# Glossary

This glossary explains the terms used in Neon Pairs, including the differences between player language and identifiers in the source.

The entries describe the current implementation and specification 2.2. Code names are shown literally so that a reader can search for them. A term can be useful in engineering discussion without belonging in the interface; the screen generally uses the shorter vocabulary described in [Voice guide](voice-guide.md).

## Play and the board

**Activation.** An attempt to use a card through the shared game action. A primary click, completed tap, Enter or Space can activate a card. `activateCard(state, index)` decides whether that attempt changes the state. Activation is broader than reveal: activating an already matched card, for example, leaves the game unchanged. Focus movement is a different operation.

**Board.** The square arrangement of card positions for one deal. In `src/game/deck.ts`, the `Board` interface contains `boardCode`, `size`, `seed` and `deck`. In interface discussion, “board” can also mean the visible grid and scroll area.

**Board code.** The text that identifies a starting deal, such as `np1-4-1`. It encodes a generation version, side length and seed. It does not contain moves or remembered progress. Loading a code starts that deal from its initial state. See [Board code format](../sharing/board-code-format.md) for its accepted syntax and [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md) for its relationship to saved progress.

**Card.** One position in the deck and its corresponding native button. Two different cards can show the same face. A row and column identify a position; a face name identifies artwork shared by two cards.

**Closed.** A card whose face is not shown. It is also the literal selection kind `closed`, which means there is no currently revealed unmatched selection. Matched cards may remain face up when the selection is closed.

**Completion / win.** The state in which every position is matched. `isWon(state)` derives this by comparing `matched.length` with `deck.length`; there is no separately stored victory field in `GameState`. The interface displays the final moves and time. See [Win conditions](../gameplay/win-conditions.md).

**Deal.** The initial card arrangement determined by a board code. Restart repeats a deal, whereas New Game creates a fresh seed. The same deal can be played repeatedly with different results.

**Deck.** The row-order array of integer face IDs. `generateBoard` begins with two copies of each included face, shuffles them and returns the frozen board description. Positions remain stable as cards reveal and match.

**Eligible card.** A card that can supply the next reveal under the current game state. It excludes matched cards, repeating the first selection and attempts during blocked intervals. This is explanatory language, not a named TypeScript type.

**Face.** The identity depicted on a revealed card. The integer ID selects a shape, marker direction and fill. Color follows the marker distinction rather than adding another independent identity. Face IDs run from 0 through 127 across the complete artwork catalogue. A smaller board uses only the required initial range of faces. See [Face catalogue](../visuals/face-catalogue.md).

**Face up.** Revealed to the player, either temporarily as part of a selection or permanently as a matched card. `faceUpCards` combines the matched positions with the currently selected positions. It is a presentation set derived from game state, not another persisted list.

**Fill.** The solid or outline treatment of the main shape. This distinguishes faces that otherwise share a shape and marker direction. In generated labels, the word is `solid` or `outline`. The card border and focus outline are separate features.

**Grid size / size.** The square board's side length. `GRID_SIZES` contains 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 and 16. The select displays dimensions such as `6x6`; the state stores the number 6. Increasing size increases the card count.

**Index / position.** A zero-based location in the row-order deck. Player-facing row and column names begin at one. The first card is index 0 and row 1, column 1. [Numbers style](numbers-style.md) gives conversion examples.

**Marker.** The small circular mark positioned around the central shape. The directions are top, top-right, right, bottom-right, bottom, bottom-left, left and top-left. The matched-card check mark is a separate state indication.

**Match / matched pair.** Two distinct positions with equal face IDs that have been successfully revealed together. `matched` stores their positions, two entries per pair. Matched cards retain their faces and gain a border and check mark. Six matched positions mean three pairs.

**Mismatch / miss.** A turn whose second eligible card has a different face from the first. The selection becomes `mismatch`, with `first`, `second` and `remainingMs`. Both cards stay visible for the pending interval before closing together. “No match” is the interface wording; mismatch is the useful state-machine term. It is an ordinary result.

**Move.** One completed two-card choice, counted on the second eligible reveal. Both matches and misses count. A first reveal alone, repeated activation of that first card and ignored activation do not add moves. The counter saturates at `MOVES_MAX`, while play continues. [Scoring and moves](../gameplay/scoring-and-moves.md) explains the counting examples.

**Pair.** Two cards carrying one face identity. In the progress display, a matched pair contributes one toward the board's total. There are half as many pairs as cards. “Matched pair” specifies that the pair has been found.

**Selection.** The currently revealed unmatched portion of a turn. `Selection` is a union of `closed`, `one` and `mismatch`. The `one` branch contains `index`; the mismatch branch contains two indices and remaining active time. Already matched cards are tracked separately. [Selection state](../gameplay/selection-state.md) describes the transitions.

**Shape.** The central geometry in a face: circle, square, triangle, diamond, star, hexagon, plus or chevron. The neutral diamond on the back of a closed card is back artwork, not evidence that the hidden face has the diamond identity.

**Turn.** The two-card choice that starts with a first eligible reveal and resolves when a different eligible card is revealed. On a miss, the visible interval continues after that result. “Turn” is useful explanatory language; the state does not store a turn-number field separate from `moves` and `selection`.

## Session, time and records

**Active time.** Time that contributes to the running game while the page is shown and unfinished imported progress is not paused. The elapsed clock starts on the first valid reveal and stops at completion. The pending mismatch uses that same active-time basis. It is not simply the amount of wall time since opening the page.

**Best.** The lowest completed move count recorded locally for a particular board size. It is not a fastest-time record, a per-seed record or a remotely verified result. The status shows `none` before a size has a record. [Best score records](../gameplay/best-score-records.md) explains the record's scope.

**Celebration.** A session flag controlling the completion banner's pulse after play finishes the board. It is distinct from `isWon`: completion describes the game's data, while celebration describes a presentation event. That distinction lets an already completed position be displayed without implying that the player just made its final turn.

**Elapsed time.** The game's accumulated active milliseconds, stored in `elapsedMs`. The screen formats this value for reading. A browser rendering tick is not itself a unit of elapsed time. The measured duration can contain fractions in memory even though snapshot export writes whole milliseconds.

**Generation.** A session counter used to distinguish successive game replacements. `replaceGame` increments it. Timer updates carry a generation so that an update belonging to an earlier game can be ignored. It is unrelated to the generation-version prefix in a board code: one identifies a browser session replacement, the other identifies a deck algorithm.

**Pause / paused.** The session condition applied when unfinished progress is loaded from a snapshot. The Resume button clears it. Page visibility separately controls active time. `paused` belongs to `Session`, not the serialized core `GameState`.

**Preferences.** The last supported size and the local best-move map. The browser storage module reads and writes them under `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. Reload uses the remembered size for a fresh deal.

**Remaining time.** The `remainingMs` field of a pending mismatch. It measures how much more active time the two unmatched faces stay visible. It does not mean time left to finish the game, and it is absent from the other selection branches.

**Session.** The browser-facing state that wraps `game` with pause state, generation, feedback, load notice, announcement counter, celebration and preferences. `src/game/session/session.ts` defines it. See [Session module](../architecture/session-module.md) for the boundary.

**Started.** The `GameState` boolean indicating that the first valid reveal has happened. A started game may be paused, hidden or complete.

## Exchange and diagnostics

**Announcement.** Accessible result feedback supplied through the status region. It describes turn outcomes and load statuses. In source, `announcement` is also a session counter used to distinguish result events, including repeated identical text. The game itself does not play speech audio.

**Draft.** The text currently being edited in the Board code input or Snapshot JSON textarea. The corresponding load action validates it before replacement. Invalid drafts remain available for correction.

**Export.** Encoding current progress and placing the JSON text in the snapshot textarea. `encodeSnapshot` supplies the serialization. The interface lets the player select and copy it manually. “Export” here does not imply a downloaded file or a clipboard notification.

**Import / load.** Validating supplied text and, on success, replacing the active game with the described deal or progress. The UI labels are Load board and Load snapshot. Engineering prose also calls restoring external progress an import.

**Logical time.** The explicit timeline used by the game core and replay. `advanceGame` receives a duration rather than consulting a browser clock. Replay action timestamps describe this timeline; they do not encode a calendar or the period during which a browser page was hidden.

**Replay.** A versioned description of one board's timed activations. Its fields include `actions` and `endMs`. The CLI runs those actions through the same game transitions and prints the resulting snapshot. Replay has no control in the current game screen.

**Seed.** The positive integer component of a board code that initializes deterministic deck generation. Equal supported size, version and seed yield the same deck. The seed identifies the starting arrangement, not the player's later choices or result.

**Snapshot.** A versioned JSON description of progress, containing `boardCode`, matched positions, selection, moves, elapsed time and started state. It regenerates the deck from the code. It does not store every past action. [Snapshot format](../sharing/snapshot-format.md) describes validation, and [Sharing FAQ](../sharing/sharing-faq.md) helps choose between a code, snapshot and replay.

**Validation.** Checking unknown input against the relevant format and state constraints before using it. It checks acceptable state, not an authenticated play history.

**Version.** A label whose subject needs to be explicit. Specification 2.2, package version `1.0.0`, snapshot `version: 1`, replay `version: 1` and the `np1` board-code prefix refer to different artifacts. A change in one does not automatically change the others. [Format versioning guide](../sharing/format-versioning-guide.md) discusses the data-format side.

# Corrupt data policy

This page explains how Neon Pairs handles unreadable or invalid stored data and how read rejection relates to a later save.

Browser storage contains strings outside the type system. A value may have been written by an older build, edited by a person, truncated by a debugging experiment or replaced by another script on the origin. The current preference reader accepts only a usable preference aggregate and otherwise returns its default. It does not try to repair individual score entries.

## Rejection at the read boundary

A failed decode produces empty application data rather than a partially interpreted value. The read path can abandon unusable content without deleting the browser string as part of that read. A stored value that fails to parse or validate is treated as empty, without any error, and stays untouched until the next save replaces it. The distinction between reading and saving matters because a save can follow immediately during application initialization.

For current preferences, “empty” is the complete fallback `{ size: DEFAULT_SIZE, bestMoves: {} }`. `DEFAULT_SIZE` is 4. The result is therefore a fresh default-size game with no known bests, rather than an empty board or a blocked screen. `readPreferences` makes that fallback before entering its `try` block and returns it from each rejection branch.

The reader has no write or removal call. However, `useSavedPreferences` runs an effect on mounting with the preferences obtained during initialization. That effect can overwrite the rejected string with valid fallback preferences after rendering. The original text remains available only until a save occurs, and the ordinary mount effect is such a save.

## Parsing is only the first filter

`parseJson` in `src/game/saved-format.ts` catches `JSON.parse` errors and returns `undefined`. A string such as `{` therefore fails without throwing an uncaught exception from the preference reader. Valid JSON can still be unusable: `null`, an array, a string, a boolean or a number does not provide the required preference object.

`isJsonObject` rejects null and arrays. After that narrowing, the reader checks `schemaVersion === PREFERENCES_VERSION` and requires `size` to have JavaScript type `number`. It then checks that size against `isValidSize` and requires `bestMoves` to be an object. A string value such as `"6"` is not accepted as a selected size even though the UI select ultimately uses string option values.

The empty string is handled even earlier. `if (!text) return fallback` covers a missing key returned as `null`, an empty stored string and a null store's absent result. It avoids parsing text that cannot represent the preference object. Whitespace-only text is truthy, reaches the parser and fails there.

These branches are worth keeping separate in a test log. They converge on the same application state, but one shows absent data, another shows malformed syntax and another shows a structural mismatch. No error copy is rendered for these preference cases.

## Whole-value validation

The reader builds a fresh `bestMoves` object and iterates through `Object.entries(value.bestMoves)`. For each entry it converts the key with `Number(size)`, then compares `String(numberSize)` with the original key. That round trip requires the canonical size spelling. It rejects `04`, `4.0`, `4e0` and strings padded with whitespace, even when numerical conversion would produce 4.

The numeric key must then be supported by `isValidSize`. Each move count must be a nonnegative safe integer, no greater than `MOVES_MAX`, and no smaller than the number of pairs for its size. `MOVES_MAX` is 999999. The lower bound is `numberSize ** 2 / 2`, because completing the board takes at least one move for each pair.

| Side length | Lowest accepted completed move count |
| --- | ---: |
| 4 | 8 |
| 6 | 18 |
| 8 | 32 |
| 10 | 50 |
| 12 | 72 |
| 14 | 98 |
| 16 | 128 |

A failure at any entry returns the fallback for the entire preference value. A valid selected size of 6 does not survive alongside an invalid 4x4 score of 1. Likewise, valid score entries are not salvaged around one bad entry. The local object being assembled is never returned on that failure path.

This behavior is observable after reload: both the size preference and all previously accepted bests can appear reset when one map entry becomes invalid. It does not indicate that the size failed its own check. [Preferences store](preferences-store.md) explains why the aggregate is read as a unit.

## Examples with different failure causes

This value parses, but its version discriminator is unsupported:

```json
{"schemaVersion":2,"size":6,"bestMoves":{}}
```

This value has the expected version and size, but the score field has the wrong shape:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":6,"bestMoves":[]}
```

This value has a valid map shape and an invalid key spelling:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":6,"bestMoves":{"04":8}}
```

This value uses a canonical supported key but an impossible completed score:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":6,"bestMoves":{"4":7}}
```

All four produce the same preference fallback. The reader does not emit different messages or a machine-readable rejection reason. A diagnostic harness can identify the failed condition by choosing one changed field at a time. The production API does not expose those distinctions to components.

By contrast, this is a valid value with no score for the selected size:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":6,"bestMoves":{"4":8}}
```

The 4x4 record is retained, the board starts at 6x6, and the 6x6 best display is `none`. Absence of a current-size best is not evidence of corruption.

## Extra properties and normalization

The preference reader does not enforce an exact property count at the top level. A value with valid expected fields and an additional property can be accepted. The returned application value includes only the selected size and the newly built score map. A normal subsequent write serializes those known fields and the schema discriminator, omitting the extra property.

This is different from the snapshot parser, which rejects unknown fields according to its own format. A shared JSON helper does not make all parsers equally strict. Tests that copy a snapshot rejection case into preferences without checking the reader could accidentally demand behavior the game does not implement.

The current reader also does not coerce score strings to numbers, round fractions or clamp out-of-range scores. A value of `"8"` is not accepted as a move count. A fraction is rejected rather than rounded. A number above the move cap invalidates the aggregate rather than being reduced to the cap. Validation produces a known state or the fallback, not a best-effort approximation of the edited input.

## The timeline of replacement

There are three useful points in a corruption test. Before initialization, the raw store contains the original text. After `readPreferences`, the caller has either accepted preferences or fallback preferences, and the raw store is still unchanged by that function. After `writePreferences`, the store may contain a valid serialized replacement if the write succeeded.

In the browser, those latter two stages are separated by React's render and effect cycle rather than by a player's explicit action. `useGame` initializes session state from the read result, then `useSavedPreferences` writes that state after mounting. A test inspecting storage only after the UI has settled can see valid defaults and miss the original corrupt text entirely.

The simplest way to prove read nonmutation is a store double whose `setItem` records calls. Invoke only `readPreferences`, inspect the original string and check that no write occurred. A separate browser test can demonstrate mount replacement. Combining both assertions into a single post-navigation observation loses the distinction this policy depends on.

## Silent rejection is local to stored preferences

Invalid input typed into the board-code and snapshot controls follows another interaction. Those controls keep the current game, preserve the draft for correction and show their defined validation status. They do not silently replace the active game with a default board. That feedback is appropriate because the person has just requested an explicit load operation.

Stored preference rejection happens during initialization with no draft to correct in the game UI. It returns a playable state quietly. There is no recovery dialog, corrupted-data banner or download of rejected text. Browser access failure also returns defaults, but concerns operation availability rather than text acceptance; see [Storage failure policy](storage-failure-policy.md).

None of these parsers establishes authenticity. A manually edited score of 8 for 4x4 is accepted if the surrounding value is valid, even without evidence that eight pairs were played. The constraints establish a plausible stored aggregate, not a verified score history.

## Evidence and useful extensions to a diagnosis

`storage.test.ts` already covers malformed JSON, null, an empty object, unsupported size, scores below the pair count, negative and fractional values, and a noncanonical key. It separately checks that a score at the move cap round-trips and one beyond it is rejected. The browser persistence contract test seeds malformed text before navigation and checks for a playable 16-card default board.

Those tests are focused evidence, not an exhaustive enumeration of every possible JSON string. A new bug report is easiest to isolate with its exact raw value and one field changed at a time. Comparing an independently written valid baseline with the failing value exposes whether the issue concerns syntax, object shape, selected size, key spelling or score bounds. [Storage testing guide](storage-testing-guide.md) gives the browser setup and store doubles for doing that without modifying the source.

# ADR 058: Give additional stored data a distinct namespace

This record explains the naming rule for new stored data while preserving the existing preferences key.

## Context

The first storage decision used a game prefix, a data-family segment and a version suffix separated by dots. The current preferences key still demonstrates that choice: `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. It contains a selected size and a map of per-size best moves in a versioned JSON value.

Additional stored families need a recognizable naming convention without turning a documentation change into an unnecessary migration of existing preferences. This record supersedes [ADR 011](adr-011-storage-keys.md). The scope is key naming; it does not add another stored family to the current game or replace snapshot export with automatic progress saving.

## Decision

The namespace distinguishes newly introduced storage from keys that a released game already reads. New stored data uses a key of the form np3:THING, where THING is a lowercase plural noun for what is stored. Keys that already exist keep their names. This lets a reader recognize the new convention while the existing preference reader continues to find its current value.

The distinction is intentionally about whether a key already exists, rather than whether its contents look old. Renaming preferences merely to make the key look consistent would require a migration, conflict handling and evidence that the saved size and records survived. No such migration is implemented in the source.

## What remains unchanged in the implementation

`PREFERENCES_KEY` is the one existing key used by `readPreferences` and `writePreferences`. The stored JSON carries `schemaVersion: 1`, `size` and `bestMoves`. Naming a storage key and validating the value are separate responsibilities. A recognizable namespace cannot establish that JSON is well formed, that a size is supported or that a score is a plausible bounded integer.

The parser treats saved data as unknown, checks supported values and falls back to usable defaults when access or validation fails. Writes are caught so the in-memory game remains playable. The namespace decision does not move those browser effects into pure game functions. [Preferences store](../persistence/preferences-store.md) and [Storage failure policy](../persistence/storage-failure-policy.md) describe the existing behavior.

## Alternatives and tradeoffs

Renaming every key at once would make the storage inspector look uniform, but would create work and risk unrelated to the new naming need. Continuing the original dotted pattern indefinitely would avoid any new convention while leaving this replacement decision without effect. The selected approach separates continuity for existing data from a clear naming choice for additions.

A single giant application value could avoid choosing new keys at all. That would couple unrelated data families to the same read, validation and write path. The current preferences envelope is appropriately small for size and best moves.

## Reading the rule accurately

The namespace marker is not a new board-code prefix, snapshot version or replay version. Those public formats retain their own identifiers. It is also not a claim that the current preferences schema has been upgraded. Confusing these layers would create a format change where only storage-key naming was intended.

The current source provides a concrete compatibility check: a reader can inspect `PREFERENCES_KEY` and see the existing name. There is no second preferences key to merge and no new data family to initialize as part of this naming decision. [Persistence envelope](../persistence/persistence-envelope.md), [Format versioning guide](../sharing/format-versioning-guide.md) and [ADR 053](adr-053-docs-in-repo.md) explain the surrounding boundaries.

This preserves the useful local-storage model while making the successor to the old naming decision explicit. Historical context remains in the superseded record; current readers can follow its replacement link here without treating the old pattern as the convention for additional data.

## The current preferences key and value shape

These are the existing declarations. The new naming decision preserves this identifier rather than silently changing where the application reads its preferences.

```ts
export const DEFAULT_SIZE = GRID_SIZES[0];
export const PREFERENCES_KEY = 'neon-pairs.preferences.v1';
export const PREFERENCES_VERSION = 1;
export interface Preferences {
  readonly size: number;
  readonly bestMoves: Readonly<Record<string, number>>;
}
export interface PreferenceStore {
  getItem(key: string): string | null;
  setItem(key: string, value: string): void;
}
```

# Voice guide

This guide explains the voice already used by Neon Pairs and how that voice supports play, recovery and accessible feedback.

The game speaks briefly because the player's attention belongs on the cards. Controls name actions, status text reports facts, and help explains the next useful interaction. The small amount of personality sits around those jobs. This page is about that balance; exact number presentation is covered in [Numbers style](numbers-style.md), and failure messages have their own [error message guide](error-message-style.md).

## The voice in the current screen

`src/game/Game.tsx` opens with the eyebrow “A little focus. A perfect pair.” The title is simply “Neon Pairs”. The introduction then becomes practical: “Reveal two cards. Match their shape and marker to keep the pair.” Those lines do different work. The eyebrow sets a mood; the introduction tells a new player what to do. Reading only the introduction is enough to begin.

The board help is equally direct: “Use a pointer or Tab to enter the board. Arrow keys move between cards. Enter or Space reveals a card.” It names the supported interactions without requiring a player to know terms such as roving focus, keydown handlers or native activation. Those implementation terms are useful in engineering documents, but they would make the board instructions harder to use.

The tone is friendly and restrained. Interface text has no exclamation marks. The completion banner closes with “Well played.” after reporting the result, so encouragement follows something that actually happened. There is no running commentary on the player's skill or on the quality of a particular miss.

That division gives copy review a useful starting point. A phrase that explains a control belongs near the control. A phrase that describes the latest turn belongs in feedback. A phrase that merely adds atmosphere has to earn its space alongside the existing eyebrow and title.

## Labels name the action

The literal labels live in `src/game/controls/control-labels.ts`. They are short enough to recognize while scanning and specific enough to distinguish actions with different consequences.

| Current label | What the wording tells the player |
| --- | --- |
| Grid size | The select changes the board dimensions. |
| New Game | Start a fresh deal at the selected size. |
| Restart | Begin the current deal again. |
| Reproduce a game | Open the tools for repeating a deal or restoring progress. |
| Board code | The nearby field contains a deal identifier. |
| Load board | Use the entered code to start its deal. |
| Snapshot JSON | The larger field contains serialized progress. |
| Export snapshot | Put the current progress into that field. |
| Load snapshot | Restore the progress entered in that field. |
| Resume | Continue the unfinished game loaded from a snapshot. |

“New Game” and “Restart” are especially easy to blur in explanatory prose. The first changes the deal; the second repeats it. A sentence such as “restart for a different arrangement” would misdescribe the existing button. [New game and restart](../gameplay/new-game-and-restart.md) explains the behavior in detail. In a writing review, the important question is whether the reader can predict the button's result from the surrounding sentence.

The mix of capitalization is part of the current interface, rather than evidence of one universal casing scheme. “New Game” has two capitals, while “Load board” has one. Quoting the real control name makes instructions easier to follow than silently regularizing those labels in prose.

## Outcomes are facts, not judgments

`src/game/session/session.ts` constructs the turn feedback. A successful nonfinal turn begins “Pair found.” and follows with the matched-pair count. An unsuccessful turn says “No match. Cards close after a short pause.” Neither message blames the player. Both identify what happened, and the second explains the temporary state of the board.

The word “short” in that message describes the experience rather than asking the player to read a technical timer value. Engineering prose can name the `MISMATCH_MS` constant and the active-time behavior. The player needs to know why the cards remain visible and that they will close. That is a useful example of the same behavior needing different levels of detail in different places.

The final turn's feedback combines the pair result with completion: “Pair found. All pairs found in N moves and time.” The visible banner uses a related sentence: “Every pair found in N moves and time. We…1527 tokens truncated…/game/session/session.ts` contains the browser load messages. The invalid notices are “Invalid board code.” and “Invalid snapshot.” `use-game.ts` chooses the appropriate one when parsing fails. It returns before resetting the clock or replacing the game.

| Attempt | Visible error | What was rejected |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Load board with an unacceptable code | `Invalid board code.` | The board-code draft. |
| Load snapshot with unacceptable progress | `Invalid snapshot.` | The snapshot draft. |

The noun is useful. A player can distinguish the board field from the larger JSON field without interpreting a generic “Something went wrong”. The wording also avoids an unsupported diagnosis: “invalid” does not assert that the text is corrupted, that the device failed, or that a particular character is responsible.

Both notices end in a period and stand as complete status text. They do not name a function, a parser exception or a schema utility. The code has more knowledge than the short UI exposes, but it does not currently present field-by-field snapshot diagnostics. An example that shows such a diagnostic would describe a different interface.

The related success notices help explain the same design. Unfinished progress says “Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue.” Completed progress says “Loaded completed snapshot.” One includes an action because the resulting state needs it. The other reports the state without that instruction. A writing change that makes every load outcome use the same generic sentence would remove useful information.

## Failure preserves the correction context

The browser keeps the entered draft and the current game when a board or snapshot load is invalid. A useful help paragraph can therefore say to correct the text in its field and use the same load action again. There is no need to describe starting over from an empty form, since the current components do not clear failed input.

The board-code path trims surrounding whitespace before calling `parseBoardCode`. The snapshot path validates the whole textarea content. These facts matter when diagnosing a report, but they are not separate error messages. For example, a board code with an unsupported side length still produces the same board-code notice as a code with an invalid prefix.

The board input is an uncontrolled field keyed to session generation. A successful game replacement refreshes it from the active board code. A failed load does not replace the generation, so the draft remains. `Reproduction.tsx` stores snapshot text in local component state. Those are two implementation routes to preserving useful correction context; neither turns the draft into accepted game state.

The notices appear beside the reproduction controls and are also passed through session feedback. A repeated invalid submission is a separate event even if its sentence is identical. Copy review can inspect the text here, while [Announcements policy](../interface/announcements-policy.md) and [Error display guide](../interface/error-display-guide.md) describe its presentation and delivery.

## The replay command has a diagnostic audience

Replay is a developer command rather than a browser control. Run it as `npm run --silent replay -- PATH`. On success it prints the final snapshot JSON to stdout and exits with status 0. On failure it leaves stdout empty, writes a diagnostic to stderr and exits with status 1. This separation allows another program to consume successful output as JSON.

`scripts/replay-cli.ts` builds most failure messages through `fail(file, reason)`. The shape is `Could not replay FILE: reason.` followed by a newline. `FILE` is the argument supplied by the caller. It is not replaced in the message with the internally resolved absolute path. Relative file lookup uses the caller folder, accounting for npm's `INIT_CWD`.

For a file named `broken.json` containing `{`, the diagnostic is:

```text
Could not replay broken.json: the file is not valid JSON.
```

For an absent file named `missing.json`, the message is:

```text
Could not replay missing.json: the file does not exist.
```

A different read failure uses “the file can't be read”. That wording reflects the actual distinction in `isMissing`: `ENOENT` gets the missing-file reason, and other caught read failures get the broader reason. It does not speculate about permissions, locking or a device problem when the adapter has not established that cause.

## Diagnostic specificity follows the parser result

`readReplay` returns either a state or a `problem`, with an optional action position. `ReplayProblem` gives those cases names such as `malformedJson`, `boardCode`, `order` and `index`. The CLI's `PROBLEMS` mapping turns them into explanations. That mapping keeps the core independent of presentation wording.

| Problem kind | Current reason text |
| --- | --- |
| `tooLarge` | `the file is larger than 1048576 bytes` |
| `malformedJson` | `the file is not valid JSON` |
| `format` | `it isn't a version 1 replay with exactly version, boardCode, actions and endMs` |
| `boardCode` | `its board code is invalid` |
| `actions` | `actions must be a list of at most 10000` |
| `endTime` | `endMs must be a nonnegative safe integer` |
| `action` | `needs exactly atMs and index as nonnegative safe integers` |
| `order` | `comes before the previous action or after endMs` |
| `index` | `names a card outside the board` |

For an action-specific problem the CLI inserts a human action ordinal before the reason. The parser's position is zero-based, but the diagnostic adds one. An invalid card index in the second action of `rule.json` therefore reads:

```text
Could not replay rule.json: action 2 names a card outside the board.
```

That number identifies the action's list position. It is not the offending card index. The distinction helps someone find the problem in a longer replay. It also explains why the diagnostic can be useful without quoting the entire action object.

When arguments are absent or there is more than one argument, the command prints its usage line instead of the file-and-reason form:

```text
Usage: npm run --silent replay -- PATH
```

There is no file-specific cause to report in that situation because the invocation itself is unacceptable. The message names the accepted command shape, making the next attempt concrete. [Replay format](../sharing/replay-format.md) covers the file contents after that invocation succeeds in reading a file.

## Internal exceptions belong to another layer

Not every string containing “Invalid” is an interface notice. `boardCode` and `generateBoard` throw `Error('Invalid board code.')` when called with an unacceptable code. `faceDesign` throws `Error('Invalid face.')` for an invalid face ID. `generateBoard` also guards against unavailable deck entries with “Deck index out of range.”

Those exceptions describe invalid internal calls or an invariant failure. They are not additional browser validation states. The normal browser load path parses the code before creating a game, and snapshot decoding returns `null` for rejected external state. Copying an internal exception into a player help page as though it were a visible notice would confuse these boundaries.

Likewise, storage failures are caught by the storage adapter and leave play available. The current browser does not turn a blocked preference write into an error dialog or an inline save warning. The fallback keeps the game available when storage fails. [Storage failure policy](../persistence/storage-failure-policy.md) covers the underlying behavior.

# Glossary

This glossary explains the terms used in Neon Pairs, including the differences between player language and identifiers in the source.

The entries describe the current implementation and specification 2.2. Code names are shown literally so that a reader can search for them. A term can be useful in engineering discussion without belonging in the interface; the screen generally uses the shorter vocabulary described in [Voice guide](voice-guide.md).

## Play and the board

**Activation.** An attempt to use a card through the shared game action. A primary click, completed tap, Enter or Space can activate a card. `activateCard(state, index)` decides whether that attempt changes the state. Activation is broader than reveal: activating an already matched card, for example, leaves the game unchanged. Focus movement is a different operation.

**Board.** The square arrangement of card positions for one deal. In `src/game/deck.ts`, the `Board` interface contains `boardCode`, `size`, `seed` and `deck`. In interface discussion, “board” can also mean the visible grid and scroll area.

**Board code.** The text that identifies a starting deal, such as `np1-4-1`. It encodes a generation version, side length and seed. It does not contain moves or remembered progress. Loading a code starts that deal from its initial state. See [Board code format](../sharing/board-code-format.md) for its accepted syntax and [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md) for its relationship to saved progress.

**Card.** One position in the deck and its corresponding native button. Two different cards can show the same face. A row and column identify a position; a face name identifies artwork shared by two cards.

**Closed.** A card whose face is not shown. It is also the literal selection kind `closed`, which means there is no currently revealed unmatched selection. Matched cards may remain face up when the selection is closed.

**Completion / win.** The state in which every position is matched. `isWon(state)` derives this by comparing `matched.length` with `deck.length`; there is no separately stored victory field in `GameState`. The interface displays the final moves and time. See [Win conditions](../gameplay/win-conditions.md).

**Deal.** The initial card arrangement determined by a board code. Restart repeats a deal, whereas New Game creates a fresh seed. The same deal can be played repeatedly with different results.

**Deck.** The row-order array of integer face IDs. `generateBoard` begins with two copies of each included face, shuffles them and returns the frozen board description. Positions remain stable as cards reveal and match.

**Eligible card.** A card that can supply the next reveal under the current game state. It excludes matched cards, repeating the first selection and attempts during blocked intervals. This is explanatory language, not a named TypeScript type.

**Face.** The identity depicted on a revealed card. The integer ID selects a shape, marker direction and fill. Color follows the marker distinction rather than adding another independent identity. Face IDs run from 0 through 127 across the complete artwork catalogue. A smaller board uses only the required initial range of faces. See [Face catalogue](../visuals/face-catalogue.md).

**Face up.** Revealed to the player, either temporarily as part of a selection or permanently as a matched card. `faceUpCards` combines the matched positions with the currently selected positions. It is a presentation set derived from game state, not another persisted list.

**Fill.** The solid or outline treatment of the main shape. This distinguishes faces that otherwise share a shape and marker direction. In generated labels, the word is `solid` or `outline`. The card border and focus outline are separate features.

**Grid size / size.** The square board's side length. `GRID_SIZES` contains 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 and 16. The select displays dimensions such as `6x6`; the state stores the number 6. Increasing size increases the card count.

**Index / position.** A zero-based location in the row-order deck. Player-facing row and column names begin at one. The first card is index 0 and row 1, column 1. [Numbers style](numbers-style.md) gives conversion examples.

**Marker.** The small circular mark positioned around the central shape. The directions are top, top-right, right, bottom-right, bottom, bottom-left, left and top-left. The matched-card check mark is a separate state indication.

**Match / matched pair.** Two distinct positions with equal face IDs that have been successfully revealed together. `matched` stores their positions, two entries per pair. Matched cards retain their faces and gain a border and check mark. Six matched positions mean three pairs.

**Mismatch / miss.** A turn whose second eligible card has a different face from the first. The selection becomes `mismatch`, with `first`, `second` and `remainingMs`. Both cards stay visible for the pending interval before closing together. “No match” is the interface wording; mismatch is the useful state-machine term. It is an ordinary result.

**Move.** One completed two-card choice, counted on the second eligible reveal. Both matches and misses count. A first reveal alone, repeated activation of that first card and ignored activation do not add moves. The counter saturates at `MOVES_MAX`, while play continues. [Scoring and moves](../gameplay/scoring-and-moves.md) explains the counting examples.

**Pair.** Two cards carrying one face identity. In the progress display, a matched pair contributes one toward the board's total. There are half as many pairs as cards. “Matched pair” specifies that the pair has been found.

**Selection.** The currently revealed unmatched portion of a turn. `Selection` is a union of `closed`, `one` and `mismatch`. The `one` branch contains `index`; the mismatch branch contains two indices and remaining active time. Already matched cards are tracked separately. [Selection state](../gameplay/selection-state.md) describes the transitions.

**Shape.** The central geometry in a face: circle, square, triangle, diamond, star, hexagon, plus or chevron. The neutral diamond on the back of a closed card is back artwork, not evidence that the hidden face has the diamond identity.

**Turn.** The two-card choice that starts with a first eligible reveal and resolves when a different eligible card is revealed. On a miss, the visible interval continues after that result. “Turn” is useful explanatory language; the state does not store a turn-number field separate from `moves` and `selection`.

## Session, time and records

**Active time.** Time that contributes to the running game while the page is shown and unfinished imported progress is not paused. The elapsed clock starts on the first valid reveal and stops at completion. The pending mismatch uses that same active-time basis. It is not simply the amount of wall time since opening the page.

**Best.** The lowest completed move count recorded locally for a particular board size. It is not a fastest-time record, a per-seed record or a remotely verified result. The status shows `none` before a size has a record. [Best score records](../gameplay/best-score-records.md) explains the record's scope.

**Celebration.** A session flag controlling the completion banner's pulse after play finishes the board. It is distinct from `isWon`: completion describes the game's data, while celebration describes a presentation event. That distinction lets an already completed position be displayed without implying that the player just made its final turn.

**Elapsed time.** The game's accumulated active milliseconds, stored in `elapsedMs`. The screen formats this value for reading. A browser rendering tick is not itself a unit of elapsed time. The measured duration can contain fractions in memory even though snapshot export writes whole milliseconds.

**Generation.** A session counter used to distinguish successive game replacements. `replaceGame` increments it. Timer updates carry a generation so that an update belonging to an earlier game can be ignored. It is unrelated to the generation-version prefix in a board code: one identifies a browser session replacement, the other identifies a deck algorithm.

**Pause / paused.** The session condition applied when unfinished progress is loaded from a snapshot. The Resume button clears it. Page visibility separately controls active time. `paused` belongs to `Session`, not the serialized core `GameState`.

**Preferences.** The last supported size and the local best-move map. The browser storage module reads and writes them under `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. Reload uses the remembered size for a fresh deal.

**Remaining time.** The `remainingMs` field of a pending mismatch. It measures how much more active time the two unmatched faces stay visible. It does not mean time left to finish the game, and it is absent from the other selection branches.

**Session.** The browser-facing state that wraps `game` with pause state, generation, feedback, load notice, announcement counter, celebration and preferences. `src/game/session/session.ts` defines it. See [Session module](../architecture/session-module.md) for the boundary.

**Started.** The `GameState` boolean indicating that the first valid reveal has happened. A started game may be paused, hidden or complete.

## Exchange and diagnostics

**Announcement.** Accessible result feedback supplied through the status region. It describes turn outcomes and load statuses. In source, `announcement` is also a session counter used to distinguish result events, including repeated identical text. The game itself does not play speech audio.

**Draft.** The text currently being edited in the Board code input or Snapshot JSON textarea. The corresponding load action validates it before replacement. Invalid drafts remain available for correction.

**Export.** Encoding current progress and placing the JSON text in the snapshot textarea. `encodeSnapshot` supplies the serialization. The interface lets the player select and copy it manually. “Export” here does not imply a downloaded file or a clipboard notification.

**Import / load.** Validating supplied text and, on success, replacing the active game with the described deal or progress. The UI labels are Load board and Load snapshot. Engineering prose also calls restoring external progress an import.

**Logical time.** The explicit timeline used by the game core and replay. `advanceGame` receives a duration rather than consulting a browser clock. Replay action timestamps describe this timeline; they do not encode a calendar or the period during which a browser page was hidden.

**Replay.** A versioned description of one board's timed activations. Its fields include `actions` and `endMs`. The CLI runs those actions through the same game transitions and prints the resulting snapshot. Replay has no control in the current game screen.

**Seed.** The positive integer component of a board code that initializes deterministic deck generation. Equal supported size, version and seed yield the same deck. The seed identifies the starting arrangement, not the player's later choices or result.

**Snapshot.** A versioned JSON description of progress, containing `boardCode`, matched positions, selection, moves, elapsed time and started state. It regenerates the deck from the code. It does not store every past action. [Snapshot format](../sharing/snapshot-format.md) describes validation, and [Sharing FAQ](../sharing/sharing-faq.md) helps choose between a code, snapshot and replay.

**Validation.** Checking unknown input against the relevant format and state constraints before using it. It checks acceptable state, not an authenticated play history.

**Version.** A label whose subject needs to be explicit. Specification 2.2, package version `1.0.0`, snapshot `version: 1`, replay `version: 1` and the `np1` board-code prefix refer to different artifacts. A change in one does not automatically change the others. [Format versioning guide](../sharing/format-versioning-guide.md) discusses the data-format side.

# Acceptance
Acceptance is a set of journeys that checks whether Neon Pairs meets its product requirements.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Finish a game, then start another one during a mismatch. The first journey checks play and completion. The second checks that an earlier timer can't change a new game.

## Play

Use these journeys with the requirements in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md):

- Finish every supported size with complete pairs.
- Reveal one card twice, then reveal a different card. Check the exact move count.
- Match a pair, then miss a pair. Check the immediate match and the 800ms active mismatch interval.
- Hide the page during a mismatch, then return and finish its remaining interval.
- Start and restart during a mismatch. Check the cleared state and later timer updates.
- Finish games with better, equal and worse move counts. Reload and check the current size's best.

## Controls

Use pointer, touch and keyboard to follow [Input](../interface/input.md) and [Controls](../interface/controls.md). Check control labels, row movement, edge stops, native Tab exit and focus after each action. Check that hidden cards reveal no identity in the DOM.

Follow the keyboard journey in I17 and check its accessibility tree. During user acceptance, confirm spoken results with a screen reader, including consecutive identical results and the final match with its win.

## Appearance

Measure the layout and review all 128 faces against [Visuals](../visuals/visuals.md). Use a 44px grayscale face sheet to distinguish shape, marker and fill. Check 16x16 boards at both stated viewport sizes, full focus outlines and the equivalent zoom layout. Check reduced motion and the static completion banner after its single pulse.

Play through completion and reset while checking [Sound](../sound/sound.md). Every action stays silent.

## Reproduction

Check [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md) with its example deck and replay. Check snapshot round trips and malformed input. Check the exact mismatch timeout before an equal-time replay action.

Load an unfinished snapshot, attempt input while paused, then Resume. Check its remaining active time and focus. Load a completed snapshot and check its static banner and unchanged best score.

## Delivery

Use a locked install, type check, unit tests and a fresh browser build as defined in [Technology](../architecture/technology.md). Open the resulting HTML directly from disk with network access blocked. Use a local HTTP origin for saved preferences.

Review the pure game functions, browser effects, file sizes and behavior placement against [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md).

Back to [Neon Pairs](../README.md).

# Test strategy
This page explains how Neon Pairs divides evidence between game tests, browser journeys, source checks and user acceptance.

The product contract is specification version 2.2. The README records a successful named compatibility run. [Known issues](known-issues.md) tracks verification limits, and [Fixtures](fixtures-guide.md) explains why replacing reviewed JSON expectations with current output would weaken the evidence.

## Start with the question

A deck test asks whether a code produces the published cards. A browser test asks whether a player can reach and activate those cards through rendered controls. An accessibility-tree capture asks what Chromium exposes to assistive software. None can substitute for the others.

The useful division follows the architecture's existing boundaries:

| Question | Existing evidence | What it cannot establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Does a turn change the right data? | Vitest tests beside `game.ts` | Native focus, scrolling or pointer dispatch |
| Does the seeded deal match the format? | Literal vectors and `tests/deal-oracle.ts` | Whether hidden identities leak into markup |
| Does the browser adapter count active time? | Pure clock tests plus controlled browser clocks | Real device scheduling latency |
| Can a player finish through the interface? | Built-page keyboard and touch journeys | Spoken screen-reader output |
| Does local storage survive reload? | HTTP-origin persistence journeys | Cross-browser behavior of disk-origin storage |
| Does the distribution stand alone? | Offline disk navigation and built-output inspection | Every browser engine or operating system |
| Does the layout survive difficult geometry? | Large-board, scrollbar, zoom and focus tests | Every possible window size |

This is a map of current checks, not a demand to create one test of each kind for every change. A correction to snapshot validation usually needs parser evidence first. A clipped focus ring needs browser geometry. A change to explanatory copy may need only the relevant reviewed expectation and a visual check. [Unit tests](unit-test-guide.md) and [Browser tests](browser-test-guide.md) show the local conventions.

## Pure behavior carries the broad matrix

`vitest.config.ts` includes `src/**/*.test.ts` and `scripts/**/*.test.ts`. The package's `test` script is `vitest run`. Most of these tests import `test` from Vitest and assertions from `node:assert/strict`. They do not mount React to prove a card transition.

The core state includes the immutable board description, its deck, matched positions, selection, moves, elapsed milliseconds and the started flag. Selection has closed, one-card and mismatch branches. Tests exercise transitions directly, allowing exact questions such as whether advancing a pending miss by 799ms leaves it open and whether the next millisecond closes both cards.

The suite checks complete pairs at all seven supported sizes. `completion.test.ts` finishes each size through `activateCard`; it does not infer that a 4x4 success proves a 16x16 finish. `deck.test.ts` checks the published seed-one vector, generator states, the inclusive maximum seed, frozen data and independent generation at each size. `deck-rejection.test.ts` targets uncommon rejection-sampling boundaries using separately stored expected decks.

The game tests also make negative cases visible. A fractional or out-of-range card index returns the old state. Repeating the first selected card adds no move. During a miss, every activation is ignored. Invalid elapsed steps leave the game unchanged. Keeping the original object in those cases is observable behavior in these tests; asserting identity can distinguish an ignored action from an unnecessary reconstruction.

Snapshot and replay tests carry a different matrix: exact object fields, integer ranges, byte limits, valid selections and action ordering. A round trip is useful, but two matching mistakes can round trip successfully. Independent expected fields and malformed inputs provide the stronger evidence. A valid started game with one revealed card and zero moves is the baseline for several invalid-counter cases, so rejection can be attributed to the changed counter rather than an unrelated invalid state.

## Session tests connect results to browser-independent policy

`src/game/session/session.ts` is a data adapter. Its tests create sessions and call `activateSession`, `replaceGame` and `tickSession` directly. This makes several integration rules cheap to check without pretending to test browser effects.

A replacement increments `generation`. A tick carrying an earlier generation has no effect. An unfinished imported game is paused and cannot accept card input or active time until resumed. A locally completed game can improve the appropriate saved move record. A completed import follows the import path instead of the live completion path. These are separate causes even when both render a completed board.

Session feedback tests inspect event progression as well as text. Two misses with the same wording still represent two turns. Focus movement and time advancement do not represent new turn results. Browser announcement tests then verify that these data changes become the intended DOM updates. Checking both layers helps distinguish a missing session event from a rendering problem.

Storage tests use the narrow `PreferenceStore` interface. A Map-backed implementation covers round trips and per-size minima; a throwing implementation covers failures without a browser. Browser tests separately exercise a denied `window.localStorage` getter. The distinction matters because failure while obtaining the store occurs before either `getItem` or `setItem` can run.

## Browser journeys use the shipped shape

The package's `test:e2e` command runs the main build, builds diagnostic entries, and then invokes Node's test runner over `tests/*.e2e.test.ts` with concurrency set to one. Playwright drives Chromium, while `node:test` owns the tests. There is no Playwright Test project configuration controlling this suite's retry or worker behavior.

Most journey files import the wrapper in `tests/browser-test.ts`. It launches a browser, creates a fresh context per case, collects page errors and closes resources. `tests/artifact-server.ts` serves the freshly built HTML on a private loopback port. `GAME_URL` points at the same build on disk. Persistence journeys use the served URL; offline-delivery checks use the disk URL.

Fresh contexts isolate browser storage, permissions and page-installed instrumentation. They do not make every global resource independent: the artifact server and browser belong to file-level hooks, and the runtime record has a shared output location. The serial command is part of the implementation being documented. [Flaky-test notes](flaky-test-notes.md) discuss the timing consequences.

The browser tests use public controls to load `np1-4-1`. They know its deck from the documented format and test fixture, rather than asking the application for hidden state. The board's hidden buttons expose positions and closed state. The tests inspect that absence directly in `input-contract.e2e.test.ts`, including the neutral back and lack of face artwork. A solver that depended on hidden SVGs would invalidate this evidence.

## Contract checks complement shared labels

Ordinary journey helpers import the control-label constants so they can focus on behavior. Contract tests also contain literal labels and limits. This prevents changing a production constant and every test lookup together from silently changing the public contract.

`control-contract.e2e.test.ts` covers native reproduction controls, their input limits, invalid statuses and action focus. `product-contract.e2e.test.ts` covers status presentation, continuing minutes and successful load size selection. `persistence-contract.e2e.test.ts` checks record comparisons, saved sizes and fresh progress after reload. These overlap broader journeys at specific seams, where a shared helper could otherwise conceal a mistake.

Overlap is useful when the assertions answer different questions. Loading a snapshot appears in parser tests, session tests and browser tests because validation, paused data and Resume focus are different behaviors. Repeating the same serializer implementation as an expected-value helper would add little protection. The suite's independent literal expectations are intended to break that circularity.

## Visual and accessibility evidence are concrete

The art entry renders every face at the minimum card size. Tests capture color, grayscale and neutral versions. Neutral silhouettes are compared for uniqueness, and separate assertions inspect marker geometry and palette application. This establishes machine-distinguishable geometry; a person still reviews whether the distinctions are usable. [Accessibility audit](accessibility-audit.md) explains that limit.

Layout tests inspect page width, card bounds, board scrolling and complete focus outlines. The large-board checks cover 360x800 and 1280x800 CSS-pixel viewports. A separate equivalent-zoom journey uses 640x400 with device scale 2. Visible-scrollbar cases remove Chromium's default scrollbar-hiding launch argument and test widths where scrollbar space changes the available board area.

The accessibility journey uses the Chromium DevTools Protocol to capture the accessibility tree during a complete keyboard game. It checks controls, revealed and matched names, disabled state exposure, results, completion, Tab exit and a fresh game. The artifact records browser and Playwright versions and explicitly records that a screen reader was not run. User acceptance owns the spoken journey. Tree assertions support that review; they do not prove speech delivery.

## Source and delivery checks

`source-audit.test.ts` inspects package pins, lockfile agreement, compiler settings and source conventions required by the architecture and technology specifications. It reads authored files rather than the compiled bundle. `source-conventions.test.ts` checks current export ownership, question-shaped predicate names, behavior-oriented test names and the small set of environment reads the runners use.

These are text checks with intentionally limited reach. The core effect scan names particular source files. It is not an analysis of every transitive call. The TypeScript source scan can reject spelling patterns, but cannot prove full semantic purity. Review remains necessary when moving behavior to a new module. [Code review](../architecture/code-review-guide.md) and [Source audit notes](../architecture/source-audit-notes.md) provide related architectural context.

The built-output test searches the emitted HTML for `fetch(` and the preload helper's `relList` marker. The offline journey blocks network access and checks that only the document request occurs while a card remains playable. Together they cover bundle content and observed loading. Neither measures first-render duration; [Performance budget](performance-budget.md) documents that evidence gap.

## Following through

Choose the smallest test that exposes the changed behavior, then follow it into the browser where native interaction or effects matter. [Regression catalogue](regression-catalogue.md) shows paired investigations, and [Release checklist](release-checklist.md) assembles the complete verification sequence. The remaining evidence gaps are tracked in [Known issues](known-issues.md).

# Technology
Technology is the build and language specification for Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.2.

The game runs offline from one HTML file. Browser controls and inline SVG provide the board, input and artwork.

## Stack

- T01 - Use React with TypeScript and DOM rendering. Use native buttons, a native select and CSS Grid. Use no component library.

- T02 - Pin these packages and keep the lockfile. The stable versions were checked on 31 October 2026:

| Package | Version | Job |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `react`, `react-dom` | `19.3.1` | Browser UI |
| `typescript` | `7.0.2` | Type checking |
| `@types/react`, `@types/react-dom` | `19.3.0` | React types |
| `vite` | `8.3.5` | Build |
| `@vitejs/plugin-react` | `6.1.2` | React build integration |
| `vite-plugin-singlefile` | `2.3.4` | One HTML distribution |
| `vitest` | `5.0.5` | Unit tests |
| `@playwright/test` | `1.64.1` | Browser tests |
| `@types/node` | `24.19.2` | Build and test types |

TypeScript 7 is a stable release, as the [release announcement](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/typescript/announcing-typescript-7-0/) describes. The [React versions page](https://react.dev/versions) lists the stable React release family.

## Language

- T03 - Use Node.js 24.19 or later and npm. Keep browser and Node compiler projects separate. Use ESM, static imports and type-only imports for types.

Use Node `26.12.1`, npm `11.20.0` and Playwright `1.64.1` with Chromium `156.0.8078.4` as the named compatibility combination. Record the locked install, build, unit tests and browser journeys with those exact versions in the project README before calling the combination tested. Other supported versions need their own results.

- T04 - Enable TypeScript strictness, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, `verbatimModuleSyntax` and `erasableSyntaxOnly`. Keep type checking separate from bundling. Vite's [TypeScript support](https://vite.dev/guide/features.html#typescript) transpiles code without checking types.

- T05 - Model project data with exact types and validate unknown data where it enters the game. Use narrowing instead of `any`, suppressed diagnostics or unchecked casts. Derive state unions from their named values.

- T06 - Keep behavior and its code, styles and tests together. Aim for 100 lines per TypeScript file and keep authored TypeScript files at or below 200 lines. Split by behavior when a file grows. Use direct imports from the file that defines a behavior.

## Commands

- T07 - Provide these commands:

| Command | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `npm ci` | Install the locked dependencies |
| `npm run dev` | Serve the game locally |
| `npm run typecheck` | Check every compiler project |
| `npm test` | Run unit tests for the game rules |
| `npm run test:e2e` | Build from current source, then run browser checks in fresh contexts against that build |
| `npm run build` | Type check and emit `dist/index.html` |
| `npm run --silent replay -- PATH` | Read replay JSON with the output and exit behavior in C14 |

The browser command must fail if its build fails. It must never fall back to an earlier `dist`. Stop development servers and watchers you start before finishing the work.

## Distribution

- T08 - `dist/index.html` contains the script, styles and artwork needed for play. It opens directly from disk without another file or a network request. Use the system font. Keep browser zoom enabled.

- T09 - Serve the game from a local HTTP origin when checking saved preferences. Storage on a `file:` URL differs between browsers, as the [localStorage documentation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/localStorage) explains. If storage is unavailable, play continues for the current session.

- T10 - Keep dependencies in development and build tooling where possible. The game uses no service, account, external asset, analytics or API key. Dependency installation can use the network. Playing the distribution doesn't use it.

The [game specification](../README.md) connects this stack to the other requirements.
