# Clock design

This page traces `browser-clock.ts` and `use-session-clock.ts`, including scheduling, visibility changes, action synchronization and cleanup.

The clock has a small arithmetic part and a browser-lifecycle part. The arithmetic keeps an observation baseline; the hook decides when to observe and when an interval counts as active play. `advanceGame` remains responsible for what a positive amount of logical time does to the game. [Time policy](time-policy.md) states the ownership boundary; this page follows the implementation.

## The arithmetic record

`browser-clock.ts` exports `CLOCK_INTERVAL_MS = 40`, `createClock` and `elapsedStep`. Its private `ActiveClock` interface contains only `observedAt: number`. It does not store accumulated active time, a mismatch deadline, a timer identifier or a pause flag.

`createClock(now)` returns `{ observedAt: now }`. `elapsedStep(clock, now, active)` subtracts the previous observation, accepts the delta only if active, finite and positive, and returns `{ clock: createClock(now), milliseconds }`. Accumulated elapsed time remains in `GameState`; the clock only supplies the next contribution.

An inactive step still updates the baseline. That is the mechanism that discards waiting time without asking the game rules to subtract it later. A backward or nonfinite delta contributes zero, but its supplied observation still becomes the baseline. The function has no hidden memory beyond the record passed by its caller.

## Fractional values survive observation

The arithmetic never floors the delta. For observations at 0, 0.3, 0.8, 1.1, 3.7 and 10.9, adding the active steps gives the same total as one active observation at 10.9, allowing ordinary floating-point tolerance. A timer frequency change therefore does not inherently change elapsed accounting.

This matters particularly for a mismatch opened between integer milliseconds. Its remaining interval is a positive number in memory and decreases by actual observed active time. Export is the separate rounding boundary: elapsed rounds downward and a positive pending remainder rounds upward.

`browser-clock.test.ts` checks fractional steps, hidden intervals, waiting before start, backward observations, NaN and independence from observation frequency. These tests do not schedule anything. Their purpose is to isolate the arithmetic contract from browser event behavior.

## Hook inputs and persistent refs

`useSessionClock(session, current, commit)` receives the rendered session, a ref to the latest session and a function that commits a new value. It creates a ref for the arithmetic clock and another for the stored visibility state, initialized from `!document.hidden`.

The expression supplied to `useRef(createClock(performance.now()))` is evaluated as the hook renders, while React retains the first ref value. Later evaluations do not by themselves reset that retained baseline. Explicit reset updates `clock.current`. This distinction helps when tracing observations in a render-heavy test: evaluating an initializer expression and replacing a ref value are different operations.

The hook derives `won = isWon(session.game)` for effect dependencies. Inside asynchronous work, `running()` uses `current.current` to read pause, start and victory state, along with the visibility ref. It does not decide activity from a session captured several renders earlier.

## Synchronization step by step

`synchronize(generation = current.current.generation)` begins with a generation check. A mismatched captured generation returns before observing or updating the baseline. Otherwise it reads a fresh browser observation and calls `elapsedStep` using the current running predicate.

It always installs the returned clock record. If `milliseconds` is nonzero, it commits `tickSession(current.current, generation, milliseconds)`. The session function performs another generation check and a pause check, then delegates to `advanceGame`.

The second check is data-layer protection. The first check also prevents an old callback from disturbing the new game's observation baseline. A session-level refusal alone would stop an incorrect game advance but would not explain ownership of the clock record.

The hook's returned `reset()` replaces the baseline with a new observation. It does not clear the game elapsed total or selection. Controller actions combine reset with the appropriate game replacement or resume transition, which is where progress semantics are defined.

## One rescheduling chain

The effect captures the rendered generation, sets `active = true` and holds an optional timer identifier. Its `schedule()` function first clears the current identifier. It then returns if the effect is inactive, the generation no longer matches or `running()` is false.

If active, it reads the current selection. A mismatch uses `Math.min(CLOCK_INTERVAL_MS, selection.remainingMs)` as the requested delay; other states use 40. The timeout callback checks `active`, synchronizes with the captured generation and schedules again.

This is a recursive timeout chain rather than a fixed interval. The next delay is chosen from current state after the previous callback. A mismatch near expiry can request its smaller remainder, and an inactive session stops producing periodic work. The nominal delay is never treated as the actual amount elapsed.

## A delayed callback

Suppose active play has a baseline of 100ms and a timeout requested for 40ms runs at 180ms. Synchronization contributes 80ms. It does not contribute one unit of 40ms merely because one callback fired. The rules update elapsed time and any pending mismatch using that measured contribution.

If the remaining mismatch was 60ms, the same 80ms advance closes it. The rules still add the whole active 80ms to elapsed time, subject to the cap. They do not reduce total elapsed to 60ms just because the selection closed partway through the interval.

This is why callbacks are observation opportunities rather than authority over time. A busy event loop can delay visible updates, but the next synchronization catches the game up from the last observation. [Mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) covers the visible duration independently of this scheduling mechanism.

## Visibility event ordering

`visibilityChanged()` first checks effect activity and generation. It then calls `synchronize(generation)` before assigning `visible.current = !document.hidden`, and finally calls `schedule()`.

On a visible-to-hidden event, synchronization sees the previously visible state and accounts for active time up to the hide observation. The flag then becomes false, and scheduling clears the pending timeout and stops.

On a hidden-to-visible event, synchronization sees the previously hidden state. It contributes zero while updating the baseline to the return observation. The flag then becomes true and scheduling resumes. This order excludes the hidden interval without relying on browser timer throttling behavior.

Reversing that assignment and synchronization would misclassify the interval ending at the event. The relevant state is the activity during the time since the previous observation, not merely the new visibility value after the event. The current order makes that distinction explicit.

## A visibility timeline

| Observation | Stored visibility used for the step | Contribution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Start accepted at 100ms | Not started before the activation | Zero for waiting before start |
| Hide event at 350ms | Visible | 250ms active play |
| Show event at 5350ms | Hidden | Zero for the hidden interval |
| Next active observation at 5390ms | Visible | 40ms active play |

The table assumes no intervening observations and an unfinished, unpaused game. It describes the same arithmetic as many short periodic steps. Hidden time is excluded because the baseline advances on return, not because the system clock stopped.

Headless Chromium does not naturally supply the hidden-tab behavior these journeys need, so browser tests override `document.hidden` and dispatch `visibilitychange` at the adapter boundary. This drives the actual handler while keeping the rule functions unchanged.

## Action synchronization is deliberate

The controller synchronizes immediately before activation. Consider a mismatch whose logical interval has expired while its scheduled callback remains queued. A click can land first. Synchronization closes the old mismatch through `advanceGame`, then `activateSession` sees the newly closed selection and accepts the click as the next first reveal.

`fractional-clock.e2e.test.ts` tests this in one browser task: it updates the controlled observation and invokes a button click before any timer can run. That makes the action-boundary behavior observable without depending on machine load.

Export has the same need for current data. The last rendered state can trail the clock by less than a scheduled interval or more under load. `exportSnapshot` synchronizes and encodes the latest ref. It does not serialize the session value captured by the prior render.

## Replacement, pause and Resume

New Game, Restart and valid loads reset the baseline before replacement. `replaceGame` increments generation, causing the prior effect to become obsolete. An earlier callback checks both activity and generation before affecting the replacement.

An unfinished snapshot import installs its saved state but pauses the session. No active scheduled loop runs while paused. Resume resets the baseline before clearing `paused`, so waiting at the Resume control is not charged to the imported game. Its saved elapsed total and mismatch remainder remain intact.

An invalid load only changes notices. It neither replaces the game nor resets its baseline. An export during active play also does not pause. The controller's action semantics therefore determine which intervals count; the reproduction panel's visibility is not itself a clock state.

## Effect dependencies and cleanup

The effect depends on `session.generation`, `session.game.started`, `session.paused` and the derived `won`. Those values describe changes that start, stop or replace the scheduling lifetime. Ordinary elapsed updates do not restart the effect on every render.

Cleanup marks `active` false, clears the timeout and removes the visibility listener. The callback's activity check handles a callback associated with a retired effect. The generation check handles a replaced game. Removing the listener prevents a later visibility event from invoking obsolete session work after unmount.

The timer identifier may be undefined before anything is scheduled. The browser clear operation is used both at the start of `schedule` and at cleanup, keeping one ownership path. There is no independent timeout per mismatch stored in the core state.

## Completion and numeric caps

When the final match is accepted, the controller has already synchronized. `isWon` then becomes true, the effect's victory dependency changes and the running predicate becomes false. Further logical advances return the won game unchanged.

At `ELAPSED_MAX_MS`, however, victory need not be true. The game can continue, including resolving pending mismatches, even though the elapsed total no longer increases. The hook does not treat the cap as a reason to stop scheduling. This is consistent with the core's independent handling of elapsed accumulation and selection remainder.

The move cap has no direct role in this hook. It is part of activation logic. Separating those bounds avoids turning a display/storage limit into an accidental lifecycle stop.

## Evidence that isolates the risks

The arithmetic tests establish numerical behavior. Session tests establish generation and pause gating. `clock-edges.e2e.test.ts` exports at amounts that are not multiples of the 40ms interval, demonstrating action synchronization. Fractional tests preserve submillisecond mismatch origin and export a final quarter-millisecond as a valid pending interval.

`idle-clock.e2e.test.ts` waits through a hidden period without inspecting the game repeatedly, then checks the remaining active interval on return. A separate case imports a paused mismatch and waits before Resume. These cases expose bugs that incidental observations during inactivity could conceal.

`timer-lifecycle.e2e.test.ts` instruments timeouts and visibility listeners in the separate session harness, unmounts the actual game and checks both counts return to zero. It also starts another mismatch in the same deal after an earlier one has closed. That case distinguishes stale work inside one generation from stale work across replacement.

When investigating drift, the useful trace contains observations, active conditions and resulting deltas. Counting callbacks or inspecting the displayed seconds is too coarse to distinguish a rounding defect from a baseline defect. The two-file design makes each of those quantities available to focused tests without adding diagnostic state to the shipped game.

# Announcements policy

This page describes how event feedback is published, repeated and kept separate from routine game rendering.

The game has many visible updates, but only some represent a new result. A clock tick is a changing value; resolving a turn is an event. Treating those as the same kind of update would make a memory game noisy and would bury the information a player needs after selecting two cards.

## Publication point

`Game.tsx` places the game result between the board instructions and the Board itself. Its paragraph has `role="status"`, `aria-live="polite"` and `aria-atomic="true"`, with the current feedback inside a span. The page has exactly one live region, the status paragraph in Game.tsx. New status text, such as whose turn it is, goes through that region. The current game publishes pair results and load outcomes there; it has no turn-owner feature.

The paragraph remains mounted while its content changes. It is inside `.game-result`, which has a minimum height of `56px`, flex alignment and margins. The wrapper reserves a readable area near the board without making the scrollable card content itself the announcement source.

Polite publication allows the browser and assistive technology to schedule the result around other speech. Atomic content indicates that the paragraph's result is treated as a complete update rather than an isolated changed number. These attributes express the intended exposure; the actual spoken experience still needs user acceptance with a screen reader.

## Session data behind the paragraph

The session owns `feedback` and an integer `announcement`. Game renders `<span key={session.announcement}>{session.feedback}</span>`. Updating the key replaces the child span even when its text is identical to the preceding result. This gives repeated events a DOM change without adding a hidden counter to the spoken text.

The counter is event identity, not a statistic presented to the player. It does not track moves, matched pairs or elapsed seconds. A failed load can advance it without adding a move, while the first card reveal changes game state without advancing it.

A broad render counter would be wrong for this job. Session renders occur for time and selection changes that should not repeat the last turn result. The explicit event field makes the distinction inspectable in `session.ts` and `use-game.ts`.

## Turn results

`activateSession` calls the pure `activateCard`. If the game object is unchanged, it returns the current session. If the result has selection kind `one`, it returns the updated game without changing feedback or announcement identity. That covers the first eligible reveal.

After the second eligible reveal, the result is either a mismatch or a match. The session builds the appropriate text and increments `announcement`. Completion is checked at this same boundary, so the winning match gets a combined result rather than two competing event publications.

| Result | Text produced by the session |
| --- | --- |
| First matched pair | `Pair found. 1 pair matched.` |
| Later nonfinal pair | `Pair found. M pairs matched.` |
| Mismatch | `No match. Cards close after a short pause.` |
| Winning pair | `Pair found. All pairs found in N moves and time.` |

Here `M` and `N` are replaced with the actual counts, and `time` is the output of `formatElapsed`. The singular branch is based on `game.matched.length === 2`. The final branch takes precedence over the nonfinal pair count.

A card's accessible name also changes when it reveals or matches. That is the focused control describing its own state, not a second turn-result producer. The text in the event paragraph summarizes what the two-card attempt achieved. [Screen reader notes](screen-reader-notes.md) follows those two sources in a complete game.

## Consecutive identical results

Two misses in a row produce the same sentence. Updating only a string state can leave the DOM text unchanged, which gives no new mutation for the second event. The keyed span avoids relying on a different visible sentence to distinguish them.

The current sequence is concrete. Initial feedback is empty. Revealing index 0 on `np1-4-1` changes selection to `one` without publishing. Revealing index 1 produces a mismatch and advances the event identity. After the interval closes, choosing those two indices again produces the same text with a later identity.

The counter advances once for each resolved attempt in that sequence, not once for each card action or timer update. A third activation during the mismatch is ignored by the game and leaves the event unchanged. The same is true of a repeated activation on the first revealed card.

There is no temporary blanking timeout between identical results. The implementation does not clear text, wait a guessed number of milliseconds and restore it. That avoids adding announcement timing to the game clock or introducing a second lifecycle that can outlive a replacement game.

## Changes that stay quiet

`tickSession` advances the game and returns a new session with that game, leaving feedback and announcement fields intact. Mismatch closure is part of this advancement. It does not publish a new “cards closed” result. The earlier mismatch sentence already told the player that closure would follow a short pause.

Arrow movement is local board focus state. It does not call the session feedback path. Clock renders update Time in GameStatus, while card memoization prevents unchanged cards from rendering again. Neither operation is a new turn result.

New Game and Restart call `replaceGame` with `imported: false`. That replacement clears the prior feedback and load notice while keeping the announcement number. A successful board-code load follows the same replacement path. These operations clear old context; the current source does not add a success sentence for a board-code load.

Clearing text is still a DOM change and may appear in a mutation trace as an empty result. It is different from republishing a turn sentence. The accessibility journey's expected record includes the new-game clearing event, so a raw count of every mutation is not a substitute for reading what each event contains.

## Load outcomes share the publication path

The controller's `notice(feedback)` helper assigns both `feedback` and `loadNotice`, then increments `announcement`. Invalid Board code publishes `Invalid board code.`; invalid Snapshot JSON publishes `Invalid snapshot.`. Repeating the same invalid submission is a new load attempt and advances the identity again.

For valid snapshot import, `replaceGame(..., true)` increments the identity and publishes either `Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue.` or `Loaded completed snapshot.`. The former corresponds to a paused unfinished game, the latter to completed progress. Valid board-code loading does not use the imported-snapshot branch.

Reproduction also renders `loadNotice` in its ordinary paragraph with id `load-notice`. The load buttons reference it through `aria-describedby`. That keeps the outcome visible beside the text tools and associates the description with their actions without creating another event publisher in that panel.

Resume clears feedback and loadNotice without increasing the event identity. It also transfers focus to the board before its button disappears. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) and [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) describe those effects independently of event publication.

## Completion and persistent reading

GameStatus shows a completion paragraph whenever `isWon(game)` is true. A newly won game can give it the celebration class; an imported completed game shows it statically. That paragraph is persistent reading content containing the final moves and time.

The winning turn's feedback already contains the match and win in one result. The status paragraph does not need to separately announce a matched pair, then publish a second completion sentence. This avoids having two updates compete at the most significant turn in the game.

A completed snapshot instead publishes its load outcome, because import is the event that just occurred. The game is visibly complete, but no new card match happened. This distinction preserves a useful account of what the user actually did.

## Automated evidence

`session.test.ts` checks that first reveal, mismatch closure and repeated mismatch events affect announcement identity as expected. It also checks import outcomes and completion transitions without involving the browser.

`tests/announcements.e2e.test.ts` observes DOM mutations in the status paragraph. It resolves a mismatch, moves focus, runs the mismatch interval and repeats the same attempt. The expected result history contains the mismatch sentence once for each resolved turn, with no extra result from movement or closure.

The same test submits each snapshot load kind and each invalid-load kind twice, checking the publication history and the visible load notice. `tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` checks that the result remains beside the board during large-phone play and that the reproduction panel has no competing result role.

The accessibility journey reads Chromium's tree for the polite and atomic properties and the result text at each turn. That establishes exposure in the tested runtime. Spoken scheduling and verbalization are assessed in user acceptance. The repository records spoken review as user acceptance.

## Diagnosing a repeated or missing result

A missing second identical result suggests checking event identity before changing the sentence. A repeated result on every clock tick suggests checking whether routine advancement touches the publication fields. A load notice visible near the textarea but absent from event output suggests checking whether the controller used `notice` or only changed local text.

For a report, the useful sequence is the action, feedback string, announcement number and observed mutations. That evidence can show whether the session failed to publish, React had no relevant change or the browser exposed the expected update but a spoken review behaved differently. The policy gives a single publication boundary; diagnosis follows it from the event to the paragraph rather than adding more announcers around the page.

# Acceptance
Acceptance is a set of journeys that checks whether Neon Pairs meets its product requirements.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Finish a game, then start another one during a mismatch. The first journey checks play and completion. The second checks that an earlier timer can't change a new game.

## Play

Use these journeys with the requirements in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md):

- Finish every supported size with complete pairs.
- Reveal one card twice, then reveal a different card. Check the exact move count.
- Match a pair, then miss a pair. Check the immediate match and the 800ms active mismatch interval.
- Hide the page during a mismatch, then return and finish its remaining interval.
- Start and restart during a mismatch. Check the cleared state and later timer updates.
- Finish games with better, equal and worse move counts. Reload and check the current size's best.

## Controls

Use pointer, touch and keyboard to follow [Input](../interface/input.md) and [Controls](../interface/controls.md). Check control labels, row movement, edge stops, native Tab exit and focus after each action. Check that hidden cards reveal no identity in the DOM.

Follow the keyboard journey in I17 and check its accessibility tree. During user acceptance, confirm spoken results with a screen reader, including consecutive identical results and the final match with its win.

## Appearance

Measure the layout and review all 128 faces against [Visuals](../visuals/visuals.md). Use a 44px grayscale face sheet to distinguish shape, marker and fill. Check 16x16 boards at both stated viewport sizes, full focus outlines and the equivalent zoom layout. Check reduced motion and the static completion banner after its single pulse.

Play through completion and reset while checking [Sound](../sound/sound.md). Every action stays silent.

## Reproduction

Check [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md) with its example deck and replay. Check snapshot round trips and malformed input. Check the exact mismatch timeout before an equal-time replay action.

Load an unfinished snapshot, attempt input while paused, then Resume. Check its remaining active time and focus. Load a completed snapshot and check its static banner and unchanged best score.

## Delivery

Use a locked install, type check, unit tests and a fresh browser build as defined in [Technology](../architecture/technology.md). Open the resulting HTML directly from disk with network access blocked. Use a local HTTP origin for saved preferences.

Review the pure game functions, browser effects, file sizes and behavior placement against [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md).

Back to [Neon Pairs](../README.md).

# Test strategy
This page explains how Neon Pairs divides evidence between game tests, browser journeys, source checks and user acceptance.

The product contract is specification version 2.2. The README records a successful named compatibility run. [Known issues](known-issues.md) tracks verification limits, and [Fixtures](fixtures-guide.md) explains why replacing reviewed JSON expectations with current output would weaken the evidence.

## Start with the question

A deck test asks whether a code produces the published cards. A browser test asks whether a player can reach and activate those cards through rendered controls. An accessibility-tree capture asks what Chromium exposes to assistive software. None can substitute for the others.

The useful division follows the architecture's existing boundaries:

| Question | Existing evidence | What it cannot establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Does a turn change the right data? | Vitest tests beside `game.ts` | Native focus, scrolling or pointer dispatch |
| Does the seeded deal match the format? | Literal vectors and `tests/deal-oracle.ts` | Whether hidden identities leak into markup |
| Does the browser adapter count active time? | Pure clock tests plus controlled browser clocks | Real device scheduling latency |
| Can a player finish through the interface? | Built-page keyboard and touch journeys | Spoken screen-reader output |
| Does local storage survive reload? | HTTP-origin persistence journeys | Cross-browser behavior of disk-origin storage |
| Does the distribution stand alone? | Offline disk navigation and built-output inspection | Every browser engine or operating system |
| Does the layout survive difficult geometry? | Large-board, scrollbar, zoom and focus tests | Every possible window size |

This is a map of current checks, not a demand to create one test of each kind for every change. A correction to snapshot validation usually needs parser evidence first. A clipped focus ring needs browser geometry. A change to explanatory copy may need only the relevant reviewed expectation and a visual check. [Unit tests](unit-test-guide.md) and [Browser tests](browser-test-guide.md) show the local conventions.

## Pure behavior carries the broad matrix

`vitest.config.ts` includes `src/**/*.test.ts` and `scripts/**/*.test.ts`. The package's `test` script is `vitest run`. Most of these tests import `test` from Vitest and assertions from `node:assert/strict`. They do not mount React to prove a card transition.

The core state includes the immutable board description, its deck, matched positions, selection, moves, elapsed milliseconds and the started flag. Selection has closed, one-card and mismatch branches. Tests exercise transitions directly, allowing exact questions such as whether advancing a pending miss by 799ms leaves it open and whether the next millisecond closes both cards.

The suite checks complete pairs at all seven supported sizes. `completion.test.ts` finishes each size through `activateCard`; it does not infer that a 4x4 success proves a 16x16 finish. `deck.test.ts` checks the published seed-one vector, generator states, the inclusive maximum seed, frozen data and independent generation at each size. `deck-rejection.test.ts` targets uncommon rejection-sampling boundaries using separately stored expected decks.

The game tests also make negative cases visible. A fractional or out-of-range card index returns the old state. Repeating the first selected card adds no move. During a miss, every activation is ignored. Invalid elapsed steps leave the game unchanged. Keeping the original object in those cases is observable behavior in these tests; asserting identity can distinguish an ignored action from an unnecessary reconstruction.

Snapshot and replay tests carry a different matrix: exact object fields, integer ranges, byte limits, valid selections and action ordering. A round trip is useful, but two matching mistakes can round trip successfully. Independent expected fields and malformed inputs provide the stronger evidence. A valid started game with one revealed card and zero moves is the baseline for several invalid-counter cases, so rejection can be attributed to the changed counter rather than an unrelated invalid state.

## Session tests connect results to browser-independent policy

`src/game/session/session.ts` is a data adapter. Its tests create sessions and call `activateSession`, `replaceGame` and `tickSession` directly. This makes several integration rules cheap to check without pretending to test browser effects.

A replacement increments `generation`. A tick carrying an earlier generation has no effect. An unfinished imported game is paused and cannot accept card input or active time until resumed. A locally completed game can improve the appropriate saved move record. A completed import follows the import path instead of the live completion path. These are separate causes even when both render a completed board.

Session feedback tests inspect event progression as well as text. Two misses with the same wording still represent two turns. Focus movement and time advancement do not represent new turn results. Browser announcement tests then verify that these data changes become the intended DOM updates. Checking both layers helps distinguish a missing session event from a rendering problem.

Storage tests use the narrow `PreferenceStore` interface. A Map-backed implementation covers round trips and per-size minima; a throwing implementation covers failures without a browser. Browser tests separately exercise a denied `window.localStorage` getter. The distinction matters because failure while obtaining the store occurs before either `getItem` or `setItem` can run.

## Browser journeys use the shipped shape

The package's `test:e2e` command runs the main build, builds diagnostic entries, and then invokes Node's test runner over `tests/*.e2e.test.ts` with concurrency set to one. Playwright drives Chromium, while `node:test` owns the tests. There is no Playwright Test project configuration controlling this suite's retry or worker behavior.

Most journey files import the wrapper in `tests/browser-test.ts`. It launches a browser, creates a fresh context per case, collects page errors and closes resources. `tests/artifact-server.ts` serves the freshly built HTML on a private loopback port. `GAME_URL` points at the same build on disk. Persistence journeys use the served URL; offline-delivery checks use the disk URL.

Fresh contexts isolate browser storage, permissions and page-installed instrumentation. They do not make every global resource independent: the artifact server and browser belong to file-level hooks, and the runtime record has a shared output location. The serial command is part of the implementation being documented. [Flaky-test notes](flaky-test-notes.md) discuss the timing consequences.

The browser tests use public controls to load `np1-4-1`. They know its deck from the documented format and test fixture, rather than asking the application for hidden state. The board's hidden buttons expose positions and closed state. The tests inspect that absence directly in `input-contract.e2e.test.ts`, including the neutral back and lack of face artwork. A solver that depended on hidden SVGs would invalidate this evidence.

## Contract checks complement shared labels

Ordinary journey helpers import the control-label constants so they can focus on behavior. Contract tests also contain literal labels and limits. This prevents changing a production constant and every test lookup together from silently changing the public contract.

`control-contract.e2e.test.ts` covers native reproduction controls, their input limits, invalid statuses and action focus. `product-contract.e2e.test.ts` covers status presentation, continuing minutes and successful load size selection. `persistence-contract.e2e.test.ts` checks record comparisons, saved sizes and fresh progress after reload. These overlap broader journeys at specific seams, where a shared helper could otherwise conceal a mistake.

Overlap is useful when the assertions answer different questions. Loading a snapshot appears in parser tests, session tests and browser tests because validation, paused data and Resume focus are different behaviors. Repeating the same serializer implementation as an expected-value helper would add little protection. The suite's independent literal expectations are intended to break that circularity.

## Visual and accessibility evidence are concrete

The art entry renders every face at the minimum card size. Tests capture color, grayscale and neutral versions. Neutral silhouettes are compared for uniqueness, and separate assertions inspect marker geometry and palette application. This establishes machine-distinguishable geometry; a person still reviews whether the distinctions are usable. [Accessibility audit](accessibility-audit.md) explains that limit.

Layout tests inspect page width, card bounds, board scrolling and complete focus outlines. The large-board checks cover 360x800 and 1280x800 CSS-pixel viewports. A separate equivalent-zoom journey uses 640x400 with device scale 2. Visible-scrollbar cases remove Chromium's default scrollbar-hiding launch argument and test widths where scrollbar space changes the available board area.

The accessibility journey uses the Chromium DevTools Protocol to capture the accessibility tree during a complete keyboard game. It checks controls, revealed and matched names, disabled state exposure, results, completion, Tab exit and a fresh game. The artifact records browser and Playwright versions and explicitly records that a screen reader was not run. User acceptance owns the spoken journey. Tree assertions support that review; they do not prove speech delivery.

## Source and delivery checks

`source-audit.test.ts` inspects package pins, lockfile agreement, compiler settings and source conventions required by the architecture and technology specifications. It reads authored files rather than the compiled bundle. `source-conventions.test.ts` checks current export ownership, question-shaped predicate names, behavior-oriented test names and the small set of environment reads the runners use.

These are text checks with intentionally limited reach. The core effect scan names particular source files. It is not an analysis of every transitive call. The TypeScript source scan can reject spelling patterns, but cannot prove full semantic purity. Review remains necessary when moving behavior to a new module. [Code review](../architecture/code-review-guide.md) and [Source audit notes](../architecture/source-audit-notes.md) provide related architectural context.

The built-output test searches the emitted HTML for `fetch(` and the preload helper's `relList` marker. The offline journey blocks network access and checks that only the document request occurs while a card remains playable. Together they cover bundle content and observed loading. Neither measures first-render duration; [Performance budget](performance-budget.md) documents that evidence gap.

## Following through

Choose the smallest test that exposes the changed behavior, then follow it into the browser where native interaction or effects matter. [Regression catalogue](regression-catalogue.md) shows paired investigations, and [Release checklist](release-checklist.md) assembles the complete verification sequence. The remaining evidence gaps are tracked in [Known issues](known-issues.md).

# Technology
Technology is the build and language specification for Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.2.

The game runs offline from one HTML file. Browser controls and inline SVG provide the board, input and artwork.

## Stack

- T01 - Use React with TypeScript and DOM rendering. Use native buttons, a native select and CSS Grid. Use no component library.

- T02 - Pin these packages and keep the lockfile. The stable versions were checked on 31 October 2026:

| Package | Version | Job |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `react`, `react-dom` | `19.3.1` | Browser UI |
| `typescript` | `7.0.2` | Type checking |
| `@types/react`, `@types/react-dom` | `19.3.0` | React types |
| `vite` | `8.3.5` | Build |
| `@vitejs/plugin-react` | `6.1.2` | React build integration |
| `vite-plugin-singlefile` | `2.3.4` | One HTML distribution |
| `vitest` | `5.0.5` | Unit tests |
| `@playwright/test` | `1.64.1` | Browser tests |
| `@types/node` | `24.19.2` | Build and test types |

TypeScript 7 is a stable release, as the [release announcement](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/typescript/announcing-typescript-7-0/) describes. The [React versions page](https://react.dev/versions) lists the stable React release family.

## Language

- T03 - Use Node.js 24.19 or later and npm. Keep browser and Node compiler projects separate. Use ESM, static imports and type-only imports for types.

Use Node `26.12.1`, npm `11.20.0` and Playwright `1.64.1` with Chromium `156.0.8078.4` as the named compatibility combination. Record the locked install, build, unit tests and browser journeys with those exact versions in the project README before calling the combination tested. Other supported versions need their own results.

- T04 - Enable TypeScript strictness, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, `verbatimModuleSyntax` and `erasableSyntaxOnly`. Keep type checking separate from bundling. Vite's [TypeScript support](https://vite.dev/guide/features.html#typescript) transpiles code without checking types.

- T05 - Model project data with exact types and validate unknown data where it enters the game. Use narrowing instead of `any`, suppressed diagnostics or unchecked casts. Derive state unions from their named values.

- T06 - Keep behavior and its code, styles and tests together. Aim for 100 lines per TypeScript file and keep authored TypeScript files at or below 200 lines. Split by behavior when a file grows. Use direct imports from the file that defines a behavior.

## Commands

- T07 - Provide these commands:

| Command | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `npm ci` | Install the locked dependencies |
| `npm run dev` | Serve the game locally |
| `npm run typecheck` | Check every compiler project |
| `npm test` | Run unit tests for the game rules |
| `npm run test:e2e` | Build from current source, then run browser checks in fresh contexts against that build |
| `npm run build` | Type check and emit `dist/index.html` |
| `npm run --silent replay -- PATH` | Read replay JSON with the output and exit behavior in C14 |

The browser command must fail if its build fails. It…1676 tokens truncated…of 40ms merely because one callback fired. The rules update elapsed time and any pending mismatch using that measured contribution.

If the remaining mismatch was 60ms, the same 80ms advance closes it. The rules still add the whole active 80ms to elapsed time, subject to the cap. They do not reduce total elapsed to 60ms just because the selection closed partway through the interval.

This is why callbacks are observation opportunities rather than authority over time. A busy event loop can delay visible updates, but the next synchronization catches the game up from the last observation. [Mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) covers the visible duration independently of this scheduling mechanism.

## Visibility event ordering

`visibilityChanged()` first checks effect activity and generation. It then calls `synchronize(generation)` before assigning `visible.current = !document.hidden`, and finally calls `schedule()`.

On a visible-to-hidden event, synchronization sees the previously visible state and accounts for active time up to the hide observation. The flag then becomes false, and scheduling clears the pending timeout and stops.

On a hidden-to-visible event, synchronization sees the previously hidden state. It contributes zero while updating the baseline to the return observation. The flag then becomes true and scheduling resumes. This order excludes the hidden interval without relying on browser timer throttling behavior.

Reversing that assignment and synchronization would misclassify the interval ending at the event. The relevant state is the activity during the time since the previous observation, not merely the new visibility value after the event. The current order makes that distinction explicit.

## A visibility timeline

| Observation | Stored visibility used for the step | Contribution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Start accepted at 100ms | Not started before the activation | Zero for waiting before start |
| Hide event at 350ms | Visible | 250ms active play |
| Show event at 5350ms | Hidden | Zero for the hidden interval |
| Next active observation at 5390ms | Visible | 40ms active play |

The table assumes no intervening observations and an unfinished, unpaused game. It describes the same arithmetic as many short periodic steps. Hidden time is excluded because the baseline advances on return, not because the system clock stopped.

Headless Chromium does not naturally supply the hidden-tab behavior these journeys need, so browser tests override `document.hidden` and dispatch `visibilitychange` at the adapter boundary. This drives the actual handler while keeping the rule functions unchanged.

## Action synchronization is deliberate

The controller synchronizes immediately before activation. Consider a mismatch whose logical interval has expired while its scheduled callback remains queued. A click can land first. Synchronization closes the old mismatch through `advanceGame`, then `activateSession` sees the newly closed selection and accepts the click as the next first reveal.

`fractional-clock.e2e.test.ts` tests this in one browser task: it updates the controlled observation and invokes a button click before any timer can run. That makes the action-boundary behavior observable without depending on machine load.

Export has the same need for current data. The last rendered state can trail the clock by less than a scheduled interval or more under load. `exportSnapshot` synchronizes and encodes the latest ref. It does not serialize the session value captured by the prior render.

## Replacement, pause and Resume

New Game, Restart and valid loads reset the baseline before replacement. `replaceGame` increments generation, causing the prior effect to become obsolete. An earlier callback checks both activity and generation before affecting the replacement.

An unfinished snapshot import installs its saved state but pauses the session. No active scheduled loop runs while paused. Resume resets the baseline before clearing `paused`, so waiting at the Resume control is not charged to the imported game. Its saved elapsed total and mismatch remainder remain intact.

An invalid load only changes notices. It neither replaces the game nor resets its baseline. An export during active play also does not pause. The controller's action semantics therefore determine which intervals count; the reproduction panel's visibility is not itself a clock state.

## Effect dependencies and cleanup

The effect depends on `session.generation`, `session.game.started`, `session.paused` and the derived `won`. Those values describe changes that start, stop or replace the scheduling lifetime. Ordinary elapsed updates do not restart the effect on every render.

Cleanup marks `active` false, clears the timeout and removes the visibility listener. The callback's activity check handles a callback associated with a retired effect. The generation check handles a replaced game. Removing the listener prevents a later visibility event from invoking obsolete session work after unmount.

The timer identifier may be undefined before anything is scheduled. The browser clear operation is used both at the start of `schedule` and at cleanup, keeping one ownership path. There is no independent timeout per mismatch stored in the core state.

## Completion and numeric caps

When the final match is accepted, the controller has already synchronized. `isWon` then becomes true, the effect's victory dependency changes and the running predicate becomes false. Further logical advances return the won game unchanged.

At `ELAPSED_MAX_MS`, however, victory need not be true. The game can continue, including resolving pending mismatches, even though the elapsed total no longer increases. The hook does not treat the cap as a reason to stop scheduling. This is consistent with the core's independent handling of elapsed accumulation and selection remainder.

The move cap has no direct role in this hook. It is part of activation logic. Separating those bounds avoids turning a display/storage limit into an accidental lifecycle stop.

## Evidence that isolates the risks

The arithmetic tests establish numerical behavior. Session tests establish generation and pause gating. `clock-edges.e2e.test.ts` exports at amounts that are not multiples of the 40ms interval, demonstrating action synchronization. Fractional tests preserve submillisecond mismatch origin and export a final quarter-millisecond as a valid pending interval.

`idle-clock.e2e.test.ts` waits through a hidden period without inspecting the game repeatedly, then checks the remaining active interval on return. A separate case imports a paused mismatch and waits before Resume. These cases expose bugs that incidental observations during inactivity could conceal.

`timer-lifecycle.e2e.test.ts` instruments timeouts and visibility listeners in the separate session harness, unmounts the actual game and checks both counts return to zero. It also starts another mismatch in the same deal after an earlier one has closed. That case distinguishes stale work inside one generation from stale work across replacement.

When investigating drift, the useful trace contains observations, active conditions and resulting deltas. Counting callbacks or inspecting the displayed seconds is too coarse to distinguish a rounding defect from a baseline defect. The two-file design makes each of those quantities available to focused tests without adding diagnostic state to the shipped game.

# Announcements policy

This page describes how event feedback is published, repeated and kept separate from routine game rendering.

The game has many visible updates, but only some represent a new result. A clock tick is a changing value; resolving a turn is an event. Treating those as the same kind of update would make a memory game noisy and would bury the information a player needs after selecting two cards.

## Publication point

`Game.tsx` places the game result between the board instructions and the Board itself. Its paragraph has `role="status"`, `aria-live="polite"` and `aria-atomic="true"`, with the current feedback inside a span. The page has exactly one live region, the status paragraph in Game.tsx. New status text, such as whose turn it is, goes through that region. The current game publishes pair results and load outcomes there; it has no turn-owner feature.

The paragraph remains mounted while its content changes. It is inside `.game-result`, which has a minimum height of `56px`, flex alignment and margins. The wrapper reserves a readable area near the board without making the scrollable card content itself the announcement source.

Polite publication allows the browser and assistive technology to schedule the result around other speech. Atomic content indicates that the paragraph's result is treated as a complete update rather than an isolated changed number. These attributes express the intended exposure; the actual spoken experience still needs user acceptance with a screen reader.

## Session data behind the paragraph

The session owns `feedback` and an integer `announcement`. Game renders `<span key={session.announcement}>{session.feedback}</span>`. Updating the key replaces the child span even when its text is identical to the preceding result. This gives repeated events a DOM change without adding a hidden counter to the spoken text.

The counter is event identity, not a statistic presented to the player. It does not track moves, matched pairs or elapsed seconds. A failed load can advance it without adding a move, while the first card reveal changes game state without advancing it.

A broad render counter would be wrong for this job. Session renders occur for time and selection changes that should not repeat the last turn result. The explicit event field makes the distinction inspectable in `session.ts` and `use-game.ts`.

## Turn results

`activateSession` calls the pure `activateCard`. If the game object is unchanged, it returns the current session. If the result has selection kind `one`, it returns the updated game without changing feedback or announcement identity. That covers the first eligible reveal.

After the second eligible reveal, the result is either a mismatch or a match. The session builds the appropriate text and increments `announcement`. Completion is checked at this same boundary, so the winning match gets a combined result rather than two competing event publications.

| Result | Text produced by the session |
| --- | --- |
| First matched pair | `Pair found. 1 pair matched.` |
| Later nonfinal pair | `Pair found. M pairs matched.` |
| Mismatch | `No match. Cards close after a short pause.` |
| Winning pair | `Pair found. All pairs found in N moves and time.` |

Here `M` and `N` are replaced with the actual counts, and `time` is the output of `formatElapsed`. The singular branch is based on `game.matched.length === 2`. The final branch takes precedence over the nonfinal pair count.

A card's accessible name also changes when it reveals or matches. That is the focused control describing its own state, not a second turn-result producer. The text in the event paragraph summarizes what the two-card attempt achieved. [Screen reader notes](screen-reader-notes.md) follows those two sources in a complete game.

## Consecutive identical results

Two misses in a row produce the same sentence. Updating only a string state can leave the DOM text unchanged, which gives no new mutation for the second event. The keyed span avoids relying on a different visible sentence to distinguish them.

The current sequence is concrete. Initial feedback is empty. Revealing index 0 on `np1-4-1` changes selection to `one` without publishing. Revealing index 1 produces a mismatch and advances the event identity. After the interval closes, choosing those two indices again produces the same text with a later identity.

The counter advances once for each resolved attempt in that sequence, not once for each card action or timer update. A third activation during the mismatch is ignored by the game and leaves the event unchanged. The same is true of a repeated activation on the first revealed card.

There is no temporary blanking timeout between identical results. The implementation does not clear text, wait a guessed number of milliseconds and restore it. That avoids adding announcement timing to the game clock or introducing a second lifecycle that can outlive a replacement game.

## Changes that stay quiet

`tickSession` advances the game and returns a new session with that game, leaving feedback and announcement fields intact. Mismatch closure is part of this advancement. It does not publish a new “cards closed” result. The earlier mismatch sentence already told the player that closure would follow a short pause.

Arrow movement is local board focus state. It does not call the session feedback path. Clock renders update Time in GameStatus, while card memoization prevents unchanged cards from rendering again. Neither operation is a new turn result.

New Game and Restart call `replaceGame` with `imported: false`. That replacement clears the prior feedback and load notice while keeping the announcement number. A successful board-code load follows the same replacement path. These operations clear old context; the current source does not add a success sentence for a board-code load.

Clearing text is still a DOM change and may appear in a mutation trace as an empty result. It is different from republishing a turn sentence. The accessibility journey's expected record includes the new-game clearing event, so a raw count of every mutation is not a substitute for reading what each event contains.

## Load outcomes share the publication path

The controller's `notice(feedback)` helper assigns both `feedback` and `loadNotice`, then increments `announcement`. Invalid Board code publishes `Invalid board code.`; invalid Snapshot JSON publishes `Invalid snapshot.`. Repeating the same invalid submission is a new load attempt and advances the identity again.

For valid snapshot import, `replaceGame(..., true)` increments the identity and publishes either `Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue.` or `Loaded completed snapshot.`. The former corresponds to a paused unfinished game, the latter to completed progress. Valid board-code loading does not use the imported-snapshot branch.

Reproduction also renders `loadNotice` in its ordinary paragraph with id `load-notice`. The load buttons reference it through `aria-describedby`. That keeps the outcome visible beside the text tools and associates the description with their actions without creating another event publisher in that panel.

Resume clears feedback and loadNotice without increasing the event identity. It also transfers focus to the board before its button disappears. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) and [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) describe those effects independently of event publication.

## Completion and persistent reading

GameStatus shows a completion paragraph whenever `isWon(game)` is true. A newly won game can give it the celebration class; an imported completed game shows it statically. That paragraph is persistent reading content containing the final moves and time.

The winning turn's feedback already contains the match and win in one result. The status paragraph does not need to separately announce a matched pair, then publish a second completion sentence. This avoids having two updates compete at the most significant turn in the game.

A completed snapshot instead publishes its load outcome, because import is the event that just occurred. The game is visibly complete, but no new card match happened. This distinction preserves a useful account of what the user actually did.

## Automated evidence

`session.test.ts` checks that first reveal, mismatch closure and repeated mismatch events affect announcement identity as expected. It also checks import outcomes and completion transitions without involving the browser.

`tests/announcements.e2e.test.ts` observes DOM mutations in the status paragraph. It resolves a mismatch, moves focus, runs the mismatch interval and repeats the same attempt. The expected result history contains the mismatch sentence once for each resolved turn, with no extra result from movement or closure.

The same test submits each snapshot load kind and each invalid-load kind twice, checking the publication history and the visible load notice. `tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` checks that the result remains beside the board during large-phone play and that the reproduction panel has no competing result role.

The accessibility journey reads Chromium's tree for the polite and atomic properties and the result text at each turn. That establishes exposure in the tested runtime. Spoken scheduling and verbalization are assessed in user acceptance. The repository records spoken review as user acceptance.

## Diagnosing a repeated or missing result

A missing second identical result suggests checking event identity before changing the sentence. A repeated result on every clock tick suggests checking whether routine advancement touches the publication fields. A load notice visible near the textarea but absent from event output suggests checking whether the controller used `notice` or only changed local text.

For a report, the useful sequence is the action, feedback string, announcement number and observed mutations. That evidence can show whether the session failed to publish, React had no relevant change or the browser exposed the expected update but a spoken review behaved differently. The policy gives a single publication boundary; diagnosis follows it from the event to the paragraph rather than adding more announcers around the page.

# Shared-device playtest notes

This page is a qualitative account of how people played Neon Pairs together and what those sessions suggest for competition design.

The sessions examined local play with the current game. The observations concern attention, learning and handoff.

## Session setting

The working setup was deliberately modest: one browser game, people seated close enough to see the screen and paper notes beside the device. Event sketches were discussed on paper because the game has no participant entry or bracket controller. The browser supplied the actual card play, its ordinary status area and the existing reproduction tools.

Three settings were considered: a laptop on a table, a tablet passed between adjacent seats and a phone held by the current player. These are contrasting situations, not a representative sample of device usage. Their value was in making different problems observable. A laptop makes spectating easy; a held phone makes physical transfer and changing viewing angles much more prominent.

The discussion concentrated on what people did without prompting. Could someone enter the board, distinguish a face, recover after a miss and understand that their board was complete? Could a person who had looked away rejoin the conversation? Those questions were more productive than asking participants whether a finished competition feature sounded appealing in the abstract.

## Laptop: learning the faces aloud

In the laptop session, Mara began with the pointer and described each revealed face aloud. Her first descriptions used only shape: circle, star, triangle. After encountering similar shapes with different markers in a larger practice board, she started adding direction. The vocabulary changed from “the star near the corner” to “the star with the marker on the right.”

Jon, sitting beside her, remembered locations in row terms instead. He pointed to a horizontal band and then counted columns. They were attending to the same artwork but encoding different information. Neither strategy suggested a problem with the deck; the difference was in how people organized memory.

This observation agrees with the face model in `src/game/board/face-design.ts`: shape and marker direction both contribute to identity, and the game also includes a fill distinction. It also explains why the introduction in `Game.tsx` mentions shape and marker. A report that two faces “looked the same” can mean that a participant initially remembered only part of the available design.

The useful follow-up question was which feature they had noticed, rather than whether they had memorized the official face name. [Face catalogue](../visuals/face-catalogue.md) and [pair identity](../gameplay/pair-identity.md) provide the source context for interpreting such reports.

## Keyboard: movement looked like hesitation

Leah used Tab to enter the board and then moved with the arrows. An observer initially wrote down several pauses as indecision about the puzzle. On closer discussion, some of those pauses were time spent checking the focus outline and moving to a remembered position. The participant knew which card she wanted before she reached it.

This was a useful correction to the observation method. Card navigation and memory retrieval are separate activities, even when they occur between the same two reveals. Counting only the delay between clicks would have concealed the difference entirely, since this participant was not primarily clicking.

Leah also revisited an already matched card while moving across the board. She treated it as a landmark rather than as a card she intended to play. The current cards remain focusable in that state. That behavior made sense in the session, but an observer looking only at focus position might have misclassified it as a failed selection.

The input trace records navigation behavior. The repository README records accessibility-tree checks; screen-reader testing has not been performed. [Board keyboard navigation](../interface/board-keyboard-navigation.md), [focus policy](../interface/focus-policy.md) and [screen reader notes](../interface/screen-reader-notes.md) distinguish those subjects.

## Tablet: the handoff was an activity of its own

In the tablet session, moving the device between people interrupted the group's visual reference. The outgoing player tilted it toward the next person, while another participant tried to read the result from an angle. The result was still present, but not everyone saw it at the same time.

The next player first adjusted the tablet on the table, then looked for the board. That sequence would have been easy to describe as slow play if the observer had measured from physical handoff. It was mostly positioning the device. The observation helped separate the social transition from actual interaction with the game.

People also used the visible completed board as a conversation piece. They pointed at remembered mistakes and explained how they finally located a pair. The exposed cards carried a short history of the attempt that a bare result number would not capture. In a group setting, that retrospective conversation was part of the appeal.

The presentation of a competition handoff remained undecided. The prototype used ordinary play and a paper event sketch. It showed what people looked at and discussed. [Competition overview](competition-overview.md) explains the intended social context.

## Phone: scrolling and tapping had different purposes

On the phone, Niko sometimes touched the board to move its visible area rather than to reveal a card. His comments made that intention clear: he was searching for a remembered row near the edge. A raw touch trace would have contained contact with several cards, but contact alone would not have described the intended action.

The research note therefore distinguishes an attempted tap, a completed activation and a scroll gesture. These are useful observational categories, not additional game states. A participant saying “I touched that one” can refer to any of them, and the distinction can explain an apparent missing move.

The observer's view was narrower on the phone too. People beside the player often saw the device's back or an oblique angle, so they talked more about the eventual result than about individual reveals. That was a different social experience from the laptop, even though the underlying card actions were unchanged. [Pointer and touch](../interface/pointer-and-touch.md) and [large board rendering](../visuals/large-board-rendering.md) cover the relevant existing behavior.

## The mismatch pause helped memory and confused tapping

Several exchanges centered on a miss. One participant used the visible interval to repeat both face descriptions aloud. Another tapped quickly again and interpreted the lack of a new reveal as a lost input. The two reactions came from different expectations about whether the turn had finished.

It was useful in the discussion to replay the participant's explanation in ordinary language: “I was still looking at those two” versus “I thought I could choose the next one.” Both describe a reading of the same moment. Neither requires a different deck or a new scoring mechanism to explain it.

## Spectators remembered more than the current player expected

People who watched closely often remembered a location that the player had forgotten. Sometimes that produced a laugh; sometimes it produced an unsolicited hint. When the device moved out of view, conversation changed from specific positions to general encouragement. The physical setting strongly influenced how much information was shared.

This is relevant to the feel of local competition. The current application has no way to know who watched the screen or who spoke during a turn. No screen arrangement can make that social history part of the board code. The notes identify a design tension.

A future research session could explore how different groups feel about spectating, but that is a research question rather than a committed feature. The existing observations support only the narrower conclusion that sharing a device also shares attention in ways that vary with posture, distance and familiarity.

## Evidence retained from the discussion

These sessions identified misunderstandings during local play. Shape-only memory, keyboard travel, device adjustment and the visible mismatch interval each explain a different kind of report. The observations are useful starting points for further sessions.

A board code can anchor an arrangement, a snapshot can anchor progress and a replay can anchor actions. The observer's account adds the human context those artifacts omit. [Competition deals](competition-deals.md), [browser test guide](../quality/browser-test-guide.md) and [acceptance](../quality/acceptance.md) explain the technical evidence.

format.definition:
start: pragma_source | plain_source
pragma_source: PRAGMA_LINE NEWLINE SOURCE
plain_source: SOURCE

PRAGMA_LINE: /[ \t]*\/\/ @exec:[^\r\n]*/
NEWLINE: /\r?\n/
SOURCE: /[\s\S]+/

tools.name: wait
tools.description:
Waits on a yielded `exec` cell and returns new output or completion.
- Use `wait` only after `exec` returns `Script running with cell ID ...`.
- `cell_id` identifies the running `exec` cell to resume.
- `yield_time_ms` controls how long to wait for more output before yielding again. Defaults to 10000 ms.
- `max_tokens` limits how much new output this wait call returns. Defaults to 10000 tokens.
- `terminate: true` stops the running cell; false or omitted waits for output.
- `wait` returns only the new output since the last yield, or the final completion or termination result for that cell.
- If the cell is still running, `wait` may yield again with the same `cell_id`.
- If the cell has already finished, `wait` returns the completed result and closes the cell.

cell_id.description: Identifier of the running exec cell.

max_tokens.description: Output token budget for this wait call. Defaults to 10000 tokens.

terminate.description: True stops the running exec cell; false or omitted waits for output.

yield_time_ms.description: Wait before yielding more output. Defaults to 10000 ms.

tools.name: request_user_input
tools.description: Request user input for one to three short questions and wait for the response. This tool is only available in Plan mode.

questions.description: Questions to show the user. Prefer 1 and do not exceed 3

header.description: Short header label shown in the UI (12 or fewer chars).

options.description: Provide 2-3 mutually exclusive choices. Put the recommended option first and suffix its label with "(Recommended)". Do not include an "Other" option in this list; the client will add a free-form "Other" option automatically.

description.description: One short sentence explaining impact/tradeoff if selected.

question.description: Single-sentence prompt shown to the user.

tools.name: request_user_input_async
tools.description: Ask the user one or more questions during ongoing work. Use this tool only to request missing information, preferences, constraints, clarification, or approval. The tool returns immediately without ending the turn or waiting for a reply; any reply arrives asynchronously as a new user message. Keep questions concise, self-contained, and easy to understand, using a level of detail appropriate to the user and task. The UI always allows a free-text answer, including when suggested options are provided. A preselected option is not submitted automatically.

questions.description: One or more self-contained questions to present together, in display order.

options.description: Suggested answers, in display order. Put the recommended answer first; the first option is preselected by default. The user can select one option or enter a free-text answer. Do not include an Other option or a free-text placeholder; the UI provides free-text input automatically. Omit options for a free-text-only question.

title.description: The complete question shown to the user, including any context needed to answer it.

tools.name: clock

tools.name: sleep
tools.description: Pause execution for a specified duration. The sleep ends early when new input arrives for the active turn. Returns the elapsed wall-clock time.

duration_ms.description: How long to sleep in milliseconds. Must be between 1 and 43200000.

tools.name: followup_task
tools.description: Send a follow-up task to an existing non-root target agent and trigger a turn if it is idle. If the target is already running, deliver the task promptly at message boundaries while sampling, or after the pending tool call completes.

message.description: Message text to send to the target agent.

target.description: Agent id or canonical task name to send a follow-up task to (from spawn_agent).

tools.description: Interrupt an agent's current turn, if any, and return its previous status. The agent remains available for messages and follow-up tasks.

target.description: Agent id or canonical task name to interrupt (from spawn_agent).
