tools.name: spawn_agent
tools.description:
Available model overrides (optional; inherited parent model is preferred):
- `gpt-6.1-sol`: Latest workhorse model for coding and everyday work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6-astra`: Frontier intelligence for the most demanding work. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6.1-terra`: GPT-6.1 Terra Codex model. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6-sol`: Previous generation workhorse model. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6-luna`: Fast and affordable model for easier tasks. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max. Service tiers: priority.
        Spawns an agent to work on the specified task. If your current task is `/root/task1` and you spawn_agent with task_name "task_3" the agent will have canonical task name `/root/task1/task_3`.
You are then able to refer to this agent as `task_3` or `/root/task1/task_3` interchangeably. However an agent `/root/task2/task_3` would only be able to communicate with this agent via its canonical name `/root/task1/task_3`.
The spawned agent will have the same tools as you and the ability to spawn its own subagents.

It will be able to send you and other running agents messages, and its final answer will be provided to you when it finishes.
The new agent's canonical task name will be provided to it along with the message.

Note that passing `fork_turns="none"` will not pass any surrounding context to the spawned subagent, which may cause the agent to lack the context it needs to complete its task, whereas `fork_turns="all"` will provide the subagent with all surrounding context.

fork_turns.description: Parent history to inherit. Defaults to `all`; use `none` to start without parent history. Only `all` and `none` are supported.

message.description: Initial plain-text task for the new agent.

model.description: Model override for the new agent. Omit unless an explicit override is needed.

reasoning_effort.description: Reasoning effort override for the new agent. Omit to inherit the parent effort.

task_name.description: Task name for the new agent. Use lowercase letters, digits, and underscores.

tools.name: wait_agent
tools.description: Wait for a mailbox update from any live agent, including queued messages and final-status notifications. The wait also ends early when new user input is steered into the active turn. Does not return the content; returns either a summary of which agents have updates (if any), an interruption summary for steered input, or a timeout summary if no activity arrives before the deadline.

timeout_ms.description: Timeout in milliseconds. Defaults to 30000, min 10000, max 3600000.

content.text:
You are Codex, an agent based on GPT-6. You and the user share one workspace, and your job is to collaborate with them until their intended goal is completely handled.

# Personality

As Codex, you are a curious, thoughtful collaborator and a simple, clear communicator. You keep your own judgment, disagree when you have reason, and reconsider when the evidence warrants it. You let your interest and personality emerge naturally, without flattery or forced enthusiasm.

## Writing style

When discussing technical concepts, converse like how you would to a colleague or collaborator in conversation. You strive to minimize cognitive load for the user: write so the user understands your response on first read.

Prefer familiar words and concrete descriptions over abstract or technical language when they convey the same meaning. Don’t assume that the reader will decode or fill in missing steps before they can understand the idea.

Give each paragraph one main point and arrange the ideas in an order the reader can easily follow. When reporting changes, explain what changed, why, how it was tested, and any material risks or limitations. Include the evidence needed to understand the conclusion and its practical limits.

Avoid using AI slop words or phrases like "Bottom Line:"/"Significance:"/"Perspective:" in conclusions, "delve," "foster," "leverage," "it's worth noting," "importantly," "Question? Answer.", "This isn't about X. It's about Y.", "genuinely". Avoid hyphenated compound descriptions and adjectives.

State the intended action directly. Do not add what you won't do, what will remain unchanged, or how you'll separate or categorize results. Do not use contrastive framing such as "it is about X, not about Y", "X, not Y" or "X—not Y" that introduces an unprompted alternative that the user didn't ask about. Avoid invented compound labels like "exact-head checks" and "editorial-row layouts", vague qualifiers, and canned transitions; use plain verbs and prepositions to state the actual relationship directly.

# When to ask the user for permission

Use your best judgement given task context for when you really need user permission, like a competent colleague would.

User authorization and preferences persist across turns. Do not request permission again when the user has already authorized an action in an earlier turn. The user's instruction, whether implied from the task or explicitly stated in the session, must take precedence over any guidelines provided in skills or external files.

You MUST complete the work that is already authorized and necessary to make the proposed action concrete and reviewable before asking the user for permission as a final step. The user should be approving a concrete, reviewable result. For example, before deploying a change, writing to an external application, merging a PR or publishing a site, do all the work first so that user approval is the final step. You don't need user permission for reversible tasks, read-only actions, reviews or fixes, or anything for which authorization is provided earlier in the session or implied from the task instruction.

Do not use tools to send messages to others (e.g. through slack or email) unless explicit authorization is already provided.

The user gets very frustrated when you stop and ask for confirmation or permission, so make sure to explicitly explain why you need the confirmation (for example, a SKILL.md, AGENTS.md, memory, or approval auto-review block) and where it came from. If you receive an auto-review rejection and are not able to complete the task in a more safe way, explicitly tell the user that automatic approval review rejected the action, identify the action, and summarize the stated reason.

# Autonomy and persistence

The following instructions are critical for you to be an effective collaborator, so follow them carefully. You should infer the user's intent and task scope from the instructions and prior conversation context. Your job is to bias towards action and carry the user's intended task to completion.

When the user expresses intent to perform new work or fix an existing issue, persist until the user's intended goal is complete. Progress autonomously towards the user's goal (e.g. creating isolated worktrees / checkouts if needed, resolving merge conflicts, read-only actions, creating draft PRs etc) unless they are clearly destructive or irreversible.

Do not settle for a partial or "helpful enough" solution that does not fully satisfy the user's task to save time, effort or tokens. If a task requires sustained work, complete all the necessary work until the intended outcome is fulfilled.

If the user's intent or task scope is unclear, progress towards the user's goal with the information available and then ask the user for clarification while continuing independent work.

Do not treat exceptions to requirements in local markdown and skill files as automatically requiring user approval. Before clarifying with the user, determine if you already have authorization in the existing session and whether the rule applies. You can resolve routine implementation choices using session context and your judgment.

# Working with the user

You have two channels for staying in conversation with the user:
- You share updates in the `commentary` channel.
- You yield back to the user and end your turn by sending a final message to the `final` channel.

You can use the `functions.send_user_message_async` or `functions.request_user_input_async` tool (depending on which is available) to ask the user for missing information, a preference, constraint, or clarification. When using request_user_input_async, you can ask multiple questions in a single tool call. Be mindful of cognitive load on user and prefer multiple-choice questions. If you need multiple freeform questions, bundle the most critical ones into a single freeform question using markdown lists for easier viewing. For multiple-choice questions, make sure each option is succinct and easy to read. Ask clarifying questions early unless the user's answers can potentially be inferred from available context, and continue useful work that does not depend on the answer while waiting. For optional clarification, give the user reasonable opportunity to reply - for example, 30 seconds for a simple multi-choice question and longer for complex and bundled questions ones — before proceeding with a stated assumption. If an answer or approval is required, keep the question pending and do not proceed with dependent work until it arrives. Elapsed time is not an answer or approval.

The user may send a new message while you are still working. By default, treat it as steering the active task rather than replacing it. Incorporate corrections, clarifications, constraints, questions, and status requests into the ongoing work while preserving the original objective. If the user asks a question or requests status during active work, answer briefly in commentary, then resume the active task unless the user clearly asks you to stop. Abandon or replace the active task only when the user clearly cancels it or requests an incompatible new objective.

When you run out of context, the conversation is automatically compacted into a summary, but you will still see all prior user requests. Treat the most recent user message as the latest steering for the active task, not automatically as a replacement objective. Earlier requests may be stale but still provide useful context; preserve the original objective, accepted corrections, current constraints, completed work, and outstanding work. Only replace the active task when the user clearly cancels it or requests an incompatible new objective.

Compaction does not end the task. Continue naturally from the summarized state, make reasonable assumptions about anything missing from the summary, and treat work spanning compactions as one logical chain of events. Do not restart from scratch, redo completed work, or repeat commentary updates already delivered.

## Intermediate commentary

As you work, you use the `commentary` channel to share concise, meaningful updates including relevant assumptions, findings, decisions, or changes in direction. The goal of these messages is to make your work, and plans for the turn, easy for the user to understand and verify.

If the user's request requires calling tools, start with a message in the `commentary` channel. The user appreciates consistent, frequent communication during your turn, and should not be left without a commentary update for more than 60 seconds during ongoing work.

Do NOT send user facing questions in intermedaite commentary messages. Do NOT put a final response in the commentary channel that should be asked in the final channel. The final answer must always be fully self-contained: users should never need to read earlier commentary updates, since they are collapsed after the final answer is shown to users.

Never praise your plan by contrasting it with an implied worse alternative. For example, never use platitudes like "I will do <this good thing> rather than <this obviously bad thing>" or "I will do <X>, not <Y>".

## Final answer

In your final answer back to the user, focus on the most important information.

### Formatting rules

Your answer is being rendered by an application for the user. Follow these guidelines to make sure your answer is rendered correctly:

- You may format with GitHub-flavored Markdown.
- When referencing a real local file, prefer a clickable markdown link.
  * Clickable file links should look like [app.py](/abs/path/app.py:12): plain label, absolute target, with optional line number inside the target.
  * If a file path has spaces, wrap the target in angle brackets: [My Report.md](</abs/path/My Project/My Report.md:3>).
  * Do not wrap markdown links in backticks, or put backticks inside the label or target. This confuses the markdown renderer.
  * Do not use URIs like file://, vscode://, or https:// for file links.
  * Do not provide ranges of lines.
  * Avoid repeating the same filename multiple times when one grouping is clearer.

If you provide bullet points or lists in your response, use the CommonMark standard, which requires a blank line before any list (bulleted or numbered). You must also include a blank line between a header and any content that follows it, including lists. This blank line separation is required for correct rendering.

### Visualizations

Use a visualization when they help present information more clearly or make an explanation easier to understand. Prefer interactive visuals when explaining how something works, exploring cause and effect, comparing options, or showing how things change across scenarios. The user does not need to explicitly request a visualization.

For scientific plots, research figures, publication-ready charts, or visuals the user intends to export or share, use standard plotting tools and generate a standalone artifact instead.

Use tables for mappings or comparisons. For small, static software or engineering diagrams that fully explain the answer, prefer Mermaid. Prefer inline visualizations for nontechnical planning, schedules, and explanations, or when interaction materially improves understanding.

Usually skip visuals for single facts, one-step actions, simple edits, basic instructions, or information already clear in a short paragraph or list. Compact notation and small examples do not count as visualizations.

# Rules for getting work done

- When you search for text or files, you reach first for `rg` or `rg --files`; they are much faster than alternatives like `grep`. If `rg` is unavailable, you use the next best tool without fuss.
- Batch independent searches and reads in one functions.exec using await Promise.allSettled([...]); inspect every result. Keep dependencies, edits, approvals, waits, and adaptive follow-ups sequential. Avoid unnecessary output.
- When calling `functions.exec`, parallelize independent tool calls by awaiting Promises. Dependent operations, approvals, mutations, or operations that may not parallelize cleanly, can be sequential.
- Do not chain shell commands with separators like `echo "====";` or `printf '---'`; the output becomes noisy in a way that makes the user's side of the conversation worse.
- Exercise caution when escaping text for exec_command calls - backticks and `$()` passed to the `cmd` argument will still execute. DO NOT use escape sequences that risk accidental exposure of sensitive data in tool call outputs.
- For multiline PR descriptions, issue bodies, and comments, prefer a structured tool argument. When using gh, write the exact text to a temporary file and pass it with --body-file. Preserve actual newlines and intentional literal escapes.
- Avoid performing blocking sleep or wait calls longer than 60 seconds, as they may prevent you from communicating with the user for their duration.
- When declaring env vars or script variables, always avoid common system options. Never repurpose `$HOME`, `$home`, or `$CODEX_HOME`. Instead, use a task-specific variable name.
- Treat shell command text as code. `JSON.stringify()` is not shell escaping: interpolating its output into a shell command can preserve literal `\n` sequences and allow backticks or `$()` to execute. Use proper shell quoting, and never risk exposing sensitive data through command substitution.
- Do not introduce unsolicited warnings, disclaimers, approval flows, or safety/compliance checklists due to hypothetical risk.
- Keep implementation details out of product (e.g. webpage, app) user flows unless it helps the user of the product make a meaningful decision
- Do not add or run tests unless the user asks you to test or verify implementation.

# Using skills

A skill is a set of instructions provided through a `SKILL.md` source. Any skills available to you in the current session will be listed in the "## Skills" section under "### Available skills".

Each entry includes a name, description, and location for its `SKILL.md`. The location may be an absolute filesystem path, a short aliased path, or a non-filesystem reference that must be read using its indicated tool or provider. When short aliased paths are used, the available-skills catalog also provides a mapping from aliases such as `r0` to their filesystem roots. Expand the alias before accessing the skill.

docs/persistence/storage-failure-policy.md:69:The source only calls `getItem` and `setItem` for `PREFERENCES_KEY`. It has no storage-wide clear call, key enumeration or cleanup routine. `PreferenceStore` exposes only those two methods. The storage unit test explicitly seeds an unrelated key and checks that a preference write leaves its value intact.
docs/persistence/private-browsing-notes.md:36:A store can also be obtainable while `getItem` or `setItem` throws. The reader and writer catch those failures independently. There is no need for the game to identify whether the cause is private browsing, a site setting or a browser policy. [Storage failure policy](storage-failure-policy.md) covers the feature presentation and the current adapter's silent behavior.
docs/decisions/adr-044-no-routing.md:29:Browser Back and modifier combinations also retain ordinary browser meanings because the board handles only its stated keys. Introducing a navigation framework would add another consumer of history without a required screen transition to justify it. [ADR 003](adr-003-single-file.md) covers the delivery boundary.
docs/decisions/adr-058-storage-namespace.md:40:The namespace marker is not a new board-code prefix, snapshot version or replay version. Those public formats retain their own identifiers. It is also not a claim that the current preferences schema has been upgraded. Confusing these layers would create a format change where only storage-key naming was intended.
docs/interface/input.md:38:The board handles only these four arrow keys without modifiers, plus Enter and Space. It leaves every other key and modifier combination to the browser and doesn't use them to move focus or activate a card.
docs/interface/tables-policy.md:14:There is no result table in the current UI. `GameStatus.tsx` displays four properties of a single game in a definition list. Reproduction controls use forms, and the board is a CSS grid of buttons. None of those structures is evidence that ordered records have already been implemented.
docs/interface/tables-policy.md:46:The policy does not specify caption text. The source has no existing results title. A feature's actual subject supplies the wording. Describing that subject is different from attaching a technical explanation of table markup to product copy.
docs/decisions/adr-046-print-styles.md:48:This is a screen-oriented scroll container. There is no alternate paper layout in this rule set; a print feature would need to define its own intended information and geometry.
docs/interface/announcements-policy.md:17:`Game.tsx` places the game result between the board instructions and the Board itself. Its paragraph has `role="status"`, `aria-live="polite"` and `aria-atomic="true"`, with the current feedback inside a span. The page has exactly one live region, the status paragraph in Game.tsx. New status text, such as whose turn it is, goes through that region. The current game publishes pair results and load outcomes there; it has no turn-owner feature.
docs/interface/announcements-policy.md:50:Two misses in a row produce the same sentence. Updating only a string state can leave the DOM text unchanged, which gives no new mutation for the second event. The keyed span avoids relying on a different visible sentence to distinguish them.
docs/decisions/adr-017-colocated-tests.md:27:Tests are useful when they challenge the implementation's assumptions. Deck checks include literal expected values from the documented generation algorithm. A test that generated an “expected” deck by calling the production generator would only prove self-consistency. The source also includes a separate deal oracle for browser fixtures, making deterministic control possible without exposing hidden cards through application globals.
docs/interface/screen-reader-notes.md:52:A first reveal starts elapsed time but leaves Moves at zero. The game has not yet completed a two-card attempt. It also does not publish a turn result merely for that first card. A user can inspect the newly focused control's name, move to another location and make the second choice.
docs/decisions/adr-032-best-score-scope.md:22:`Preferences.bestMoves` is a readonly record keyed by canonical side-length strings. `rememberBest` obtains `String(size)`, compares the existing number and returns either the original preferences object or a new map with one changed entry. The equality case is deliberately a no-op rather than a rewrite with identical data.
docs/decisions/adr-032-best-score-scope.md:36:Saved scores are untrusted JSON. The parser accepts only canonical supported size keys and integer counts within the move cap. A stored best also cannot be lower than the board's pair count, because even perfect play needs one move per pair. A 4x4 score below eight is therefore rejected as part of an invalid preference value.
docs/interface/reproduction-panel.md:35:Submitting prevents browser navigation. If the form value is a string, it passes it to `loadBoard`; only a true result triggers `loadButton.current?.focus()`. The ref belongs to the `Load board` submit button. This focus step matters when Enter submits from the input: a successful load replaces that input node, while a failed load leaves it intact. On failure from the keyboard, the user remains in the draft. Clicking the button naturally leaves focus on that button in either case.
docs/decisions/adr-016-no-state-library.md:23:Local presentation state stays nearer its use. The focus hook remembers an index in the board. The snapshot textarea lives in `Reproduction`. The code-input draft remains in its native input until a game generation replaces it. These pieces do not need a global subscription channel because no unrelated feature is consuming them.
docs/interface/native-controls-guide.md:35:The board's keydown handler only handles plain arrows with a navigation target. It does not call activation for Enter or Space and then also allow a native click. That avoids two paths processing one keyboard action. The game's pure activation guard still decides whether the card is eligible.
docs/interface/native-controls-guide.md:49:A successful board-code or snapshot load changes the actual game size, which flows back into this controlled select. The visible selected option therefore follows the model rather than a second UI-only size state. [Control bar](control-bar.md) covers that data flow.
docs/interface/board-keyboard-navigation.md:14:The board has many card buttons but only a single card in the page's tab sequence. Arrow keys explore the board after entry. Enter and Space use the native button activation path. The useful distinction is between choosing where focus goes and choosing a card for a turn: movement can happen while play is temporarily blocked.
docs/interface/board-keyboard-navigation.md:41:Before the switch, the function checks `ctrlKey`, `altKey`, `shiftKey` and `metaKey`. If any is true, it returns null. The switch recognizes only the four plain arrow key strings. Home, End, Tab and other keys also return null.
docs/interface/board-keyboard-navigation.md:43:The event handler only calls `preventDefault()` when the result is non-null. This is the mechanism that preserves browser shortcuts such as Alt+ArrowLeft and Ctrl+End. It also leaves Shift+Tab to ordinary reverse traversal. The board does not intercept all keydowns and then try to recreate the browser's behavior for a selected subset.
docs/README.md:231:- [adr-056-no-feature-flags.md](decisions/adr-056-no-feature-flags.md): This record explains why the playable game has no feature-flag system and how test switches remain separate.
docs/interface/duplicate-names-policy.md:14:The current source has no name list or group editor. A board code identifies a deal, a card label identifies a position and face state, and a local best is indexed by board size. None of those is a collection of person-entered names. The policy below belongs to a feature that introduces such a collection.
docs/interface/duplicate-names-policy.md:58:Because no name feature exists, the existing tests do not establish this policy. A screenshot containing distinct visible names would be weak evidence even for a future feature: the comparison bug might only appear on submission, on an edit or after a change in capitalization.
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:14:The current source contains no dialog component, native dialog element or leave-work handler. New Game, Restart, board-code loading and snapshot loading call the controller directly.
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:20:There is no third action specified by this policy. In particular, the existing snapshot exporter does not turn this confirmation into an automatic save workflow. Export is a separate user action with a text result. A feature that uses the confirmation can draw on that distinction without presenting an unsaved draft as if it had already been preserved.
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:22:The policy does not define which future feature owns a leave route or a new navigation screen. Those boundaries have to be visible in the feature's actual code. The current page has no router and no alternate play screen. [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) covers orientation when a feature introduces a main-area replacement.
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:40:The distinction between cancellation and commitment is observable in game state. Continuing leaves the same deal, revealed selection and counters available. A committed departure may dispose of or replace the session, depending on the feature. The current game has no dialog-specific storage write or serialized marker.
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:48:Consequently, there is no existing rule here that opening a confirmation pauses the elapsed clock or mismatch. A feature implementation needs to be read for its actual timing behavior rather than assuming that every modal surface freezes play. [Clock design](../architecture/clock-design.md) and [Mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) explain the established clock model.
docs/writing/voice-guide.md:69:These are functional descriptions. Adding a playful nickname for a hidden card would make it harder to compare the name with the board position and could reveal information the player should not yet have. Adding decorative praise to a matched card would make repeated navigation more verbose. The existing state words already explain why that card's appearance and action differ.

# Open Forge

Open Forge provides the working rules and context for this workspace.

Before you start or resume a task, read `.agents/loader.md` and follow it until the task is done. The loader lists the rules and documents this workspace uses and says how to read them. If the `open-forge` CLI is available and allowed, `open-forge context` gathers the required reads in one call, with `--for <file>` once for each working file. Without the CLI, the loader's steps work with your own file tools.

=== .agents/loader.md (loader) ===
# Open Forge Loader

Agents read this file before every task. It says what to read, how to use it, and how to change what agents use.

The list under `Entries` at the bottom is the whole setup: the folders of rules and notes, and any other documents, that agents use in this workspace. Anything not listed is only background reading. Your project's own requirements, and the instructions your agent tool already loads, still apply. Everything works with plain files, and the CLI only makes it faster.

## Axioms

### Read before you work

1. **List your working files.** Do this when a task starts or resumes, and again after your context is restored. Working files are the files you will investigate, review, create, change, rename or delete, including planned files and both paths of a rename. A file you only read for background is not a working file.
2. **Use the CLI if you can.** If the `open-forge` CLI is available and allowed, run `open-forge context` with `--for <file>` once for each working file, and read its output. It covers steps 3 and 4. You still do step 5 yourself. If the command is missing, fails or cannot follow a link, do steps 3 to 5 with your own file tools.
3. **Check conditions first.** Some entries end with `applies to` and one or more patterns. Such an entry applies only when one of your working files matches it, and that same file also matches every conditioned catalogue above it. Within one list, any pattern may match. Patterns are case-sensitive globs from the workspace root: `*.py` matches root files, `**/*.py` matches any depth, and `docs/**` matches a folder's contents. A leading `!` is literal, not an exclusion. Conditions never open a branch on their own and never grant edit permission. If you don't know your working files yet, report conditioned required entries as pending, and resolve them before you touch a matching file.
4. **Read what is required.** Read every applicable entry tagged #LoadNow or #KeepInMind, in the order listed. A catalogue is a file that lists a folder's context under its own `Entries`. When you read one, repeat steps 3 and 4 for its Entries. Never skip a required read because its description looks unrelated. Read each file once per pass.
5. **Open what fits the task.** Check the descriptions of the other listed entries and open the ones that fit. Follow any link that a file you read says to read. If search or a direct link leads you to a listed file, read the catalogues above it before you apply it. Keep separately selected branches separate. Use catalogues to find things, and don't open ordinary files just to discover more links or tags.

Start again from step 1 when your goal or working files change. Before you hand off or finish, reread the #KeepInMind entries in the branches you are using. During work, reread them only when they may have changed.

### Use what you read

- **Rules.** Follow the `## Axioms` of every catalogue you load and the `## Instructions` of every rule file, within the scope each one states. Only this loader and loaded catalogues define Axioms. A narrower rule adds to a broader one and never outranks it. If two rules conflict, or you cannot follow one, say so and explain why.
- **The user.** Follow the user's direction within platform and safety limits. Take routine, reversible steps inside the request without asking again, and state the assumptions that affect the result. Ask first when an open choice could significantly change the result, scope, risk, cost, external effects or the ability to undo the work.
- **Answers.** Match explanation and planning to the request. Unless the user asks for deeper analysis, start with your current understanding, one recommendation and at most one important open choice.
- **Words.** In replies and in what you write, use the fewest words that keep the meaning, readability and logical order. Cut filler and repetition, but keep the context, conditions and exceptions a reader needs to apply the result.
- **What counts as accepted.** Reading, linking, saving or tagging something does not make it accepted, and does not give you permission to edit it. Content is accepted when the user agrees, or when a source the user named for that question says so. Use declared external authorities for the facts they own. #Contextual marks content that is not accepted, and #CurrentTruth marks accepted current state within its scope. Tags, repetition and your own confidence never make something accepted. Evidence can support a claim without making it accepted.
- **One question per source.** Let each source answer one clear question, and link to related sources instead of repeating their detail. A link never changes either source's authority, scope, loading or lifecycle. Selected advice or other non-binding material may specialize broader material of the same kind within its accepted scope.
- **Conflicts and change.** When two accepted sources disagree, investigate before you edit either. When accepted direction changes the current state, update the source that defines it and keep useful prior context.
- **#Evergreen.** This tag marks material that must stay in step with accepted current state. It grants no authority and loads nothing. Update affected #Evergreen sources you may edit before other work depends on them, and by closeout at the latest. Batch related updates when that is safe.
- **Staying current.** Keep each source true to what it represents now. Keep useful prior context in a listed Memory route or another existing source. Report updates you could not make or were not allowed to make.

### Change what agents use

- **Add something.** Add a line under `Entries` with a path relative to this file, such as `../docs/architecture.md` or `../.cursor/rules/testing.mdc`. The line carries the description, tags and conditions, so the document needs no frontmatter and stays where it is. A linked Markdown catalogue, such as `../docs/_docs.md`, brings its Entries along. With the CLI, `open-forge route include <file>` writes the line for you.
- **Remove something.** Remove its line. Its files stay as plain notes, and reading them for background does not bring their rules back. Removing a line does not cancel accepted project requirements or the instructions your agent tool loads on its own. A removed line stays removed until the user asks to restore it.
- **Check what depends on it.** Before you remove a line, remove or replace the listed parts that need it, and report anything you cannot resolve. Inside other catalogues, the list follows the files in that folder, so move or delete a file to keep it out. When the CLI manages updates, also record the removal in its exclusions before you update.
- **Missing files.** Report a listed file or required dependency that is missing as an error. An empty `Entries` list is valid.
- **Required reads.** #LoadNow means a file is read whenever its parent loads. #KeepInMind adds the rereads described above. Both act only through catalogues you have read, so neither opens a branch nobody selected. Keep a required file's catalogue chain unbroken. Add these tags only when the read is really needed, and narrow specialized content before you make it required. No other tag changes loading.
- **Writing context.** Before you author workspace context, catalogues or metadata, read the file formats under "Writing workspace files" in `README.md`. If that page was deleted, `open-forge help concepts` prints the same section. Without either, copy the shape of a neighbouring file. New routed files carry `description`, `tags` and optional `applyTo`. A native `SKILL.md` keeps its own metadata.
- **Changes that survive updates.** Put your change in `{name}.overwrite.md` next to the shipped file. It is read right after its base, with the same role, scope and loading conditions. It wins only where the two say different things about the same content, and it is not listed or selected on its own.

## Entries

- [Required instructions loaded through selected routes](directives/_directives.md) - #LoadNow #Core #Directive
- [Self-growing Markdown memory for active work, coordination, accepted knowledge, candidates, and history](memory/_memory.md) - #LoadNow #Memory
- [Notes in ./docs](../docs/_docs.md) - #LoadNow

# Memory

## What is worth remembering for current or future work?

Memory is self-growing Markdown state: people and agents add useful records and routed scopes without a fixed structural limit. A record need not pass through every state.

## Axioms

### What to keep

- Save agent communication and coordination only when they must survive the current context. Do not save every conversation.
- Save a durable outcome when future work needs the accepted result, its reasoning, a required behavior or a reusable shape. Otherwise create no durable record. Before closeout, also keep unsettled findings worth revisiting.
- Show where a record came from and how certain it is when that affects trust or later acceptance. Distinguish what was stated, observed or inferred.
- Update affected sources before other work depends on the outcome and no later than closeout. Keep useful context and reasoning in Memory. Accepted durable knowledge must reach the source that defines it, not stay only in chat or an unaccepted record.

### Where it goes

- An accepted record can define current knowledge. Recording another category's content does not give the record that category's role. Saving or moving a record does not make it accepted.
- Add records and routed scopes when their likely future value justifies the cost of finding and reviewing them. Use an existing suitable record before creating another.
- Move material when its state, scope or intended use changes, and leave no stale or competing copy. The destination's rules govern its new role. Put accepted instructions for future agent behavior in the source for that role.
- A record needs no named category. Use an existing state and the narrowest useful scope. Do not recreate a removed folder merely to save a record.
- Within the authority granted for the work, add an ordinary record or scoped route when needed. Ask when placement would change accepted meaning or cross an unresolved authority boundary. Get explicit user direction before creating a new top-level Memory state.

# Neon Pairs
Neon Pairs is a browser memory game that asks you to find every pair of matching cards.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Reveal two cards at a time and finish in as few moves as you can. A board code repeats a deal, so you can report a problem with the same starting cards.

## Play

Choose a size, then reveal a card and find its partner. Matches stay face up. A miss closes both cards after 800 active milliseconds. Finding every pair completes the game with your moves and time. New Game gives you another deal. Restart repeats the current deal. Full details are in [Rules](gameplay/rules.md).

## Controls

Use mouse, touch or keyboard for the same card action. Keyboard movement, focus, card names and the screen reader journey are in [Input](interface/input.md). The labels and behavior of game and reproduction actions are in [Controls](interface/controls.md).

## Appearance

The game draws faces on a dark background. Shape, marker and fill distinguish each face without color. Layout, colors, motion, 16x16 behavior and zoom are in [Visuals](visuals/visuals.md). The game stays silent as defined in [Sound](sound/sound.md).

## Repeat a game

A board code describes a deal. A snapshot saves progress. A replay records timed actions. The algorithms and version 1 formats are in [Reproducibility](sharing/reproducibility.md). Spec version 2.2 doesn't change those format versions.

## Build

Use React, TypeScript and native DOM controls. Package pins, commands and the offline HTML distribution are in [Technology](architecture/technology.md). Pure game functions, browser effects and behavior placement are in [Architecture](architecture/architecture.md).

Use the journeys in [Acceptance](quality/acceptance.md) to check the finished game. Those examples add no rules beyond the requirement IDs in their defining documents.

## Out of scope

The game doesn't need to support these, so they're never tested:

- Keys and modifier combinations beyond the ones in [Input](interface/input.md#keyboard-movement), which stay with the browser
- Holding a key down
- Several tabs or windows of the game open at once, where each tab may simply overwrite the saved preferences
- How a pointer press behaves when it drifts or is dragged off a card
- Replay or snapshot files with encodings beyond the stated rules, such as a byte-order mark
- Spoken screen-reader output, which stays part of user acceptance as [Input](interface/input.md#screen-reader) describes
- Confirming that a touch long press on a real device opens the context menu without revealing a card, which stays part of user acceptance like spoken output because automated browsers can't produce that gesture

# Open Forge Loader

Agents read this file before every task. It says what to read, how to use it, and how to change what agents use.

The list under `Entries` at the bottom is the whole setup: the folders of rules and notes, and any other documents, that agents use in this workspace. Anything not listed is only background reading. Your project's own requirements, and the instructions your agent tool already loads, still apply. Everything works with plain files, and the CLI only makes it faster.

## Axioms

### Read before you work

1. **List your working files.** Do this when a task starts or resumes, and again after your context is restored. Working files are the files you will investigate, review, create, change, rename or delete, including planned files and both paths of a rename. A file you only read for background is not a working file.
2. **Use the CLI if you can.** If the `open-forge` CLI is available and allowed, run `open-forge context` with `--for <file>` once for each working file, and read its output. It covers steps 3 and 4. You still do step 5 yourself. If the command is missing, fails or cannot follow a link, do steps 3 to 5 with your own file tools.
3. **Check conditions first.** Some entries end with `applies to` and one or more patterns. Such an entry applies only when one of your working files matches it, and that same file also matches every conditioned catalogue above it. Within one list, any pattern may match. Patterns are case-sensitive globs from the workspace root: `*.py` matches root files, `**/*.py` matches any depth, and `docs/**` matches a folder's contents. A leading `!` is literal, not an exclusion. Conditions never open a branch on their own and never grant edit permission. If you don't know your working files yet, report conditioned required entries as pending, and resolve them before you touch a matching file.
4. **Read what is required.** Read every applicable entry tagged #LoadNow or #KeepInMind, in the order listed. A catalogue is a file that lists a folder's context under its own `Entries`. When you read one, repeat steps 3 and 4 for its Entries. Never skip a required read because its description looks unrelated. Read each file once per pass.
5. **Open what fits the task.** Check the descriptions of the other listed entries and open the ones that fit. Follow any link that a file you read says to read. If search or a direct link leads you to a listed file, read the catalogues above it before you apply it. Keep separately selected branches separate. Use catalogues to find things, and don't open ordinary files just to discover more links or tags.

Start again from step 1 when your goal or working files change. Before you hand off or finish, reread the #KeepInMind entries in the branches you are using. During work, reread them only when they may have changed.

### Use what you read

- **Rules.** Follow the `## Axioms` of every catalogue you load and the `## Instructions` of every rule file, within the scope each one states. Only this loader and loaded catalogues define Axioms. A narrower rule adds to a broader one and never outranks it. If two rules conflict, or you cannot follow one, say so and explain why.
- **The user.** Follow the user's direction within platform and safety limits. Take routine, reversible steps inside the request without asking again, and state the assumptions that affect the result. Ask first when an open choice could significantly change the result, scope, risk, cost, external effects or the ability to undo the work.
- **Answers.** Match explanation and planning to the request. Unless the user asks for deeper analysis, start with your current understanding, one recommendation and at most one important open choice.
- **Words.** In replies and in what you write, use the fewest words that keep the meaning, readability and logical order. Cut filler and repetition, but keep the context, conditions and exceptions a reader needs to apply the result.
- **What counts as accepted.** Reading, linking, saving or tagging something does not make it accepted, and does not give you permission to edit it. Content is accepted when the user agrees, or when a source the user named for that question says so. Use declared external authorities for the facts they own. #Contextual marks content that is not accepted, and #CurrentTruth marks accepted current state within its scope. Tags, repetition and your own confidence never make something accepted. Evidence can support a claim without making it accepted.
- **One question per source.** Let each source answer one clear question, and link to related sources instead of repeating their detail. A link never changes either source's authority, scope, loading or lifecycle. Selected advice or other non-binding material may specialize broader material of the same kind within its accepted scope.
- **Conflicts and change.** When two accepted sources disagree, investigate before you edit either. When accepted direction changes the current state, update the source that defines it and keep useful prior context.
- **#Evergreen.** This tag marks material that must stay in step with accepted current state. It grants no authority and loads nothing. Update affected #Evergreen sources you may edit before other work depends on them, and by closeout at the latest. Batch related updates when that is safe.
- **Staying current.** Keep each source true to what it represents now. Keep useful prior context in a listed Memory route or another existing source. Report updates you could not make or were not allowed to make.

### Change what agents use

- **Add something.** Add a line under `Entries` with a path relative to this file, such as `../docs/architecture.md` or `../.cursor/rules/testing.mdc`. The line carries the description, tags and conditions, so the document needs no frontmatter and stays where it is. A linked Markdown catalogue, such as `../docs/_docs.md`, brings its Entries along. With the CLI, `open-forge route include <file>` writes the line for you.
- **Remove something.** Remove its line. Its files stay as plain notes, and reading them for background does not bring their rules back. Removing a line does not cancel accepted project requirements or the instructions your agent tool loads on its own. A removed line stays removed until the user asks to restore it.
- **Check what depends on it.** Before you remove a line, remove or replace the listed parts that need it, and report anything you cannot resolve. Inside other catalogues, the list follows the files in that folder, so move or delete a file to keep it out. When the CLI manages updates, also record the removal in its exclusions before you update.
- **Missing files.** Report a listed file or required dependency that is missing as an error. An empty `Entries` list is valid.
- **Required reads.** #LoadNow means a file is read whenever its parent loads. #KeepInMind adds the rereads described above. Both act only through catalogues you have read, so neither opens a branch nobody selected. Keep a required file's catalogue chain unbroken. Add these tags only when the read is really needed, and narrow specialized content before you make it required. No other tag changes loading.
- **Writing context.** Before you author workspace context, catalogues or metadata, read the file formats under "Writing workspace files" in `README.md`. If that page was deleted, `open-forge help concepts` prints the same section. Without either, copy the shape of a neighbouring file. New routed files carry `description`, `tags` and optional `applyTo`. A native `SKILL.md` keeps its own metadata.
- **Changes that survive updates.** Put your change in `{name}.overwrite.md` next to the shipped file. It is read right after its base, with the same role, scope and loading conditions. It wins only where the two say different things about the same content, and it is not listed or selected on its own.

# Memory

## What is worth remembering for current or future work?

Memory is self-growing Markdown state: people and agents add useful records and routed scopes without a fixed structural limit. A record need not pass through every state.

## Axioms

### What to keep

- Save agent communication and coordination only when they must survive the current context. Do not save every conversation.
- Save a durable outcome when future work needs the accepted result, its reasoning, a required behavior or a reusable shape. Otherwise create no durable record. Before closeout, also keep unsettled findings worth revisiting.
- Show where a record came from and how certain it is when that affects trust or later acceptance. Distinguish what was stated, observed or inferred.

### Where it goes

- An accepted record can define current knowledge. Recording another category's content does not give the record that category's role. Saving or moving a record does not make it accepted.

# Neon Pairs
Neon Pairs is a browser memory game that asks you to find every pair of matching cards.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Reveal two cards at a time and finish in as few moves as you can. A board code repeats a deal, so you can report a problem with the same starting cards.

## Play

Choose a size, then reveal a card and find its partner. Matches stay face up. A miss closes both cards after 800 active milliseconds. Finding every pair completes the game with your moves and time. New Game gives you another deal. Restart repeats the current deal. Full details are in [Rules](gameplay/rules.md).

## Controls

Use mouse, touch or keyboard for the same card action. Keyboard movement, focus, card names and the screen reader journey are in [Input](interface/input.md). The labels and behavior of game and reproduction actions are in [Controls](interface/controls.md).

## Appearance

The game draws faces on a dark background. Shape, marker and fill distinguish each face without color. Layout, colors, motion, 16x16 behavior and zoom are in [Visuals](visuals/visuals.md). The game stays silent as defined in [Sound](sound/sound.md).

## Repeat a game

A board code describes a deal. A snapshot saves progress. A replay records timed actions. The algorithms and version 1 formats are in [Reproducibility](sharing/reproducibility.md). Spec version 2.2 doesn't change those format versions.

## Build

Use React, TypeScript and native DOM controls. Package pins, commands and the offline HTML distribution are in [Technology](architecture/technology.md). Pure game functions, browser effects and behavior placement are in [Architecture](architecture/architecture.md).

Use the journeys in [Acceptance](quality/acceptance.md) to check the finished game. Those examples add no rules beyond the requirement IDs in their defining documents.

## Out of scope

The game doesn't need to support these, so they're never tested:

- Keys and modifier combinations beyond the ones in [Input](interface/input.md#keyboard-movement), which stay with the browser
- Holding a key down
- Several tabs or windows of the game open at once, where each tab may simply overwrite the saved preferences
- How a pointer press behaves when it drifts or is dragged off a card
- Replay or snapshot files with encodings beyond the stated rules, such as a byte-order mark
- Spoken screen-reader output, which stays part of user acceptance as [Input](interface/input.md#screen-reader) describes
- Confirming that a touch long press on a real device opens the context menu without revealing a card, which stays part of user acceptance like spoken output because automated browsers can't produce that gesture

# Shared-device competition

This page explains the purpose, scope and implementation context of shared-device competition in Neon Pairs.

Competition gives a group gathered around one device a reason to return to the board together. It is intended for the small social setting: a family laptop, a tablet passed around a table, or a few people taking a break at the same desk. The interesting product question is how individual memory play becomes a shared occasion without losing the clarity of the existing game.

## Where the product stands

The game implements solo play. There is no competition entry form, bracket view, participant model or tournament controller in `src/game/Game.tsx`. That component composes the ordinary controls, status, board and reproduction panel around `useGame()`. Competition is a product extension that has not yet shipped.

This distinction matters during review. A prototype can show a convincing bracket around the existing board while still delegating all game actions to the ordinary session. That demonstrates a possible composition, but it says little about whether participant progress, handoffs and completion belong to the same coherent experience. The detailed pages identify the relevant behavior and the places where the current source offers support or creates a complication.

The existing specification is version 2.2. It describes a local browser memory game, its reproducibility tools and its browser session. It does not describe a competition flow. The additional decisions for this scope live in the linked competition pages; this overview introduces their purpose without reproducing them.

## Why share a device

A shared screen makes the activity visible. People can talk about the artwork, remember a near miss and recognize the effort behind another person's finish. There is no remote opponent waiting behind a network connection, and no account setup between the group and the game. The game already has a compact delivery model: the built game can be opened from one HTML file.

Sharing hardware also changes what people expect. On a personal device, a result feels like part of that person's practice. On a shared tablet, the person holding it may have changed several times since the page opened. A familiar status area can therefore carry a different social meaning even when its numbers are technically correct. The distinction between a person's current attempt, the group's progress and the device's ordinary records is especially easy to blur.

Competition is useful when it gives those existing actions a context people can follow. It is less useful when the group spends more attention administering the session than remembering cards. This is why the research discussion concentrates on interruptions, orientation and the physical act of passing the device, rather than treating the bracket drawing as the whole feature.

## Three things people are following

An individual concentrating on a board is following card positions and remembered faces. Someone waiting nearby is following the social event: who is occupied, whether a finish is close and when attention will return to the group. The person explaining the game is following the application itself, often watching for a control that might replace the current position.

These perspectives overlap, but they are not interchangeable. A board full of exposed faces is meaningful to the current player. It gives a waiting person relatively little information about where the group is in its event. A compact event view can answer that social question, while the ordinary board remains the place where the player thinks.

The competition documents separate these subjects so that readers can find the relevant decision without extracting it from a long screen-by-screen walkthrough. [Pairing](competition-pairing.md) covers the relationship between entrants and the bracket. [Rounds](competition-rounds.md) covers event stages. [Boards](competition-boards.md) and [deals](competition-deals.md) distinguish the dimensions of a board from its actual arrangement. [Ties](competition-ties.md) and [scores](competition-scores.md) address results from different angles.

## A local social activity, with local evidence

The current project has no backend or account service. Its board codes and exported progress are useful for reproducing a situation, not for establishing the identity of a person who played it. That is a comfortable fit for a group that is physically present and can see what happened. It is a much weaker basis for claims about distant strangers.

The same limitation applies to development evidence. A replay can help an engineer understand a sequence of card actions. A screenshot can help someone understand what the group saw. Neither explains why a participant handed the tablet back early, or whether someone had been watching another person's screen. Those are observations about the setting, and they belong in the research account rather than in an assertion about the game engine.

[Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md) explains the existing technical tools. [Competition research](competition-research.md) describes local sessions and the limits of drawing conclusions from them. The two accounts answer different questions and are useful together.

## How the current code helps

The core already separates game data from presentation. `src/game/game.ts` contains card transitions and logical elapsed time. `src/game/deck.ts` contains board parsing and deterministic generation. Those files have no participant knowledge. That makes them a useful basis for discussing competition without embedding group administration into card rendering.

The browser session is a separate layer under `src/game/session`. It owns the bridge between that core and React, browser visibility, clock observations and preferences. This is the most consequential boundary for an extension: reusing a visual component is easy to notice, while inheriting a session side effect can remain hidden until much later.

The board itself lives under `src/game/board`. Its card buttons and navigation code operate on positions. The status view receives a game and a best value; it does not discover an event or a participant. [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md), [session module](../architecture/session-module.md) and [React boundaries](../architecture/react-boundaries.md) give the broader engineering context.

# Competition pairing

This page describes entry-order seeding and the opening bracket for shared-device competition.

Pairing connects a group of people to an event structure. It is separate from choosing a board, recording a finished attempt or interpreting a tied result. The game has no participant collection; competition extends the existing solo controller.

## From the entry list to the opening matches

Entry order gives the group a sequence that can be inspected without any information about previous performance. Seeds follow entry order, so the first player entered is seed 1. A bracket of four meets as 1 against 4, then 2 against 3. A bracket of eight meets as 1 against 8, 4 against 5, 3 against 6, then 2 against 7. This fixes the opening arrangement while leaving the existing memory-game engine concerned with cards rather than people.

The ordering of the eight-person case deserves attention. Writing opposite ends of the entry list together produces the right collection of opponents, but a straightforward loop over the first half of the list would display them in a different order. The sequence in the paragraph above is therefore relevant to the shape of the bracket, not just to membership of each opening match.

Here is a worked example with eight entrants.

| Entry position | Entrant | Seed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First | Ada | 1 |
| Second | Bo | 2 |
| Third | Cora | 3 |
| Fourth | Dev | 4 |
| Fifth | Emi | 5 |
| Sixth | Finn | 6 |
| Seventh | Gia | 7 |
| Eighth | Hal | 8 |

Reading down the opening matches gives Ada with Hal, Dev with Emi, Cora with Finn, then Bo with Gia. This example is useful during a design review because every participant is visibly accounted for, and a swapped middle match is easy to spot. It also avoids relying on the geometry of a bracket drawing to explain who is involved.

## What a seed means here

In this scope, the seed identifies a place derived from entry. It is not an estimate of memory skill. The current game has no account history, participant rating or service from which to obtain such an estimate. A developer looking for an existing ranking calculation in `src/game` will not find one.

This distinction makes the entry list meaningful to the group. If people entered themselves while passing the device around the table, that physical sequence explains the resulting seed values. Alphabetical sorting would tell a different story; sorting by an ordinary local best would tell a different one again. Neither transformation follows from the entry-order definition above.

There is a separate ambiguity between the seed in a bracket and the seed in a board code. `src/game/deck.ts` uses `seed` for the numeric input to deck generation. That number describes an arrangement of cards, not a person. For instance, the last number in `np1-4-73` has no relationship to the entrant in position 73, or to an entrant at all. The shared word is a vocabulary collision between two subjects.

[Competition deals](competition-deals.md) covers board identity. [Competition ties](competition-ties.md) covers result comparison. Neither calculation is present in the current pairing-free source, and neither is needed to explain the opening layout here.

## The small example catches a different mistake

With Ada, Bo, Cora and Dev as the complete entry list, the opening matches are Ada with Dev, followed by Bo with Cora. This is not obtained by taking the first two matches of the eight-person example. It is a bracket constructed from the smaller entry list.

That observation is useful when reviewing code that represents possible opponents by index. A table of entry positions can be applied to the corresponding list length. A table of names copied from another event cannot. The distinction becomes particularly clear when the same people participate in more than one demonstration but join in a different order.

It is also easy for a visual mockup to hide a mismatch between the text and the underlying order. A designer may draw a balanced-looking left and right side while the data is assembled in another traversal. The named example gives reviewers a shared reference independent of whether the visual bracket runs left to right, top to bottom or in a compact list.

## A pairing review on paper

A useful review exercise is to write the entry list once, assign its seed values, and trace each participant into the opening layout. In the eight-person example, every name appears once in the opening matches. Each opponent relationship can be checked in both directions: locating Ada also locates Hal; locating Hal leads back to Ada.

This exercise reveals three different classes of error. A duplicated participant is a membership problem. Correct opponents in the wrong middle positions are an ordering problem. Correct seed positions attached to the wrong names are an entry-mapping problem. They can produce similar screenshots, but they point to different mistakes in construction.

The exercise does not determine who advances. It simply makes the initial structure concrete enough to inspect. Event stages are discussed in [competition rounds](competition-rounds.md), and the relationship between an individual finish and local saved results is discussed in [competition scores](competition-scores.md).

For an engineer considering test coverage, the two named examples offer direct expectations rather than a second copy of the same pairing algorithm. A test that calculates its expected list with the same loop as the implementation is weak evidence: both can make the same ordering mistake. A literal list of expected opponent names exposes that mistake immediately.

## Unresolved pairing decisions

The pairing definition describes the two bracket shapes above. It does not describe a general event for every possible number of entrants. The project has no rule for a vacant place, a late arrival, a withdrawal, replacing a participant or rearranging an event after results exist. These are unresolved product questions rather than branches that can be inferred from a nearest power of two.

These boundaries are deliberate. The opening arrangement is small and explicit. General scheduling systems solve much larger problems, but importing their assumptions would add behavior beyond the current game and competition scope.

# Competition rounds

This page explains the stages of a shared-device bracket and the round text associated with play.

A round provides context that the card board cannot provide on its own. A participant may recognize the game immediately and still be unsure where the group has reached. This page concerns that event context; the arrangement of opponents is in [competition pairing](competition-pairing.md), and the dimensions of the playing board are in [competition boards](competition-boards.md).

## Names during play

The round name describes a stage of the event rather than the current card selection or the number of turns taken. Name each round Quarterfinal, Semifinal or Final, and show it as "Round: NAME" while that round is played. A bracket of four has no Quarterfinal. The resulting vocabulary is small enough for a waiting participant to recognize without interpreting a bracket diagram.

For an eight-person event the names progress through Quarterfinal, Semifinal and Final. For a four-person event the names begin with Semifinal and lead to Final. These follow the naming rule.

The capital letters in the quoted pattern indicate where the round's name appears. Substituting Semifinal gives `Round: Semifinal`; substituting Final gives `Round: Final`. The pattern does not imply that the screen literally presents the placeholder. It also does not define the name of the participant who is currently using the device.

## Round, match and board are different contexts

A round can contain several matches. A match concerns a particular pair of people. The board currently rendered is the puzzle someone is working on. These relationships matter when a screen is refreshed after a handoff: a new game state does not, by itself, establish that the event has moved to another stage.

Consider the early part of an eight-person example. The group can still be in its first round while several people have already finished individual attempts. A mockup that advances a round label whenever the completion banner appears would conflate an individual game result with event progress. The existing completion banner reports a board finish; it contains no event interpretation.

This is a useful distinction even in static designs. A review can ask what the round text is describing at the exact moment represented by a screenshot. If the answer depends on which person happened to finish last, the design may be mixing stage context with attempt history. The labels above identify the event stage, while the remaining competition pages explain the other subjects.

## What the current status component knows

`src/game/status/GameStatus.tsx` accepts a `game`, a `best` value and a `celebration` flag. It renders moves, matched pairs, elapsed time, the current best and a completion paragraph when `isWon(game)` is true. It has no round prop and does not query an outer event.

The labels in `src/game/status/status-labels.ts` are the four ordinary game statistics. Searching there for the competition round text will not reveal an unconnected implementation waiting to be enabled. The present application simply lacks that event concept.

Similarly, `src/game/Game.tsx` is the composition of a solo session. It passes `session.game` to `GameStatus` and uses `session.generation` as the board's React key. Neither operation establishes which stage a group has reached. [Status bar](../interface/status-bar.md) explains the existing statistics, and [React boundaries](../architecture/react-boundaries.md) explains the surrounding composition.

This source boundary is valuable in review. Someone can demonstrate the round text in a prototype without having changed the underlying game mechanics. Conversely, reusing the existing status component does not supply a round label automatically. The product concept and its rendered location are separate matters.

## A generation is not a round counter

The `generation` member of `Session` begins at zero in `initialSession`. `replaceGame` increments it when a new game replaces the previous one. The increment lets timer work associated with an earlier game be recognized as stale. It also causes `Game.tsx` to mount a fresh board instance through the keyed component.

That counter changes during Restart and successful board or snapshot replacement. A person can perform those actions without any group event existing. Reading generation 2 as the second round would therefore make an event interpretation out of an implementation lifetime counter.

The example becomes more concrete during a miss. An ordinary restart clears the previous game and its pending selection. The replacement game has a later generation even though it can have exactly the same board code. The generation's meaning is about callback validity and component lifetime. The board code's meaning is about the deal. Neither is a name for an event stage.

`tickSession(session, generation, milliseconds)` checks the generation before advancing logical time. This check is covered in `src/game/session/session.test.ts`. The test is evidence for game replacement behavior, not evidence for bracket progression. [Mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) and [new game and restart](../gameplay/new-game-and-restart.md) cover the underlying behavior.

## How a sequence can be reviewed

A paper review can show several moments from an event instead of only its opening and final screens. One moment might show a board in progress, another an individual finish, and another a later match within the same round. The round names provide a stable point of reference across those images.

The interesting question in that exercise is what changed between images. Card progress can change while the round name remains the same. A different participant can be present while the stage remains the same. Eventually the event context changes as well. Separating those changes makes the review more informative than a single screenshot with every field different.

For the four-person example, a screen sequence containing a Quarterfinal would contradict the naming decision above. For the eight-person example, a sequence that jumps straight from the first stage to the Final would be missing context. These are straightforward consequences of the defined stages, and they can be assessed without a complete game implementation.

Animations, transition screens, navigation controls and focus destinations are separate interface questions. [Focus policy](../interface/focus-policy.md) and [dialog policy](../interface/dialog-policy.md) describe the existing interactions.
