item.aggregated_output: --- docs/interface/controls.md --- --- open-forge: description: Game options and reproduction controls tags: - Game - Controls --- # Controls Controls is a specification that defines the game options and reproduction tools in Neon Pairs. Status: spec version 2.2. You can start another deal, repeat the current one or load saved progress. Each control keeps the same label, so you can find the same action after a game changes. ## Deal controls The main controls are: - C01 - Label the native size select "Grid size". Give it options `4x4`, `6x6`, `8x8`, `10x10`, `12x12`, `14x14` and `16x16`, with numeric side length `N` as each value. After a successful board-code or snapshot load, select the loaded board's size. - C02 - Label the fresh-deal button "New Game". It creates a fresh seed and keeps the current size. - C03 - Label the repeat-deal button "Restart". It starts the same board code again. Changing size, starting and restarting follow the session rules in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md). ## Reproduction tools - C04 - Put reproduction controls inside a native `details` element that starts collapsed. Give its summary the exact text "Reproduce a game". The controls use the board-code and snapshot formats defined in [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md). A board code starts a deal. A snapshot loads progress on a deal. ## Load a board - C05 - Label the text input "Board code" and limit it to 32 characters. Show the current board code after a new deal, Restart or a successful load. Keep an edited draft when a card action changes the game. - C06 - Label its button "Load board". Validate the entered code before replacing the current game with that deal's starting state. For example, loading `np1-4-1` starts its hidden four-column board. Entering that code alone keeps the current game until you select Load board. ## Snapshot tools - C07 - Label the textarea "Snapshot JSON" and limit it to 65536 characters. The parser also applies the UTF-8 byte limit in the snapshot format. - C08 - Label the export button "Export snapshot". Fill the textarea with readable version 1 snapshot JSON that you can select and copy manually. Export leaves the game state and clock unchanged. It requires no Clipboard API. Export `elapsedMs` and a pending mismatch's `remainingMs` as whole milliseconds. A pending mismatch always exports at least 1ms. - C09 - Label the import button "Load snapshot". Validate the complete draft before replacing the current game. Load unfinished progress paused and show "Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue." Load completed progress as completed without pausing and show "Loaded completed snapshot." - C10 - Show a "Resume" button only while an imported unfinished game is paused. Selecting it clears that pause. Unfinished play continues from the loaded state. While paused, block every card activation and allow board focus movement. On Resume, move focus to the board's remembered tab stop before removing the Resume button. A loaded completed game stays completed and shows no Resume button. - C11 - On invalid input, keep the current game and the entered draft for correction. Show the exact status for that control: | Control | Status | | --- | --- | | Load board | Invalid board code. | | Load snapshot | Invalid snapshot. | - C12 - A loaded completed snapshot keeps the win banner static and plays no celebration. Import doesn't write a best score. Resuming an unfinished snapshot and later winning records a local best under R10. For example, loading a completed game with fewer moves than the saved best shows that game without replacing the saved record. ## Focus - C13 - Keep focus on the button used for starting, restarting, loading or exporting. These actions don't move focus to the board. Resume follows C10 because its button disappears. The board's remembered tab stop follows the focus rules in [Input](input.md#focus). ## Replay - C14 - Keep replay in the developer CLI and game core. V1 has no replay controls in the game UI. Run `npm run --silent replay -- PATH` to read a replay file. On valid input, print only the final snapshot JSON to stdout and exit 0. On invalid input, print nothing to stdout, write a message to stderr and exit nonzero. The complete game pack starts in [Neon Pairs](../README.md). --- docs/interface/control-bar.md --- --- open-forge: description: The deal buttons, size selector, responsive arrangement and session callbacks in Controls.tsx. tags: - Controls - Layout - Session --- # Control bar This page explains how `Controls.tsx` presents the deal actions and how those actions connect to the session. The bar is deliberately small: a labeled size selector, New Game and Restart. It sits above the statistics and board in `src/game/Game.tsx`, so the actions that replace a deal are available before entering the board. Reproduction tools have a different rhythm and occupy their own disclosure below the board; see [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md). ## Component boundary `src/game/controls/Controls.tsx` accepts three props: `size`, `newGame(size?: number)` and `restart()`. It does not own a second copy of the selected size, choose a seed, reset a timer or update preferences. Its select is controlled by the `size` prop. That prop comes from `session.game.size`, which makes the displayed choice agree with the board after a size change, board-code load or snapshot import. The optional argument on `newGame` explains the two call sites. The select converts `event.currentTarget.value` with `Number(...)` and calls `newGame` with that value. New Game calls `newGame()` without an argument. The default in `use-game.ts` takes the current game's size. Restart calls its separate callback. There is no DOM inspection to decide which size to use when either button is pressed. The select and buttons are native elements. The two buttons explicitly use `type="button"`; they do not submit the reproduction form farther down the page. The wrapper is a `div` with class `controls`, not a toolbar widget with a separate keyboard model. Tab follows ordinary document order through the select, New Game and Restart. Board navigation begins after those controls, as described in [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md). ## Labels and options `src/game/controls/control-labels.ts` exports `DealControl`. The visible strings are `Grid size`, `New Game` and `Restart`. The label is associated with `id="grid-size"` through `htmlFor="grid-size"`. A user or browser test can therefore find the select by its visible name instead of a CSS class or its position in the bar. The options come directly from `GRID_SIZES` in `deck.ts`. Their values are the numeric side lengths rendered as native option values, and their text is the side repeated with a lowercase `x`: | Display | Value | Cards | | --- | --- | --- | | 4x4 | 4 | 16 | | 6x6 | 6 | 36 | | 8x8 | 8 | 64 | | 10x10 | 10 | 100 | | 12x12 | 12 | 144 | | 14x14 | 14 | 196 | | 16x16 | 16 | 256 | Those are deal sizes, rather than zoom settings. Choosing 16 changes the game to a 16-row, 16-column deck; it does not squeeze the existing sixteen cards into a different arrangement. The larger boards can exceed the available width inside their scroll container. [Pointer and touch](pointer-and-touch.md) explains the consequences for reaching cards. The component itself receives `size: number`, but the session's `newGame` function checks `isValidSize(size)` before making a replacement. That guard is outside the control and also protects callers that do not originate in the native select. The option list is not the only validation boundary. ## Desktop arrangement `controls.css` uses flex layout with `align-items: end`, `flex-wrap: wrap`, a `12px` gap and a `16px` bottom margin. The size group is another flex row with `align-items: center` and a `12px` gap. The label sits beside its select rather than above it. The outer alignment brings the actions to the same bottom line if control heights differ. No explicit column count or button width is needed in this layout. Labels and the browser's select affordance contribute to their natural widths. Wrapping is enabled before the phone media query applies, so the bar can also adapt to a constrained content area on a wider window. The maximum content width and page padding come from `game.css`, not the controls stylesheet. The shared `.control` class comes from `control.css`: `min-height: 44px`, `padding: 8px 12px`, a `1px` neutral border, an `8px` radius, panel background, text color and inherited font. The select and buttons get a pointer cursor. The stylesheet does not replace the select's browser interaction with a drawn menu. Its popup remains the native control's responsibility. ## Phone arrangement At `max-width: 599px`, `.controls` changes to `align-items: stretch`. The size group occupies the full line with `width: 100%` and `justify-content: space-between`; its label and select move to opposite ends of that row. The direct child buttons each get `flex: 1`, sharing the following row when there is room. The media query acts on the current DOM hierarchy. Moving a button into an extra wrapper would change the effect of `.controls > button`. A review of such a refactor can compare computed widths and wrapping before deciding that it preserves the arrangement. The apparent simplicity of a wrapper change can hide a layout change on phones. The breakpoint is not a board-size breakpoint. A 4x4 and a 16x16 game use the same control bar at the same viewport width. The board handles its own width independently. This separation keeps the controls available even when a player has scrolled to the far end of a large board. ## What the actions replace In `use-game.ts`, `newGame` creates a code using `freshBoardCode(size, current.current.game.seed)`, constructs the new game, resets the clock adapter and commits `replaceGame(...)`. Restart constructs a game from `current.current.game.boardCode` instead. Both begin with a closed selection, no matched positions, zero moves, zero elapsed time and `started: false` because that is what `createGame` returns. `replaceGame` increments `session.generation`. The Board in `Game.tsx` is keyed by this generation, so it mounts with a fresh remembered tab stop. The BoardCodeForm input is also keyed by generation and receives the current board code as its default value. A reset is therefore observable in several places without each component inventing its own reset event. The size is saved through the session preferences path. The current size's best record is read independently for the statistics. Choosing a size with no stored record shows `Best: none`; returning to a size with a record displays that size's value. For the exact display boundary, see [Status bar](status-bar.md) and [Best score records](../gameplay/best-score-records.md). A pending mismatch cannot later alter the replacement deal. Clock reset and generation checks in the session make stale updates harmless. This is why replacing a deal during its short mismatch display is a meaningful controls test, rather than merely checking that the card count changes. ## Focus and continuity Clicking New Game or Restart leaves focus on the action button. The components do not call `.focus()` on the board after a reset. A user can press the same action again or Tab forward to the new first card. A size change likewise uses the native select interaction rather than an application focus transfer. Initial page load also does not select a card on the user's behalf. The board's first card is ready as its tab stop, but readiness is separate from current focus. [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) describes this distinction and the different treatment needed when Resume removes its own button. There is no confirmation step in either callback today. Pressing an action replaces the current deal immediately. Do not infer a pending dialog from the text of an action or from the fact that the old game had moves. The separate [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) records the policy for future actions that leave unfinished work. ## A useful review path The controls checks in `tests/controls.e2e.test.ts` inspect the native option values as well as their displayed text. `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` checks the literal labels. `tests/keyboard.e2e.test.ts` checks the relationship between Restart and the remembered board entry point. Layout coverage includes a narrow `320x640` viewport in `tests/layout.e2e.test.ts` and the equivalent zoom layout in `tests/zoom.e2e.test.ts`. These checks cover different failures. A label refactor could preserve a screenshot while breaking name-based selection. A wrapper refactor could preserve all labels while changing the mobile row. A session refactor could keep the bar visually identical while allowing an earlier timer to touch a new deal. Reading the component, CSS and callback together makes those differences visible. For a manual check, choose a nondefault size, reveal a mismatching pair, then use Restart before it closes. The deck repeats and the counters reset. Use New Game at that same size and confirm that its code changes. Tab into the board after each action to observe the reset entry point. Finally load a valid code of another size from the reproduction panel and look back at Grid size: the controlled select follows the loaded game without another local state update. --- docs/interface/announcements-policy.md --- --- open-forge: description: Status publication, repeated event identity, turn results and load feedback. tags: - Input - Accessibility - Status --- # Announcements policy This page describes how event feedback is published, repeated and kept separate from routine game rendering. The game has many visible updates, but only some represent a new result. A clock tick is a changing value; resolving a turn is an event. Treating those as the same kind of update would make a memory game noisy and would bury the information a player needs after selecting two cards. ## Publication point `Game.tsx` places the game result between the board instructions and the Board itself. Its paragraph has `role="status"`, `aria-live="polite"` and `aria-atomic="true"`, with the current feedback inside a span. The page has exactly one live region, the status paragraph in Game.tsx. New status text, such as whose turn it is, goes through that region. The current game publishes pair results and load outcomes there; it has no turn-owner feature. The paragraph remains mounted while its content changes. It is inside `.game-result`, which has a minimum height of `56px`, flex alignment and margins. The wrapper reserves a readable area near the board without making the scrollable card content itself the announcement source. Polite publication allows the browser and assistive technology to schedule the result around other speech. Atomic content indicates that the paragraph's result is treated as a complete update rather than an isolated changed number. These attributes express the intended exposure; the actual spoken experience still needs user acceptance with a screen reader. ## Session data behind the paragraph The session owns `feedback` and an integer `announcement`. Game renders `{session.feedback}`. Updating the key replaces the child span even when its text is identical to the preceding result. This gives repeated events a DOM change without adding a hidden counter to the spoken text. The counter is event identity, not a statistic presented to the player. It does not track moves, matched pairs or elapsed seconds. A failed load can advance it without adding a move, while the first card reveal changes game state without advancing it. A broad render counter would be wrong for this job. Session renders occur for time and selection changes that should not repeat the last turn result. The explicit event field makes the distinction inspectable in `session.ts` and `use-game.ts`. ## Turn results `activateSession` calls the pure `activateCard`. If the game object is unchanged, it returns the current session. If the result has selection kind `one`, it returns the updated game without changing feedback or announcement identity. That covers the first eligible reveal. After the second eligible reveal, the result is either a mismatch or a match. The session builds the appropriate text and increments `announcement`. Completion is checked at this same boundary, so the winning match gets a combined result rather than two competing event publications. | Result | Text produced by the session | | --- | --- | | First matched pair | `Pair found. 1 pair matched.` | | Later nonfinal pair | `Pair found. M pairs matched.` | | Mismatch | `No match. Cards close after a short pause.` | | Winning pair | `Pair found. All pairs found in N moves and time.` | Here `M` and `N` are replaced with the actual counts, and `time` is the output of `formatElapsed`. The singular branch is based on `game.matched.length === 2`. The final branch takes precedence over the nonfinal pair count. A card's accessible name also changes when it reveals or matches. That is the focused control describing its own state, not a second turn-result producer. The text in the event paragraph summarizes what the two-card attempt achieved. [Screen reader notes](screen-reader-notes.md) follows those two sources in a complete game. ## Consecutive identical results Two misses in a row produce the same sentence. Updating only a string state can leave the DOM text unchanged, which gives no new mutation for the second event. The keyed span avoids relying on a different visible sentence to distinguish them. The current sequence is concrete. Initial feedback is empty. Revealing index 0 on `np1-4-1` changes selection to `one` without publishing. Revealing index 1 produces a mismatch and advances the event identity. After the interval closes, choosing those two indices again produces the same text with a later identity. The counter advances once for each resolved attempt in that sequence, not once for each card action or timer update. A third activation during the mismatch is ignored by the game and leaves the event unchanged. The same is true of a repeated activation on the first revealed card. There is no temporary blanking timeout between identical results. The implementation does not clear text, wait a guessed number of milliseconds and restore it. That avoids adding announcement timing to the game clock or introducing a second lifecycle that can outlive a replacement game. ## Changes that stay quiet `tickSession` advances the game and returns a new session with that game, leaving feedback and announcement fields intact. Mismatch closure is part of this advancement. It does not publish a new “cards closed” result. The earlier mismatch sentence already told the player that closure would follow a short pause. Arrow movement is local board focus state. It does not call the session feedback path. Clock renders update Time in GameStatus, while card memoization prevents unchanged cards from rendering again. Neither operation is a new turn result. New Game and Restart call `replaceGame` with `imported: false`. That replacement clears the prior feedback and load notice while keeping the announcement number. A successful board-code load follows the same replacement path. These operations clear old context; the current source does not add a success sentence for a board-code load. Clearing text is still a DOM change and may appear in a mutation trace as an empty result. It is different from republishing a turn sentence. The accessibility journey's expected record includes the new-game clearing event, so a raw count of every mutation is not a substitute for reading what each event contains. ## Load outcomes share the publication path The controller's `notice(feedback)` helper assigns both `feedback` and `loadNotice`, then increments `announcement`. Invalid Board code publishes `Invalid board code.`; invalid Snapshot JSON publishes `Invalid snapshot.`. Repeating the same invalid submission is a new load attempt and advances the identity again. For valid snapshot import, `replaceGame(..., true)` increments the identity and publishes either `Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue.` or `Loaded completed snapshot.`. The former corresponds to a paused unfinished game, the latter to completed progress. Valid board-code loading does not use the imported-snapshot branch. Reproduction also renders `loadNotice` in its ordinary paragraph with id `load-notice`. The load buttons reference it through `aria-describedby`. That keeps the outcome visible beside the text tools and associates the description with their actions without creating another event publisher in that panel. Resume clears feedback and loadNotice without increasing the event identity. It also transfers focus to the board before its button disappears. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) and [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) describe those effects independently of event publication. ## Completion and persistent reading GameStatus shows a completion paragraph whenever `isWon(game)` is true. A newly won game can give it the celebration class; an imported completed game shows it statically. That paragraph is persistent reading content containing the final moves and time. The winning turn's feedback already contains the match and win in one result. The status paragraph does not need to separately announce a matched pair, then publish a second completion sentence. This avoids having two updates compete at the most significant turn in the game. A completed snapshot instead publishes its load outcome, because import is the event that just occurred. The game is visibly complete, but no new card match happened. This distinction preserves a useful account of what the user actually did. ## Automated evidence `session.test.ts` checks that first reveal, mismatch closure and repeated mismatch events affect announcement identity as expected. It also checks import outcomes and completion transitions without involving the browser. `tests/announcements.e2e.test.ts` observes DOM mutations in the status paragraph. It resolves a mismatch, moves focus, runs the mismatch interval and repeats the same attempt. The expected result history contains the mismatch sentence once for each resolved turn, with no extra result from movement or closure. The same test submits each snapshot load kind and each invalid-load kind twice, checking the publication history and the visible load notice. `tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` checks that the result remains beside the board during large-phone play and that the reproduction panel has no competing result role. The accessibility journey reads Chromium's tree for the polite and atomic properties and the result text at each turn. That establishes exposure in the tested runtime. Spoken scheduling and verbalization are assessed in user acceptance. The repository records spoken review as user acceptance. ## Diagnosing a repeated or missing result A missing second identical result suggests checking event identity before changing the sentence. A repeated result on every clock tick suggests checking whether routine advancement touches the publication fields. A load notice visible near the textarea but absent from event output suggests checking whether the controller used `notice` or only changed local text. For a report, the useful sequence is the action, feedback string, announcement number and observed mutations. That evidence can show whether the session failed to publish, React had no relevant change or the browser exposed the expected update but a spoken review behaved differently. The policy gives a single publication boundary; diagnosis follows it from the event to the paragraph rather than adding more announcers around the page. --- docs/interface/focus-policy.md --- --- open-forge: description: Current action focus and board memory, plus the policy for main-screen replacements. tags: - Input - Focus - Policy --- # Focus policy This page records focus behavior in the current game and the policy for a feature that changes the main screen. Focus tells a keyboard user where input will go next. It is related to game selection but is not stored as part of a turn or snapshot. The current interface deliberately keeps deal-action focus, remembered board focus and card reveal state as distinct things. ## Existing page and future screens `Game.tsx` currently renders one main area with an h1, deal controls, statistics, instructions, turn output, the Board and reproduction controls. It has no alternate-screen branch or screen-level h2 focus target. Replacing a deal remounts the board within that page; it does not replace the page with a different screen. A feature that introduces a screen replacement has a different orientation problem from resetting a deck. When a feature replaces what the main area shows, focus moves to that screen's h2, which has tabindex="-1". This gives the new screen a programmatic landing place without adding that heading to ordinary Tab traversal. The current deal and load callbacks can still be understood on their own terms; they are not evidence that such a screen transition already exists. The policy applies to the feature-level replacement described here. Expanding native details, updating statistics, closing a mismatch or displaying the completed-game paragraph does not currently create a new screen. Those operations retain the page structure and follow the existing behavior below. [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) covers a separate interaction with its own opening focus. ## Initial load is quiet The hook `useBoardFocus(size)` initializes `focused` to zero. Board gives index 0 a tab index of zero and the other card buttons a tab index of minus one. This makes the first card available on entry, but no mount effect calls its focus method. The browser's current focus therefore remains where it is at initial load. The page does not jump down to the board before a player has found Grid size or New Game. The board help paragraph describes how to enter and operate it. Its region uses `aria-describedby="board-help"` to associate those instructions with the board. A remembered entry point is often described casually as “focus on the first card.” In this code that wording is incomplete. There is an entry point ready at the first card, while actual focus may be on the document, a deal button or another native control. Keeping those concepts separate prevents accidental mount-time focus stealing. ## Deal actions retain their location New Game and Restart are native buttons that call the session controller. Neither callback moves focus into the board. After either action, a keyboard user remains on the button they used and can repeat the action or Tab toward the board. The size select uses its native interaction and likewise does not issue a board focus call. The replacement increments `session.generation`, used as Board's React key. The newly mounted hook begins with a remembered index of zero. Thus the next board entry goes to the first card, even if the previous deal's memory was near its end. Actual action focus and future board entry are updated through different mechanisms. A valid board-code load also increments generation. BoardCodeForm focuses its Load board ref on successful submission because its input is keyed by generation and will be replaced. That is especially important when the action was Enter in the input. An invalid submission keeps the input node and does not call the button ref, so correction can continue in place. Clicking the load button starts with focus on that button, and an invalid click leaves it there. The distinction is based on the action's origin and successful input replacement, not on a general rule that all errors move focus into a field. [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) follows those cases in detail. ## Remembered board focus Board focus memory is a local hook state containing a card index. The `onFocus` callback updates it whenever a card receives focus. Board renders exactly that index with `tabIndex={0}`. All other cards remain programmatically focusable with `tabIndex={-1}`. Arrow movement uses the DOM order of the deck and never changes game selection on its own. Tab and Shift+Tab are left to the browser, so the board is one stop in the page sequence rather than a trap. Returning to it finds the last focused card, even if that card is now matched. Matched positions stay in the navigation geometry. A player does not need to relearn how many arrow presses separate two coordinates after a match. During a mismatch, focus can also move while activation is blocked. The same is true while imported unfinished progress waits for Resume. [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) provides the calculations and edge behavior. ## Resume transfers before removal Resume is the current exception to retaining focus on the action button. It exists only while `session.paused` is true. Clearing that flag removes the button, so leaving focus there would leave a disappearing target. In `Game.tsx`, the local `resume()` function first calls `board.current?.focusRemembered()` and then `controller.resume()`. Board's imperative method focuses the remembered card with `preventScroll: true` and then brings it into view. Only after that does the controller clear the paused state and notices. The ordering is observable. `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` installs a focus listener and confirms that Resume is still present when the card receives focus. A visual assertion after the fact would not establish this timing. The focus-entry test also remembers a far card on a large imported board, scrolls away and confirms that Resume returns to that location with nearest alignment. The remembered location after import is initially the first card because the import replaced the board. The player can change it while paused. Resume uses that current memory rather than the snapshot's revealed index or a hard-coded first card. A snapshot stores game progress, not the browser's last navigation location. ## Visible focus and scroll clearance `game.css` defines `:focus-visible` as a `3px` white outline with a `2px` offset. `card.css` gives cards `scroll-margin: 6px`. This combination accommodates the ring when the card is brought to the edge of the scroll area. The focus hook uses `card.matches(':focus-visible')` before scrolling in `cardFocused`. Keyboard movement can scroll immediately; pointer focus avoids moving a card under a held press. Board scrolls a clicked card after the click completes. The timing is part of reliable focus behavior, not only a visual polish detail. `useNearestScroll` stores the board's last reported scroll position, restores it and then invokes `scrollIntoView` with nearest alignment. The source records the Chromium-specific reason: Tab or Shift+Tab can center a newly focused card before the handler runs. Starting from the prior view preserves the player's location as much as possible. The helper leaves the outer page's scrolling to the browser. A review therefore measures both the card inside the board viewport and its visibility inside the window. A ring can be uncut by the board yet still sit partly below the window if the outer document did not move appropriately. ## Focus is not completion feedback Winning does not move focus to the completion paragraph in GameStatus. The final card stays the current control, and the completed summary becomes available in document order. The final turn's feedback is published through the game's event output. The component does not force the player to leave the board simply because all pairs are now matched. Likewise, a mismatch closing does not restore focus to either of its cards. Focus may have moved elsewhere while the pair was visible. The game-state update closes the faces while the user's navigation choice survives. An ordinary clock tick also leaves focus untouched. These examples are useful when evaluating a proposed effect that focuses something whenever `game` changes. Game changes for elapsed time, first reveals, turn results and resets. An effect tied to that broad object would combine very different events and could interrupt typing or navigation. The existing code places its explicit focus operations at narrower action boundaries. ## Review evidence The keyboard browser check covers Tab exit, rem ... command output truncated for persistence ... its the narrow layout, while a large board confines its own overflow to its viewport. A longer draft can remain in an input even when not all of its characters are visible at once; native text editing can scroll within the field. That is different from making the whole outer page wider. A multiline snapshot can expand or scroll internally without turning its label into a floating overlay. The equivalent zoom test at `640x400`, device scale 2, checks readable controls, statistics and completion output. It also uses the snapshot tools at that constrained layout. `tests/controls.e2e.test.ts` verifies labels, native limits and selectable export text. Together the sources cover geometry and editing behavior without defining a new generic form framework. For a proposed name field, these label and native-control patterns are relevant background, but there is no implemented name form to copy. [Text entry policy](text-entry-policy.md), [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) and [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md) own its separate acceptance rules. The current interface has no name-field placeholder, character counter, error precedence or field order. --- docs/interface/native-controls-guide.md --- --- open-forge: description: Native element choices and the browser behavior retained around React callbacks. tags: - Controls - Semantics - Architecture --- # Native controls guide This page explains the native HTML elements used by Neon Pairs and the behavior they supply to the interface. The source combines React event wiring with browser controls. It does not draw input controls on canvas or implement a replacement select menu. The resulting code leaves common editing, activation and disclosure behavior with the browser while keeping game decisions in the session and core. ## The current element choices | Element | Use in the game | Application responsibility around it | | --- | --- | --- | | `button` | Cards and actions | Decide what the activation changes | | `select` with `option` | Grid size | Supply supported sizes and start a deal | | `label` | Grid size and text fields | Associate visible names with field ids | | `input` | Board-code draft | Read and validate the submitted code | | `textarea` | Snapshot draft and export | Hold text and pass it to the snapshot decoder | | `form` | Board-code submission | Prevent navigation and handle the result | | `details` with `summary` | Reproduction disclosure | Supply content and layout | | `dl` with `dt` and `dd` | Current game statistics | Derive the displayed values | These choices describe the current DOM. Policies for other kinds of content are documented in [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) and [Tables policy](tables-policy.md), without implying that those elements already appear in Game. ## Buttons unify activation Card renders a native button with `type="button"`. Its `onClick` sends an index to the shared activation path. Enter and Space can activate the same control through normal button behavior, so there is no separate keydown implementation of reveal. The board's keydown handler only handles plain arrows with a navigation target. It does not call activation for Enter or Space and then also allow a native click. That avoids two paths processing one keyboard action. The game's pure activation guard still decides whether the card is eligible. Action buttons outside the board use explicit types too. The Board code loader is `type="submit"` inside its form. New Game, Restart, Export snapshot, Load snapshot and Resume are `type="button"`. This makes submission intent visible in JSX rather than relying on where the browser happens to find an enclosing form. A native button's semantics do not automatically implement ARIA-disabled behavior. Card uses `aria-disabled={matched}` while remaining focusable, and the game ignores matched activations. [Disabled state guide](disabled-state-guide.md) explains that deliberate split. ## The select keeps its native interaction Controls renders a labeled select whose value comes from `game.size`. Each option comes from `GRID_SIZES` and has a numeric side length value with `NxN` display text. The browser supplies its dropdown interaction and option-selection behavior. The component handles change by converting the selected value to a number and calling `newGame`. There is no local menu-open flag, active-option state or custom pointer hit testing. The controller still checks supported sizes, because native options are an interface aid rather than the only trust boundary. The select inherits the shared font and panel colors through `.control`. Styling the border and background does not replace its role or its label relationship. The current CSS does not remove it in favor of an invisible field beneath a separately focusable drawn menu. A successful board-code or snapshot load changes the actual game size, which flows back into this controlled select. The visible selected option therefore follows the model rather than a second UI-only size state. [Control bar](control-bar.md) covers that data flow. ## Text editing remains text editing Board code is an input, and Snapshot JSON is a textarea. They retain selection, caret movement and browser editing operations. The textarea can resize vertically and receives readable export text without a clipboard permission dependency. The card's `user-select: none` styling is scoped to `.card`. It does not disable selecting an exported snapshot. The code-field spell-check and autocomplete settings reflect its format-oriented use; the snapshot field disables spell checking as well. None of those attributes validates the entered data. BoardCodeForm uses FormData and prevents the form's default navigation in `onSubmit`. Pressing Enter in the input reaches that same submission path. The snapshot tools instead use local React state and explicit action buttons, preserving multiline Enter behavior in the textarea. Controlled and uncontrolled fields both appear here. Reproduction controls the textarea value with state. BoardCodeForm uses `defaultValue` on an input keyed by generation. Native element choice does not determine which React state pattern is appropriate. The intended draft lifecycle does; see [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md). ## A disclosure is already an interaction The reproduction panel uses details with a summary, starts collapsed and relies on native expansion. There is no handler toggling an `expanded` variable or emulating summary key activation. The CSS styles the panel and summary without changing their source order. The summary's visible text supplies its purpose. The load notice and Resume live outside the collapsible body, so closing it does not hide the pause continuation action. This is a layout and component-boundary decision around the native disclosure, not a custom disclosure implementation. A disclosure leaves the surrounding document operable and expands in flow. It is not equivalent to a modal overlay. That distinction matters when reading a feature description: choosing a different native element changes more than a border shape or animation. ## DOM cards and artwork Board is a CSS grid of DOM buttons, and each visible face is an inline SVG child. Hidden cards omit the face component entirely. The button name comes from position, state and, when available, face description; the SVG is hidden from accessibility and cannot receive focus. The face drawing is therefore not the input surface's semantic replacement. A user activates the button, not an independently focusable path inside the SVG. This keeps the artwork and interaction connected without requiring canvas coordinate mapping or an invisible parallel button list. The matched check mark is also an aria-hidden, nonfocusable SVG. It reinforces state visually while the button name and disabled property express it through the control. [Card artwork](../visuals/card-artwork.md) and [Screen reader notes](screen-reader-notes.md) describe those channels more fully. ## Native elements still need application work The browser does not know that a pair matches, that a snapshot import is paused or that a game replacement invalidates an old timer. Those decisions remain in `game.ts`, `session.ts` and `use-game.ts`. A correct native element can still call the wrong controller action. Nor does a button automatically implement the board's remembered entry point. `useBoardFocus` supplies the tab-index pattern and arrows, while the browser supplies basic focus and activation. The scroll helper addresses a specific Chromium centering behavior rather than replacing all browser scrolling. Labels and descriptions also need correct associations. A visible label next to an input is not sufficient if its `htmlFor` points elsewhere. A load notice remains useful because the buttons reference its actual id. Native semantics reduce custom behavior, but they do not excuse checking the JSX relationships. The same applies to CSS. Minimum height, shrinking fields, wrapping rows and visible outlines are explicit styles. A native input can still overflow a narrow page if its sizing constraints are wrong. [Form layout guide](form-layout-guide.md) and [Target size policy](target-size-policy.md) cover those aspects. ## Why alternatives would carry more work Replacing the select with a drawn menu would move option navigation, expansion, selection and focus handling into application code. Replacing summary with a styled generic container would require recreating its activation and expanded-state exposure. Those are concrete costs even if the replacement initially resembles the current design. A canvas board would also need a separate way to expose each card's position, name, state and focus behavior. The current DOM makes those properties inspectable directly. This is the benefit behind the existing choice, not a claim that native elements alone solve every accessibility issue. The source does not contain a component library or a custom form abstraction that all new controls must use. Shared labels and CSS are small local tools. [ADR 006](../decisions/adr-006-native-controls.md) is the decision reference, while [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md) explains the separation between browser effects and pure game behavior. ## Evidence in review The controls tests locate fields and buttons by names and roles, inspect native option values and check selectable export text. Keyboard tests rely on normal Tab exit and native button activation. The accessibility journey captures the browser's exposed control roles and states. These checks are more informative than asserting only that a div has the right class. They verify the interaction surface that the player receives. At the same time, they remain browser and tree evidence, with spoken confirmation assigned to user acceptance in the repository README. For a refactor, compare element type, explicit button type, field association, key handling and callback as a connected path. If a visual wrapper is the only intended change, those details reveal whether it also changed submission, tab order or mobile flex behavior. The native structure makes the comparison concrete. --- docs/interface/text-entry-policy.md --- --- open-forge: description: Accepted name representation and its separation from board-code and JSON input. tags: - Forms - Names - Policy --- # Text entry policy This page records the treatment of person-entered names and distinguishes it from the game's existing code and JSON fields. Neon Pairs currently asks for a board code and snapshot text, not a player name. There is no name field, group-name store or name rendering component in the source. The name policy below applies when such input is introduced; it does not describe a transformation already applied to the reproduction textarea. ## One name representation A name can arrive with incidental spaces from typing, pasting or an input method. Keeping several representations of that same entered name would make later display and comparison harder to reason about. Every name a person types is stored and shown after trimming both ends, collapsing each run of inner whitespace to one space and normalizing to NFC. The stored value and visible value therefore describe the same processed name rather than exposing the original draft in one view and a different spelling in another. The policy is about a person's name. It does not turn all user input into name text, and it does not change the board-code grammar or snapshot serialization. The current fields demonstrate why that distinction matters: significant punctuation and structural whitespace belong to their own formats. For names, the other checks are documented separately in [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) and [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md). This page explains representation and input boundaries without duplicating their conditions or error messages. ## Examples of representation The following examples use quotes only to make surrounding whitespace visible. The quotes are not part of the entered name. | Entered draft | Displayed and stored form | What changed | | --- | --- | --- | | ` Mira ` | `Mira` | Space around the name is removed | | `Ada Lovelace` | `Ada Lovelace` | An interior run becomes one separating space | | `Jean Luc` | `Jean Luc` | Ordinary spacing stays ordinary | | `Cafe` followed by a combining acute on the e | `Café` | Canonically equivalent text gets a composed representation where available | | `O'Neil` | `O'Neil` | The apostrophe is retained | The last example matters because representation cleanup is not an instruction to remove meaningful punctuation or rewrite a person's preferred spelling. The policy does not transliterate scripts, strip accents or convert names to ASCII. Those would be additional transformations beyond what is stated. NFC addresses canonical equivalence in Unicode text. It is not the compatibility normalization form. Text that merely looks similar is not necessarily canonically equivalent, and this policy does not define visual resemblance as identity. That boundary prevents a representation step from quietly becoming a broad name-matching heuristic. A name can also contain multiple words. Collapsing a whitespace run does not merge words together; it leaves a separating space. Treating the policy as “delete all whitespace” would change `Ada Lovelace` into a different string and would not implement the stated behavior. ## Drafts and accepted values A draft is what someone is still editing. A stored value is what an action has accepted. The policy determines the representation of accepted and displayed names, but it does not prescribe that the caret jump after every keystroke or that an input method's partial composition be rewritten while it is active. That distinction leaves room to implement an editing experience without confusing it with persistence. A reviewer can inspect where a completed entry crosses from local draft state into the feature's model and where the model is rendered. If display uses an old raw draft while storage uses the processed value, the two surfaces no longer have the relationship described above. The current Reproduction component provides a useful example of draft ownership, though its data is not a name. Its snapshot string lives in local React state and is sent to the decoder on Load snapshot. BoardCodeForm instead reads its native form field at submission. Either storage approach can host an input boundary; the choice of controlled or uncontrolled field does not by itself implement name representation. No name persistence shape exists in `session/storage.ts`. Its preferences concern size and best move counts. Those fields contain no name preference key, snapshot property or import format. ## Board codes follow a different path The Board code input is a native text input with `maxLength={32}`, spell checking disabled and autocomplete off. On submission, `use-game.ts` calls `code.trim()` before `parseBoardCode(code)`. That is the only cleanup in that loading path. The grammar is a version prefix, supported side length and seed separated by hyphens. For example, surrounding spaces around `np1-6-1` are accepted by the control, but an internal space changes the grammar and is rejected. The loader does not collapse arbitrary interior text or repair the seed. Successful submission replaces the game and refreshes the field from the current code because the input is keyed by generation. Unsuccessful submission preserves the draft. This gives a concrete reference for separating a draft from an accepted representation without applying name transformations to a deal identifier. See [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md). Board-code parsing is also available as a core function. Calling `parseBoardCode` directly is not the same as passing through the UI loader's trim step. When reading a failure report, the entry point matters. A format parser and an input adapter can have distinct responsibilities without the application guessing what malformed identifiers meant. ## Snapshot text remains structured data Snapshot JSON has a native textarea length limit and a decoder byte limit. It can include whitespace for readability, and export deliberately produces multiple lines. Its structure is validated before the game is replaced. Applying name cleanup to the entire JSON draft would conflate two kinds of input. Whitespace can occur between tokens or inside a JSON string, with different meanings. The existing code passes the complete draft to `decodeSnapshot`; it does not first treat it as display prose or a person's name. The same is true for error preservation. On malformed JSON, the text remains editable and the current game remains present. That behavior supports correction of a structured draft. Accepted names use the normalized representation described above. [Import safety policy](../sharing/import-safety-policy.md) and [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) explain the current parser and feedback boundaries. Keeping those links close to the input descriptions is more useful than inventing one universal cleanup function for every field on the page. ## Unicode review considerations Canonical equivalence is easiest to miss when examples are written as visually identical letters. A composed accented character and a base character followed by a combining mark may render alike while having different underlying sequences. A useful representation check includes both forms and inspects the accepted value rather than only its screenshot. The policy also leaves capitalization alone at this representation step. A comparison operation may have its own policy, but that does not require changing a person's displayed capitalization. Keeping display representation and comparison purpose distinct avoids presenting a comparison key as someone's chosen name. Likewise, a font's treatment of a character does not change the text stored. A missing glyph, a ligature or a different script's shaping belongs to rendering and typography. The representation policy can be implemented correctly while a layout still needs work to display the name legibly. [Typography](../visuals/typography.md) provides the visual context. The current game has no name-character allowlist or prohibited-name list. Adding one while implementing spacing cleanup would be a separate product decision, not a consequence of Unicode normalization. ## Implementation evidence to look for There are no name-specific tests in the repository because no name entry has been implemented. The useful evidence for a future implementation would connect its draft, accepted model and displayed text using the cases above. A check confined to an input's current value can miss a storage path that retains an older raw string. Repeated processing should not progressively change the accepted spelling. The transformations described here have a stable result once applied. If editing, saving and displaying the same accepted name repeatedly removes more content each time, that points to an implementation doing more than the stated representation work. The current code's strongest relevant lesson is explicit boundaries: BoardCodeForm submits a draft, the controller validates, replacement updates the model, and rendered controls follow that model. Names need their own representation boundary within the feature that introduces them. The present board-code and snapshot controls use their own input boundaries. --- docs/interface/name-length-policy.md --- --- open-forge: description: Name-length acceptance, Unicode counting units and boundary examples. tags: - Forms - Names - Unicode --- # Name length policy This page defines how the name-length check is interpreted and separates it from native text-field limits. The current game has no person-name field or name validator. Its existing text limits belong to Board code and Snapshot JSON. They are useful examples of browser entry constraints, but neither is an implementation of the name policy on this page. ## The checked value The length check concerns the accepted name representation, after the processing described in [Text entry policy](text-entry-policy.md). Counting the raw draft instead can produce a different result from counting the value that the feature will store and display. A name has 2 to 20 Unicode code points after normalization. Anything else blocks the action and shows "Use 2 to 20 characters." This check therefore belongs at the point where a draft would become an accepted name, rather than being inferred from the field's apparent width. The message is the user-facing explanation of this failure. The numerical bounds are inclusive: the endpoints pass, and values outside them fail. The policy does not define an exception for a one-character name, a separate limit for a family name or an alternate bound for another script. A failure blocks the action that is trying to accept the name. It is not a request to silently cut the entered value to fit. Truncating a longer string would accept a different name and would conceal which action failed. The policy specifies feedback and blocking rather than a repair that guesses the user's intended spelling. ## Code points, code units and visible text JavaScript string `.length` counts UTF-16 code units. That is not always the number required here. Many characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane occupy two code units but one Unicode code point. For example, `A😀` has three code units and two code points. A user-perceived symbol can also contain several code points. An emoji sequence joined with a zero-width joiner may look like one symbol while contributing multiple points. A base letter plus a combining mark can be another example, depending on whether canonical composition produces a single point in the accepted form. The policy chooses code points, not rendered glyph count or grapheme cluster count. A font can draw two code points as one ligature, and an input method can produce a composed-looking sequence. Neither observation changes which unit the check uses. Reviewing only a screenshot cannot establish that the correct unit was counted. In JavaScript, iterating a string by code point is different from indexing its individual UTF-16 units. `Array.from(value).length` or a spread-based count illustrates that distinction for well-formed text. This is an explanatory example, not a requirement to allocate an array in a particular implementation. The source has no name helper. ## Boundary examples The examples below assume that the value shown is already in its accepted representation. They illustrate the count, not an additional character allowlist. | Value | Code-point count | Length result | | --- | --- | --- | | Empty string | 0 | Fails | | `A` | 1 | Fails | | `Al` | 2 | Passes | | `A😀` | 2 | Passes | | Twenty ASCII letters | 20 | Passes | | Twenty-one ASCII letters | 21 | Fails | | Twenty supplementary-plane symbols | 20 | Passes | The supplementary-plane example can expose a validator that accidentally uses `.length`: it sees forty code units instead. The opposite mistake is counting a joined visual sequence as one merely because it occupies one displayed cell. A correct boundary check is about the string's code points after representation processing. “Passes” here means that the length condition is satisfied. It does not imply that an action with other applicable checks is guaranteed to succeed. The [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md) addresses a separate group-level condition without changing the unit used by this check. ## The order is observable A raw draft may have surrounding or repeated spacing that will not be retained in its accepted form. Counting before the representation step can reject a value that would fit after processing, or accept a value whose later transformations were not what the length helper expected. The policy's ordering avoids having the stored name disagree with the checked name. A reviewer can follow one candidate from field submission to accepted model and then display. The decisive value is the same one used for the count. An implementation that checks one temporary string but saves a different raw draft has two representations and cannot establish the stated condition simply by having a correctly named length function. There is no instruction here to run the full action after every individual keystroke. Composition and editing are part of the input experience. The check governs acceptance, while timing of draft feedback is not otherwise specified by the current code or this policy. ## Scope of current evidence There is no name-length test in the repository. Keyboard and reproduction checks establish native field labels, draft preservation and load outcomes. They do not verify the name count merely because they type strings into controls. When this policy is implemented, its evidence can name the processed candidate and observed outcome at the boundary. That is enough to distinguish a counting defect from a display problem or another group-level validation failure. The policy stays narrow: one accepted value, one counting unit, one inclusive interval and the stated blocking message. --- docs/interface/duplicate-names-policy.md --- --- open-forge: description: Group-scoped name comparison, case handling and evidence for repeat detection. tags: - Forms - Names - Validation --- # Duplicate names policy This page explains the group-level name comparison policy and the distinctions a reviewer needs when checking it. The current source has no name list or group editor. A board code identifies a deal, a card label identifies a position and face state, and a local best is indexed by board size. None of those is a collection of person-entered names. The policy below belongs to a feature that introduces such a collection. ## Comparison boundary The group being edited supplies the comparison scope; the draft alone cannot establish whether it repeats an existing entry. The candidate's accepted representation comes from [Text entry policy](text-entry-policy.md). Names in one group compare without regard to case, after normalization. A repeat blocks the action and shows "Each name must be different." This lets the same visible spelling with different capitalization be recognized as a repeat without requiring that all displayed names be rewritten in one case. The scope is one group. Neon Pairs has no global name registry across devices, browser origins or unrelated groups. A local comparison can answer whether an entry repeats within the group being acted on without implying that the person owns a unique account name. The check concerns names, rather than board positions or face identities. Two cards intentionally share a face, and a replay can intentionally activate the same position more than once. Those repetitions follow their own game rules. A generic “remove duplicates everywhere” helper would not express this policy's subject or scope. ## Display value and comparison value Case-insensitive comparison does not by itself prescribe changing a name's displayed capitalization. `Mira` and `mira` can compare as the same candidate while the accepted display spelling remains the one chosen by the person who entered it. Showing a lowercased comparison key as the name would conflate two purposes. A useful implementation trace therefore distinguishes the value displayed, the value accepted into the group and whatever representation is used to compare it. The comparison representation is an internal tool. It is not a new user-visible identifier, a format field or a replacement for the accepted name. The policy does not specify locale selection or a particular Unicode case-folding API. That matters for names whose case behavior differs across languages or scripts. Name normalization retains diacritics and does not transliterate names. Examples with ordinary Latin letters illustrate the unambiguous case while case behavior across Unicode varies. The representation step is also not a license to treat all visually similar strings as equal. Latin and Cyrillic lookalikes, differing accents and compatibility characters can resemble one another without being the same processed string. Visual similarity would be a broader identity rule than the policy states. ## Small examples | Existing accepted name | Candidate | What the example demonstrates | | --- | --- | --- | | `Mira` | `Mira` | A direct repeat | | `Mira` | `mira` | Capitalization does not distinguish the names | | `Mira` | `MIRA` | The comparison is not limited to the first letter | | `Ada Lovelace` | The same name after representation processing | The comparison uses accepted name text | | `Mira` in another group | `Mira` in this group | The stated scope is the group being edited | These cases are illustrations of the policy rather than a complete Unicode test corpus. They also do not decide length validity; [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) covers that independent check. A candidate can satisfy length and still repeat an existing name. A group with several entries can expose a bug that a two-entry example misses. If only the immediately preceding name is checked, a repeat of the first entry can slip through after a different middle entry. The policy speaks about the group, so the relevant evidence is membership across that group rather than adjacency in the rendered form. ## Blocking has a concrete meaning A repeated candidate does not become an accepted additional name as part of the failed action. The exact feedback above explains why acceptance stopped. Automatically adding a suffix, changing capitalization or deleting one of the existing names would implement a different outcome from the one stated. This policy does not decide which error wins when several checks fail at once. It also does not add live validation on every keystroke, a suggestion picker or a search across previous games. Those are separate interaction choices, and none is present in the source. The current reproduction handlers demonstrate an explicit acceptance boundary: parse first, replace only on success, otherwise publish a notice. A name feature can be reviewed with the same question—where does a candidate become accepted?—without reusing the board parser or claiming that load errors are name errors. [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) provides the current feedback mechanics. ## Evidence a reviewer can assess Because no name feature exists, the existing tests do not establish this policy. A screenshot containing distinct visible names would be weak evidence even for a future feature: the comparison bug might only appear on submission, on an edit or after a change in capitalization. Useful examples include an exact repeat, a case-only repeat, a repeat that is not adjacent in the displayed list and a different accepted name. An edit scenario reveals whether the current entry is being confused with another entry. A separate-group example reveals whether an implementation accidentally enforces a broader scope than the policy states. For a defect report, the accepted group values, candidate value, action and observed message make the comparison reproducible. Display order can be recorded as context, but it does not define identity. The policy stays about equality within the group, and its representation and length dependencies remain in their own linked pages.

The complete game pack starts in [Neon Pairs](../README.md). --- docs/interface/control-bar.md --- --- open-forge: description: The deal buttons, size selector, responsive arrangement and session callbacks in Controls.tsx. tags: - Controls - Layout - Session --- # Control bar This page explains how `Controls.tsx` presents the deal actions and how those actions connect to the session. The bar is deliberately small: a labeled size selector, New Game and Restart. It sits above the statistics and board in `src/game/Game.tsx`, so the actions that replace a deal are available before entering the board. Reproduction tools have a different rhythm and occupy their own disclosure below the board; see [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md). ## Component boundary `src/game/controls/Controls.tsx` accepts three props: `size`, `newGame(size?: number)` and `restart()`. Finally load a valid code of another size from the reproduction panel and look back at Grid size: the controlled select follows the loaded game without another local state update. --- docs/interface/announcements-policy.md --- --- open-forge: description: Status publication, repeated event identity, turn results and load feedback. tags: - Input - Accessibility - Status --- # Announcements policy This page describes how event feedback is published, repeated and kept separate from routine game rendering. Names need their own representation boundary within the feature that introduces them. The present board-code and snapshot controls use their own input boundaries. --- docs/interface/name-length-policy.md --- --- open-forge: description: Name-length acceptance, Unicode counting units and boundary examples. tags: - Forms - Names - Unicode --- # Name length policy This page defines how the name-length check is interpreted and separates it from native text-field limits. The current game has no person-name field or name validator. Its existing text limits belong to Board code and Snapshot JSON. They are useful examples of browser entry constraints, but neither is an implementation of the name policy on this page. ## The checked value The length check concerns the accepted name representation, after the processing described in [Text entry policy](text-entry-policy.md). Counting the raw draft instead can produce a different result from counting the value that the feature will store and display. A name has 2 to 20 Unicode code points after normalization. Anything else blocks the action and shows "Use 2 to 20 characters." This check therefore belongs at the point where a draft would become an accepted name, rather than being inferred from the field's apparent width. The message is the user-facing explanation of this failure. The numerical bounds are inclusive: the endpoints pass, and values outside them fail. The policy does not define an exception for a one-character name, a separate limit for a family name or an alternate bound for another script. A failure blocks the action that is trying to accept the name. It is not a request to silently cut the entered value to fit. Truncating a longer string would accept a different name and would conceal which action failed. The policy specifies feedback and blocking rather than a repair that guesses the user's intended spelling. ## Code points, code units and visible text JavaScript string `.length` counts UTF-16 code units. That is not always the number required here. Many characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane occupy two code units but one Unicode code point. For example, `A😀` has three code units and two code points. A user-perceived symbol can also contain several code points. An emoji sequence joined with a zero-width joiner may look like one symbol while contributing multiple points. A base letter plus a combining mark can be another example, depending on whether canonical composition produces a single point in the accepted form. The policy chooses code points, not rendered glyph count or grapheme cluster count. A font can draw two code points as one ligature, and an input method can produce a composed-looking sequence. Neither observation changes which unit the check uses. Reviewing only a screenshot cannot establish that the correct unit was counted. In JavaScript, iterating a string by code point is different from indexing its individual UTF-16 units. `Array.from(value).length` or a spread-based count illustrates that distinction for well-formed text. This is an explanatory example, not a requirement to allocate an array in a particular implementation. The source has no name helper. ## Boundary examples The examples below assume that the value shown is already in its accepted representation. When this policy is implemented, its evidence can name the processed candidate and observed outcome at the boundary. That is enough to distinguish a counting defect from a display problem or another group-level validation failure. The policy stays narrow: one accepted value, one counting unit, one inclusive interval and the stated blocking message. --- docs/interface/duplicate-names-policy.md --- --- open-forge: description: Group-scoped name comparison, case handling and evidence for repeat detection. tags: - Forms - Names - Validation --- # Duplicate names policy This page explains the group-level name comparison policy and the distinctions a reviewer needs when checking it. The current source has no name list or group editor. A board code identifies a deal, a card label identifies a position and face state, and a local best is indexed by board size. None of those is a collection of person-entered names. The policy below belongs to a feature that introduces such a collection. ## Comparison boundary The group being edited supplies the comparison scope; the draft alone cannot establish whether it repeats an existing entry. The candidate's accepted representation comes from [Text entry policy](text-entry-policy.md). Names in one group compare without regard to case, after normalization. A repeat blocks the action and shows "Each name must be different." This lets the same visible spelling with different capitalization be recognized as a repeat without requiring that all displayed names be rewritten in one case. The scope is one group. Neon Pairs has no global name registry across devices, browser origins or unrelated groups. A local comparison can answer whether an entry repeats within the group being acted on without implying that the person owns a unique account name. The check concerns names, rather than board positions or face identities. Two cards intentionally share a face, and a replay can intentionally activate the same position more than once. Those repetitions follow their own game rules. A generic “remove duplicates everywhere” helper would not express this policy's subject or scope. ## Display value and comparison value Case-insensitive comparison does not by itself prescribe changing a name's displayed capitalization. `Mira` and `mira` can compare as the same candidate while the accepted display spelling remains the one chosen by the person who entered it. Showing a lowercased comparison key as the name would conflate two purposes. A useful implementation trace therefore distinguishes the value displayed, the value accepted into the group and whatever representation is used to compare it. The comparison representation is an internal tool. It is not a new user-visible identifier, a format field or a replacement for the accepted name. The policy does not specify locale selection or a particular Unicode case-folding API. That matters for names whose case behavior differs across languages or scripts. Name normalization retains diacritics and does not transliterate names. Examples with ordinary Latin letters illustrate the unambiguous case while case behavior across Unicode varies. The representation step is also not a license to treat all visually similar strings as equal. Latin and Cyrillic lookalikes, differing accents and compatibility characters can resemble one another without being the same processed string. Visual similarity would be a broader identity rule than the policy states. ## Small examples | Existing accepted name | Candidate | What the example demonstrates | | --- | --- | --- | | `Mira` | `Mira` | A direct repeat | | `Mira` | `mira` | Capitalization does not distinguish the names | | `Mira` | `MIRA` | The comparison is not limited to the first letter | | `Ada Lovelace` | The same name after representation processing | The comparison uses accepted name text | | `Mira` in another group | `Mira` in this group | The stated scope is the group being edited | These cases are illustrations of the policy rather than a complete Unicode test corpus. They also do not decide length validity; [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) covers that independent check. A candidate can satisfy length and still repeat an existing name. A group with several entries can expose a bug that a two-entry example misses. If only the immediately preceding name is checked, a repeat of the first entry can slip through after a different middle entry. The policy speaks about the group, so the relevant evidence is membership across that group rather than adjacency in the rendered form. ## Blocking has a concrete meaning A repeated candidate does not become an accepted additional name as part of the failed action. The exact feedback above explains why acceptance stopped. Automatically adding a suffix, changing capitalization or deleting one of the existing names would implement a different outcome from the one stated. This policy does not decide which error wins when several checks fail at once. It also does not add live validation on every keystroke, a suggestion picker or a search across previous games. Those are separate interaction choices, and none is present in the source. The current reproduction handlers demonstrate an explicit acceptance boundary: parse first, replace only on success, otherwise publish a notice. A name feature can be reviewed with the same question—where does a candidate become accepted?—without reusing the board parser or claiming that load errors are name errors. [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) provides the current feedback mechanics. ## Evidence a reviewer can assess Because no name feature exists, the existing tests do not establish this policy. A screenshot containing distinct visible names would be weak evidence even for a future feature: the comparison bug might only appear on submission, on an edit or after a change in capitalization. Useful examples include an exact repeat, a case-only repeat, a repeat that is not adjacent in the displayed list and a different accepted name. An edit scenario reveals whether the current entry is being confused with another entry. A separate-group example reveals whether an implementation accidentally enforces a broader scope than the policy states. For a defect report, the accepted group values, candidate value, action and observed message make the comparison reproducible. Display order can be recorded as context, but it does not define identity. The policy stays about equality within the group, and its representation and length dependencies remain in their own linked pages.
