On failure from the keyboard, the user remains in the draft. Clicking the button naturally leaves focus on that button in either case.
docs/interface/reproduction-panel.md:51:The textarea is full width and vertically resizable. It provides ordinary text selection and copy behavior. Export places readable JSON into this field; the user can select it manually. There is no permission prompt for clipboard access and no dependency on an available Clipboard API.
docs/persistence/storage-failure-policy.md:19:The preference adapter still exposes no blocked-status result: `readPreferences` returns preferences and `writePreferences` returns `void`. The tournament adapter returns history with an `available` flag and a boolean write result. Its warning applies to tournament history; it does not claim that the separate preference write failed.
docs/persistence/storage-failure-policy.md:53:There is no queue, timer-driven retry, backoff or unload handler. Another dependency change can cause another attempt, but the code does not poll for a browser setting to change. A returned `null` store is captured in state for the lifetime of that mounted game; enabling storage later does not replace that state value automatically.
docs/persistence/storage-failure-policy.md:57:The writer's lack of a success result also means the existing UI cannot distinguish a rejected write from a successful one. This is a deliberate limit of the current adapter, not a hidden confirmation mechanism. Any investigation that needs that distinction can observe the supplied store in a test.
docs/persistence/storage-failure-policy.md:69:The storage adapters call `getItem` and `setItem` only for their own preference or tournament-history key. Neither uses a storage-wide clear call, key enumeration or cleanup routine. Their store interfaces expose only those two methods. The preference storage test explicitly seeds an unrelated key and checks that a preference write leaves its value intact.
docs/interface/target-size-policy.md:66:The reproduction summary is another useful case. Its text and disclosure marker occupy only part of a padded native summary element. The element supplies the disclosure interaction. Replacing it with a visually similar small icon could change both target size and semantics; the current source does neither.
docs/interface/target-size-policy.md:80:Those checks establish the existing tested elements at their stated layouts. They do not automatically cover a future control merely because it shares a color or appears next to a tested button. The source selectors and actual bounding box identify the scope of evidence.
docs/interface/target-size-policy.md:84:The current game makes many of these checks straightforward by keeping interaction on native DOM elements. There is no canvas hit-map to reconcile with a drawn target. [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) explains that architectural advantage, while [Contrast audit](../visuals/contrast-audit.md) and [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) cover other properties that a dimension alone cannot establish.
docs/interface/native-controls-guide.md:37:The board's keydown handler only handles plain arrows with a navigation target. It does not call activation for Enter or Space and then also allow a native click. That avoids two paths processing one keyboard action. The game's pure activation guard still decides whether the card is eligible.
docs/interface/native-controls-guide.md:47:The component handles change by converting the selected value to a number and calling `newGame`. There is no local menu-open flag, active-option state or custom pointer hit testing. The controller still checks supported sizes, because native options are an interface aid rather than the only trust boundary.
docs/interface/native-controls-guide.md:65:The reproduction panel uses details with a summary, starts collapsed and relies on native expansion. There is no handler toggling an `expanded` variable or emulating summary key activation. The CSS styles the panel and summary without changing their source order.
docs/interface/native-controls-guide.md:77:The matched check mark is also an aria-hidden, nonfocusable SVG. It reinforces state visually while the button name and disabled property express it through the control. [Card artwork](../visuals/card-artwork.md) and [Screen reader notes](screen-reader-notes.md) describe those channels more fully.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:16:## Existing page and future screens
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:22:Expanding native details, updating statistics, closing a mismatch or displaying the completed-game paragraph does not create a new screen. Within Tournament, the Start turn button hands focus to the new board, Next turn and Next match focus the following Start turn button, and completion focuses Back to game. [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) covers the separate opening focus for its confirmation.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:36:The replacement increments `session.generation`, used as Board's React key. The newly mounted hook begins with a remembered index of zero. Thus the next board entry goes to the first card, even if the previous deal's memory was near its end. Actual action focus and future board entry are updated through different mechanisms.
docs/persistence/corrupt-data-policy.md:109:Stored preference rejection happens during initialization with no draft to correct in the game UI. It returns a playable state quietly. There is no recovery dialog, corrupted-data banner or download of rejected text. Browser access failure also returns defaults, but concerns operation availability rather than text acceptance; see [Storage failure policy](storage-failure-policy.md).
docs/interface/text-entry-policy.md:18:A name can arrive with incidental spaces from typing, pasting or an input method. Keeping several representations of that same entered name would make later display and comparison harder to reason about. Every name a person types is stored and shown after trimming both ends, collapsing each run of inner whitespace to one space and normalizing to NFC. The stored value and visible value therefore describe the same processed name rather than exposing the original draft in one view and a different spelling in another.
docs/interface/text-entry-policy.md:20:The policy is about a person's name. It does not turn all user input into name text, and it does not change the board-code grammar or snapshot serialization. The current fields demonstrate why that distinction matters: significant punctuation and structural whitespace belong to their own formats.
docs/interface/text-entry-policy.md:26:The following examples use quotes only to make surrounding whitespace visible. The quotes are not part of the entered name.
docs/interface/text-entry-policy.md:36:The last example matters because representation cleanup is not an instruction to remove meaningful punctuation or rewrite a person's preferred spelling. The policy does not transliterate scripts, strip accents or convert names to ASCII. Those would be additional transformations beyond what is stated.
docs/interface/text-entry-policy.md:38:NFC addresses canonical equivalence in Unicode text. It is not the compatibility normalization form. Text that merely looks similar is not necessarily canonically equivalent, and this policy does not define visual resemblance as identity. That boundary prevents a representation step from quietly becoming a broad name-matching heuristic.
docs/interface/text-entry-policy.md:48:Tournament's player inputs are controlled draft fields. On submission, `validatePlayerNames` returns the normalized values that become the tournament participants and are then displayed in the bracket. The choice of controlled or uncontrolled field does not by itself implement name representation.
docs/interface/text-entry-policy.md:50:Player names do not enter `session/storage.ts` or the solo preference value. They are carried by tournament JSON and by completed tournament records in the separate tournament-history key.
docs/interface/text-entry-policy.md:66:Applying name cleanup to the entire JSON draft would conflate two kinds of input. Whitespace can occur between tokens or inside a JSON string, with different meanings. The existing code passes the complete draft to `decodeSnapshot`; it does not first treat it as display prose or a person's name.
docs/interface/text-entry-policy.md:76:The policy also leaves capitalization alone at this representation step. A comparison operation may have its own policy, but that does not require changing a person's displayed capitalization. Keeping display representation and comparison purpose distinct avoids presenting a comparison key as someone's chosen name.
docs/interface/text-entry-policy.md:78:Likewise, a font's treatment of a character does not change the text stored. A missing glyph, a ligature or a different script's shaping belongs to rendering and typography. The representation policy can be implemented correctly while a layout still needs work to display the name legibly. [Typography](../visuals/typography.md) provides the visual context.
docs/interface/text-entry-policy.md:80:The current game has no name-character allowlist or prohibited-name list. Adding one while implementing spacing cleanup would be a separate product decision, not a consequence of Unicode normalization.
docs/interface/text-entry-policy.md:84:The current test record does not establish name-specific behavior. Review can connect the setup draft, accepted tournament model, bracket display and exported value using the cases above. A check confined to an input's current value can miss a storage path that retains an older raw string.
docs/interface/text-entry-policy.md:86:Repeated processing should not progressively change the accepted spelling. The transformations described here have a stable result once applied. If editing, saving and displaying the same accepted name repeatedly removes more content each time, that points to an implementation doing more than the stated representation work.
docs/persistence/persistence-overview.md:13:The game stores solo preferences under `neon-pairs.preferences.v1` and completed tournament history under `np3:tournaments`. Preferences remember the selected board size and the lowest completed move count for each size; they do not contain a saved game. Tournament history keeps the ten most recent completed brackets. Reloading solo play starts a fresh deal at the remembered size, while finished tournaments remain in Past tournaments.
docs/persistence/persistence-overview.md:23:Here the next page load starts a new 6x6 game. The best displayed while playing that size is 20. Choosing 4x4 exposes the independent best of 9. There is no record for 8x8, so the status displays `none` for that size. The selected size does not have to be the only size represented in the score map.
docs/persistence/persistence-overview.md:40:- An unfinished tournament is not saved automatically. Export Tournament JSON to preserve its setup or progress outside the current page.
docs/persistence/persistence-overview.md:66:The app does not synchronize preference or tournament-history changes between open tabs. Each tab reads its initial value and writes its own in-memory state. One tab can overwrite another tab's changes; the specification explicitly leaves several simultaneous game windows outside the supported journeys.
docs/persistence/storage-quota-notes.md:43:A nominal allowance is not a reservation for Neon Pairs. Browser policy can prevent writes from the beginning. Other values on the same origin can consume capacity. Private browsing can give data a shorter lifetime even if writing works. A small serialized value therefore supports the claim that the application contributes little storage, but does not prove a future write will succeed.
docs/persistence/storage-quota-notes.md:57:There is no test that fills a physical browser storage area to its exact capacity. There is no recorded capacity sweep for Firefox or Safari in the test suite. The README reports Chromium journeys on its named compatibility combination; that is functional evidence for the game, not a general quota benchmark. An engineer should not attach a browser-specific measured threshold to these results.
docs/interface/pointer-and-touch.md:20:There is no face-specific pointer handler. Whether the click reveals a card is decided in the session and game functions. Matched cards, the already revealed first card, out-of-range indices and activation during a mismatch have no game effect. Imported paused games are blocked at the session boundary. A click handler can therefore run without a counter or selection changing.
docs/interface/pointer-and-touch.md:30:There is no application constant for gesture distance or press duration. Adding one would change the interaction model and would need evidence beyond a visual review.
docs/interface/pointer-and-touch.md:76:Matched cards retain their full-opacity face and green border when hovered. Clicking one does not add a move. Their continued presence as buttons allows a pointer user to revisit a remembered position and a keyboard user to traverse a consistent grid. [Disabled state guide](disabled-state-guide.md) discusses why semantic unavailability is not implemented as removal from focus order.
docs/persistence/private-browsing-notes.md:14:Private browsing and blocked storage are different conditions. A private context may allow the preference write and a same-session reload to work, then remove that data when the private session ends. A blocked context may reject the storage getter or a method immediately. Neon Pairs does not detect private browsing or branch on a browser mode name; it responds to the storage operations available to the mounted page.
docs/persistence/private-browsing-notes.md:30:There is no server copy, browser-account synchronization or preference export path in the game that restores the earlier aggregate. A board code reproduces a deal, not the private context's remembered settings. A snapshot restores one game position, not the browser's collection of local bests. [Sharing FAQ](../sharing/sharing-faq.md) and [Persistence overview](persistence-overview.md) explain these boundaries.
docs/persistence/private-browsing-notes.md:36:A store can also be obtainable while `getItem` or `setItem` throws. The reader and writer catch those failures independently. There is no need for the game to identify whether the cause is private browsing, a site setting or a browser policy. [Storage failure policy](storage-failure-policy.md) covers the feature presentation and the current adapter's silent behavior.
docs/interface/board-keyboard-navigation.md:14:The board has many card buttons but only a single card in the page's tab sequence. Arrow keys explore the board after entry. Enter and Space use the native button activation path. The useful distinction is between choosing where focus goes and choosing a card for a turn: movement can happen while play is temporarily blocked.
docs/interface/board-keyboard-navigation.md:41:Before the switch, the function checks `ctrlKey`, `altKey`, `shiftKey` and `metaKey`. If any is true, it returns null. The switch recognizes only the four plain arrow key strings. Home, End, Tab a
... command output truncated for persistence ...
ot` fills the textarea with a point-in-time representation. The player can select and copy that text manually. There is no dependency on the Clipboard API, no upload step and no account exchange. Export does not put the live session into the imported pause state. If the source game keeps running while the text is copied, the later source position may differ from the exported one.
docs/sharing/data-exchange-policy.md:72:All copied or loaded data is untrusted. “Valid snapshot” means that the object satisfies the documented state constraints, not that its claimed result has a verified play history. The same is true of tournament JSON: validation establishes a structurally consistent bracket, not that its participants achieved the recorded results. A hand-edited object can be accepted if its fields remain consistent.
docs/sharing/data-exchange-policy.md:74:Replays give a more explicit history, but they still contain author-supplied actions and times. The evaluator applies normal rules, including ignored activations, and does not attest who supplied the file. There is no authentication or signed result in the current exchange model. Local best moves are local game records, not a remote ranking service.
docs/architecture/react-boundaries.md:19:The component tree is intentionally direct. There is no React context carrying a global game store and no router. `Controls` receives size and solo actions. `GameStatus` receives a game, an optional best and a celebration flag. `Board` receives a game and activation action. `Reproduction` receives current code context and exchange actions. `Tournament` owns its setup draft, tournament controller, transfer box, confirmation and history view.
docs/architecture/react-boundaries.md:27:The board has data-only helpers too. `keyboard.ts` computes a target from keys and coordinates. `card-state.ts` computes a state description. `face-design.ts` maps an integer identity to design values. These helpers can be tested without rendering `Board` or building a synthetic browser tree.
docs/architecture/react-boundaries.md:45:| `use-session-clock.ts` | Clock/visibility refs and timer effect |
docs/architecture/react-boundaries.md:88:This behavior is also why tests use documented board codes rather than a diagnostic global. A test can reconstruct a deal independently and activate matching positions through the public interface. There is no application solver endpoint that a production user or test needs to query.
docs/sharing/format-versioning-guide.md:27:This is why replacing a JSON `version` with a product release string fails. The current readers compare the parsed value directly with their numeric constant. The string `"1"` is also different from number `1`. There is no negotiation, version range or “closest supported version” branch.
docs/sharing/format-versioning-guide.md:37:The general policies for future exchange objects and field diagnostics are in [Data exchange policy](data-exchange-policy.md) and [Import safety](import-safety-policy.md). They are separate from the accepted version 1 wire definitions. Reading a policy page does not make the current decoder accept fields absent from its exact-key lists.
docs/sharing/format-versioning-guide.md:71:The source currently supplies only single-version readers, not a general migration framework. Any future version handling will need concrete design work at the affected format. The existing boundaries remain the starting evidence: [Snapshot format](snapshot-format.md), [Replay format](replay-format.md) and [Reproducibility](reproducibility.md).

# Tables policy

This page records the markup policy for ordered result data and explains why the current game statistics use a different structure.

The solo UI uses a definition list for one game's statistics. Tournament uses an HTML table for bracket rows, with a caption and scoped column headings. The card board remains a CSS grid of buttons; those different structures serve different data.

## Policy for result data

When the content represents records with comparable columns, its relationships need to survive reading beyond the visual arrangement. CSS alone can align text while leaving those relationships absent from the document structure. Ranked or bracket data is a table element with a caption and th scope="col" header cells. The caption identifies the collection being read, while the column headers connect each record's values to their meaning.

This is a content-specific policy. It does not make the game board a data table because it has rows and columns, and it does not require converting every compact summary to tabular markup. The distinction begins with what the content means: interactive card coordinates, a property's value and a record in an ordered result collection are different things.

No such result feature is present in `Game.tsx`. The policy applies when result data is introduced. [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) discusses the broader preference for native semantics without adding another result format.

## Why the statistics are a definition list

GameStatus renders Moves, Pairs, Time and Best as four `dt`/`dd` groups inside a `dl`. Each term names a property of the same current game. There are no peer result rows and no column whose meaning changes with the row being read.

The layout happens to use flex and can wrap. At a wide width, those groups may look like cells in a horizontal strip. At a narrow width, they can flow to multiple lines. Neither visual arrangement changes the definition-list relationship. Replacing the wrapper with a table solely to preserve one desktop arrangement would confuse layout with content structure.

The Best value is one saved move count selected by current size. It does not present a list of people or a comparison across many records. `session.preferences.bestMoves[String(game.size)]` chooses the value before it reaches GameStatus. A single local best is not an implemented ordered-results screen.

[Status bar](status-bar.md) documents those expressions and labels. The present statistics model has no result columns.

## Why the card board is not a table

Board renders a named region containing an inner `div.board` and native card buttons. CSS Grid places those buttons in row order. Each card has its own coordinate and state in its accessible name, and keyboard movement follows a dedicated spatial model.

The table policy does not turn that interactive surface into a data table. A card is activated, can reveal a face and participates in remembered focus. A result cell is read as part of a record. They have different purposes even if both appear in a rectangle.

There is also no ARIA grid role on the current board. Its native buttons and movement handler implement the specified interaction without declaring a separate composite widget role. [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) traces that behavior. A review of result markup should not accidentally rename or restructure the card controls because the word “row” appears in both contexts.

## What the caption contributes

An ordered collection needs context. A visible title elsewhere on a page can be helpful, but a table caption directly identifies the collection associated with the table. That matters when reading the table independently or navigating between document structures.

The bracket caption is “Tournament bracket.” A table's caption should identify the data the table presents; technical details about markup belong in documentation rather than product copy.

A caption also does not supply missing column meaning. A reader needs to know whether a number represents moves, a position in an ordering or another property. The required header cells carry the column relationships; the caption names the whole collection. Combining all labels into a caption would leave the row values harder to interpret.

## Column relationships and reading order

The `scope="col"` attribute makes the header's direction explicit. It communicates that the header applies to values down its column. A bold `td`, a styled `div` or text positioned above a column can look similar while having a different structure.

A reviewer can inspect the table DOM and the browser's accessibility representation separately from the screenshot. The screenshot establishes visible arrangement. The DOM establishes element choices and attributes. The accessibility view helps establish that the browser exposes a meaningful table structure. No single one of these views proves all aspects of the interface.

Row headers, column order, numeric alignment and sorting controls depend on the result feature. The current game has no result implementation with those details.

## Narrow layouts and long values

The current game already separates outer page width from board overflow. Result data would have its own content and width behavior; it cannot simply inherit the card board's scroll logic by sharing a class name. A table's relationship between headers and values remains meaningful even when its viewport is narrow.

There is no table stylesheet in the source and no prescribed responsive table transformation here. A reviewer can still observe whether a proposed layout makes values readable and associated with their headers. Changing a collection into a stack of unrelated labels solely at a breakpoint can affect more than appearance, so both DOM and visual behavior are relevant evidence.

Name text can also vary in width without changing its accepted value. Typography and wrapping are layout concerns. The name policies remain separate from table structure; accepted names retain their displayed representation. [Typography](../visuals/typography.md) and [Form layout guide](form-layout-guide.md) explain nearby layout decisions in the existing interface.

The existing accessibility journey covers game controls and completion, not a result table. Evidence for a future result view would identify its actual markup and readable rows; the current statistics tests cannot establish that structure. [Accessibility audit](../quality/accessibility-audit.md) provides the wider review context.

# Error display guide

This page explains how failed board-code and snapshot loads are reported without replacing the current game.

The current UI has two validation outcomes that are errors: `Invalid board code.` and `Invalid snapshot.`. They describe the attempted load, not a broken game. The player can correct the draft and retry while the current deal remains available.

## The visible location

Reproduction renders a paragraph with `id="load-notice"` and class `load-notice` inside `.load-status`. That container follows the native details element. It is adjacent to the reproduction tools but outside their collapsible body.

Both Load board and Load snapshot carry `aria-describedby="load-notice"`. Their visible names remain the action labels; the description associates the nearby outcome with those actions. The field labels stay Board code and Snapshot JSON rather than being replaced with an error sentence.

Because the paragraph is outside details, it remains in document flow when the panel is closed. A person does not have to reopen the JSON field merely to see the most recent load notice or Resume. The `.load-status` flex row wraps, has a `12px` gap and a `56px` minimum height; its paragraph can grow and shrink within the available width.

The same load outcome is also published through the game's feedback path. [Announcements policy](announcements-policy.md) describes that event handling. The local paragraph's role here is visible context beside the load tools, not a second independent validation system.

## Who decides that a load failed

BoardCodeForm reads its draft through FormData and calls the `loadBoard` prop. The controller in `use-game.ts` trims surrounding whitespace and checks `parseBoardCode`. Failure calls `notice(SessionNotice.invalidBoard)` and returns false before clock reset or replacement.

Reproduction passes the complete snapshot draft to `loadSnapshot`. The controller calls `decodeSnapshot`. Failure calls `notice(SessionNotice.invalidSnapshot)` and returns false, again before resetting or replacing the game. The textarea component does not try to validate JSON structure itself.

`SessionNotice` in `session.ts` owns the literal messages. The shared `notice` helper sets both `feedback` and `loadNotice` and advances announcement identity. The exact words therefore come from the session boundary that knows the operation failed, rather than being duplicated in each field's change handler.

This ordering is important. If a load reset the timer before parsing, even an invalid draft could alter play. If it replaced the game before reporting failure, the notice would not describe the preservation behavior promised by the controls specification. The current callbacks validate first.

## What a failure preserves

A failed board-code load leaves the input's DOM node intact because generation does not change. Its edited value remains available. A failed snapshot load leaves Reproduction's local string state intact. Neither failure clears the draft to make the panel look clean.

The game object, board size, matched positions, selection, moves and elapsed state are not replaced by the error path. The existing game can continue to advance active time. An invalid input is not an imported pause, and it does not freeze a pending mismatch merely because a notice appeared.

Focus memory also survives because Board is not remounted. A player who last visited a far card can return there after correcting a form. The current saved size is unchanged by a failed load; successful replacement is what updates that preference.

The load notice is a session field separate from the game. Adding it can produce a render without changing card state. This is why comparing the complete session object for identity is different from asserting that gameplay was replaced. [Game state model](../gameplay/game-state-model.md) and [Session module](../architecture/session-module.md) explain those boundaries.

## Focus depends on how submission began

A click on Load board ordinarily leaves focus on the button. If the code is invalid, BoardCodeForm does not issue another focus call. A keyboard Enter submission from inside Board code leaves focus in the field on failure, so the user can continue editing.

On successful Enter submission, the input is about to be replaced because it is keyed by generation. BoardCodeForm explicitly focuses its Load board ref when the callback returns true. That is a success-path focus correction, not an error-summary jump.

Load snapshot is a `type="button"` action. Its handler passes local text to the controller and does not move focus elsewhere on failure or success. The snapshot textarea stays mounted. Export likewise keeps its action focus and fills the field rather than focusing or selecting it automatically.

These cases show why “errors focus the field” would be an inaccurate description of this interface. The source preserves the user's current interaction where it can. [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) covers the complete set of current focus transfers.

## Notices are outcomes, not sticky field annotations

`loadNotice` is one session string used for the latest published load outcome. It is not an error object keyed separately by field. The UI does not render two simultaneous field-specific error paragraphs or an error list above the panel.

After an invalid Board code attempt followed by an invalid snapshot attempt, the visible notice is the snapshot message. The Board code draft can still be invalid; the notice records the most recent action rather than continuously describing all field values.

Editing the snapshot string changes local state but does not itself clear the controller's notice. Editing Board code is native uncontrolled editing and likewise does not call a notice-clearing function. The outcome can remain visible while the user works on a correction.

Export replaces textarea text but does not explicitly clear `loadNotice`. Card turns update feedback without rewriting the load notice. New Game, Restart and a successful board-code replacement clear both through `replaceGame(..., false)`. Successful snapshot loading replaces the notice with its load outcome, and Resume clears it when continuing play.

This lifecycle explains a report that an old load message is still visible after editing. The message is action feedback, not a live validator attached to every keystroke. Adding an on-change clearing behavior would be a change to this lifecycle, not a fix to a missing CSS state.

## Format validity is more than native limits

Board code has a 32-character entry cap, but many shorter strings are invalid. An unsupported size, zero seed, leading zeros or malformed separators fail the parser even when the input is well below its native maximum. The loader's surrounding trim is a deliberate adapter step, not broad syntax repair.

Snapshot JSON has a 65536-character textarea limit and a UTF-8 byte bound in the decoder. Malformed JSON is only one failure kind. Unsupported versions, unknown properties, inconsistent matched positions, invalid selections and out-of-range counters can also produce the same UI error.

The UI intentionally gives the short outcome rather than exposing the decoder's internal reasoning. There is no implemented per-property error report or highlighted JSON line number. [Import safety policy](../sharing/import-safety-policy.md) and [Snapshot format](../sharing/snapshot-format.md) are the useful debugging references for engineers handling a rejected draft.

A completed valid snapshot is not an error merely because its result exceeds the local stored best. It loads as completed with a completion notice and static banner. An unfinished valid snapshot loads paused with an instruction to resume. The notice area carries both success and failure outcomes, so `.load-notice` is a more accurate name than a field-specific error class.

## Existing visual and semantic treatment

The notice paragraph uses the surrounding document styles and the load-status layout. The current fields do not receive `aria-invalid`, an error border class or an inline replacement label on failure. Those absences are part of the existing markup, not evidence that validation did not run.

The paragraph can wrap and has `min-width: 0` in its flex row. Resume can wrap alongside it on a constrained viewport. There is no absolute positioning that places a message over the field. [Form layout guide](form-layout-guide.md) explains how the notice row relates to the grid inside the disclosure.

Name-related errors do not exist in the current component tree. Their policies are in [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) and [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md). The load forms use their own messages and have no shared name-error component.

## Evidence for preservation and retry

`tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` populates progress, submits both invalid drafts and compares exported state before and after. It also advances the browser clock to show that the preserved game is still running. That distinguishes failure preservation from an accidental reset or pause.

`tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` submits a valid code with Enter, then an invalid code, checking both focus and the unchanged card count. `tests/controls.e2e.test.ts` checks exact notices, retained drafts and action focus. Repeated invalid submissions are covered in the announcement and accessibility journeys.

A useful defect report includes the draft, action origin, notice text and a before/after state observation. For example, an invalid snapshot followed by an unchanged exported selection is evidence of preservation. A notice alone cannot prove it, and a preserved game alone cannot prove that the user was told what happened. Reviewing both gives the error path its full meaning.
The hook is a small effect:

```ts
useEffect(() => {
  writePreferences(store, preferences);
}, [preferences, store]);
```

There is no queue, timer-driven retry, backoff or unload handler. Another dependency change can cause another attempt, but the code does not poll for a browser setting to change. A returned `null` store is captured in state for the lifetime of that mounted game; enabling storage later does not replace that state value automatically.

If the captured store object exists and its methods change behavior, a later effect can succeed using the same object. For example, a test double can reject its first write and accept a later one. That is different from reacquiring a previously inaccessible property. Both cases can be modeled without making the game rules aware of browser error names.

The writer's lack of a success result also means the existing UI cannot distinguish a rejected write from a successful one. This is a deliberate limit of the current adapter, not a hidden confirmation mechanism. Any investigation that needs that distinction can observe the supplied store in a test.

## Read failure and corrupt data have different evidence

A denied read and an invalid JSON value both lead to fallback preferences. Only the former establishes that an operation could not be completed. A parse failure establishes that the browser returned text which the application could not use. Confusing the two can lead to a misleading message about browser settings when the actual issue is an edited value.

Similarly, a quota error does not mean the existing value is invalid. The old string may remain perfectly readable while the new result exists only in memory. A person may see a better current best and then see the older best after reload. That sequence is a useful way to reproduce a failed update without damaging a valid baseline.

[Corrupt data policy](corrupt-data-policy.md) follows the rejection branches in detail. [Storage quota notes](storage-quota-notes.md) explains why the small size of this app's own payload cannot establish that a shared origin has available space.

## Errors do not authorize deleting other data

The storage adapters call `getItem` and `setItem` only for their own preference or tournament-history key. Neither uses a storage-wide clear call, key enumeration or cleanup routine. Their store interfaces expose only those two methods. The preference storage test explicitly seeds an unrelated key and checks that a preference write leaves its value intact.

This matters in shared local environments, where another page can occupy the same origin. A rejected preference write does not cause Neon Pairs to free space by deleting that page's values. The current fallback is simply to continue without a successful save. The app also does not switch to cookies, a server endpoint or another browser database after failure.

When reproducing capacity problems, a disposable origin or isolated browser context keeps artificial fill data away from a person's real preferences. That is a testing technique rather than an extra product recovery path. The test can remove the keys it created afterward; the shipped game contains no such test cleanup behavior.

## Evidence in the test suite

`storage.test.ts` uses a denied store whose read and write methods both throw. It checks that reading yields the default size and that writing does not throw. It also covers `readPreferences(null)`. This verifies the API boundary directly, without needing to configure an actual browser's privacy settings.

The browser environment test covers a different boundary: acquisition of `window.localStorage`. It installs the throwing getter before loading the game, loads a fixed board and matches a known pair. The harness gathers uncaught page errors and checks that none occurred. That demonstrates continued play after an acquisition failure, not persistence in that denied context.

These tests don't establish every browser policy or a physical disk limit. They also don't assert the saved-record feature notice described earlier. Reading the test title alone can obscure those limits; the actual injection point and assertions show what each test proves. [Storage testing guide](storage-testing-guide.md) extends that evidence into an investigation workflow.

# Focus policy

This page records focus behavior in the current game and the policy for a feature that changes the main screen.

Focus tells a keyboard user where input will go next. It is related to game selection but is not stored as part of a turn or snapshot. The current interface deliberately keeps deal-action focus, remembered board focus and card reveal state as distinct things.

## Existing page and future screens

`Game.tsx` switches the main area between Play and Tournament. Both screens have an h2 with `tabIndex="-1"`; when the screen changes, focus moves to its heading. The initial Play screen does not move focus on page load.

A screen replacement has a different orientation problem from resetting a deck. When a feature replaces what the main area shows, focus moves to that screen's h2, which has tabindex="-1". This gives the new screen a programmatic landing place without adding that heading to ordinary Tab traversal.

Expanding native details, updating statistics, closing a mismatch or displaying the completed-game paragraph does not create a new screen. Within Tournament, the Start turn button hands focus to the new board, Next turn and Next match focus the following Start turn button, and completion focuses Back to game. [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) covers the separate opening focus for its confirmation.

## Initial load is quiet

The hook `useBoardFocus(size)` initializes `focused` to zero. Board gives index 0 a tab index of zero and the other card buttons a tab index of minus one. This makes the first card available on entry, but no mount effect calls its focus method.

The browser's current focus therefore remains where it is at initial load. The page does not jump down to the board before a player has found Grid size or New Game. The board help paragraph describes how to enter and operate it. Its region uses `aria-describedby="board-help"` to associate those instructions with the board.

A remembered entry point is often described casually as “focus on the first card.” In this code that wording is incomplete. There is an entry point ready at the first card, while actual focus may be on the document, a deal button or another native control. Keeping those concepts separate prevents accidental mount-time focus stealing.

## Deal actions retain their location

New Game and Restart are native buttons that call the session controller. Neither callback moves focus into the board. After either action, a keyboard user remains on the button they used and can repeat the action or Tab toward the board. The size select uses its native interaction and likewise does not issue a board focus call.

The replacement increments `session.generation`, used as Board's React key. The newly mounted hook begins with a remembered index of zero. Thus the next board entry goes to the first card, even if the previous deal's memory was near its end. Actual action focus and future board entry are updated through different mechanisms.

A valid board-code load also increments generation. BoardCodeForm focuses its Load board ref on successful submission because its input is keyed by generation and will be replaced. That is especially important when the action was Enter in the input. An invalid submission keeps the input node and does not call the button ref, so correction can continue in place.

Clicking the load button starts with focus on that button, and an invalid click leaves it there. The distinction is based on the action's origin and successful input replacement, not on a general rule that all errors move focus into a field. [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) follows those cases in detail.

## Remembered board focus

Board focus memory is a local hook state containing a card index. The `onFocus` callback updates it whenever a card receives focus. Board renders exactly that index with `tabIndex={0}`. All other cards remain programmatically focusable with `tabIndex={-1}`.

Arrow movement uses the DOM order of the deck and never changes game selection on its own. Tab and Shift+Tab are left to the browser, so the board is one stop in the page sequence rather than a trap. Returning to it finds the last focused card, even if that card is now matched.

Matched positions stay in the navigation geometry. A player does not need to relearn how many arrow presses separate two coordinates after a match. During a mismatch, focus can also move while activation is blocked. The same is true while imported unfinished progress waits for Resume. [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) provides the calculations and edge behavior.

## Resume transfers before removal

Resume is the current exception to retaining focus on the action button. It exists only while `session.paused` is true. Clearing that flag removes the button, so leaving focus there would leave a disappearing target.

In `Game.tsx`, the local `resume()` function first calls `board.current?.focusRemembered()` and then `controller.resume()`. Board's imperative method focuses the remembered card with `preventScroll: true` and then brings it into view. Only after that does the controller clear the paused state and notices.

The ordering is observable. `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` installs a focus listener and confirms that Resume is still present when the card receives focus. A visual assertion after the fact would not establish this timing. The focus-entry test also remembers a far card on a large imported board, scrolls away and confirms that Resume returns to that location with nearest alignment.

The remembered location after import is initially the first card because the import replaced the board. The player can change it while paused. Resume uses that current memory rather than the snapshot's revealed index or a hard-coded first card. A snapshot stores game progress, not the browser's last navigation location.

## Visible focus and scroll clearance

`game.css` defines `:focus-visible` as a `3px` white outline with a `2px` offset. `card.css` gives cards `scroll-margin: 6px`. This combination accommodates the ring when the card is brought to the edge of the scroll area.

The focus hook uses `card.matches(':focus-visible')` before scrolling in `cardFocused`. Keyboard movement can scroll immediately; pointer focus avoids moving a card under a held press. Board scrolls a clicked card after the click completes. The timing is part of reliable focus behavior, not only a visual polish detail.

`useNearestScroll` stores the board's last reported scroll position, restores it and then invokes `scrollIntoView` with nearest alignment. The source records the Chromium-specific reason: Tab or Shift+Tab can center a newly focused card before the handler runs. Starting from the prior view preserves the player's location as much as possible.

The helper leaves the outer page's scrolling to the browser. A review therefore measures both the card inside the board viewport and its visibility inside the window. A ring can be uncut by the board yet still sit partly below the window if the outer document did not move appropriately.

## Focus is not completion feedback

Winning does not move focus to the completion paragraph in GameStatus. The final card stays the current control, and the completed summary becomes available in document order. The final turn's feedback is published through the game's event output. The component does not force the player to leave the board simply because all pairs are now matched.

Likewise, a mismatch closing does not restore focus to either of its cards. Focus may have moved elsewhere while the pair was visible. The game-state update closes the faces while the user's navigation choice survives. An ordinary clock tick also leaves focus untouched.

# Shared-device playtest notes

This page is a qualitative account of how people played Neon Pairs together and what those sessions suggest for competition design.

The sessions examined local play with the current game. The observations concern attention, learning and handoff.

## Session setting

The working setup was deliberately modest: one browser game, people seated close enough to see the screen and paper notes beside the device. Event sketches were discussed on paper because the game has no participant entry or bracket controller. The browser supplied the actual card play, its ordinary status area and the existing reproduction tools.

Three settings were considered: a laptop on a table, a tablet passed between adjacent seats and a phone held by the current player. These are contrasting situations, not a representative sample of device usage. Their value was in making different problems observable. A laptop makes spectating easy; a held phone makes physical transfer and changing viewing angles much more prominent.

The discussion concentrated on what people did without prompting. Could someone enter the board, distinguish a face, recover after a miss and understand that their board was complete? Could a person who had looked away rejoin the conversation? Those questions were more productive than asking participants whether a finished competition feature sounded appealing in the abstract.

## Laptop: learning the faces aloud

In the laptop session, Mara began with the pointer and described each revealed face aloud. Her first descriptions used only shape: circle, star, triangle. After encountering similar shapes with different markers in a larger practice board, she started adding direction. The vocabulary changed from “the star near the corner” to “the star with the marker on the right.”

Jon, sitting beside her, remembered locations in row terms instead. He pointed to a horizontal band and then counted columns. They were attending to the same artwork but encoding different information. Neither strategy suggested a problem with the deck; the difference was in how people organized memory.

This observation agrees with the face model in `src/game/board/face-design.ts`: shape and marker direction both contribute to identity, and the game also includes a fill distinction. It also explains why the introduction in `Game.tsx` mentions shape and marker. A report that two faces “looked the same” can mean that a participant initially remembered only part of the available design.

The useful follow-up question was which feature they had noticed, rather than whether they had memorized the official face name. [Face catalogue](../visuals/face-catalogue.md) and [pair identity](../gameplay/pair-identity.md) provide the source context for interpreting such reports.

## Keyboard: movement looked like hesitation

Leah used Tab to enter the board and then moved with the arrows. An observer initially wrote down several pauses as indecision about the puzzle. On closer discussion, some of those pauses were time spent checking the focus outline and moving to a remembered position. The participant knew which card she wanted before she reached it.

This was a useful correction to the observation method. Card navigation and memory retrieval are separate activities, even when they occur between the same two reveals. Counting only the delay between clicks would have concealed the difference entirely, since this participant was not primarily clicking.

Leah also revisited an already matched card while moving across the board. She treated it as a landmark rather than as a card she intended to play. The current cards remain focusable in that state. That behavior made sense in the session, but an observer looking only at focus position might have misclassified it as a failed selection.

The input trace records navigation behavior. The repository README records accessibility-tree checks; screen-reader testing has not been performed. [Board keyboard navigation](../interface/board-keyboard-navigation.md), [focus policy](../interface/focus-policy.md) and [screen reader notes](../interface/screen-reader-notes.md) distinguish those subjects.

## Tablet: the handoff was an activity of its own

# Tables policy

This page records the markup policy for ordered result data and explains why the current game statistics use a different structure.

The solo UI uses a definition list for one game's statistics. Tournament uses an HTML table for bracket rows, with a caption and scoped column headings. The card board remains a CSS grid of buttons; those different structures serve different data.

## Policy for result data

When the content represents records with comparable columns, its relationships need to survive reading beyond the visual arrangement. CSS alone can align text while leaving those relationships absent from the document structure. Ranked or bracket data is a table element with a caption and th scope="col" header cells. The caption identifies the collection being read, while the column headers connect each record's values to their meaning.

This is a content-specific policy. It does not make the game board a data table because it has rows and columns, and it does not require converting every compact summary to tabular markup. The distinction begins with what the content means: interactive card coordinates, a property's value and a record in an ordered result collection are different things.

No such result feature is present in `Game.tsx`. The policy applies when result data is introduced. [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) discusses the broader preference for native semantics without adding another result format.

## Why the statistics are a definition list

GameStatus renders Moves, Pairs, Time and Best as four `dt`/`dd` groups inside a `dl`. Each term names a property of the same current game. There are no peer result rows and no column whose meaning changes with the row being read.

The layout happens to use flex and can wrap. At a wide width, those groups may look like cells in a horizontal strip. At a narrow width, they can flow to multiple lines. Neither visual arrangement changes the definition-list relationship. Replacing the wrapper with a table solely to preserve one desktop arrangement would confuse layout with content structure.

The Best value is one saved move count selected by current size. It does not present a list of people or a comparison across many records. `session.preferences.bestMoves[String(game.size)]` chooses the value before it reaches GameStatus. A single local best is not an implemented ordered-results screen.

[Status bar](status-bar.md) documents those expressions and labels. The present statistics model has no result columns.

## Why the card board is not a table

Board renders a named region containing an inner `div.board` and native card buttons. CSS Grid places those buttons in row order. Each card has its own coordinate and state in its accessible name, and keyboard movement follows a dedicated spatial model.

The table policy does not turn that interactive surface into a data table. A card is activated, can reveal a face and participates in remembered focus. A result cell is read as part of a record. They have different purposes even if both appear in a rectangle.

There is also no ARIA grid role on the current board. Its native buttons and movement handler implement the specified interaction without declaring a separate composite widget role. [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) traces that behavior. A review of result markup should not accidentally rename or restructure the card controls because the word “row” appears in both contexts.

## What the caption contributes

An ordered collection needs context. A visible title elsewhere on a page can be helpful, but a table caption directly identifies the collection associated with the table. That matters when reading the table independently or navigating between document structures.

The bracket caption is “Tournament bracket.” A table's caption should identify the data the table presents; technical details about markup belong in documentation rather than product copy.

A caption also does not supply missing column meaning. A reader needs to know whether a number represents moves, a position in an ordering or another property. The required header cells carry the column relationships; the caption names the whole collection. Combining all labels into a caption would leave the row values harder to interpret.

## Column relationships and reading order

The `scope="col"` attribute makes the header's direction explicit. It communicates that the header applies to values down its column. A bold `td`, a styled `div` or text positioned above a column can look similar while having a different structure.

A reviewer can inspect the table DOM and the browser's accessibility representation separately from the screenshot. The screenshot establishes visible arrangement. The DOM establishes element choices and attributes. The accessibility view helps establish that the browser exposes a meaningful table structure. No single one of these views proves all aspects of the interface.

Row headers, column order, numeric alignment and sorting controls depend on the result feature. The current game has no result implementation with those details.

## Narrow layouts and long values

The current game already separates outer page width from board overflow. Result data would have its own content and width behavior; it cannot simply inherit the card board's scroll logic by sharing a class name. A table's relationship between headers and values remains meaningful even when its viewport is narrow.

There is no table stylesheet in the source and no prescribed responsive table transformation here. A reviewer can still observe whether a proposed layout makes values readable and associated with their headers. Changing a collection into a stack of unrelated labels solely at a breakpoint can affect more than appearance, so both DOM and visual behavior are relevant evidence.

Name text can also vary in width without changing its accepted value. Typography and wrapping are layout concerns. The name policies remain separate from table structure; accepted names retain their displayed representation. [Typography](../visuals/typography.md) and [Form layout guide](form-layout-guide.md) explain nearby layout decisions in the existing interface.

The existing accessibility journey covers game controls and completion, not a result table. Evidence for a future result view would identify its actual markup and readable rows; the current statistics tests cannot establish that structure. [Accessibility audit](../quality/accessibility-audit.md) provides the wider review context.

`loadNotice` is one session string used for the latest published load outcome. It is not an error object keyed separately by field. The UI does not render two simultaneous field-specific error paragraphs or an error list above the panel.

After an invalid Board code attempt followed by an invalid snapshot attempt, the visible notice is the snapshot message. The Board code draft can still be invalid; the notice records the most recent action rather than continuously describing all field values.

Editing the snapshot string changes local state but does not itself clear the controller's notice. Editing Board code is native uncontrolled editing and likewise does not call a notice-clearing function. The outcome can remain visible while the user works on a correction.

Export replaces textarea text but does not explicitly clear `loadNotice`. Card turns update feedback without rewriting the load notice. New Game, Restart and a successful board-code replacement clear both through `replaceGame(..., false)`. Successful snapshot loading replaces the notice with its load outcome, and Resume clears it when continuing play.

This lifecycle explains a report that an old load message is still visible after editing. The message is action feedback, not a live validator attached to every keystroke. Adding an on-change clearing behavior would be a change to this lifecycle, not a fix to a missing CSS state.

## Format validity is more than native limits

Board code has a 32-character entry cap, but many shorter strings are invalid. An unsupported size, zero seed, leading zeros or malformed separators fail the parser even when the input is well below its native maximum. The loader's surrounding trim is a deliberate adapter step, not broad syntax repair.

Snapshot JSON has a 65536-character textarea limit and a UTF-8 byte bound in the decoder. Malformed JSON is only one failure kind. Unsupported versions, unknown properties, inconsistent matched positions, invalid selections and out-of-range counters can also produce the same UI error.

The UI intentionally gives the short outcome rather than exposing the decoder's internal reasoning. There is no implemented per-property error report or highlighted JSON line number. [Import safety policy](../sharing/import-safety-policy.md) and [Snapshot format](../sharing/snapshot-format.md) are the useful debugging references for engineers handling a rejected draft.

A completed valid snapshot is not an error merely because its result exceeds the local stored best. It loads as completed with a completion notice and static banner. An unfinished valid snapshot loads paused with an instruction to resume. The notice area carries both success and failure outcomes, so `.load-notice` is a more accurate name than a field-specific error class.

## Existing visual and semantic treatment

The notice paragraph uses the surrounding document styles and the load-status layout. The current fields do not receive `aria-invalid`, an error border class or an inline replacement label on failure. Those absences are part of the existing markup, not evidence that validation did not run.

The paragraph can wrap and has `min-width: 0` in its flex row. Resume can wrap alongside it on a constrained viewport. There is no absolute positioning that places a message over the field. [Form layout guide](form-layout-guide.md) explains how the notice row relates to the grid inside the disclosure.

Name-related errors do not exist in the current component tree. Their policies are in [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) and [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md). The load forms use their own messages and have no shared name-error component.

## Evidence for preservation and retry

`tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` populates progress, submits both invalid drafts and compares exported state before and after. It also advances the browser clock to show that the preserved game is still running. That distinguishes failure preservation from an accidental reset or pause.

`tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` submits a valid code with Enter, then an invalid code, checking both focus and the unchanged card count. `tests/controls.e2e.test.ts` checks exact notices, retained drafts and action focus. Repeated invalid submissions are covered in the announcement and accessibility journeys.

A useful defect report includes the draft, action origin, notice text and a before/after state observation. For example, an invalid snapshot followed by an unchanged exported selection is evidence of preservation. A notice alone cannot prove it, and a preserved game alone cannot prove that the user was told what happened. Reviewing both gives the error path its full meaning.
The hook is a small effect:

```ts
useEffect(() => {
  writePreferences(store, preferences);
}, [preferences, store]);
```

There is no queue, timer-driven retry, backoff or unload handler. Another dependency change can cause another attempt, but the code does not poll for a browser setting to change. A returned `null` store is captured in state for the lifetime of that mounted game; enabling storage later does not replace that state value automatically.

If the captured store object exists and its methods change behavior, a later effect can succeed using the same object. For example, a test double can reject its first write and accept a later one. That is different from reacquiring a previously inaccessible property. Both cases can be modeled without making the game rules aware of browser error names.

The writer's lack of a success result also means the existing UI cannot distinguish a rejected write from a successful one. This is a deliberate limit of the current adapter, not a hidden confirmation mechanism. Any investigation that needs that distinction can observe the supplied store in a test.

## Read failure and corrupt data have different evidence

A denied read and an invalid JSON value both lead to fallback preferences. Only the former establishes that an operation could not be completed. A parse failure establishes that the browser returned text which the application could not use. Confusing the two can lead to a misleading message about browser settings when the actual issue is an edited value.

Similarly, a quota error does not mean the existing value is invalid. The old string may remain perfectly readable while the new result exists only in memory. A person may see a better current best and then see the older best after reload. That sequence is a useful way to reproduce a failed update without damaging a valid baseline.

[Corrupt data policy](corrupt-data-policy.md) follows the rejection branches in detail. [Storage quota notes](storage-quota-notes.md) explains why the small size of this app's own payload cannot establish that a shared origin has available space.

## Errors do not authorize deleting other data

The storage adapters call `getItem` and `setItem` only for their own preference or tournament-history key. Neither uses a storage-wide clear call, key enumeration or cleanup routine. Their store interfaces expose only those two methods. The preference storage test explicitly seeds an unrelated key and checks that a preference write leaves its value intact.

This matters in shared local environments, where another page can occupy the same origin. A rejected preference write does not cause Neon Pairs to free space by deleting that page's values. The current fallback is simply to continue without a successful save. The app also does not switch to cookies, a server endpoint or another browser database after failure.

When reproducing capacity problems, a disposable origin or isolated browser context keeps artificial fill data away from a person's real preferences. That is a testing technique rather than an extra product recovery path. The test can remove the keys it created afterward; the shipped game contains no such test cleanup behavior.

## Evidence in the test suite

`storage.test.ts` uses a denied store whose read and write methods both throw. It checks that reading yields the default size and that writing does not throw. It also covers `readPreferences(null)`. This verifies the API boundary directly, without needing to configure an actual browser's privacy settings.

The browser environment test covers a different boundary: acquisition of `window.localStorage`. It installs the throwing getter before loading the game, loads a fixed board and matches a known pair. The harness gathers uncaught page errors and checks that none occurred. That demonstrates continued play after an acquisition failure, not persistence in that denied context.

These tests don't establish every browser policy or a physical disk limit. They also don't assert the saved-record feature notice described earlier. Reading the test title alone can obscure those limits; the actual injection point and assertions show what each test proves. [Storage testing guide](storage-testing-guide.md) extends that evidence into an investigation workflow.

# Focus policy

This page records focus behavior in the current game and the policy for a feature that changes the main screen.

Focus tells a keyboard user where input will go next. It is related to game selection but is not stored as part of a turn or snapshot. The current interface deliberately keeps deal-action focus, remembered board focus and card reveal state as distinct things.

## Existing page and future screens

`Game.tsx` switches the main area between Play and Tournament. Both screens have an h2 with `tabIndex="-1"`; when the screen changes, focus moves to its heading. The initial Play screen does not move focus on page load.

A screen replacement has a different orientation problem from resetting a deck. When a feature replaces what the main area shows, focus moves to that screen's h2, which has tabindex="-1". This gives the new screen a programmatic landing place without adding that heading to ordinary Tab traversal.

Expanding native details, updating statistics, closing a mismatch or displaying the completed-game paragraph does not create a new screen. Within Tournament, the Start turn button hands focus to the new board, Next turn and Next match focus the following Start turn button, and completion focuses Back to game. [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) covers the separate opening focus for its confirmation.

## Initial load is quiet

The hook `useBoardFocus(size)` initializes `focused` to zero. Board gives index 0 a tab index of zero and the other card buttons a tab index of minus one. This makes the first card available on entry, but no mount effect calls its focus method.

The browser's current focus therefore remains where it is at initial load. The page does not jump down to the board before a player has found Grid size or New Game. The board help paragraph describes how to enter and operate it. Its region uses `aria-describedby="board-help"` to associate those instructions with the board.

A remembered entry point is often described casually as “focus on the first card.” In this code that wording is incomplete. There is an entry point ready at the first card, while actual focus may be on the document, a deal button or another native control. Keeping those concepts separate prevents accidental mount-time focus stealing.

## Deal actions retain their location

New Game and Restart are native buttons that call the session controller. Neither callback moves focus into the board. After either action, a keyboard user remains on the button they used and can repeat the action or Tab toward the board. The size select uses its native interaction and likewise does not issue a board focus call.

The replacement increments `session.generation`, used as Board's React key. The newly mounted hook begins with a remembered index of zero. Thus the next board entry goes to the first card, even if the previous deal's memory was near its end. Actual action focus and future board entry are updated through different mechanisms.

A valid board-code load also increments generation. BoardCodeForm focuses its Load board ref on successful submission because its input is keyed by generation and will be replaced. That is especially important when the action was Enter in the input. An invalid submission keeps the input node and does not call the button ref, so correction can continue in place.

Clicking the load button starts with focus on that button, and an invalid click leaves it there. The distinction is based on the action's origin and successful input replacement, not on a general rule that all errors move focus into a field. [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) follows those cases in detail.

## Remembered board focus

Board focus memory is a local hook state containing a card index. The `onFocus` callback updates it whenever a card receives focus. Board renders exactly that index with `tabIndex={0}`. All other cards remain programmatically focusable with `tabIndex={-1}`.

Arrow movement uses the DOM order of the deck and never changes game selection on its own. Tab and Shift+Tab are left to the browser, so the board is one stop in the page sequence rather than a trap. Returning to it finds the last focused card, even if that card is now matched.

Matched positions stay in the navigation geometry. A player does not need to relearn how many arrow presses separate two coordinates after a match. During a mismatch, focus can also move while activation is blocked. The same is true while imported unfinished progress waits for Resume. [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) provides the calculations and edge behavior.

## Resume transfers before removal

Resume is the current exception to retaining focus on the action button. It exists only while `session.paused` is true. Clearing that flag removes the button, so leaving focus there would leave a disappearing target.

In `Game.tsx`, the local `resume()` function first calls `board.current?.focusRemembered()` and then `controller.resume()`. Board's imperative method focuses the remembered card with `preventScroll: true` and then brings it into view. Only after that does the controller clear the paused state and notices.

The ordering is observable. `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` installs a focus listener and confirms that Resume is still present when the card receives focus. A visual assertion after the fact would not establish this timing. The focus-entry test also remembers a far card on a large imported board, scrolls away and confirms that Resume returns to that location with nearest alignment.

The remembered location after import is initially the first card because the import replaced the board. The player can change it while paused. Resume uses that current memory rather than the snapshot's revealed index or a hard-coded first card. A snapshot stores game progress, not the browser's last navigation location.

## Visible focus and scroll clearance

`game.css` defines `:focus-visible` as a `3px` white outline with a `2px` offset. `card.css` gives cards `scroll-margin: 6px`. This combination accommodates the ring when the card is brought to the edge of the scroll area.

The focus hook uses `card.matches(':focus-visible')` before scrolling in `cardFocused`. Keyboard movement can scroll immediately; pointer focus avoids moving a card under a held press. Board scrolls a clicked card after the click completes. The timing is part of reliable focus behavior, not only a visual polish detail.

`useNearestScroll` stores the board's last reported scroll position, restores it and then invokes `scrollIntoView` with nearest alignment. The source records the Chromium-specific reason: Tab or Shift+Tab can center a newly focused card before the handler runs. Starting from the prior view preserves the player's location as much as possible.

The helper leaves the outer page's scrolling to the browser. A review therefore measures both the card inside the board viewport and its visibility inside the window. A ring can be uncut by the board yet still sit partly below the window if the outer document did not move appropriately.

## Focus is not completion feedback

Winning does not move focus to the completion paragraph in GameStatus. The final card stays the current control, and the completed summary becomes available in document order. The final turn's feedback is published through the game's event output. The component does not force the player to leave the board simply because all pairs are now matched.

Likewise, a mismatch closing does not restore focus to either of its cards. Focus may have moved elsewhere while the pair was visible. The game-state update closes the faces while the user's navigation choice survives. An ordinary clock tick also leaves focus untouched.

# Shared-device playtest notes

This page is a qualitative account of how people played Neon Pairs together and what those sessions suggest for competition design.

The sessions examined local play with the current game. The observations concern attention, learning and handoff.

## Session setting

The working setup was deliberately modest: one browser game, people seated close enough to see the screen and paper notes beside the device. Event sketches were discussed on paper because the game has no participant entry or bracket controller. The browser supplied the actual card play, its ordinary status area and the existing reproduction tools.

Three settings were considered: a laptop on a table, a tablet passed between adjacent seats and a phone held by the current player. These are contrasting situations, not a representative sample of device usage. Their value was in making different problems observable. A laptop makes spectating easy; a held phone makes physical transfer and changing viewing angles much more prominent.

The discussion concentrated on what people did without prompting. Could someone enter the board, distinguish a face, recover after a miss and understand that their board was complete? Could a person who had looked away rejoin the conversation? Those questions were more productive than asking participants whether a finished competition feature sounded appealing in the abstract.

## Laptop: learning the faces aloud

In the laptop session, Mara began with the pointer and described each revealed face aloud. Her first descriptions used only shape: circle, star, triangle. After encountering similar shapes with different markers in a larger practice board, she started adding direction. The vocabulary changed from “the star near the corner” to “the star with the marker on the right.”

Jon, sitting beside her, remembered locations in row terms instead. He pointed to a horizontal band and then counted columns. They were attending to the same artwork but encoding different information. Neither strategy suggested a problem with the deck; the difference was in how people organized memory.

This observation agrees with the face model in `src/game/board/face-design.ts`: shape and marker direction both contribute to identity, and the game also includes a fill distinction. It also explains why the introduction in `Game.tsx` mentions shape and marker. A report that two faces “looked the same” can mean that a participant initially remembered only part of the available design.

The useful follow-up question was which feature they had noticed, rather than whether they had memorized the official face name. [Face catalogue](../visuals/face-catalogue.md) and [pair identity](../gameplay/pair-identity.md) provide the source context for interpreting such reports.

## Keyboard: movement looked like hesitation

Leah used Tab to enter the board and then moved with the arrows. An observer initially wrote down several pauses as indecision about the puzzle. On closer discussion, some of those pauses were time spent checking the focus outline and moving to a remembered position. The participant knew which card she wanted before she reached it.

This was a useful correction to the observation method. Card navigation and memory retrieval are separate activities, even when they occur between the same two reveals. Counting only the delay between clicks would have concealed the difference entirely, since this participant was not primarily clicking.

Leah also revisited an already matched card while moving across the board. She treated it as a landmark rather than as a card she intended to play. The current cards remain focusable in that state. That behavior made sense in the session, but an observer looking only at focus position might have misclassified it as a failed selection.

The input trace records navigation behavior. The repository README records accessibility-tree checks; screen-reader testing has not been performed. [Board keyboard navigation](../interface/board-keyboard-navigation.md), [focus policy](../interface/focus-policy.md) and [screen reader notes](../interface/screen-reader-notes.md) distinguish those subjects.

## Tablet: the handoff was an activity of its own

Waits on a yielded `exec` cell and returns new output or completion.

- If the cell is still running, `wait` may yield again with the same `cell_id`.
