# Tables policy

This page records the markup policy for ordered result data and explains why the current game statistics use a different structure.

The solo UI uses a definition list for one game's statistics. Tournament uses an HTML table for bracket rows, with a caption and scoped column headings. The card board remains a CSS grid of buttons; those different structures serve different data.

## Policy for result data

When the content represents records with comparable columns, its relationships need to survive reading beyond the visual arrangement. CSS alone can align text while leaving those relationships absent from the document structure. Ranked or bracket data is a table element with a caption and th scope="col" header cells. The caption identifies the collection being read, while the column headers connect each record's values to their meaning.

This is a content-specific policy. It does not make the game board a data table because it has rows and columns, and it does not require converting every compact summary to tabular markup. The distinction begins with what the content means: interactive card coordinates, a property's value and a record in an ordered result collection are different things.

No such result feature is present in `Game.tsx`. The policy applies when result data is introduced. [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) discusses the broader preference for native semantics without adding another result format.

## Why the statistics are a definition list

GameStatus renders Moves, Pairs, Time and Best as four `dt`/`dd` groups inside a `dl`. Each term names a property of the same current game. There are no peer result rows and no column whose meaning changes with the row being read.

The layout happens to use flex and can wrap. At a wide width, those groups may look like cells in a horizontal strip. At a narrow width, they can flow to multiple lines. Neither visual arrangement changes the definition-list relationship. Replacing the wrapper with a table solely to preserve one desktop arrangement would confuse layout with content structure.

The Best value is one saved move count selected by current size. It does not present a list of people or a comparison across many records. `session.preferences.bestMoves[String(game.size)]` chooses the value before it reaches GameStatus. A single local best is not an implemented ordered-results screen.

[Status bar](status-bar.md) documents those expressions and labels. The present statistics model has no result columns.

## Why the card board is not a table

Board renders a named region containing an inner `div.board` and native card buttons. CSS Grid places those buttons in row order. Each card has its own coordinate and state in its accessible name, and keyboard movement follows a dedicated spatial model.

The table policy does not turn that interactive surface into a data table. A card is activated, can reveal a face and participates in remembered focus. A result cell is read as part of a record. They have different purposes even if both appear in a rectangle.

There is also no ARIA grid role on the current board. Its native buttons and movement handler implement the specified interaction without declaring a separate composite widget role. [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) traces that behavior. A review of result markup should not accidentally rename or restructure the card controls because the word “row” appears in both contexts.

## What the caption contributes

An ordered collection needs context. A visible title elsewhere on a page can be helpful, but a table caption directly identifies the collection associated with the table. That matters when reading the table independently or navigating between document structures.

The bracket caption is “Tournament bracket.” A table's caption should identify the data the table presents; technical details about markup belong in documentation rather than product copy.

A caption also does not supply missing column meaning. A reader needs to know whether a number represents moves, a position in an ordering or another property. The required header cells carry the column relationships; the caption names the whole collection. Combining all labels into a caption would leave the row values harder to interpret.

## Column relationships and reading order

The `scope="col"` attribute makes the header's direction explicit. It communicates that the header applies to values down its column. A bold `td`, a styled `div` or text positioned above a column can look similar while having a different structure.

A reviewer can inspect the table DOM and the browser's accessibility representation separately from the screenshot. The screenshot establishes visible arrangement. The DOM establishes element choices and attributes. The accessibility view helps establish that the browser exposes a meaningful table structure. No single one of these views proves all aspects of the interface.

Row headers, column order, numeric alignment and sorting controls depend on the result feature. The current game has no result implementation with those details.

## Narrow layouts and long values

The current game already separates outer page width from board overflow. Result data would have its own content and width behavior; it cannot simply inherit the card board's scroll logic by sharing a class name. A table's relationship between headers and values remains meaningful even when its viewport is narrow.

There is no table stylesheet in the source and no prescribed responsive table transformation here. A reviewer can still observe whether a proposed layout makes values readable and associated with their headers. Changing a collection into a stack of unrelated labels solely at a breakpoint can affect more than appearance, so both DOM and visual behavior are relevant evidence.

Name text can also vary in width without changing its accepted value. Typography and wrapping are layout concerns. The name policies remain separate from table structure; accepted names retain their displayed representation. [Typography](../visuals/typography.md) and [Form layout guide](form-layout-guide.md) explain nearby layout decisions in the existing interface.

The existing accessibility journey covers game controls and completion, not a result table. Evidence for a future result view would identify its actual markup and readable rows; the current statistics tests cannot establish that structure. [Accessibility audit](../quality/accessibility-audit.md) provides the wider review context.

# Error display guide

This page explains how failed board-code and snapshot loads are reported without replacing the current game.

The current UI has two validation outcomes that are errors: `Invalid board code.` and `Invalid snapshot.`. They describe the attempted load, not a broken game. The player can correct the draft and retry while the current deal remains available.

## The visible location

Reproduction renders a paragraph with `id="load-notice"` and class `load-notice` inside `.load-status`. That container follows the native details element. It is adjacent to the reproduction tools but outside their collapsible body.

Both Load board and Load snapshot carry `aria-describedby="load-notice"`. Their visible names remain the action labels; the description associates the nearby outcome with those actions. The field labels stay Board code and Snapshot JSON rather than being replaced with an error sentence.

Because the paragraph is outside details, it remains in document flow when the panel is closed. A person does not have to reopen the JSON field merely to see the most recent load notice or Resume. The `.load-status` flex row wraps, has a `12px` gap and a `56px` minimum height; its paragraph can grow and shrink within the available width.

The same load outcome is also published through the game's feedback path. [Announcements policy](announcements-policy.md) describes that event handling. The local paragraph's role here is visible context beside the load tools, not a second independent validation system.

## Who decides that a load failed

BoardCodeForm reads its draft through FormData and calls the `loadBoard` prop. The controller in `use-game.ts` trims surrounding whitespace and checks `parseBoardCode`. Failure calls `notice(SessionNotice.invalidBoard)` and returns false before clock reset or replacement.

Reproduction passes the complete snapshot draft to `loadSnapshot`. The controller calls `decodeSnapshot`. Failure calls `notice(SessionNotice.invalidSnapshot)` and returns false, again before resetting or replacing the game. The textarea component does not try to validate JSON structure itself.

`SessionNotice` in `session.ts` owns the literal messages. The shared `notice` helper sets both `feedback` and `loadNotice` and advances announcement identity. The exact words therefore come from the session boundary that knows the operation failed, rather than being duplicated in each field's change handler.

This ordering is important. If a load reset the timer before parsing, even an invalid draft could alter play. If it replaced the game before reporting failure, the notice would not describe the preservation behavior promised by the controls specification. The current callbacks validate first.

## What a failure preserves

A failed board-code load leaves the input's DOM node intact because generation does not change. Its edited value remains available. A failed snapshot load leaves Reproduction's local string state intact. Neither failure clears the draft to make the panel look clean.

The game object, board size, matched positions, selection, moves and elapsed state are not replaced by the error path. The existing game can continue to advance active time. An invalid input is not an imported pause, and it does not freeze a pending mismatch merely because a notice appeared.

Focus memory also survives because Board is not remounted. A player who last visited a far card can return there after correcting a form. The current saved size is unchanged by a failed load; successful replacement is what updates that preference.

The load notice is a session field separate from the game. Adding it can produce a render without changing card state. This is why comparing the complete session object for identity is different from asserting that gameplay was replaced. [Game state model](../gameplay/game-state-model.md) and [Session module](../architecture/session-module.md) explain those boundaries.

## Focus depends on how submission began

A click on Load board ordinarily leaves focus on the button. If the code is invalid, BoardCodeForm does not issue another focus call. A keyboard Enter submission from inside Board code leaves focus in the field on failure, so the user can continue editing.

On successful Enter submission, the input is about to be replaced because it is keyed by generation. BoardCodeForm explicitly focuses its Load board ref when the callback returns true. That is a success-path focus correction, not an error-summary jump.

Load snapshot is a `type="button"` action. Its handler passes local text to the controller and does not move focus elsewhere on failure or success. The snapshot textarea stays mounted. Export likewise keeps its action focus and fills the field rather than focusing or selecting it automatically.

These cases show why “errors focus the field” would be an inaccurate description of this interface. The source preserves the user's current interaction where it can. [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) covers the complete set of current focus transfers.

## Notices are outcomes, not sticky field annotations

`loadNotice` is one session string used for the latest published load outcome. It is not an error object keyed separately by field. The UI does not render two simultaneous field-specific error paragraphs or an error list above the panel.

After an invalid Board code attempt followed by an invalid snapshot attempt, the visible notice is the snapshot message. The Board code draft can still be invalid; the notice records the most recent action rather than continuously describing all field values.

Editing the snapshot string changes local state but does not itself clear the controller's notice. Editing Board code is native uncontrolled editing and likewise does not call a notice-clearing function. The outcome can remain visible while the user works on a correction.

Export replaces textarea text but does not explicitly clear `loadNotice`. Card turns update feedback without rewriting the load notice. New Game, Restart and a successful board-code replacement clear both through `replaceGame(..., false)`. Successful snapshot loading replaces the notice with its load outcome, and Resume clears it when continuing play.

This lifecycle explains a report that an old load message is still visible after editing. The message is action feedback, not a live validator attached to every keystroke. Adding an on-change clearing behavior would be a change to this lifecycle, not a fix to a missing CSS state.

## Format validity is more than native limits

Board code has a 32-character entry cap, but many shorter strings are invalid. An unsupported size, zero seed, leading zeros or malformed separators fail the parser even when the input is well below its native maximum. The loader's surrounding trim is a deliberate adapter step, not broad syntax repair.

Snapshot JSON has a 65536-character textarea limit and a UTF-8 byte bound in the decoder. Malformed JSON is only one failure kind. Unsupported versions, unknown properties, inconsistent matched positions, invalid selections and out-of-range counters can also produce the same UI error.

The UI intentionally gives the short outcome rather than exposing the decoder's internal reasoning. There is no implemented per-property error report or highlighted JSON line number. [Import safety policy](../sharing/import-safety-policy.md) and [Snapshot format](../sharing/snapshot-format.md) are the useful debugging references for engineers handling a rejected draft.

A completed valid snapshot is not an error merely because its result exceeds the local stored best. It loads as completed with a completion notice and static banner. An unfinished valid snapshot loads paused with an instruction to resume. The notice area carries both success and failure outcomes, so `.load-notice` is a more accurate name than a field-specific error class.

## Existing visual and semantic treatment

The notice paragraph uses the surrounding document styles and the load-status layout. The current fields do not receive `aria-invalid`, an error border class or an inline replacement label on failure. Those absences are part of the existing markup, not evidence that validation did not run.

The paragraph can wrap and has `min-width: 0` in its flex row. Resume can wrap alongside it on a constrained viewport. There is no absolute positioning that places a message over the field. [Form layout guide](form-layout-guide.md) explains how the notice row relates to the grid inside the disclosure.

Name-related errors do not exist in the current component tree. Their policies are in [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) and [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md). The load forms use their own messages and have no shared name-error component.

## Evidence for preservation and retry

`tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` populates progress, submits both invalid drafts and compares exported state before and after. It also advances the browser clock to show that the preserved game is still running. That distinguishes failure preservation from an accidental reset or pause.

`tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` submits a valid code with Enter, then an invalid code, checking both focus and the unchanged card count. `tests/controls.e2e.test.ts` checks exact notices, retained drafts and action focus. Repeated invalid submissions are covered in the announcement and accessibility journeys.

A useful defect report includes the draft, action origin, notice text and a before/after state observation. For example, an invalid snapshot followed by an unchanged exported selection is evidence of preservation. A notice alone cannot prove it, and a preserved game alone cannot prove that the user was told what happened. Reviewing both gives the error path its full meaning.

# Form layout guide

This page explains the label, field and action arrangements used by the current controls.

The game has the always-visible deal bar, text tools inside Reproduce a game and a Tournament setup form. They share native elements and the `.control` style, but their DOM and layout differ. This guide describes those differences so a markup refactor can preserve the actual interaction rather than just one screenshot.

## A map of the current groups

| Group | Markup and layout | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grid size | Label and select in a flex row | `Controls.tsx`, `controls.css` |
| Deal actions | Three buttons in the outer wrapped flex row | `Controls.tsx` |
| Tournament setup | Players select, labeled name inputs and submit button | `TournamentSetup.tsx`, `tournament.css` |
| Board code | Form with label above a field/action row | `BoardCodeForm.tsx`, `reproduction.css` |
| Snapshot JSON | Label and textarea in the panel's body grid | `Reproduction.tsx` |
| Snapshot actions | Two buttons in a wrapped flex row | `Reproduction.tsx` |
| Load outcome | Paragraph and conditional Resume in a wrapped row | `Reproduction.tsx` |

Only Board code is wrapped in a form element. The snapshot field is controlled React state in Reproduction, and its buttons explicitly call callbacks. Enter in a multiline textarea remains text editing rather than submitting the snapshot. Enter in Board code invokes the form's submit path.

## Labels are visible and associated

Grid size uses `htmlFor="grid-size"` and a select with that id. Board code uses `htmlFor="board-code"`, and Snapshot JSON uses `htmlFor="snapshot-json"`. The visible text supplies the fields' names; placeholders do not stand in for labels.

Board code also has `name="boardCode"` because its form reads that field through FormData. Its id serves label association; its name serves native form data lookup. Those are different roles, and changing one does not automatically update the other.

The snapshot textarea has no need for a FormData name in its current path because its value is held in React state and passed directly to `loadSnapshot`. Adding a name attribute alone would not turn its surrounding buttons into a form submission. [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) explains the behavioral value of the current element choices.

The labels come from `control-labels.ts`. Keeping visible text in those constants does not change the label/field relationship. A review can inspect both the imported value and the actual id association, because a correct label string next to the wrong id is still a broken field relationship.

## Deal bar: horizontal until it wraps

The outer `.controls` container uses `display: flex`, bottom alignment, wrapping and a `12px` gap. The nested `.size-control` is a centered flex row with its own `12px` gap. On a wide layout, label, select and action buttons appear in one compact band above the statistics.

At widths up to 599px, the outer container stretches…6032 tokens truncated…hose the wrong records. [Storage testing guide](storage-testing-guide.md) describes the store doubles that make this separation observable.

## What bests retain

The best map cannot answer how many attempts occurred, which deal produced a best, how long that attempt took, or whether two equal results happened on different days. None of those fields is retained. A new feature that needs a collection has a different persistence concern from calculating a size-specific minimum.

Keeping that distinction explicit avoids a misleading implementation shortcut: interpreting every best-map update as if it were an append to a historical list. The code's result is an aggregate with replacement semantics. The saved-list rule belongs to collections, while the current aggregate remains documented and tested according to its own source behavior.

# Mismatch interval

This page explains the 800 active milliseconds during which two different revealed faces remain visible, including pauses and exact expiry.

`MISMATCH_MS` is 800 in `src/game/game.ts`. A miss stores that duration as `selection.remainingMs`. The interval is part of game state and advances through the same logical time operation as elapsed time. It is not a standalone callback that remembers two DOM nodes to close later.

## The pending state

After two eligible positions with different face values are revealed, selection contains `kind: mismatch`, `first`, `second`, and `remainingMs`. The move has already been counted. Matched positions are unchanged.

While selection remains mismatch, `activateCard` returns the same state for every activation. A third card is not revealed or saved for later. Repeated activation of either exposed card does not extend the interval. Focus can move independently of that game-state rejection.

Both faces are included by `faceUpCards`, alongside all previously matched positions. When selection closes, both temporary faces leave that derived set in one state transition. Matched faces remain up.

The start of this interval is the second reveal. Time spent considering the first revealed card contributes to elapsed time but does not consume any of the 800 milliseconds, since there is no mismatch yet.

## Exact core arithmetic

For a started, unfinished game and a finite positive delta, `advanceGame` updates elapsed time and then subtracts the same delta from a pending remainder:

```ts
const remainingMs = state.selection.remainingMs - milliseconds;
const selection =
  remainingMs > 0
    ? { ...state.selection, remainingMs }
    : { kind: SelectionKind.closed };
```

A positive result stays pending. Zero and negative results close selection. A single advance of 800 from a new mismatch closes it; an advance of 799 followed by 1 has the same selection outcome.

The whole delta contributes to elapsed time, subject to the elapsed cap. If a callback arrives 900 milliseconds after a new mismatch, the function closes it and adds 900 elapsed milliseconds. It does not discard the 100 milliseconds after expiry, since the game remains active between turns.

No extra move is added on expiry. The move was charged when the second card was revealed. There is also no new turn-result feedback event on a clock tick; closing is the delayed consequence of the already reported miss.

## A visible-time example

On `np1-4-1`, reveal positions 0 and 1. Their face values differ. From that second activation:

| Active duration since miss | Selection result |
| ---: | --- |
| 0 ms | Mismatch, 800 remaining |
| 250 ms | Mismatch, 550 remaining |
| 799 ms | Mismatch, 1 remaining |
| 800 ms | Closed |

These durations exclude hidden-page intervals and an imported snapshot's pause. They are not promises about when the browser paints a frame. The logical boundary is exact; the visible update happens when the browser runs and renders the relevant work.

A one-card selection has no comparable timeout. Waiting 800 milliseconds with one card revealed leaves that card revealed. [Selection state](selection-state.md) distinguishes the alternatives.

## Browser scheduling

`useSessionClock` in `src/game/session/use-session-clock.ts` uses a recursive timeout. Its usual interval is `CLOCK_INTERVAL_MS`, currently 40. When a mismatch is present, the next delay is the smaller of 40 and its remaining duration.

The timeout is a chance to observe `performance.now`, not a claim that exactly its requested delay passed. `elapsedStep` subtracts the previous observation from the actual reading and passes that positive active delta through `tickSession` to `advanceGame`.

There is no fixed number of ticks defining a mismatch. Twenty nominal 40-millisecond waits and a delayed larger update are different schedules that can produce the same active duration. Basing the interval on measured time prevents slower rendering from stretching the logical memory window by counting callbacks.

The hook reads the latest session through a ref when it schedules and synchronizes. It does not preserve the two indices from the original miss in an independent closing closure. A later time update applies to the current selection.

## Synchronization before a click

`useGame.activate` calls `clock.synchronize()` before `activateSession`. This ordering handles an overdue mismatch even if the timeout has not run.

For example, assume a miss starts at monotonic reading 362.25. Its logical expiry is 1162.25. A click at 1163.25 first advances the pending duration past zero, then can reveal a new eligible first card. The stale rendered appearance immediately before that task does not force the click to be ignored.

A click while positive time still remains is ignored after synchronization. It does not become an action waiting to execute at expiry. The distinction is the measured active duration at the activation, not the location of a timer callback in the task queue.

`tests/fractional-clock.e2e.test.ts` explicitly checks an overdue click in the same task that changes the test clock, leaving no opportunity for an earlier timeout to resolve the selection first.

## Hiding and showing the page

The hook tracks `document.hidden` through a visibility listener. On a visibility change it synchronizes using the previous visibility state, updates its stored visibility, and schedules as appropriate.

On hiding, that final synchronization includes the active portion since the last observation. While hidden, the scheduling predicate is false. On showing, synchronization observes the hidden period as inactive, updates the observation point, and then restarts visible scheduling.

If 200 active milliseconds of a mismatch passed before hiding, it has 600 remaining on return even after a long hidden interval. Another 599 visible milliseconds leave it pending; the next active millisecond closes it.

The elapsed clock uses the same accounting, so the hidden period is excluded from both. A page merely losing focus is not itself the predicate in this hook; the relevant browser signal is page visibility. [Elapsed time rules](elapsed-time-rules.md) covers that distinction.

## Loading and resuming a mismatch

A valid snapshot can carry a mismatch with a remaining whole duration from 1 through 800. `replaceGame` pauses an imported unfinished game, retaining the restored selection. `activateSession` and `tickSession` return early while the session is paused.

Resume resets the browser clock's observation point and clears `paused`. The time spent reading the loaded position is therefore excluded. A restored remainder of 300 needs another 300 active milliseconds after Resume; it does not receive a fresh 800-millisecond allowance.

If the page is hidden when an imported pause is cleared, visibility still prevents active time. Resume removes one gate, while the clock's running predicate also checks page visibility, started, and completion.

Export first synchronizes the active clock. It rounds a fractional positive remainder upward to a whole millisecond. A live remainder of 0.25 exports as 1, preserving a pending selection that the decoder accepts. Export does not restart the interval or pause the live game. See [Snapshot selection notes](../sharing/snapshot-selection-notes.md).

## Replacement and stale work

Restart during a mismatch discards that selection and creates a hidden game on the same code. New Game and size changes also clear it while choosing another seed. Successful loads replace it with the loaded position.

Each replacement increments `session.generation`. The timer path rejects a generation that differs from the current session. Effect cleanup additionally marks the old effect inactive, clears its timeout, and removes its visibility listener. An old deal cannot consume part of a replacement game's mismatch or close its new first card.

Within one deal, there is no independent old mismatch deadline that can later close another turn. Time advancement reads the current selection and applies only the measured delta since the last observation. `tests/timer-lifecycle.e2e.test.ts` checks a later mismatch after an earlier interval has finished, as well as cleanup on unmount.

## Caps do not disable the interval

Elapsed saturation uses `min(ELAPSED_MAX_MS, elapsedMs + milliseconds)`, but mismatch subtraction still uses the original positive delta. A miss can therefore close even when the elapsed counter has no room to increase. The displayed clock's remaining capacity is not the source of mismatch time.

Move saturation is independent too. At 999,999 moves a miss still creates the normal pending state and closes normally. Neither counter limit allows an extra reveal during the interval or turns a miss into completion.

## Timing evidence

`game.test.ts` checks the exact 799-plus-1 boundary. `tests/idle-clock.e2e.test.ts` checks untouched hidden and paused intervals. Fractional-clock and lifecycle tests add synchronization and replacement cases.

For a report, include the code, two positions, active durations, and visibility or Resume events. Total wall-clock waiting alone can include periods deliberately excluded from the remainder.

# Best score records

This page explains how the current session stores the lowest completed move count for each supported board size.

Records live in preferences, alongside the last selected size. They survive a reload when browser storage is available. They do not contain a saved deal, an action history, or elapsed-time rankings. The game shows the current size's entry as `Best: N`, and shows `Best: none` when that size has no entry.

The scoring distinction is described in [Scoring and moves](scoring-and-moves.md). Broader browser storage behavior belongs to [Persistence overview](../persistence/persistence-overview.md).

## Data in memory

`src/game/session/storage.ts` declares:

```ts
export interface Preferences {
  readonly size: number;
  readonly bestMoves: Readonly<Record<string, number>>;
}
```

`size` is the selected side length. `bestMoves` maps its decimal string to a move count. Missing entries represent sizes with no record. Zero is not used as a sentinel: even the smallest completed board needs eight moves, so a zero entry would be invalid saved data.

For example:

```json
{
  "size": 6,
  "bestMoves": {
    "4": 12,
    "6": 20
  }
}
```

This says the current preferred size is 6, with separate records of 12 moves for 4x4 and 20 for 6x6. It says nothing about which board code produced either result or how long either game took.

The record scope is a side length. All board codes at that size share the same comparison entry. Restarting the same deal and playing a fresh seed both compete with that entry. The current implementation has no per-code record map.

## Recording a played completion

The call to `rememberBest` is in `activateSession`. After `activateCard` produces a completed game, the session passes its preferences, the game's size, and the final move count to that helper.

This placement matters. Core completion can be calculated without storage, and a replay can finish without writing a browser record. The browser session decides when an actual activation resulting in victory is eligible to update its preferences.

`rememberBest` reads the old value at `String(size)`. Its comparison is:

```ts
if (previous !== undefined && previous <= moves) return preferences;
```

A smaller result creates a replacement preferences object containing a copied map with the improved value. An absent previous entry also creates a record. An equal or larger result returns the original preferences object. There is no elapsed-time tiebreaker.

| Existing size-4 best | Played result | Resulting best |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Missing | 14 | 14 |
| 14 | 12 | 12 |
| 12 | 12 | 12 |
| 12 | 15 | 12 |

All other size entries are preserved by the spread. Improving size 4 does not alter size 6's value or the preferred size. Successful game replacement updates preferred size separately through `replaceGame`.

## Completion imports are a different path

Loading a completed snapshot uses `replaceGame`, not `activateSession`. It displays completion and retains the imported moves in that game, but does not call `rememberBest`. A completed import can therefore show fewer moves than the current local best while the best display remains the local record.

Loading unfinished progress pauses it. After Resume, a later final match does go through `activateSession` and can establish or improve the local record. The move count considered is the full imported-and-continued count, not only the attempts made after Resume.

This is a distinction between state replacement and a played completion. Snapshot validation checks consistency of the position; it does not attest to the history of its moves. [Snapshot format](../sharing/snapshot-format.md) explains that validation boundary.

Activating a position on an already completed imported game does not turn it into a new completion event. Every valid position is matched, so `activateCard` returns the same game and the session exits before record handling.

## Persistence representation

The current storage key is `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. `PREFERENCES_VERSION` is 1, and the saved object includes that version under `schemaVersion`:

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "size": 6,
  "bestMoves": {
    "4": 12,
    "6": 20
  }
}
```

`writePreferences` serializes this object and passes it to `setItem`. `useSavedPreferences` calls the writer in an effect when the preference object or store changes. Card reveals and time ticks normally preserve the same preference reference, so they are not individual score writes.

The equal-or-worse return path in `rememberBest` also preserves that reference. Winning can still update session feedback and celebration, while the unchanged preferences do not create a new preference dependency for the saving effect.

At page startup, `browserStore` attempts to obtain `window.localStorage`. Access itself can throw, so it returns `null` on failure. `readPreferences` also catches retrieval and parsing failures. The fallback is `{ size: 4, bestMoves: {} }`.

The application writes only the designated preference key through this module. It has no clearing action for all storage and does not need to modify keys belonging to other applications. Details of storage envelopes and failure scenarios are in [Preferences store](../persistence/preferences-store.md) and [Storage failure policy](../persistence/storage-failure-policy.md).

## What is accepted from saved JSON

The reader treats parsed JSON as unknown data. It first checks that the outer value is an object with the expected schema version and a numeric supported size. It then requires `bestMoves` to be an object.

For each entry, it converts the key to a number and checks all of the following existing conditions:

- Converting that number back to a string yields the original key.
- The number is one of the supported side lengths.
- The score is a nonnegative safe integer.
- The score is at most 999,999.
- The score is at least the number of pairs for that size.

The round-trip key check rejects a key such as `"04"`, even though converting it with `Number` gives a supported size. Keys are canonical decimal side lengths in the data this reader accepts.

The minimum bounds are 8, 18, 32, 50, 72, 98, and 128 for sizes 4 through 16. A fractional score, a string containing digits, a negative number, and an implausibly low completed count are all rejected. The upper bound is shared with `MOVES_MAX` from `game.ts`.

The reader does not apply snapshot-style exact-key validation to the outer preference object. Its explicit checks concern version, size, and the record map. This is one reason the saved preference representation and the snapshot representation should not be treated as interchangeable formats.

## Failure is handled as one invalid preference value

If any record entry fails a check, `readPreferences` returns the full fallback. It does not salvage other entries from that object. An otherwise valid selected size is also lost in that fallback result.

For example, a saved object with size 6, a valid size-6 best of 20, and a size-4 best of 1 falls back to default size 4 with no bests. The invalid size-4 entry makes the stored preferences unusable as a whole.

This is different from a size with no entry. An empty record map is valid and retains a valid saved size. Loading a saved size of 6 with `{}` is a normal way to have a six-column startup board without any records.

Neither malformed saved data nor blocked storage prevents play. `writePreferences` catches write errors, and a `null` store makes the operation inert. The active session can still hold an improved record in memory and display it. If the browser did not persist it, a later reload cannot recover that in-memory change.

## Reload and replacement

Reload creates a fresh deal at the saved size, retaining the record map. New Game and Restart also retain the map while clearing progress. Successful loads select their game's size, changing which entry is visible; invalid loads retain the current size.

A completed import can therefore change the displayed best by selecting another size without establishing a record. [New Game and Restart](new-game-and-restart.md) compares these paths.

## Caps, ties, and ordinary comparisons

A capped result of 999,999 is a valid record if the size has no previous entry. A later result below it improves the record. Another capped result ties and retains the existing preferences object.

Elapsed time is irrelevant to this ordering. A 12-move completion at several minutes and a 12-move completion at a shorter time have equal score for this map. The stored representation has no duration field in which to remember the difference.

There is also no list of past attempts. The map contains at most one score for each supported size because each size is one key. It does not retain the second-best result, a date, a player name, or a streak.

## Evidence available in the source

`storage.test.ts` checks separate size records, better/equal/worse comparisons, round-trip saving, invalid values, the maximum, and denied storage. `session.test.ts` distinguishes played completion, completed imports, and completion after continuing imported progress. Browser persistence tests check the UI and actual store path.

For a missing record, compare the in-memory map after victory, the serialized preferences at the active origin, and the reader's result after reload. That separates a failed write from a validation fallback or a current-size display lookup.

# Tables policy

This page records the markup policy for ordered result data and explains why the current game statistics use a different structure.

The solo UI uses a definition list for one game's statistics. Tournament uses an HTML table for bracket rows, with a caption and scoped column headings. The card board remains a CSS grid of buttons; those different structures serve different data.

## Policy for result data

When the content represents records with comparable columns, its relationships need to survive reading beyond the visual arrangement. CSS alone can align text while leaving those relationships absent from the document structure. Ranked or bracket data is a table element with a caption and th scope="col" header cells. The caption identifies the collection being read, while the column headers connect each record's values to their meaning.

This is a content-specific policy. It does not make the game board a data table because it has rows and columns, and it does not require converting every compact summary to tabular markup. The distinction begins with what the content means: interactive card coordinates, a property's value and a record in an ordered result collection are different things.

No such result feature is present in `Game.tsx`. The policy applies when result data is introduced. [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) discusses the broader preference for native semantics without adding another result format.

## Why the statistics are a definition list

GameStatus renders Moves, Pairs, Time and Best as four `dt`/`dd` groups inside a `dl`. Each term names a property of the same current game. There are no peer result rows and no column whose meaning changes with the row being read.

The layout happens to use flex and can wrap. At a wide width, those groups may look like cells in a horizontal strip. At a narrow width, they can flow to multiple lines. Neither visual arrangement changes the definition-list relationship. Replacing the wrapper with a table solely to preserve one desktop arrangement would confuse layout with content structure.

The Best value is one saved move count selected by current size. It does not present a list of people or a comparison across many records. `session.preferences.bestMoves[String(game.size)]` chooses the value before it reaches GameStatus. A single local best is not an implemented ordered-results screen.

[Status bar](status-bar.md) documents those expressions and labels. The present statistics model has no result columns.

## Why the card board is not a table

Board renders a named region containing an inner `div.board` and native card buttons. CSS Grid places those buttons in row order. Each card has its own coordinate and state in its accessible name, and keyboard movement follows a dedicated spatial model.

The table policy does not turn that interactive surface into a data table. A card is activated, can reveal a face and participates in remembered focus. A result cell is read as part of a record. They have different purposes even if both appear in a rectangle.

There is also no ARIA grid role on the current board. Its native buttons and movement handler implement the specified interaction without declaring a separate composite widget role. [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) traces that behavior. A review of result markup should not accidentally rename or restructure the card controls because the word “row” appears in both contexts.

## What the caption contributes

An ordered collection needs context. A visible title elsewhere on a page can be helpful, but a table caption directly identifies the collection associated with the table. That matters when reading the table independently or navigating between document structures.

The bracket caption is “Tournament bracket.” A table's caption should identify the data the table presents; technical details about markup belong in documentation rather than product copy.

A caption also does not supply missing column meaning. A reader needs to know whether a number represents moves, a position in an ordering or another property. The required header cells carry the column relationships; the caption names the whole collection. Combining all labels into a caption would leave the row values harder to interpret.

## Column relationships and reading order

The `scope="col"` attribute makes the header's direction explicit. It communicates that the header applies to values down its column. A bold `td`, a styled `div` or text positioned above a column can look similar while having a different structure.

A reviewer can inspect the table DOM and the browser's accessibility representation separately from the screenshot. The screenshot establishes visible arrangement. The DOM establishes element choices and attributes. The accessibility view helps establish that the browser exposes a meaningful table structure. No single one of these views proves all aspects of the interface.

Row headers, column order, numeric alignment and sorting controls depend on the result feature. The current game has no result implementation with those details.

## Narrow layouts and long values

The current game already separates outer page width from board overflow. Result data would have its own content and width behavior; it cannot simply inherit the card board's scroll logic by sharing a class name. A table's relationship between headers and values remains meaningful even when its viewport is narrow.

There is no table stylesheet in the source and no prescribed responsive table transformation here. A reviewer can still observe whether a proposed layout makes values readable and associated with their headers. Changing a collection into a stack of unrelated labels solely at a breakpoint can affect more than appearance, so both DOM and visual behavior are relevant evidence.

Name text can also vary in width without changing its accepted value. Typography and wrapping are layout concerns. The name policies remain separate from table structure; accepted names retain their displayed representation. [Typography](../visuals/typography.md) and [Form layout guide](form-layout-guide.md) explain nearby layout decisions in the existing interface.

The existing accessibility journey covers game controls and completion, not a result table. Evidence for a future result view would identify its actual markup and readable rows; the current statistics tests cannot establish that structure. [Accessibility audit](../quality/accessibility-audit.md) provides the wider review context.

# Form layout guide

This page explains the label, field and action arrangements used by the current controls.

The game has the always-visible deal bar, text tools inside Reproduce a game and a Tournament setup form. They share native elements and the `.control` style, but their DOM and layout differ. This guide describes those differences so a markup refactor can preserve the actual interaction rather than just one screenshot.

## A map of the current groups

| Group | Markup and layout | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grid size | Label and select in a flex row | `Controls.tsx`, `controls.css` |
| Deal actions | Three buttons in the outer wrapped flex row | `Controls.tsx` |
| Tournament setup | Players select, labeled name inputs and submit button | `TournamentSetup.tsx`, `tournament.css` |
| Board code | Form with label above a field/action row | `BoardCodeForm.tsx`, `reproduction.css` |
| Snapshot JSON | Label and textarea in the panel's body grid | `Reproduction.tsx` |
| Snapshot actions | Two buttons in a wrapped flex row | `Reproduction.tsx` |
| Load outcome | Paragraph and conditional Resume in a wrapped row | `Reproduction.tsx` |

Only Board code is wrapped in a form element. The snapshot field is controlled React state in Reproduction, and its buttons explicitly call callbacks. Enter in a multiline textarea remains text editing rather than submitting the snapshot. Enter in Board code invokes the form's submit path.

## Labels are visible and associated

Grid size uses `htmlFor="grid-size"` and a select with that id. Board code uses `htmlFor="board-code"`, and Snapshot JSON uses `htmlFor="snapshot-json"`. The visible text supplies the fields' names; placeholders do not stand in for labels.

Board code also has `name="boardCode"` because its form reads that field through FormData. Its id serves label association; its name serves native form data lookup. Those are different roles, and changing one does not automatically update the other.

The snapshot textarea has no need for a FormData name in its current path because its value is held in React state and passed directly to `loadSnapshot`. Adding a name attribute alone would not turn its surrounding buttons into a form submission. [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) explains the behavioral value of the current element choices.

The labels come from `control-labels.ts`. Keeping visible text in those constants does not change the label/field relationship. A review can inspect both the imported value and the actual id association, because a correct label string next to the wrong id is still a broken field relationship.

## Deal bar: horizontal until it wraps

The outer `.controls` container uses `display: flex`, bottom alignment, wrapping and a `12px` gap. The nested `.size-control` is a centered flex row with its own `12px` gap. On a wide layout, label, select and action buttons appear in one compact band above the statistics.

At widths up to 599px, the outer container stretches its children. The size group takes the full line and distributes its label and select with space-between alignment. The direct child buttons grow equally. The DOM order stays Grid size, New Game, Tournament, Restart while the layout moves into two lines.

That stability matters for keyboard order. The CSS changes wrapping, not the tab sequence or source order. A visual rearrangement implemented by moving DOM nodes could affect where Tab goes; the present media query does not need to do that.

The group is not a native form. Changing the select calls the controller immediately. There is no Apply button or submission that combines the selected size with one of the deal actions. [Control bar](control-bar.md) documents those callbacks and what they replace.

## Board-code form: one label, one submission

BoardCodeForm renders a grid form with a `6px` gap. Its first child is the label. The next is `.control-row`, a wrapping flex container with a `12px` gap and bottom alignment. Inside are the input and the Load board submit button.

The input has `flex: 1` and `width: 16ch`. The preferred width reflects code-like text, while flex growth gives it available space. The shared control stylesheet sets `min-width: 0` for inputs and textareas so their intrinsic width does not force the page wider than its container.

The button is the form's explicit submit action. Its ref supports successful keyboard submission when the input is replaced. The form prevents normal page navigation, reads `boardCode` and calls the loader. The label stays outside the row so a wrapped button does not detach it from the field's visual group.

On the phone breakpoint, direct child buttons of `.control-row` get `flex: 1`. This selector is shared with the snapshot action row. A wrapper inserted between the row and a button would change this rule's target; a DOM cleanup can therefore have a mobile layout consequence even when desktop placement looks unchanged.

## Snapshot field: a larger editing surface

Reproduction's body is a grid with a `12px` gap and `4px 16px 16px` padding. The Snapshot JSON label and textarea are adjacent children of this grid. The textarea uses five rows, fills its available width and can resize vertically.

Export replaces its value with readable JSON. Import reads the current value. There is no automatic serialization on every game render, so the field can hold a draft while the player inspects cards or changes a deal. Its controlled state is independent of the board-code input's generation-keyed default value.

The two snapshot buttons follow in a `.control-row`. Both are `type="button"`, which makes the action semantics explicit even if the surrounding layout later changes. The current component does not depend on a textarea Enter press to decide which snapshot action to perform.

A manual copy workflow uses native text selection. The card-specific `user-select: none` rule does not apply to this field. Vertical resize and long structured text can make the disclosure tall, but the field remains an ordinary part of document flow.

## Shared control styling

`.control` sets minimum height, padding, border, radius, panel background, text color and inherited font. It is imported by both Controls and the reproduction components. The selectors for button and select add a pointer cursor, while the input and textarea selector handles shrinking.

The shared class does not create a universal component with all semantics and validation built in. A select still has native options, an input still has its own maximum length, and a textarea still has multiline editing. Their association, callbacks and error descriptions remain in the JSX.

`game.css` sets global border-box sizing and a system sans-serif font at `16px` with a `24px` line height. Form controls inherit the font instead of taking a separate browser default. The focus outline is shared through `:focus-visible`, so a form layout also needs enough space for that outline to be seen.

## Outcome text is outside the disclosure

The load notice paragraph and Resume are in `.load-status`, following details rather than living inside `.reproduction-body`. The row has a `12px` gap, wraps and reserves at least `56px` of height. The paragraph grows and has `min-width: 0`.

This placement makes a paused-load outcome usable after the disclosure closes. It also means a selector that searches only inside details will not find Resume or the notice. Tests deliberately inspect the adjacent load-status location. [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) follows its content and the load buttons' `aria-describedby` relationships.

Turn output is elsewhere, near the board instructions. The layout does not put every changing sentence inside the form body. The distinction is useful when testing a large phone board: result visibility near the board and load feedback near the text tools are separate observations.

## Reflow and review examples

At a narrow width, the page should be read as a vertical flow of labeled groups rather than a fixed matrix of coordinates. The existing wrapped rows and shrinking fields let content determine height. The default board fits the narrow layout, while a large board confines its own overflow to its viewport.

A longer draft can remain in an input even when not all of its characters are visible at once; native text editing can scroll within the field. That is different from making the whole outer page wider. A multiline snapshot can expand or scroll internally without turning its label into a floating overlay.

The equivalent zoom test at `640x400`, device scale 2, checks readable controls, statistics and completion output. It also uses the snapshot tools at that constrained layout. `tests/controls.e2e.test.ts` verifies labels, native limits and selectable export text. Together the sources cover geometry and editing behavior without defining a new generic form framework.

Tournament setup uses a Players select and labeled Player 1 through Player 8 inputs, showing the number selected. It validates the accepted names on Start tournament and reports errors through the page status. [Text entry policy](text-entry-policy.md), [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) and [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md) define those acceptance rules.

# Storage failure policy

This page describes how unavailable browser storage affects play and how saved-record features present that limitation.

The game isolates storage failures from active play. Preference writes can fail without stopping solo play. Tournament history also catches access and write failures; its screen shows “Progress won't be saved on this device.” near Past tournaments when that storage is unavailable.

## Features with saved records

For a feature that presents saved records, the unavailable-storage state belongs near the data it affects. The active interaction can still use its current in-memory state even though later visits cannot rely on finding that state again. When browser storage is blocked, a feature keeps working in memory and shows "Progress won't be saved on this device." where its saved records would appear. This ties the explanation to the missing persistence rather than turning it into a failure of the whole game.

The preference adapter still exposes no blocked-status result: `readPreferences` returns preferences and `writePreferences` returns `void`. The tournament adapter returns history with an `available` flag and a boolean write result. Its warning applies to tournament history; it does not claim that the separate preference write failed.

The existing status display remains driven by session state. A best achieved during a visit can appear there after a failed write because it is already in `session.preferences`. A visible best is evidence of the in-memory result; persistence across a later reload needs separate evidence. [Persistence overview](persistence-overview.md) describes the data boundary.

## Three browser operations can fail independently

The first operation is acquiring the storage object. `browserStore` in `src/game/session/use-saved-preferences.ts` returns `window.localStorage` inside a `try` block. If the property getter throws, the function catches the exception and returns `null`. A denied property getter is tested in `tests/browser-environment.e2e.test.ts` by defining a getter that throws a `SecurityError` before the game initializes.

The second operation is reading the key. A browser can expose an object whose `getItem` later throws. `readPreferences` protects that call and returns `{ size: DEFAULT_SIZE, bestMoves: {} }` on failure. Its optional call also accommodates a `null` store. A successful read can return no value, a malformed string or valid preferences; those are separate outcomes from a thrown read.

The third operation is writing a serialized replacement. `writePreferences` encloses both serialization and `setItem` in its `try` block. A thrown error is swallowed so it cannot interrupt play. A browser may accept reads and refuse writes, so successful startup does not establish successful saving. Quota exhaustion is one possible write failure; browser policy is another.

These stages explain why a single boolean based on the existence of the storage property would be a weak diagnostic. The game doesn't use such a probe. It attempts the real operation at the boundary and catches failure there.

## What the current fallback preserves

Storage failure does not bypass the game's own rules. Card eligibility, move counting, matching, elapsed time and completion still use their normal state transitions. The fallback affects the initial preference value and the durability of subsequent changes. It does not substitute a different deck algorithm or change how many moves a result takes.

After a denied startup read, the game starts at the default size with no saved bests. Choosing another supported size updates the active session. Completing a game can produce a best for that size in memory. New Game and Restart preserve those in-memory preferences because `replaceGame` copies the session preference object rather than rereading the browser store.

If storage remains unavailable, a page reload starts another session from the fallback. The earlier in-memory best is gone with the old page. This is the expected consequence of unsuccessful saving, even though play in the earlier page was complete and valid. A report that a score survived Restart but disappeared on reload is consistent with a write failure.

An imported unfinished snapshot remains usable under the same conditions. The snapshot text is decoded into game state, then the session handles pause and resume. That path does not require a successful preference write. The accepted board size may be retained only in the current session if the browser refuses the later save.

## No implicit retry service

The hook is a small effect:

```ts
useEffect(() => {
  writePreferences(store, preferences);
}, [preferences, store]);
```

There is no queue, timer-driven retry, backoff or unload handler. Another dependency change can cause another attempt, but the code does not poll for a browser setting to change. A returned `null` store is captured in state for the lifetime of that mounted game; enabling storage later does not replace that state value automatically.

If the captured store object exists and its methods change behavior, a later effect can succeed using the same object. For example, a test double can reject its first write and accept a later one. That is different from reacquiring a previously inaccessible property. Both cases can be modeled without making the game rules aware of browser error names.

The writer's lack of a success result also means the existing UI cannot distinguish a rejected write from a successful one. This is a deliberate limit of the current adapter, not a hidden confirmation mechanism. Any investigation that needs that distinction can observe the supplied store in a test.

## Read failure and corrupt data have different evidence

A denied read and an invalid JSON value both lead to fallback preferences. Only the former establishes that an operation could not be completed. A parse failure establishes that the browser returned text which the application could not use. Confusing the two can lead to a misleading message about browser settings when the actual issue is an edited value.

Similarly, a quota error does not mean the existing value is invalid. The old string may remain perfectly readable while the new result exists only in memory. A person may see a better current best and then see the older best after reload. That sequence is a useful way to reproduce a failed update without damaging a valid baseline.

[Corrupt data policy](corrupt-data-policy.md) follows the rejection branches in detail. [Storage quota notes](storage-quota-notes.md) explains why the small size of this app's own payload cannot establish that a shared origin has available space.

## Errors do not authorize deleting other data

The storage adapters call `getItem` and `setItem` only for their own preference or tournament-history key. Neither uses a storage-wide clear call, key enumeration or cleanup routine. Their store interfaces expose only those two methods. The preference storage test explicitly seeds an unrelated key and checks that a preference write leaves its value intact.

This matters in shared local environments, where another page can occupy the same origin. A rejected preference write does not cause Neon Pairs to free space by deleting that page's values. The current fallback is simply to continue without a successful save. The app also does not switch to cookies, a server endpoint or another browser database after failure.

When reproducing capacity problems, a disposable origin or isolated browser context keeps artificial fill data away from a person's real preferences. That is a testing technique rather than an extra product recovery path. The test can remove the keys it created afterward; the shipped game contains no such test cleanup behavior.

## Evidence in the test suite

`storage.test.ts` uses a denied store whose read and write methods both throw. It checks that reading yields the default size and that writing does not throw. It also covers `readPreferences(null)`. This verifies the API boundary directly, without needing to configure an actual browser's privacy settings.

The browser environment test covers a different boundary: acquisition of `window.localStorage`. It installs the throwing getter before loading the game, loads a fixed board and matches a known pair. The harness gathers uncaught page errors and checks that none occurred. That demonstrates continued play after an acquisition failure, not persistence in that denied context.

These tests don't establish every browser policy or a physical disk limit. They also don't assert the saved-record feature notice described earlier. Reading the test title alone can obscure those limits; the actual injection point and assertions show what each test proves. [Storage testing guide](storage-testing-guide.md) extends that evidence into an investigation workflow.

# Retention policy

This page explains retention for saved feature lists and contrasts it with the compact best-score aggregate in the current game.

Retention describes how much accepted data remains after a save. It is separate from parsing a malformed value, clearing site data in browser settings or losing a private browsing session. The game currently remembers one best move count per supported size rather than preserving individual completed attempts. A browser dump of those bests cannot reconstruct the order or number of games played.

## Saved lists

A list can grow as a feature saves additional records, even when every individual record is small. Its retention boundary applies during saving, rather than acting as an expiration clock while the player is idle. A stored list keeps its newest 10 records and drops older ones when a new record is saved. This bounds the retained collection while leaving the active interaction independent of an ever-growing history.

Completed tournament history is a saved list with a ten-record limit. It does not turn the `bestMoves` object into a history or add a timestamp to it. Record types, sort fields and tie-breaking conventions are separate from the amount retained.

The list representation is discussed in [Persistence envelope](persistence-envelope.md). Parsing and validation failures are covered in [Corrupt data policy](corrupt-data-policy.md), because retention of accepted records and recovery from rejected input are different operations.

## Preferences retain bests; tournaments retain completed events

`Preferences.bestMoves` is a `Readonly<Record<string, number>>`. The key is the canonical decimal side length, such as `4` or `12`, and the value is the best completed move count for that size. The selected board size lives separately in `Preferences.size`. Selecting another size does not discard the previous size's best.

The supported set has seven entries. Once read validation has succeeded, the score map can therefore contain at most seven different supported size keys. It can also contain fewer, including none. This bound follows from `GRID_SIZES` and canonical key validation, not from trimming an attempt history. Multiple completed games at the same size compete for the same map entry.

For example, suppose a browser has a 4x4 best of 10. Finishing later in 9 moves replaces that one number. Finishing in 11 moves leaves 9 in place. Finishing in 9 moves again also leaves it in place. Those outcomes do not append three records; there is still only one 4x4 entry. [Best score records](../gameplay/best-score-records.md) explains the completion rule in gameplay terms.

The selected size can change while all best entries remain identical. A visit that chooses 16x16 and then reloads may store `size: 16` alongside a score map containing only a 4x4 result. That is a valid aggregate. The remembered preference describes the next board size, while the map describes earlier eligible completions.

`src/game/competition/storage.ts` stores only completed tournament records in `np3:tournaments`. Saving a new completion places it first and retains at most ten records; unfinished tournaments stay in memory unless the player exports Tournament JSON. Reload therefore keeps finished brackets without creating an automatic checkpoint for an event in progress.

## Why no clock drives current retention

The preference format contains no creation date, last-played time or expiry value. `readPreferences` does not inspect the current time. It cannot tell whether a valid best was written a minute ago or on a much earlier visit. There is no scheduled cleanup effect, idle purge or age-based deletion in `use-saved-preferences.ts`.

This makes the data easy to explain: a valid best remains available across normal reloads until another relevant event changes the storage or the value is rejected. A better result can replace it. Browser policy or a person's site-data action can remove it. Another tab can overwrite the aggregate. None of those is an application age policy.

The distinction matters when comparing evidence from two visits. A gap between visits does not by itself identify the cause of a missing best. If the origin changed, the second visit may have read another storage area. If the value was edited into an invalid shape, the reader may have used its fallback. If the browser cleared data, the key may simply be absent. [Storage quota notes](storage-quota-notes.md) discusses environment-driven loss without treating it as list pruning.

## Save time is an application event

The preference writer runs from a React effect whose dependencies are the preferences object and store. This is not a page-exit flush. On initial mounting, the effect writes the current preference state. Later, a new preference object causes another effect run. There is no dependency on active elapsed milliseconds or every move in the game.

`replaceGame` always constructs a preference object with the new game's size. New Game and Restart consequently pass through a save-capable path even when the size value stays the same. Valid board-code and snapshot loads do so as well. Invalid loads update feedback without replacing preferences.

`rememberBest` returns the original object for equal or worse results. The session can still render a completed game, but the preference identity need not change. This keeps the storage effect aligned with meaningful preference updates in that path. It is not a universal deduplication layer: replacement actions can still write the same serialized preference contents again.

Tournament retention runs when the final match is completed. The preference effect has no generic event log or timer that scans browser keys, and tournament storage is handled by its feature-specific adapter.

## Retained locally does not mean backed up

The app has no account or service that copies the aggregate elsewhere. A best kept in one profile remains local to that browser's storage context. Opening the same HTML in another browser does not fetch it. Exporting a snapshot copies game progress, not a backup of the browser's accumulated bests or selected-size history.

The UI has no general preference export, browser-data restore or clear-records control. A developer can inspect or change storage manually, but those are debugging actions rather than product controls.

## Retention and capacity are related, but different

A bounded collection makes its record count predictable. It does not guarantee every write succeeds: browser access can be blocked before capacity matters, and another application on the same origin may consume storage. A small value can fail to write even though its own size is well below a browser's nominal limit.

Conversely, a successful write does not prove indefinite lifetime. The browser can later clear data, a private context can end, or the person can remove site storage. Those environmental conditions are outside the saved-list retention operation. [Private browsing notes](private-browsing-notes.md) describes how a value can survive a reload yet disappear when the browsing session ends.

The current score aggregate illustrates the same separation at a smaller scale. It has a naturally small set of keys and bounded integer values, yet `setItem` remains inside a `try` block. Capacity savings reduce the amount being written; they do not change the need to continue play if the browser refuses it.

## Checking retention with feature records

The existing test suite establishes preference behavior rather than a list API. `storage.test.ts` checks independent minimums for two sizes and object identity for equal and worse results. Browser journeys check that completed bests survive reloads and game resets. None of those tests asserts a sequence of saved feature records.

For a feature-list review, concrete before-and-after examples can expose the retention boundary without adding fields to the product format. Records can be identified by the already defined domain representation in that feature's tests. The useful observation is which accepted records are present after a save, compared with the preceding accepted collection. Examples can use the feature's existing record fields.

It is also useful to keep failed writes separate from successful retention checks. A denied store can leave the feature's in-memory state ahead of the browser value. Inspecting the old browser string then proves only that the write failed, not that the retention calculation chose the wrong records. [Storage testing guide](storage-testing-guide.md) describes the store doubles that make this separation observable.

## What bests retain

The best map cannot answer how many attempts occurred, which deal produced a best, how long that attempt took, or whether two equal results happened on different days. None of those fields is retained. A new feature that needs a collection has a different persistence concern from calculating a size-specific minimum.

Keeping that distinction explicit avoids a misleading implementation shortcut: interpreting every best-map update as if it were an append to a historical list. The code's result is an aggregate with replacement semantics. The saved-list rule belongs to collections, while the current aggregate remains documented and tested according to its own source behavior.
