# Text entry policy

This page records the treatment of person-entered names and distinguishes it from the game's existing code and JSON fields.

Tournament setup asks for player names and applies this policy when Start tournament accepts the group. The name fields are separate from board-code and JSON fields; the policy does not describe a transformation applied to reproduction text.

## One name representation

A name can arrive with incidental spaces from typing, pasting or an input method. Keeping several representations of that same entered name would make later display and comparison harder to reason about. Every name a person types is stored and shown after trimming both ends, collapsing each run of inner whitespace to one space and normalizing to NFC. The stored value and visible value therefore describe the same processed name rather than exposing the original draft in one view and a different spelling in another.

The policy is about a person's name. It does not turn all user input into name text, and it does not change the board-code grammar or snapshot serialization. The current fields demonstrate why that distinction matters: significant punctuation and structural whitespace belong to their own formats.

For names, the other checks are documented separately in [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) and [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md). This page explains representation and input boundaries without duplicating their conditions or error messages.

## Examples of representation

The following examples use quotes only to make surrounding whitespace visible. The quotes are not part of the entered name.

| Entered draft | Displayed and stored form | What changed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `  Mira  ` | `Mira` | Space around the name is removed |
| `Ada   Lovelace` | `Ada Lovelace` | An interior run becomes one separating space |
| `Jean Luc` | `Jean Luc` | Ordinary spacing stays ordinary |
| `Cafe` followed by a combining acute on the e | `Café` | Canonically equivalent text gets a composed representation where available |
| `O'Neil` | `O'Neil` | The apostrophe is retained |

The last example matters because representation cleanup is not an instruction to remove meaningful punctuation or rewrite a person's preferred spelling. The policy does not transliterate scripts, strip accents or convert names to ASCII. Those would be additional transformations beyond what is stated.

NFC addresses canonical equivalence in Unicode text. It is not the compatibility normalization form. Text that merely looks similar is not necessarily canonically equivalent, and this policy does not define visual resemblance as identity. That boundary prevents a representation step from quietly becoming a broad name-matching heuristic.

A name can also contain multiple words. Collapsing a whitespace run does not merge words together; it leaves a separating space. Treating the policy as “delete all whitespace” would change `Ada Lovelace` into a different string and would not implement the stated behavior.

## Drafts and accepted values

A draft is what someone is still editing. A stored value is what an action has accepted. The policy determines the representation of accepted and displayed names, but it does not prescribe that the caret jump after every keystroke or that an input method's partial composition be rewritten while it is active.

That distinction leaves room to implement an editing experience without confusing it with persistence. A reviewer can inspect where a completed entry crosses from local draft state into the feature's model and where the model is rendered. If display uses an old raw draft while storage uses the processed value, the two surfaces no longer have the relationship described above.

Tournament's player inputs are controlled draft fields. On submission, `validatePlayerNames` returns the normalized values that become the tournament participants and are then displayed in the bracket. The choice of controlled or uncontrolled field does not by itself implement name representation.

Player names do not enter `session/storage.ts` or the solo preference value. They are carried by tournament JSON and by completed tournament records in the separate tournament-history key.

## Board codes follow a different path

The Board code input is a native text input with `maxLength={32}`, spell checking disabled and autocomplete off. On submission, `use-game.ts` calls `code.trim()` before `parseBoardCode(code)`. That is the only cleanup in that loading path.

The grammar is a version prefix, supported side length and seed separated by hyphens. For example, surrounding spaces around `np1-6-1` are accepted by the control, but an internal space changes the grammar and is rejected. The loader does not collapse arbitrary interior text or repair the seed.

Successful submission replaces the game and refreshes the field from the current code because the input is keyed by generation. Unsuccessful submission preserves the draft. This gives a concrete reference for separating a draft from an accepted representation without applying name transformations to a deal identifier. See [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md).

Board-code parsing is also available as a core function. Calling `parseBoardCode` directly is not the same as passing through the UI loader's trim step. When reading a failure report, the entry point matters. A format parser and an input adapter can have distinct responsibilities without the application guessing what malformed identifiers meant.

## Snapshot text remains structured data

Snapshot JSON has a native textarea length limit and a decoder byte limit. It can include whitespace for readability, and export deliberately produces multiple lines. Its structure is validated before the game is replaced.

Applying name cleanup to the entire JSON draft would conflate two kinds of input. Whitespace can occur between tokens or inside a JSON string, with different meanings. The existing code passes the complete draft to `decodeSnapshot`; it does not first treat it as display prose or a person's name.

The same is true for error preservation. On malformed JSON, the text remains editable and the current game remains present. That behavior supports correction of a structured draft. Accepted names use the normalized representation described above.

[Import safety policy](../sharing/import-safety-policy.md) and [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) explain the current parser and feedback boundaries. Keeping those links close to the input descriptions is more useful than inventing one universal cleanup function for every field on the page.

## Unicode review considerations

Canonical equivalence is easiest to miss when examples are written as visually identical letters. A composed accented character and a base character followed by a combining mark may render alike while having different underlying sequences. A useful representation check includes both forms and inspects the accepted value rather than only its screenshot.

The policy also leaves capitalization alone at this representation step. A comparison operation may have its own policy, but that does not require changing a person's displayed capitalization. Keeping display representation and comparison purpose distinct avoids presenting a comparison key as someone's chosen name.

Likewise, a font's treatment of a character does not change the text stored. A missing glyph, a ligature or a different script's shaping belongs to rendering and typography. The representation policy can be implemented correctly while a layout still needs work to display the name legibly. [Typography](../visuals/typography.md) provides the visual context.

The current game has no name-character allowlist or prohibited-name list. Adding one while implementing spacing cleanup would be a separate product decision, not a consequence of Unicode normalization.

## Implementation evidence to look for

The current test record does not establish name-specific behavior. Review can connect the setup draft, accepted tournament model, bracket display and exported value using the cases above. A check confined to an input's current value can miss a storage path that retains an older raw string.

Repeated processing should not progressively change the accepted spelling. The transformations described here have a stable result once applied. If editing, saving and displaying the same accepted name repeatedly removes more content each time, that points to an implementation doing more than the stated representation work.

The code keeps these input boundaries separate: BoardCodeForm parses a deal identifier, Reproduction decodes structured progress, and Tournament setup normalizes and validates a participant group. Each rendered value follows its own accepted representation.

docs/persistence/retention-policy.md:50:Tournament retention runs when the final match is completed. The preference effect has no generic event log or timer that scans browser keys, and tournament storage is handled by its feature-specific adapter.
docs/persistence/retention-policy.md:68:The existing preference tests establish aggregate behavior rather than tournament-list retention. `storage.test.ts` checks independent minimums for two sizes and object identity for equal and worse results. The tournament history adapter implements a newest-ten list, but no test evidence is claimed here. Browser journeys check that solo bests survive reloads and game resets.
docs/persistence/retention-policy.md:76:The solo best map cannot answer how many solo attempts occurred, which deal produced a best, how long that attempt took, or whether two equal results happened on different days. Tournament results do retain each match's moves and time in the separate tournament history. A preferences map and an event collection serve different persistence needs.
docs/persistence/retention-policy.md:78:Keeping that distinction explicit avoids a misleading implementation shortcut: interpreting every solo best-map update as if it were an append to a historical list. The code's result is an aggregate with replacement semantics. The saved-list rule belongs to tournament records, while the solo aggregate remains documented according to its own source behavior.
docs/persistence/storage-failure-policy.md:13:The game isolates storage failures from active play. Preference writes can fail without stopping solo play. Tournament history also catches access and write failures; its screen shows “Progress won't be saved on this device.” near Past tournaments when that storage is unavailable.
docs/persistence/storage-failure-policy.md:17:For a feature that presents saved records, the unavailable-storage state belongs near the data it affects. The active interaction can still use its current in-memory state even though later visits cannot rely on finding that state again. When browser storage is blocked, a feature keeps working in memory and shows "Progress won't be saved on this device." where its saved records would appear. This ties the explanation to the missing persistence rather than turning it into a failure of the whole game.
docs/persistence/storage-failure-policy.md:19:The preference adapter still exposes no blocked-status result: `readPreferences` returns preferences and `writePreferences` returns `void`. The tournament adapter returns history with an `available` flag and a boolean write result. Its warning applies to tournament history; it does not claim that the separate preference write failed.
docs/persistence/storage-failure-policy.md:57:The preference writer's lack of a success result means the solo UI cannot distinguish a rejected preference write from a successful one. Tournament history writes return a boolean, which updates the availability warning shown beside Past tournaments. Any investigation that needs the preference-write distinction can observe the supplied store in a test.
docs/persistence/storage-failure-policy.md:69:The storage adapters call `getItem` and `setItem` only for their own preference or tournament-history key. Neither uses a storage-wide clear call, key enumeration or cleanup routine. Their store interfaces expose only those two methods. The preference storage test explicitly seeds an unrelated key and checks that a preference write leaves its value intact.
docs/persistence/corrupt-data-policy.md:107:Invalid input typed into the board-code and snapshot controls follows another interaction. Those controls keep the current game, preserve the draft for correction and show their defined validation status. They do not silently replace the active game with a default board. That feedback is appropriate because the person has just requested an explicit load operation.
docs/persistence/persistence-overview.md:11:This page explains the small amount of browser data Neon Pairs saves and the boundary between remembered preferences and an active game.
docs/persistence/persistence-overview.md:13:The game stores solo preferences under `neon-pairs.preferences.v1` and completed tournament history under `np3:tournaments`. Preferences remember the selected board size and the lowest completed move count for each size; they do not contain a saved game. Tournament history keeps the ten most recent completed brackets. Reloading solo play starts a fresh deal at the remembered size, while finished tournaments remain in Past tournaments.
docs/persistence/persistence-overview.md:40:- An unfinished tournament is not saved automatically. Export Tournament JSON to preserve its setup or progress outside the current page.
docs/persistence/persistence-overview.md:56:The preferences answer two recurring questions: which size did this browser use, and what is its best completed move count for this size? They can answer both without retaining every solo attempt. Tournament history separately retains completed brackets and their participant results. Neither store writes a game snapshot on every move or on page exit.
docs/persistence/persistence-overview.md:66:The app does not synchronize preference or tournament-history changes between open tabs. Each tab reads its initial value and writes its own in-memory state. One tab can overwrite another tab's changes; the specification explicitly leaves several simultaneous game windows outside the supported journeys.
docs/persistence/_persistence.md:23:- [Tournament history retention and solo aggregate best-score lifetime.](retention-policy.md) - #Persistence #Retention
docs/README.md:30:A board code describes a deal. A snapshot saves progress. A replay records timed actions. Their algorithms and formats are in [Reproducibility](sharing/reproducibility.md). Tournament JSON has its own `neon-pairs/tournament` format version 1, described with the [tournament requirements](competition/competition-overview.md).
docs/README.md:32:## Tournament
docs/README.md:34:Tournament mode runs a four- or eight-player knockout on one device. Each match gives both players the same deal in sequence, and the bracket records moves, active time and the winner. Finished brackets stay in a local Past tournaments list; Tournament JSON exports or loads setups and progress. The [competition requirements](competition/competition-overview.md) define pairings, rounds, board sizes, ties and score isolation.

docs/interface/controls.md:22:- C15 - Put a "Tournament" button beside New Game. Open the Tournament screen, where four or eight players can enter a knockout event on the shared device. Each match uses one deal for both turns; the bracket records moves, time and winner. See [Shared-device competition](../competition/competition-overview.md).
docs/interface/tables-policy.md:14:The solo UI uses a definition list for one game's statistics. Tournament uses an HTML table for bracket rows, with a caption and scoped column headings. The card board remains a CSS grid of buttons; those different structures serve different data.
docs/interface/tables-policy.md:18:When the content represents records with comparable columns, its relationships need to survive reading beyond the visual arrangement. CSS alone can align text while leaving those relationships absent from the document structure. Ranked or bracket data is a table element with a caption and th scope="col" header cells. The caption identifies the collection being read, while the column headers connect each record's values to their meaning.
docs/interface/tables-policy.md:44:The bracket caption is “Tournament bracket.” A table's caption should identify the data the table presents; technical details about markup belong in documentation rather than product copy.
docs/interface/tables-policy.md:54:The current bracket does not use row headers, numeric sorting or other table controls. Its column order groups each player's moves and time beside that player's name, then gives the match winner its own column.
docs/interface/tables-policy.md:58:The current game separates outer page width from board overflow. The bracket has its own wrapper and horizontal overflow behavior in `tournament.css`; it cannot inherit the card board's scroll logic by sharing a class name. A table's relationship between headers and values remains meaningful when its viewport is narrow.
docs/interface/tables-policy.md:60:The bracket keeps its columns and can scroll horizontally when its minimum width exceeds the viewport. The DOM relationships remain intact while scrolling, and the two player result groups stay beside their names. Both that structure and its visible narrow-layout behavior are relevant review evidence.
docs/interface/tables-policy.md:64:The existing accessibility journey covers game controls and completion, but does not establish browser accessibility-tree exposure for the tournament table. A review of the bracket should inspect its actual markup and readable rows; solo statistics checks cannot establish that structure. [Accessibility audit](../quality/accessibility-audit.md) provides the wider review context.
docs/interface/announcements-policy.md:17:`Game.tsx` places one paragraph with `role="status"`, `aria-live="polite"` and `aria-atomic="true"` before the active screen. Solo feedback and tournament event messages use the same live region. Tournament also shows the persistent visual label `Now playing: NAME` and the round label near its board; its controller announces turn changes, completed turns, match winners and the champion through the shared status paragraph.
docs/interface/announcements-policy.md:25:The solo session owns `feedback` and an integer `announcement`. Game uses that identity for solo messages and a separate local identity for tournament events. Updating the keyed span replaces the child even when its text is identical to the preceding result. This gives repeated events a DOM change without adding a hidden counter to the spoken text.
docs/interface/form-layout-guide.md:14:The game has the always-visible deal bar, text tools inside Reproduce a game and a Tournament setup form. They share native elements and the `.control` style, but their DOM and layout differ. This guide describes those differences so a markup refactor can preserve the actual interaction rather than just one screenshot.
docs/interface/form-layout-guide.md:22:| Tournament setup | Players select, labeled name inputs and submit button | `TournamentSetup.tsx`, `tournament.css` |
docs/interface/form-layout-guide.md:23:| Tournament JSON | Label and controlled textarea with Export and Load actions | `Tournament.tsx`, `tournament.css` |
docs/interface/form-layout-guide.md:29:Board code and Tournament setup are wrapped in form elements. Snapshot and Tournament JSON fields are controlled React state in their respective components, and their buttons explicitly call callbacks. Enter in a multiline textarea remains text editing rather than submitting JSON. Enter in either form invokes its submit path.
docs/interface/form-layout-guide.md:39:Tournament JSON is also held in local React state. Export fills that field, while Load reads its current value; neither action submits the Tournament setup form. The text area has a 65,536-character native maximum and remains an ordinary multiline editing surface.
docs/interface/form-layout-guide.md:47:At widths up to 599px, the outer container stretches its children. The size group takes the full line and distributes its label and select with space-between alignment. The direct child buttons grow equally. The DOM order stays Grid size, New Game, Tournament, Restart while the layout moves into two lines.
docs/interface/form-layout-guide.md:97:Tournament setup uses a Players select and labeled Player 1 through Player 8 inputs, showing the number selected. It validates the accepted names on Start tournament and reports errors through the page status. [Text entry policy](text-entry-policy.md), [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) and [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md) define those acceptance rules.
docs/interface/name-length-policy.md:13:Tournament asks for player names in its setup form. `validatePlayerNames` in `src/game/competition/names.ts` applies this policy after the text representation has been normalized. Board code and JSON fields keep their separate limits.
docs/interface/name-length-policy.md:31:In JavaScript, iterating a string by code point is different from indexing its individual UTF-16 units. `Array.from(value).length` counts the accepted name in the tournament validator.
docs/interface/name-length-policy.md:61:The validator runs when Start tournament is submitted, so the error is announced and the form remains available for correction. Name-length test coverage is not part of the existing recorded evidence; keyboard and reproduction checks do not establish this count.
docs/interface/control-bar.md:14:The bar has a labeled size selector, New Game, Tournament and Restart. It sits above the statistics and board in `src/game/Game.tsx`; the Tournament action opens a separate shared-device screen. Reproduction tools have a different rhythm and occupy their own disclosure below the board; see [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md).
docs/interface/control-bar.md:18:`src/game/controls/Controls.tsx` accepts `size`, `newGame(size?: number)`, `restart()` and `openTournament()`. It does not own a second copy of the selected size, choose a seed, reset a timer or update preferences. Its select is controlled by the `size` prop. That prop comes from `session.game.size`, which makes the displayed choice agree with the board after a size change, board-code load or snapshot import.
docs/interface/control-bar.md:22:The select and buttons are native elements. The buttons explicitly use `type="button"`; they do not submit the reproduction form farther down the page. The wrapper is a `div` with class `controls`, not a toolbar widget with a separate keyboard model. Tab follows ordinary document order through the select, New Game, Tournament and Restart. Board navigation begins after those controls, as described in [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md).
docs/interface/control-bar.md:26:`src/game/controls/control-labels.ts` exports `DealControl`. The visible strings are `Grid size`, `New Game`, `Tournament` and `Restart`. The label is associated with `id="grid-size"` through `htmlFor="grid-size"`. A user or browser test can therefore find the select by its visible name instead of a CSS class or its position in the bar.
docs/interface/control-bar.md:76:New Game and Restart still replace the current deal immediately. Tournament switches screens without replacing the solo game. Leaving an unfinished tournament uses the confirmation described in [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md).
docs/interface/error-display-guide.md:11:This page explains how failed board-code, snapshot and tournament operations are reported while preserving the current work.
docs/interface/error-display-guide.md:13:The current UI reports invalid board codes and snapshots, invalid tournament names and tournament JSON, and unknown tournament JSON fields. These messages describe the attempted operation, not a broken game. A player can correct the draft and retry while the current deal or tournament remains available.
docs/interface/error-display-guide.md:71:Snapshot JSON has a 65,536-character textarea limit and a UTF-8 byte bound in the decoder. Malformed JSON is only one failure kind. Unsupported versions, unknown properties, inconsistent matched positions, invalid selections and out-of-range counters can also produce the same UI error. Tournament JSON has the same character and byte bound. An unknown property at any recognized object level reports `Unknown field: NAME.`; other malformed or inconsistent tournament values report `Invalid tournament.`.
docs/interface/error-display-guide.md:83:Tournament name errors are published through the shared page status. The setup keeps each input draft in component state after a failed Start tournament submission; it does not attach a separate inline error paragraph to each name. The exact length and uniqueness rules are in [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) and [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md).
docs/interface/native-controls-guide.md:21:| `select` with `option` | Grid size and tournament player count | Supply supported values and start a deal or configure a group |
docs/interface/native-controls-guide.md:23:| `input` | Board-code draft and tournament player names | Read and validate the submitted value |
docs/interface/native-controls-guide.md:24:| `textarea` | Snapshot and tournament JSON drafts | Hold text and pass it to the appropriate decoder |
docs/interface/native-controls-guide.md:25:| `form` | Board-code and tournament setup | Prevent navigation and handle the result |
docs/interface/native-controls-guide.md:28:| `dialog` | Tournament leave and replace confirmation | Supply modal behavior and initial focus |
docs/interface/native-controls-guide.md:29:| `table` | Tournament bracket | Associate round, player, moves, time and winner columns |
docs/interface/native-controls-guide.md:31:These choices describe the current DOM. [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) and [Tables policy](tables-policy.md) explain the confirmation and bracket semantics.
docs/interface/native-controls-guide.md:39:Action buttons outside the board use explicit types too. The Board code loader and Start tournament are submit buttons in their forms. New Game, Tournament, Restart, Start turn, Next turn, Next match, Back to game, Export and Load buttons use `type="button"`. This makes submission intent visible in JSX rather than relying on where the browser happens to find an enclosing form.
docs/interface/disabled-state-guide.md:84:These details help distinguish a correct ignored action from a lost input. A click on a hidden eligible card in a closed active game should reveal it. A click on a matched card should not change the turn. Both can deliver the same native event; their game-state eligibility differs.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:16:## Play and Tournament screen replacement
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:18:`Game.tsx` switches the main area between Play and Tournament. Both screens have an h2 with `tabIndex="-1"`; when the screen changes, focus moves to its heading. The initial Play screen does not move focus on page load.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:22:Expanding native details, updating statistics, closing a mismatch or displaying the completed-game paragraph does not create a new screen. Within Tournament, the Start turn button hands focus to the new board, Next turn and Next match focus the following Start turn button, and completion focuses Back to game. [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) covers the separate opening focus for its confirmation.
docs/interface/duplicate-names-policy.md:14:Tournament setup collects a group of player names, and `validatePlayerNames` in `src/game/competition/names.ts` checks uniqueness within that entry list. The policy applies to that tournament group; it does not create a global name registry.
docs/interface/duplicate-names-policy.md:54:Tournament setup applies the checks when Start tournament is submitted. Invalid names publish the relevant notice and leave the form available for correction. This acceptance boundary is separate from the board-code parser and its load errors. [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) provides the feedback context.
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:14:Tournament uses a native `dialog` when leaving unfinished work or replacing an active event with loaded JSON. The Play controls retain their existing direct behavior: New Game, Restart and reproduction loads do not ask for confirmation.
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:22:Tournament owns its dialog state in `Tournament.tsx`; the app still has no router. Changing between Play and Tournament focuses the new screen's h2. [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) covers that main-area replacement.
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:42:Dialog state is local to `Tournament.tsx` and is not part of either game session or exported tournament data. The solo `Session` fields remain `game`, `paused`, `generation`, `feedback`, `loadNotice`, `announcement`, `celebration` and `preferences`. Its `paused` flag still represents unfinished snapshot import.
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:48:Opening the Tournament confirmation does not pause elapsed time or a pending mismatch: the shared clock continues while the tournament screen remains active and visible. [Clock design](../architecture/clock-design.md) and [Mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) explain the clock model.
docs/interface/text-entry-policy.md:14:Tournament setup asks for player names and applies this policy when Start tournament accepts the group. The name fields are separate from board-code and JSON fields; the policy does not describe a transformation applied to reproduction text.
docs/interface/text-entry-policy.md:48:Tournament's player inputs are controlled draft fields. On submission, `validatePlayerNames` returns the normalized values that become the tournament participants and are then displayed in the bracket. The choice of controlled or uncontrolled field does not by itself implement name representation.
docs/interface/text-entry-policy.md:50:Player names do not enter `session/storage.ts` or the solo preference value. They are carried by tournament JSON and by completed tournament records in the separate tournament-history key.
docs/interface/text-entry-policy.md:84:The current test record does not establish name-specific behavior. Review can connect the setup draft, accepted tournament model, bracket display and exported value using the cases above. A check confined to an input's current value can miss a storage path that retains an older raw string.
docs/interface/text-entry-policy.md:88:The code keeps these input boundaries separate: BoardCodeForm parses a deal identifier, Reproduction decodes structured progress, and Tournament setup normalizes and validates a participant group. Each rendered value follows its own accepted representation.
docs/interface/interface-review-checklist.md:12:This page is a review route through the Play and Tournament controls, input behavior and related interface policies.
docs/interface/interface-review-checklist.md:20:- Identify whether the change affects `Controls`, `Reproduction`, `BoardCodeForm`, `GameStatus`, `Tournament`, `Board`, `Card` or the focus hook.
docs/interface/interface-review-checklist.md:25:Tournament owns the name form, leave confirmation and bracket table. Their behavior belongs to the feature components and the policies linked below.
docs/interface/interface-review-checklist.md:56:## Tournament setup and play
docs/interface/interface-review-checklist.md:58:Use [Shared-device competition](../competition/competition-overview.md) and [Text entry policy](text-entry-policy.md) for the tournament requirements.
docs/interface/interface-review-checklist.md:63:- Start a player's turn and complete the same board code for both players in a match. Check moves, active time, tie-break order and the bracket winner.
docs/interface/interface-review-checklist.md:65:- Leave an unfinished tournament, keep playing from Escape or Keep playing, and confirm with Leave to return to setup.
docs/interface/interface-review-checklist.md:66:- Export setup and active progress to Tournament JSON. Load valid text; invalid text must leave the current state and draft unchanged.
docs/interface/interface-review-checklist.md:67:- Complete a tournament, reload, and confirm it remains in Past tournaments with its bracket.
docs/interface/interface-review-checklist.md:110:Tournament setup accepts player names under [Text entry policy](text-entry-policy.md), [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) and [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md). For bracket result content, consult [Tables policy](tables-policy.md).

# Comparing tied competition results

This page describes competition result comparison and explains the active-time information available from the current game.

A result comparison uses information from completed play. The game core exposes a finished board's moves and elapsed time; `compareResults` in `src/game/competition/rules.ts` applies the tournament order and entry-seed tie-break.

## Comparison order

Moves are the first useful distinction between two completed attempts, but they can be equal. When both players of a match finish in the same number of moves, the lower active time wins, and if that is also equal the higher seed wins. Seed 1 is the highest seed. The comparison is ordered: an earlier distinction settles the result before a later one is considered.

These example results illustrate the first two levels. The elapsed values are milliseconds in game data.

| Participant | Moves | Active elapsed milliseconds | Result in this example |
| ----------- | ----- | --------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| Ada         | 12    | 70200                       | Ahead on moves         |
| Bo          | 13    | 58100                       | Faster, but more moves |

| Participant | Moves | Active elapsed milliseconds | Result in this example          |
| ----------- | ----- | --------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| Cora        | 15    | 65200                       | Ahead on active time            |
| Dev         | 15    | 65900                       | Same moves, greater active time |

The examples deliberately separate efficiency from speed. An implementation that adds moves and seconds together, or sorts by time first, would produce a different comparison. There is no weighted combined score in the existing core or in the decision above.

## When every recorded value looks equal

Two equal move counts and equal active times lead to the seed branch described above.

A fixture with two completely equal game results exercises the seed branch, whereas examples with unequal times never reach it. [Competition pairing](competition-pairing.md) supplies the bracket context.

The seed settles the equality case without an extra round of play, shared outcome or random choice. `createTournament` keeps entry order as seed order, and `compareResults` uses the players' entry indices only after moves and active time match.

## Active time in the current game

`GameState.elapsedMs` is advanced by `advanceGame` in `src/game/game.ts`. That function does nothing before play has started or after `isWon` becomes true. The first valid reveal sets `started: true`; ignored activations do not create another start event.

In the browser, `src/game/session/use-game-clock.ts` observes `performance.now()` for both solo and tournament games. Its running check combines screen activity, page visibility, pause state, the started flag and completion. `elapsedStep` in `browser-clock.ts` calculates the interval since the previous observation and contributes it only when active. This is elapsed active play, not a stopwatch started when the HTML file was opened.

Both game controllers synchronize before applying a card activation. As a result, the final valid activation is evaluated after accounting for the elapsed interval leading up to it. Tournament results retain the completed game's in-memory elapsed value, and tournament JSON carries that value with the match result.

The 40ms scheduling constant is an update cadence, not the unit of the stored elapsed value. `performance.now()` can return fractional milliseconds, and the core preserves positive finite deltas. `browser-clock.test.ts` exercises fractional values and compares many observations with one observation over the same overall span.

## Display precision is a separate concern

`formatElapsed` in `src/game/elapsed-time.ts` discards sub-second detail for presentation. It is therefore possible for two visibly identical clock strings to correspond to different `elapsedMs` values. A screenshot of the ordinary status area cannot establish exact equality of active time.

The example with Cora and Dev demonstrates this issue: their stored times differ by 700ms even though a coarser presentation can hide that difference. Reading the rendered text back into a result comparison would throw away information the game already holds.

Snapshot serialization changes precision too, although less dramatically. `encodeSnapshot` floors `elapsedMs` to a whole millisecond. It rounds a pending mismatch's remaining interval upward so that interval remains representable. The game in memory may have fractional time that the snapshot no longer contains.

Solo snapshot values, tournament result values and visible text have different precision, so an implementation review needs to identify which representation it compares. Tournament tie resolution uses the in-memory result, while the bracket formats time for reading.

## Pauses and interruptions

The current browser session excludes hidden-page time and time spent waiting for Resume after an unfinished snapshot import. It does not offer an ordinary manual pause control. Sitting with the visible started board while talking still contributes active elapsed time, even when no cards are activated during that conversation.

A miss also contributes time. The two exposed nonmatching faces remain visible for 800 active milliseconds, during which activation is blocked. That wait is part of the same active timeline as elapsed play. Hiding the page pauses both the elapsed clock and the remaining mismatch interval.

These facts explain some apparent discrepancies in human timing. An observer measuring from the moment the device is handed over will include time before the first reveal. A wall stopwatch will include time while the page is hidden. A person looking only at clicks may overlook the visible thinking intervals between them. Those observations can all differ from `elapsedMs` without demonstrating a clock defect.

[Elapsed time rules](../gameplay/elapsed-time-rules.md), [clock design](../architecture/clock-design.md) and [mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) describe the existing mechanisms.

## Completion and boundary values

`isWon` checks whether matched positions cover the deck. Before that condition holds, a board can have many matched pairs and a plausible-looking move count while still being unfinished. A current status reading is not equivalent to a completed result merely because the player has stopped interacting.

The core caps moves at 999999 and elapsed time at 359999999ms. Matching and completion continue at those caps. These limits can increase the number of equal numeric values in artificial boundary fixtures. They do not create an uncapped hidden counter from which a comparison could recover a distinction.

`src/game/move-cap.test.ts` covers completion at the move boundary. The browser and core clock tests cover elapsed behavior separately. These tests establish single-game values; they do not cover the tournament result comparator.

## Useful evidence for a disagreement

A disputed outcome can involve several separate questions: whether both attempts completed, which values were captured, how those values were compared and whether the participants understood the result. A screenshot may help with the last question, but it is weak evidence for sub-second equality. A snapshot gives structured game values but applies the integer export precision described above.

A replay can reconstruct card actions on a logical active timeline. In the current core it begins with a code, advances time before each action and advances again to its ending timestamp. It provides no record of the human circumstances around those actions. [Replay format](../sharing/replay-format.md) explains the available evidence without turning it into a competition log.

For a result review, the move-first example, the time-second example and an exact-equality example exercise distinct branches. Together they are more informative than many examples where one participant is better on every measure. They also make comparison errors visible in the bracket.

# Shared-device competition

This page explains the purpose, scope and implementation context of shared-device competition in Neon Pairs.

Competition gives a group gathered around one device a reason to return to the board together. It is intended for the small social setting: a family laptop, a tablet passed around a table, or a few people taking a break at the same desk. The interesting product question is how individual memory play becomes a shared occasion without losing the clarity of the existing game.

## Where the product stands

The game supports solo play and a four- or eight-player Tournament mode. `src/game/Game.tsx` switches between the Play and Tournament screens. The feature's participant names, bracket, per-turn game and transfer state live under `src/game/competition`; tournament turns use the existing game rules and board.

Each match assigns one board code to both players, whose games run sequentially. The bracket records moves and active time, applies the documented tie-breaks, and advances its winner. Finished tournaments are stored separately from solo preferences; exported tournament JSON can also carry setup or in-progress state.

The specification is version 2.2. Its linked competition pages define the shared-device flow and its boundaries; this overview introduces their purpose without repeating their detailed rules.

## Why share a device

A shared screen makes the activity visible. People can talk about the artwork, remember a near miss and recognize the effort behind another person's finish. There is no remote opponent waiting behind a network connection, and no account setup between the group and the game. The game already has a compact delivery model: the built game can be opened from one HTML file.

Sharing hardware also changes what people expect. On a personal device, a result feels like part of that person's practice. On a shared tablet, the person holding it may have changed several times since the page opened. A familiar status area can therefore carry a different social meaning even when its numbers are technically correct. The distinction between a person's current attempt, the group's progress and the device's ordinary records is especially easy to blur.

Competition is useful when it gives those existing actions a context people can follow. It is less useful when the group spends more attention administering the session than remembering cards. This is why the research discussion concentrates on interruptions, orientation and the physical act of passing the device, rather than treating the bracket drawing as the whole feature.

## Three things people are following

An individual concentrating on a board is following card positions and remembered faces. Someone waiting nearby is following the social event: who is occupied, whether a finish is close and when attention will return to the group. The person explaining the game is following the application itself, often watching for a control that might replace the current position.

These perspectives overlap, but they are not interchangeable. A board full of exposed faces is meaningful to the current player. It gives a waiting person relatively little information about where the group is in its event. A compact event view can answer that social question, while the ordinary board remains the place where the player thinks.

The competition documents separate these subjects so that readers can find the relevant decision without extracting it from a long screen-by-screen walkthrough. [Pairing](competition-pairing.md) covers the relationship between entrants and the bracket. [Rounds](competition-rounds.md) covers event stages. [Boards](competition-boards.md) and [deals](competition-deals.md) distinguish the dimensions of a board from its actual arrangement. [Ties](competition-ties.md) and [scores](competition-scores.md) address results from different angles.

## A local social activity, with local evidence

The current project has no backend or account service. Its board codes and exported progress are useful for reproducing a situation, not for establishing the identity of a person who played it. That is a comfortable fit for a group that is physically present and can see what happened. It is a much weaker basis for claims about distant strangers.

The same limitation applies to development evidence. A replay can help an engineer understand a sequence of card actions. A screenshot can help someone understand what the group saw. Neither explains why a participant handed the tablet back early, or whether someone had been watching another person's screen. Those are observations about the setting, and they belong in the research account rather than in an assertion about the game engine.

[Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md) explains the existing technical tools. [Competition research](competition-research.md) describes local sessions and the limits of drawing conclusions from them. The two accounts answer different questions and are useful together.

## How the current code helps

The core already separates game data from presentation. `src/game/game.ts` contains card transitions and logical elapsed time. `src/game/deck.ts` contains board parsing and deterministic generation. Those files have no participant knowledge. That makes them a useful basis for discussing competition without embedding group administration into card rendering.

The solo browser session remains under `src/game/session`. The competition feature owns a separate session and uses the shared clock adapter, so tournament completions do not update solo size or best moves. Its completed history uses the separate `np3:tournaments` key.

The board itself lives under `src/game/board`. Its card buttons and navigation code operate on positions. The solo status view still receives a game and best value; `TournamentPlay` supplies the round, current player and bracket around the same Board. [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md), [session module](../architecture/session-module.md) and [React boundaries](../architecture/react-boundaries.md) give the broader engineering context.

# Data exchange policy

This page explains which Neon Pairs data crosses a file or text boundary and how the existing formats relate to future exports.

The game has four exchange formats with deliberately different jobs. A board code identifies a starting deal. A snapshot describes a position on that deal. A replay describes activations on a logical timeline and produces a position when evaluated. Tournament JSON carries participant setup, bracket progress and the current turn. Choosing the smallest useful format keeps a report understandable: a wrong shuffle needs a code, a wrong revealed state needs a snapshot, a timeout ordering problem usually needs a replay, and a tournament handoff needs tournament JSON.

The detailed contract is [Reproducibility](reproducibility.md). This page describes the boundary between those formats, browser session data and developer tooling. It is not an additional wire-format definition.

## Existing formats and new exports

The current snapshot and replay formats are JSON objects with numeric `version: 1`. The board code is a string whose prefix is `np1`. Their definitions predate the general policy for new JSON exports. Every new exported JSON object has a "format" of "neon-pairs/KIND", naming what it holds, and a whole-number "version", with its keys in alphabetical order at every level. Formats that already exist stay as they are. In particular, adding a discriminator to a version 1 snapshot would make it fail the existing exact-key check, and changing the board-code string into JSON would remove its usefulness in the Board code field.

Tournament transfer uses `format: "neon-pairs/tournament"` and `version: 1`. It keeps setup, tournament state and an optional current-game snapshot in one bounded object. This does not change the snapshot or replay formats.

There is an important distinction between naming a new exchange format and modifying a known one. `snapshot.ts` is still the authority for the fields of an exported snapshot. `replay.ts` is still the authority for a replay input. The general policy does not silently widen either accepted object. See [Format versioning](format-versioning-guide.md) for the compatibility decisions around those boundaries.

Current snapshot output is readable JSON produced by `JSON.stringify` with a two-space indentation argument. It writes fields in the construction order used by `encodeSnapshot`: `version`, `boardCode`, `matched`, `selection`, `moves`, `elapsedMs`, `started`. This order is not alphabetical. An importer accepts any object-key order when the required keys and values are present. The distinction matters when comparing documents: a change in whitespace or object-key order need not change the represented state.

## Choose the artifact by the question

| Question                                            | Useful artifact                | What it cannot establish                             |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| Did two runtimes generate the same deal?            | Board code                     | Which cards the player activated                     |
| Can another browser show this position?             | Snapshot                       | The complete earlier action sequence                 |
| Does a click at the mismatch boundary get accepted? | Replay                         | The browser's real scheduling behavior               |
| Does a loaded position show the right controls?     | Snapshot plus browser steps    | How that position was originally reached             |
| Can another device continue an event?               | Tournament JSON                | Whether its supplied results came from verified play |
| Did a local best survive reload?                    | A storage-focused reproduction | An exported snapshot carries no best record          |

A board code is short enough to copy into a report without a separate file. Its meaning is stable because the prefix fixes generation. A snapshot contains enough progress to avoid playing back a long game. A replay is the most explicit description of action order, but the browser does not currently record or load replay files through its reproduction panel. Developer tooling evaluates them through the core and CLI.

A screenshot may accompany any of these, but it does not replace their machine-readable information. A picture of two cards cannot tell an engineer the exact pending milliseconds. A board code plus an action sequence can distinguish a bad card layout from a bad state transition. The appropriate artifact depends on whether the disputed behavior is generation, state, time or presentation.

## What the exchange formats carry

A board code carries generation version, supported side length and seed. `generateBoard` derives the immutable deck. The result contains face identifiers in position order; the code does not carry artwork, card names or a language setting. Loading it creates a fresh hidden state with no moves and no elapsed time. The algorithm and literal example are documented in [Board code format](board-code-format.md).

A snapshot carries `boardCode`, matched position indices, a tagged selection, moves, elapsed milliseconds and the `started` flag, alongside its format version. It does not duplicate the deck. Pair count and completion are derived after loading. Omitting those derived values avoids accepting a record in which the supplied pair total disagrees with the matched positions. [Snapshot format](snapshot-format.md) gives the complete field and validation reference.

A replay carries `boardCode`, an ordered array of `{atMs, index}` actions and `endMs`, alongside its version. It starts from the hidden deal rather than from an imported snapshot. The action timeline advances game time before each activation. The final time is advanced even when no action occurs there. This is how a replay can describe a mismatch closing after the final click. [Replay format](replay-format.md) covers the timeline and diagnostic result.

Tournament JSON carries the eight-slot setup draft, the participant list, each round and match, match results, board codes and phase. When a turn is active, it includes that game's snapshot-shaped state. The decoder validates exact keys, bracket progression, code sizes and uniqueness, result bounds, and agreement between setup names and event names before it replaces the current tournament. The JSON byte limit is 65536.

Exchange objects do not contain a browser storage key, a saved size preference, a per-size best record, a focus location or an animation flag. Tournament JSON does contain participant names and match results, but it does not attest that a person played them. Solo snapshot loading can update the preferred size; loading tournament JSON leaves solo preferences separate.

## Browser text is an explicit boundary

The reproduction panel is a native `details` element with the summary “Reproduce a game”. It contains the Board code input and Snapshot JSON textarea. Editing either field only edits a draft. `Load board` or `Load snapshot` performs the actual load. The Tournament screen has a separate Tournament JSON textarea with explicit Export tournament and Load tournament buttons. This separation lets a player inspect and correct copied text without replacing current state on each keystroke.

`Export snapshot` fills the textarea with a point-in-time representation. The player can select and copy that text manually. There is no dependency on the Clipboard API, no upload step and no account exchange. Export does not put the live session into the imported pause state. If the source game keeps running while the text is copied, the later source position may differ from the exported one.

The Board code control permits 32 characters and trims surrounding whitespace in `useGame.loadBoard`. The parser used inside JSON does not perform that trim. The Snapshot JSON control permits 65536 characters, while decoding separately enforces 65536 UTF-8 bytes. These are different measurements. A text field limit is an input affordance; the decoder remains the format boundary for programmatically supplied text too.

Successful load resets the board's remembered tab stop to its first position through a new session generation. Load and export buttons retain focus, with Resume handling its own disappearing-button focus transition. Focus is not serialized, so sharing a position cannot restore where the sender last tabbed. See [Reproduction panel](../interface/reproduction-panel.md) and [Focus policy](../interface/focus-policy.md) for interface details.

## Core functions and effectful adapters

The pure format functions operate on strings and game data. `parseBoardCode` returns size and seed or `null`; `decodeSnapshot` returns a reconstructed state or `null`; `readReplay` returns a final state or a classified problem; `decodeTournamentTransfer` returns validated event state or `null`. They do not operate browser controls, write storage or read files.

The browser adapter in `session/use-game.ts` decides when accepted data replaces a session. The CLI adapter in `scripts/replay-cli.ts` reads UTF-8 text and converts accepted replay results through `encodeSnapshot`. Pasting that output into the browser adds normal snapshot import behavior, including a pause for unfinished progress. The replay evaluator itself has no pause field.

## Trust and interpretation

All copied or loaded data is untrusted. “Valid snapshot” means that the object satisfies the documented state constraints, not that its claimed result has a verified play history. The same is true of tournament JSON: validation establishes a structurally consistent bracket, not that its participants achieved the recorded results. A hand-edited object can be accepted if its fields remain consistent.

Replays give a more explicit history, but they still contain author-supplied actions and times. The evaluator applies normal rules, including ignored activations, and does not attest who supplied the file. There is no authentication or signed result in the current exchange model. Local best moves are local game records, not a remote ranking service.

A board code also reveals enough information for a developer to regenerate the whole deck. That is its purpose. The browser still keeps hidden face identity out of hidden-card DOM content. Those facts are compatible: the shareable deterministic deal is a debugging tool, while the ordinary board presents the information available during play. [Import safety](import-safety-policy.md) describes validation and replacement behavior in more detail.

## Following a reported disagreement

For a generation mismatch, begin in `src/game/deck.ts` and compare the literal vector. For a rejected position, follow `snapshot.ts` into `snapshot-selection.ts` and `saved-format.ts`. For an unexpected action result, follow `replay.ts` into `advanceGame` and `activateCard` in `game.ts`. For a tournament transfer, follow `competition/format.ts` into its validation modules and the existing snapshot decoder.

A useful report preserves the original artifact and says which boundary was exercised. “The CLI rejected this replay” and “the browser rejected the CLI's output” refer to different decoders. Keeping that distinction often removes an entire round of reproduction work.

# Import safety policy

This page explains how Neon Pairs validates untrusted exchange text before a browser session or replay result can use it.

The important boundary is between a draft and accepted game data. A text field can contain arbitrary edits, and a replay file can contain arbitrary bytes decoded as text. Neither is treated as a `GameState` just because JSON parsing succeeds. Shape checks, numeric checks and game-specific consistency checks happen before the browser commits a replacement.

## Field diagnostics and the current implementation

A field outside a format's declared shape is a validation failure, including inside a selection or replay action. The diagnostic policy makes that particular mistake identifiable to a person correcting copied data. An import with a field its format doesn't define shows "Unknown field: NAME." for the first such field and leaves the current state unchanged. This applies to the field diagnostic; it does not make an incomplete object or an unsupported version acceptable. The format's own required fields and state constraints still determine acceptance.

Tournament transfer checks nested key sets before decoding and reports `Unknown field: NAME.` for an unexpected key. The existing snapshot decoder still returns `null` and the browser displays `Invalid snapshot.` for all snapshot failures; `readReplay` provides problem categories rather than the offending key name. Those older adapters reject extensions without identifying the offending field.

The existing code does not define a traversal order, object-path syntax or combined-error format for a field-specific diagnostic. Its boolean exact-key helper cannot report a first key. Those details cannot be inferred from a `null` result. For current behavior, examine the published notice and replay problem category rather than expecting a key name.

## Validation before replacement

`useGame.loadSnapshot(text)` calls `decodeSnapshot(text)` first. A failed result calls the notice helper and returns `false`. Only a successful result reaches `clock.reset()` and `replaceGame(current.current, game, true)`. There is no earlier step that installs the imported code or clears the existing matched positions.

`useGame.loadBoard(code)` follows the same broad shape with a board-code parser. It trims the control's draft, checks the result, and only then resets the clock and constructs a replacement game. A valid board-code string is sufficient for a fresh deal; a snapshot needs the additional position checks because it claims progress.

`decodeTournamentTransfer` validates the complete tournament JSON before replacement. `firstUnknownTournamentField` checks keys at the transfer, snapshot, setup, tournament, round, match and result levels. An unknown key reports its name; other invalid tournament data reports `Invalid tournament.`. Both failures retain the JSON draft and the active event. Replacing an unfinished tournament requires confirmation, so a valid import also has an explicit decision boundary.

Failure changes visible feedback and the announcement counter. It does not replace the game, reset the running clock, save a different size or discard the edited draft. “Keeps the game” therefore does not mean that every field of the containing `Session` has reference equality: notices are session fields too. Nor does it freeze the active game while someone corrects text. A running game can continue to gain elapsed time after an unsuccessful load.

This distinction is visible in `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts`: the test enters bad board and snapshot drafts, verifies the notices and retained text, then advances the clock and verifies that the prior game is still running. A test that expected elapsed time to remain fixed indefinitely after rejection would assert behavior the product does not have.

## The shared JSON boundary

The small helpers in `src/game/saved-format.ts` separate JSON mechanics from game validation:

| Helper                            | Meaning at this boundary                                            |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `isWithinBytes(text, maxBytes)`   | Measures UTF-8 encoded length, inclusively                          |
| `parseJson(text)`                 | Returns parsed unknown data, or `undefined` after a parse exception |
| `isJsonObject(value)`             | Accepts non-null objects except arrays                              |
| `hasExactKeys(value, keys)`       | Checks own-key count and presence of every expected own key         |
| `isNonnegativeSafeInteger(value)` | Accepts numeric safe integers greater than or equal to zero         |

`JSON.parse` can produce `null`, a list, a string, a boolean or a number. Those are valid JSON texts and invalid snapshot or replay roots. The object guard is what distinguishes them from a malformed text error. This is especially visible in replay results: `{` produces `malformedJson`, whereas `null` produces `format`.

`parseJson` does not execute input as code. A string containing script-like characters is still a string and fails where an object or number is required. The decoder does not merge the parsed object into the live session wholesale. It constructs the accepted state from a generated board and the fields it has validated.

Exact keys are checked as a set, not as an ordering constraint. Missing fields fail as well as extra fields. Nested objects are checked at their own format boundaries. A `closed` selection with an `index` is invalid even if that index would be an eligible position in a different selection variant. A replay action with an annotation field is invalid even if `atMs` and `index` are otherwise good.

The helpers operate on the parsed object, not the original token stream. JSON duplicate property names are consequently handled by `JSON.parse` before exact-key checking; the decoder does not retain a record of earlier overwritten occurrences. Likewise, numeric notation such as `1.0` becomes the number `1`. The integer predicate checks the value it receives rather than enforcing a preferred spelling of a JSON number.

## Resource bounds are checked at the text boundary

Snapshot decoding and tournament transfer measure input before parsing and reject text above `65_536` bytes. Replay reading checks `REPLAY_MAX_BYTES`, which is `1_048_576`, before parsing. The replay parser then rejects more than `REPLAY_MAX_ACTIONS`, which is `10_000`. Trailing JSON whitespace is legal within a byte budget and still consumes that budget.

These checks bound the accepted format, but they should not be described as a streaming parser. `TextEncoder` allocates an encoded representation for measurement. The CLI also calls `readFile` before `readReplay` checks text size. A very large input can therefore already have been read into memory when it is rejected. The code provides explicit acceptance limits rather than a promise that arbitrary input has no allocation cost.

The browser textarea's `maxLength` is a separate character limit. Multibyte text can satisfy that limit and exceed the decoder's byte limit. The existing byte helper test uses an accented character to establish that bytes, rather than JavaScript string length, control acceptance. [Snapshot format](snapshot-format.md) discusses how this interacts with readable export text.

## Snapshot checks depend on the regenerated deal

After validating the version and board code, `decodeSnapshot` generates the board used to interpret positions. `readMatched` checks unique in-range positions and requires both copies of every represented face. An even-length list alone is not enough: on `np1-4-1`, `[2, 6]` is a pair while `[0, 1]` is not.

`readSelection` checks availability against that matched list. A mismatch needs different positions with different faces and an integer remaining interval from `1` through `800`. It cannot describe a same-face pair awaiting closure, because normal play resolves matching cards immediately. When every position is matched, availability also prevents any nonclosed selection.

The full decoder checks counter bounds, a minimum move count and consistency with `started`. These checks establish the stated constraints without reconstructing every earlier action. [Snapshot format](snapshot-format.md) gives the complete validation sequence; [Snapshot selection notes](snapshot-selection-notes.md) explains the board-dependent helpers.

## Replay checks and isolated evaluation

`readReplay` checks root shape, version, board code, action count and `endMs` before walking actions. Each action then needs its exact object shape, safe nonnegative numbers, a nondecreasing timestamp no later than `endMs`, and a position inside the deck. Its index into the action array is included in action-specific failures.

Evaluation can already have computed earlier actions when a later action fails. That is safe because the evolving state is local to `readReplay`; no browser session has been committed. The function returns a problem rather than that partial state. This is different from a streaming UI that visibly applies each imported action as it reads.

An in-range activation during a mismatch is valid replay data even though the game ignores it. So are an activation of an already matched card and a repeated activation of the current first card. Validation checks whether the action is well formed; `activateCard` decides whether it changes play. Treating every ignored activation as a corrupt replay would conflate these two jobs.

Action timestamps may be much larger than the elapsed clock cap. The replay evaluator advances the logical timeline using safe integers, while `advanceGame` caps the resulting elapsed counter. That distinction prevents a legitimate long timeline from being rejected merely because the visible clock has saturated. [Replay format](replay-format.md) explains exact timeout edges and equal-time order.

## Failure reports that preserve the evidence

For current snapshot failures the decoder deliberately supplies no reason. The most effective local investigation isolates a single change against a known accepted object: replace just the selection, just the code, or just one counter. The tests in `snapshot.test.ts` use this pattern so that an unrelated invalid baseline cannot hide a missing check.

Replay reports have more detail. `readReplay` distinguishes file size, JSON syntax, root format, board code, actions array, end time, individual action shape, time order and index bounds. The CLI translates these into stderr text and uses a one-based action number for readers. Internal action positions remain zero-based. Mixing these conventions can lead an engineer to inspect the wrong action.

Retaining original text matters when a failure depends on bytes or syntax. Parsing and reserializing a padded document can remove the very length excess that caused its rejection. A screenshot of a notice cannot establish whether an extra property was nested or at the root. For the current accepted shapes, use [Board code format](board-code-format.md), [Snapshot format](snapshot-format.md), [Replay format](replay-format.md) and [Data exchange policy](data-exchange-policy.md); for the browser steps around them, use [Sharing FAQ](sharing-faq.md).

# Dialog policy

This page records the confirmation policy for leaving unfinished work and its relationship to the game's existing actions.

Tournament uses a native `dialog` when leaving unfinished work or replacing an active event with loaded JSON. The Play controls retain their existing direct behavior: New Game, Restart and reproduction loads do not ask for confirmation.

## The confirmation boundary

A confirmation is useful only when it corresponds to a real decision about abandoning work. Its content and focus need to make the conservative path understandable before the player commits to leaving. Leaving unfinished work asks first in a native dialog element with two buttons, Keep playing and Leave. Keep playing takes focus when it opens, and Escape keeps playing. The decision is about the unfinished work being left; opening a disclosure to inspect a code is not itself that decision.

There is no third action specified by this policy. In particular, the existing snapshot exporter does not turn this confirmation into an automatic save workflow. Export is a separate user action with a text result. A feature that uses the confirmation can draw on that distinction without presenting an unsaved draft as if it had already been preserved.

Tournament owns its dialog state in `Tournament.tsx`; the app still has no router. Changing between Play and Tournament focuses the new screen's h2. [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) covers that main-area replacement.

## What the present controls actually do

`Controls.tsx` renders New Game and Restart as native buttons. Their callbacks in `use-game.ts` reset the clock adapter and commit a replacement game. They do not consult `started`, Moves, Pairs or a dialog result before doing so. The existing game replaces immediately when those buttons are used.

BoardCodeForm validates before replacing. Its `loadBoard` callback returns false for invalid input and true after successful replacement. Snapshot loading decodes the whole draft before replacing as well. These paths protect against invalid external data; they are not implementations of a leave confirmation.

The native `details` panel is also not a modal. It expands in document flow and leaves the rest of the page operable. Calling its summary a dialog trigger would misdescribe both the DOM and its focus behavior. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) documents the actual disclosure.

This distinction matters during incremental work. A new dialog in one feature does not silently change the semantics of every old control. When reading a change, follow the event handler to see whether it reaches a confirmation boundary, a parser, or the replacement directly. Similar visual labels do not establish the same lifecycle.

## Native behavior and application decisions

The policy names a native element because the interface already relies on browser semantics for buttons, forms, selects and details. A dialog has a different interaction boundary from an ordinary panel. Its opening, cancellation and closing need to be considered as a coherent interaction rather than a div painted over the board.

Using the element alone does not decide what leaving means for a game. The application still owns the transition that discards or replaces state. In the current implementation, that transition is represented by controller operations and `replaceGame`. Visual disappearance of an overlay is not evidence that a session was replaced, just as visual appearance is not evidence that play was paused.

The distinction between cancellation and commitment is observable in game state. Continuing leaves the same deal, revealed selection and counters available. A committed departure may dispose of or replace the session, depending on the feature. The current game has no dialog-specific storage write or serialized marker.

Dialog state is local to `Tournament.tsx` and is not part of either game session or exported tournament data. The solo `Session` fields remain `game`, `paused`, `generation`, `feedback`, `loadNotice`, `announcement`, `celebration` and `preferences`. Its `paused` flag still represents unfinished snapshot import.

## Timing questions exposed by an overlay

A mismatch stores its remaining active milliseconds in game selection. The session clock advances it when the page is visible and the imported-pause flag is clear. Merely placing a dialog above the board is not one of those conditions in the current source.

Opening the Tournament confirmation does not pause elapsed time or a pending mismatch: the shared clock continues while the tournament screen remains active and visible. [Clock design](../architecture/clock-design.md) and [Mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) explain the clock model.

Replacement does have a well-defined lifecycle today. `clock.reset()` and the session generation prevent old pending updates from affecting a replacement game. If a leave decision leads to that existing path, stale-timer protection still belongs to the session. The dialog does not need to know the two selected card indices to implement that protection.

The period between opening and making a decision is therefore worth observing in review. It can expose accidental differences between the visual state, current game state and timers. The observation is useful even when the feature's intended behavior is simply to preserve the current clock semantics.

## Focus ownership

Opening the confirmation establishes a temporary interaction context. The policy above states its initial focus and cancellation result. That avoids relying on DOM order alone to make the safe continuation choice the first keyboard target.

After a decision, the durability of the source control matters. Existing action buttons generally remain mounted after a deal replacement, while Resume removes itself. Game handles Resume by moving focus before the button is removed. That is a concrete example of a disappearing source, though it is not a dialog implementation.

A leave feature may keep or remove its trigger as part of its surrounding screen. Its focus return depends on which controls remain mounted. A review can inspect the final active element and its visibility.

The board also remembers focus independently of actual focus. Opening another surface would not, by itself, mean its last card index should become a selected turn. A player returning to the board still needs the distinction between orientation and activation described in [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md).

## Review notes for a proposed implementation

The most useful review evidence separates opening, continuing and leaving. A single screenshot of the open surface cannot establish which element is focused, whether Escape follows the continuation path, or whether the underlying controller already replaced the game before a decision.

A source trace can identify the first state-changing call relative to the decision. A keyboard trace can identify the active element at opening and after cancellation. A populated game, especially one with a pending mismatch, makes unintended early replacement visible. These are ways of observing the stated policy and existing game lifecycle, rather than additional product requirements.

Current browser tests establish focus retention on ordinary buttons, invalid draft preservation, Resume's transfer order and stale-timer protection. They do not establish a dialog journey. Any future report of dialog coverage has to point at the corresponding implementation and evidence, rather than citing those tests because they also involve focus.

The relevant background is [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) for element choice, [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) for page orientation and [New game and restart](../gameplay/new-game-and-restart.md) for the existing replacement boundary. Together they make it possible to review a concrete leave interaction alongside the existing game lifecycle.
