# Announcements policy

This page describes how event feedback is published, repeated and kept separate from routine game rendering.

The game has many visible updates, but only some represent a new result. A clock tick is a changing value; resolving a turn is an event. Treating those as the same kind of update would make a memory game noisy and would bury the information a player needs after selecting two cards.

## Publication point

`Game.tsx` places one paragraph with `role="status"`, `aria-live="polite"` and `aria-atomic="true"` before the active screen. Solo feedback and tournament event messages use the same live region. Tournament also shows the persistent visual label `Now playing: NAME` and the round label near its board; its controller announces turn changes, completed turns, match winners and the champion through the shared status paragraph.

The paragraph remains mounted while its content changes. It is inside `.game-result`, which has a minimum height of `56px`, flex alignment and margins. The wrapper reserves a readable area near the board without making the scrollable card content itself the announcement source.

Polite publication allows the browser and assistive technology to schedule the result around other speech. Atomic content indicates that the paragraph's result is treated as a complete update rather than an isolated changed number. These attributes express the intended exposure; the actual spoken experience still needs user acceptance with a screen reader.

## Session data behind the paragraph

The solo session owns `feedback` and an integer `announcement`. Game uses that identity for solo messages and a separate local identity for tournament events. Updating the keyed span replaces the child even when its text is identical to the preceding result. This gives repeated events a DOM change without adding a hidden counter to the spoken text.

The counter is event identity, not a statistic presented to the player. It does not track moves, matched pairs or elapsed seconds. A failed load can advance it without adding a move, while the first card reveal changes game state without advancing it.

A broad render counter would be wrong for this job. Session renders occur for time and selection changes that should not repeat the last turn result. The explicit event field makes the distinction inspectable in `session.ts` and `use-game.ts`.

## Turn results

`activateSession` calls the pure `activateCard`. If the game object is unchanged, it returns the current session. If the result has selection kind `one`, it returns the updated game without changing feedback or announcement identity. That covers the first eligible reveal.

After the second eligible reveal, the result is either a mismatch or a match. The session builds the appropriate text and increments `announcement`. Completion is checked at this same boundary, so the winning match gets a combined result rather than two competing event publications.

| Result              | Text produced by the session                       |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| First matched pair  | `Pair found. 1 pair matched.`                      |
| Later nonfinal pair | `Pair found. M pairs matched.`                     |
| Mismatch            | `No match. Cards close after a short pause.`       |
| Winning pair        | `Pair found. All pairs found in N moves and time.` |

Here `M` and `N` are replaced with the actual counts, and `time` is the output of `formatElapsed`. The singular branch is based on `game.matched.length === 2`. The final branch takes precedence over the nonfinal pair count.

A card's accessible name also changes when it reveals or matches. That is the focused control describing its own state, not a second turn-result producer. The text in the event paragraph summarizes what the two-card attempt achieved. [Screen reader notes](screen-reader-notes.md) follows those two sources in a complete game.

## Consecutive identical results

Two misses in a row produce the same sentence. Updating only a string state can leave the DOM text unchanged, which gives no new mutation for the second event. The keyed span avoids relying on a different visible sentence to distinguish them.

The current sequence is concrete. Initial feedback is empty. Revealing index 0 on `np1-4-1` changes selection to `one` without publishing. Revealing index 1 produces a mismatch and advances the event identity. After the interval closes, choosing those two indices again produces the same text with a later identity.

The counter advances once for each resolved attempt in that sequence, not once for each card action or timer update. A third activation during the mismatch is ignored by the game and leaves the event unchanged. The same is true of a repeated activation on the first revealed card.

There is no temporary blanking timeout between identical results. The implementation does not clear text, wait a guessed number of milliseconds and restore it. That avoids adding announcement timing to the game clock or introducing a second lifecycle that can outlive a replacement game.

## Changes that stay quiet

`tickSession` advances the game and returns a new session with that game, leaving feedback and announcement fields intact. Mismatch closure is part of this advancement. It does not publish a new “cards closed” result. The earlier mismatch sentence already told the player that closure would follow a short pause.

Arrow movement is local board focus state. It does not call the session feedback path. Clock renders update Time in GameStatus, while card memoization prevents unchanged cards from rendering again. Neither operation is a new turn result.

New Game and Restart call `replaceGame` with `imported: false`. That replacement clears the prior feedback and load notice while keeping the announcement number. A successful board-code load follows the same replacement path. These operations clear old context; the current source does not add a success sentence for a board-code load.

Clearing text is still a DOM change and may appear in a mutation trace as an empty result. It is different from republishing a turn sentence. The accessibility journey's expected record includes the new-game clearing event, so a raw count of every mutation is not a substitute for reading what each event contains.

## Load outcomes share the publication path

The controller's `notice(feedback)` helper assigns both `feedback` and `loadNotice`, then increments `announcement`. Invalid Board code publishes `Invalid board code.`; invalid Snapshot JSON publishes `Invalid snapshot.`. Repeating the same invalid submission is a new load attempt and advances the identity again.

For valid snapshot import, `replaceGame(..., true)` increments the identity and publishes either `Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue.` or `Loaded completed snapshot.`. The former corresponds to a paused unfinished game, the latter to completed progress. Valid board-code loading does not use the imported-snapshot branch.

Reproduction also renders `loadNotice` in its ordinary paragraph with id `load-notice`. The load buttons reference it through `aria-describedby`. That keeps the outcome visible beside the text tools and associates the description with their actions without creating another event publisher in that panel.

Resume clears feedback and loadNotice without increasing the event identity. It also transfers focus to the board before its button disappears. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) and [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) describe those effects independently of event publication.

## Completion and persistent reading

GameStatus shows a completion paragraph whenever `isWon(game)` is true. A newly won game can give it the celebration class; an imported completed game shows it statically. That paragraph is persistent reading content containing the final moves and time.

The winning turn's feedback already contains the match and win in one result. The status paragraph does not need to separately announce a matched pair, then publish a second completion sentence. This avoids having two updates compete at the most significant turn in the game.

A completed snapshot instead publishes its load outcome, because import is the event that just occurred. The game is visibly complete, but no new card match happened. This distinction preserves a useful account of what the user actually did.

## Automated evidence

`session.test.ts` checks that first reveal, mismatch closure and repeated mismatch events affect announcement identity as expected. It also checks import outcomes and completion transitions without involving the browser.

`tests/announcements.e2e.test.ts` observes DOM mutations in the status paragraph. It resolves a mismatch, moves focus, runs the mismatch interval and repeats the same attempt. The expected result history contains the mismatch sentence once for each resolved turn, with no extra result from movement or closure.

The same test submits each snapshot load kind and each invalid-load kind twice, checking the publication history and the visible load notice. `tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` checks that the result remains beside the board during large-phone play and that the reproduction panel has no competing result role.

The accessibility journey reads Chromium's tree for the polite and atomic properties and the result text at each turn. That establishes exposure in the tested runtime. Spoken scheduling and verbalization are assessed in user acceptance. The repository records spoken review as user acceptance.

## Diagnosing a repeated or missing result

A missing second identical result suggests checking event identity before changing the sentence. A repeated result on every clock tick suggests checking whether routine advancement touches the publication fields. A load notice visible near the textarea but absent from event output suggests checking whether the controller used `notice` or only changed local text.

# Source layout

This page is a map of the current Neon Pairs source tree and the responsibilities of its files.

Paths here are relative to the project root. They describe authored source and configured outputs. [Module layout policy](module-layout-policy.md) explains placement decisions; this page is for finding the implementation.

## Entry and project root

`index.html` contains the document metadata, the `root` element and the development module entry `/src/main.tsx`. It declares English, a responsive viewport, the theme color `#090B14` and the title Neon Pairs. The source HTML references a module; the production HTML is assembled by Vite and the single-file plugin.

`src/main.tsx` looks up the root, throws `Missing application root.` if it is absent and renders `<Game />` under React `StrictMode`. There is no second application page or router mounted beside it. The game begins at `src/game/Game.tsx`.

The root also holds `package.json`, `package-lock.json`, four compiler configuration files, three Vite configurations and `vitest.config.ts`. `.prettierrc.json` configures formatting; `.prettierignore` and `.gitignore` identify generated or local work. The README records setup, commands, delivery, replay and the named runtime evidence.

## Game composition

`Game.tsx` calls `useGame`, switches between Play and Tournament, and imports `game.css`. It keeps the solo session mounted while its screen is inactive, pausing its active clock. Tournament screen components and their feature-specific state live under `competition/`.

Its one extra coordination operation is Resume. It asks the board's imperative ref to focus the remembered card, then calls the controller's resume action. That keeps the DOM focus handoff outside the core state. `Board` is keyed by `session.generation`, so a replacement remounts the board's local state.

`game.css` defines root colors and spacing values, system typography, page geometry, global focus styling and the reserved turn-feedback area. The more specific board, control and status rules live beside their components. [CSS organization](css-organization.md) records selectors and cascade relationships.

## Core modules directly under src/game

| File                    | What a reader finds there                                                                                     |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `deck.ts`               | Supported sizes, seed bounds, board-code parser and formatter, seeded shuffle and immutable board description |
| `selection.ts`          | The closed, one-card and mismatch discriminated union                                                         |
| `game.ts`               | `GameState`, caps, creation, victory, face-up positions, activation and logical advancement                   |
| `elapsed-time.ts`       | Display formatting from elapsed milliseconds                                                                  |
| `saved-format.ts`       | Small shared JSON, object, key, integer and byte helpers                                                      |
| `snapshot-selection.ts` | Validation of matched positions and nested selection                                                          |
| `snapshot.ts`           | Snapshot version and bound, serialization and complete-state validation                                       |
| `replay.ts`             | Replay limits, structured problems, ordered actions and final state                                           |

These files use ordinary TypeScript functions and data. The core is not a React context or reducer hook. It can be imported by the session adapter and by the replay CLI without mounting the application.

`generateBoard` returns a frozen description with a frozen deck. `GameState` extends that description. Runtime progress is returned as new objects by transitions; ignored actions can return the existing object. This pattern explains why the board's memoized sets can survive clock-only updates.

## Core test files

`game.test.ts` checks card transitions and logical advancement. `completion.test.ts` finishes every supported size. `move-cap.test.ts` exercises play and records at the maximum move count. `elapsed-time.test.ts` covers the formatter and related elapsed behavior.

`deck.test.ts` checks parsing and generation. `deck-rejection.test.ts` references independently generated vectors for rejection-sampling boundaries. `game.fixture.ts` contains the example code, literal deck, pair positions, initial generator states and shared numerical specification vectors.

`snapshot.test.ts` and `snapshot-selection.test.ts` cover the outer state and nested validation. `replay.test.ts` and `replay-order.test.ts` cover replay acceptance and ordering. These files live near the rules even when a narrow regression deserves a different test filename from the principal module.

## Session directory

`session/session.ts` defines `Session`, the import notices and the pure session operations `initialSession`, `replaceGame`, `tickSession` and `activateSession`. It connects a game transition to feedback, completion state and preferences without itself calling the browser.

`session/use-game.ts` is the React controller. It reads initial preferences, creates the initial fresh board, keeps the latest session ref in step with state, exposes actions and composes the clock and saving hooks. Successful loads replace the game; failed loads publish notices. Exports and activations synchronize the clock first.

`session/browser-clock.ts` defines the 40ms scheduling interval and arithmetic over observed timestamps. `session/use-game-clock.ts` supplies observations, tracks page and screen activity, schedules timeouts and removes pending work on effect cleanup. `session/use-session-clock.ts` adapts the shared hook to solo `Session` updates. `session/browser-clock.test.ts` checks the arithmetic independently.

`session/fresh-board.ts` converts browser entropy into a valid board code, rejecting out-of-range candidates and an optional previous seed. `session/storage.ts` defines the preference key, version, default size, store interface, validators and best-score update. `session/use-saved-preferences.ts` obtains browser storage safely and writes changes in an effect.

`session/session.test.ts` covers state replacement, paused input, generations, repeated feedback events and completion handling. `session/storage.test.ts` uses in-memory and throwing stores to cover persistence decisions. [Session module](session-module.md) follows the exact call paths and state fields.

## Competition directory

`competition/rules.ts` owns tournament phases, match results, winner comparison and advancement. `pairing.ts` creates seeded brackets and stage-sized unique deals. `names.ts` normalizes and validates participant names. The format modules encode and validate tournament JSON, while `storage.ts` retains completed history under its own key. `tournament-session.ts`, `use-tournament.ts` and the Tournament components connect those rules to the shared game and clock.

`Tournament.tsx`, `TournamentSetup.tsx`, `TournamentPlay.tsx`, `Bracket.tsx` and `TournamentHistory.tsx` render the setup, turn flow, bracket and past events. `competition/tournament.css` styles the tournament screen and table.

## Board directory

`board/Board.tsx` maps the immutable deck into cards. It derives a face-up set and a matched set, obtains the focus hook, exposes a remembered-focus method and supplies the `--grid-size` custom property. It keeps the activation callback stable while calling the latest controller action through a ref.

`board/Card.tsx` is memoized. It renders a native button, obtains its class and accessible description from `describeCard`, renders the face only when supplied and adds a matched mark for matched positions. It delegates navigation and focus to callbacks from the board.

`board/Face.tsx` converts a face design into inline SVG primitives. `board/face-design.ts` maps one of 128 face numbers to shape, marker, color, fill style, coordinates and label. `board/card-state.ts` derives a card's closed, revealed or matched description from supplied presentation data.

`board/keyboard.ts` computes arrow-navigation targets with edge stops and modifier handling. `board/use-board-focus.ts` owns the remembered position and DOM focus calls. `board/nearest-scroll.ts` remembers the viewport scroll position so focus can use nearest alignment after Chromium's automatic focus scrolling.

`board/board.css` owns the scrolling board viewport and grid tracks. `board/card.css` owns the button, concealed back, revealed/matched surfaces, corner mark and card transition. The directory's `keyboard.test.ts`, `card-state.test.ts` and `face-design.test.ts` check the numerical and descriptive helpers. Browser tests observe actual focus, artwork and scrolling.

## Controls and status

`controls/Controls.tsx` renders the grid-size select, New Game, Tournament and Restart. It reads the size options from `GRID_SIZES`. `controls/control-labels.ts` owns the exact deal and reproduction control strings consumed by components and tests.

`controls/BoardCodeForm.tsx` renders the board-code field and submit button. Its input is keyed by generation, and successful submission moves focus to the load button because the old input is replaced. An invalid submission leaves the draft available for correction.

`controls/Reproduction.tsx` holds the snapshot textarea draft in local state, renders the details disclosure and export/load buttons, and shows the load notice and conditional Resume button outside the disclosure. It uses the game code and generation passed from the parent rather than reconstructing them.

`controls/control.css` defines the common control surface. `controls/controls.css` lays out deal controls. `controls/reproduction.css` lays out the disclosure, form rows, textarea and notice region.

`status/GameStatus.tsx` renders moves, pair progress, elapsed text, best moves and the completion paragraph. `status/status-labels.ts` owns statistic labels. `status/status.css` styles the statistic layout and completion treatment. The component receives the optional best as `number | undefined` and displays `none` when it is absent.

## Scripts directory

`scripts/replay.ts` is the command entry. It passes command-line arguments to `runReplay` and assigns the returned status to `process.exitCode`. `scripts/replay-cli.ts` handles one input path, caller-directory resolution, file reads, human-readable stderr failures and final snapshot output. `scripts/replay.test.ts` exercises the executable in child processes.

`scripts/source-files.ts` recursively reads ordinary files from a supplied folder and rejects links or special entries. `scripts/source-audit.test.ts` inspects packages, compiler settings, source length, unsafe constructs and selected effect boundaries. `scripts/source-conventions.test.ts` checks recognized exports/imports, yes-or-no naming, test names and environment reads.

These scripts are not imported by the application entry. Some import core functions because they are clients of the same public data behavior. That direction lets command-line replay reuse the rules without putting Node APIs into browser modules.

## Application-level test support

`tests/browser-test.ts` adapts Node tests to Playwright, manages browsers and contexts, records runtime versions, gathers page errors and provides artifact paths. `tests/artifact-server.ts` serves the built HTML over loopback. `tests/game-fixture.ts` contains public-control setup helpers, disk URLs and completion helpers.

`tests/deal-oracle.ts` independently computes a specified deal with BigInt. `tests/focus-bounds.ts`, `tests/readability.ts`, `tests/accessibility-tree.ts` and `tests/ui-snapshot.ts` provide focused measurement or comparison support. They are tools used by journeys, not application modules.

The many `.e2e.test.ts` files are grouped by the observable behavior they examine: controls, input, play, persistence, snapshots, lifecycle, clock edges, layout, motion, artwork, status, accessibility, touch and zoom. [Test policy](test-policy.md) explains the runner and evidence boundaries instead of repeating every assertion here.

## Diagnostic entries and configured outputs

`art/index.html` and `art/face-sheet.tsx` form a separate face-sheet build with `art/face-sheet.css`. It imports the real card and design definitions to render every face at a controlled size. `vite.art.config.ts` writes this entry to `.art`.

`art/session/index.html` and `art/session/session-harness.tsx` form a separate lifecycle harness. It mounts `Game` beside an unmount button. `vite.session.config.ts` writes it to `.session`. The harness exists so the browser suite can measure cleanup rather than infer it from a page navigation.

The production build writes `dist/index.html`. Local dependencies live under `node_modules`; browser downloads, temporary browser files, npm cache and test work have separate ignored directories. `test-results` holds browser runtime and journey artifacts. These directories have operational roles but are not additional application source layers.

There is no generated route tree, backend, API client, asset service or utility framework to discover beyond this map. For command ordering see [Build pipeline](build-pipeline.md); for import and runtime separation see [React boundaries](react-boundaries.md).

# Session module

This page explains how `src/game/session` connects the pure game model to React, browser lifecycle and saved preferences.

The directory contains both pure transformations and browser adapters. `session.ts` can be called without React; `use-game.ts` provides the solo controller; the shared clock and preference hooks perform browser effects. Tournament has its own session and controller under `src/game/competition`, while reusing the same game rules and clock implementation.

## The Session value

`Session` contains eight fields. `game` is the complete `GameState`. `paused` gates an imported unfinished game. `generation` identifies replacement lifetimes. `feedback` is the current published result or notice. `loadNotice` retains load-related text for the reproduction controls. `announcement` distinguishes feedback events. `celebration` records whether this session just completed through play. `preferences` contains selected size and best moves.

These fields are not redundant copies of the core. `isWon(game)` derives victory from matched positions; there is no second `won` boolean in the session. `celebration` answers a different question from victory: a completed import is won but has no new-completion treatment. `paused` likewise describes how the browser entered the game, not whether the snapshot describes a legal state.

The game formats serialize game progress, not the whole session. A generation, browser pause, draft form text or feedback event does not appear in an exported snapshot. This lets the same snapshot be reconstructed in another session without carrying browser bookkeeping into the core model.

## Initialization

`initialSession(code, preferences)` creates a game with `createGame`. It initializes `paused` and `celebration` to false, `generation` and `announcement` to zero and both message fields to empty strings. It retains the supplied preferences.

The React controller obtains its browser store once through a lazy `useState(browserStore)`. A second lazy state initializer reads preferences, requests a fresh board for the valid saved size and calls `initialSession`. The first board therefore depends on the saved size but not on an automatically restored progress record. Solo progress remains in memory until explicitly exchanged through a snapshot.

`browserStore` catches failure while obtaining `window.localStorage` and returns `null` if access is blocked. `readPreferences` can use that null store and return the default. Initialization is consequently resilient to the storage access failure that browsers can raise before `getItem` is even called.

## The current ref and React state

`useGame` maintains both React's `session` value and a `current` ref. Its `commit(next)` first compares object identity. If nothing changed it returns. Otherwise it updates the ref and then calls `setSession(next)`.

This order gives event handlers and timer callbacks immediate access to the latest committed session even before React has rendered it. Several operations can happen in a single browser task. Reading only the session captured by the last render could make an export or subsequent activation use an older game.

The ref is not an independent state machine. Every change still passes through the same commit operation, and React renders the corresponding state. The clock hook receives the ref and commit function so it can apply deltas to current data rather than a stale closure. [React boundaries](react-boundaries.md) follows the component consequences.

## Card activation

The exposed `activate(index)` synchronizes the clock, then commits `activateSession(current.current, index)`. Synchronization can close an overdue mismatch before the core decides whether the new activation is allowed. It also accounts for the interval before a final winning match.

`activateSession` rejects input while paused. It calls `activateCard` and returns the same session if the game is unchanged. For a first reveal, whose resulting selection is `one`, it returns a session with only the new game. There is no completed-turn message yet.

For a completed attempt, it derives victory and chooses feedback. A mismatch reports that the cards will close after a short pause. A match reports the matched pair count with singular/plural wording. A final match combines the pair result with the total moves and formatted elapsed time. The function increments `announcement` once for that turn.

A winning activation calls `rememberBest`, and `celebration` becomes true. The source implements direct game-derived transitions rather than a separate event bus.

## Why feedback has an event counter

Two consecutive mismatch attempts can produce identical text. A string comparison alone would make them look like the same event. The session counter gives `Game.tsx` a changing key for the span containing the text, so repeated outcomes remain distinct render events.

A first reveal does not increment the counter. A timer closing a mismatch does not increment it either: `tickSession` changes the game, while the turn result remains the same feedback. A new deal clears the text silently without incrementing the counter. Imports increment it to publish the load notice.

`loadNotice` serves the reproduction area separately from turn feedback. It is populated by imports and invalid load attempts and cleared on replacement without import or on Resume. A later turn result can change `feedback` without treating ordinary play as a new load message.

## Replacing a game

`replaceGame(session, game, imported)` preserves the surrounding session, installs the supplied game and increments generation. It sets the saved size to the new game's size, clears celebration and computes import pause and notices.

If `imported` is false, the replacement is unpaused, its load notice is empty and the last turn feedback is cleared. If true and unfinished, the session is paused with the loaded-snapshot notice. If true and already won, it is unpaused with the completed-snapshot notice. The latter is a static completed state rather than a completion event through activation.

A replacement does not itself call `rememberBest`. This matters for completed imports, whose supplied moves are not treated as a newly played local result. Finishing an unfinished imported game through activations does reach the ordinary completion path and can record its resulting best moves.

The generation increment has two consumers. Timer logic can reject work associated with an earlier game, and `Game.tsx` uses it to remount the board. `BoardCodeForm` also keys the input by generation so a replacement supplies a fresh current-code value. A restart of the same code still gets a new lifetime.

## Controller actions

| Controller action    | Validation or preparation                                                  | Session effect                                         |
| -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `newGame(size?)`     | Validate size, choose a fresh code excluding the current seed, reset clock | Replace with a new initial game                        |
| `restart()`          | Recreate the current code, reset clock                                     | Replace with a new initial game of that deal           |
| `loadBoard(code)`    | Trim and parse code; reset clock only on success                           | Replace, or publish invalid-code notice                |
| `loadSnapshot(text)` | Decode complete state; reset clock only on success                         | Import replacement, or publish invalid-snapshot notice |
| `exportSnapshot()`   | Synchronize active clock                                                   | Encode latest game and return text                     |
| `activate(index)`    | Synchronize active clock                                                   | Apply session activation                               |
| `resume()`           | Reset observation baseline                                                 | Clear pause and load feedback                          |

The exposed load methods return a boolean. `BoardCodeForm` uses that result to move focus only after successful loading. Snapshot loading is a button action on the current textarea string, so it does not replace the draft with a normalized serialization automatically.

The private `notice(feedback)` helper changes both message fields and increments `announcement` while preserving the game. It does not bump generation or reset the clock. An invalid submission therefore leaves progress and board focus lifetime intact.

## Logical ticks

`tickSession(session, generation, milliseconds)` returns unchanged data when the captured generation differs from the current one or when the session is paused. It then delegates to `advanceGame`. If that function returns the existing game, the existing session is returned too.

A logical tick can update elapsed time and close a mismatch. It does not publish a new turn result, save a score or create a fresh board. Those decisions remain with activation and replacement. This small contract makes it possible to test stale-callback rejection without starting a browser timer.

The shared `useGameClock` hook applies an additional generation check before obtaining an observation. Its effect has an active flag and clears scheduled work at cleanup. Solo uses `useSessionClock` as a typed wrapper; Tournament supplies its own tick transition. Session rejection is the final data-level protection, not the only lifecycle defense. [Clock design](clock-design.md) details scheduling, visibility, screen activity and fractional steps.

## Preferences and effects

`Preferences` contains `size` and `bestMoves`. The key is `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`, and the stored object includes `schemaVersion: 1`. A valid size comes from `GRID_SIZES`; each best score uses a canonical size key and a finite safe integer count between that board's pair count and `MOVES_MAX`.

`rememberBest` returns the original preferences when an existing score is less than or equal to the new count. Otherwise it returns a new preferences object and best map. This reference stability means an ordinary clock tick or an equal result need not trigger another preference effect.

`useSavedPreferences` runs `writePreferences` after preference or store changes. Writing is intentionally outside the transition functions. A session activation can decide the new best without synchronously depending on browser storage. The writer catches failures, so the in-memory game remains playable even when persistence fails.

The reader returns a complete fallback on invalid saved content, including an invalid entry within the best map. It does not salvage a subset of scores from a partly invalid preference object. The writer touches only its own key, and the store interface has no removal or enumeration method.

## Focus is a neighboring concern

The board hook owns its remembered index; `Game` coordinates Resume through the board's limited focus ref before calling the controller. Replacement remounts the board through generation, while Resume retains it. Form drafts likewise remain local to controls. [React boundaries](react-boundaries.md) explains those lifetimes without adding presentation state to the session.

## Evidence and investigation

`session.test.ts` covers stale generations, paused activations and ticks, completion through play, completed imports and repeated feedback events. It checks that a final imported unfinished game can record a best, and it checks capped move counts. Its feedback snapshot test uses a JSON fixture.

`storage.test.ts` supplies stores that work and stores whose methods throw. Browser environment tests additionally make acquisition of localStorage fail. This separates the browser integration failure from validation and operation failures in the narrow store interface.

For an incorrect result, inspecting `activateCard` establishes the game transition first. If the game is right but the notice, celebration or preference is wrong, `activateSession` and `replaceGame` are the next places to inspect. If the data is right but an interaction sees old values, the controller's synchronization and commit path become relevant. The directory's separation makes those questions answerable without debugging the entire component tree at once.

docs/gameplay/selection-state.md:54:There is no deadline attached to closed selection. Waiting before a first reveal leaves the game unstarted; waiting between turns of a started game adds elapsed time. The `started` flag, completion result, and browser session determine that distinction.
docs/gameplay/selection-state.md:72:A one-card selection does not expire on its own. `advanceGame` updates elapsed time but leaves this selection in place. docs/gameplay/selection-state.md:84:Equal deck values move both positions into `matched` and close selection immediately. There is no temporary matching alternative or 800-millisecond wait before the next turn.
docs/gameplay/mismatch-interval.md:64:There is no fixed number of ticks defining a mismatch. docs/gameplay/board-size-catalogue.md:80:The minimum result is 72 moves, saved separately for size 12. There is no unlock step or dependency on completing a smaller board before this option can be chosen.
docs/quality/browser-test-guide.md:117:There is no automatic trace or screenshot-on-every-failure configuration in this wrapper. docs/gameplay/win-conditions.md:20:Every card position must belong to a found pair. Moves and elapsed time can be large, small, or capped without changing that result. There is no losing state caused by either counter.
docs/gameplay/win-conditions.md:40:There is no stored `won` boolean or independent final-score object. `GameStatus`, the clock hook, and the session functions derive completion by calling `isWon` on the game. docs/gameplay/win-conditions.md:80:There is no sound effect attached to the win path. The current game is silent, as described in [Sound](../sound/sound.md).
docs/quality/test-strategy.md:57:The package's `test:e2e` command runs the main build, builds diagnostic entries, and then invokes Node's test runner over `tests/*.e2e.test.ts` with concurrency set to one. docs/quality/browser-support.md:48:Some cases use the Chromium DevTools Protocol directly. docs/sharing/format-versioning-guide.md:29:This is why replacing a JSON `version` with a product release string fails. docs/sharing/format-versioning-guide.md:39:The general policies for future exchange objects and field diagnostics are in [Data exchange policy](data-exchange-policy.md) and [Import safety](import-safety-policy.md). docs/sharing/format-versioning-guide.md:73:The source currently supplies only single-version readers, not a general migration framework. docs/quality/known-issues.md:43:This is an acceptance boundary, not a reason to insert synthetic speech into the game. The game remains silent; assistive software reads the exposed interface. docs/quality/known-issues.md:57:The runner imports and launches Chromium. Some tests also use the Chromium DevTools Protocol for accessibility and touch input. docs/sharing/snapshot-format.md:106:Elapsed time is independently bounded. There is no rule that a certain move count requires a minimum positive number of milliseconds. docs/sharing/snapshot-selection-notes.md:59:A closed selection is accepted only with the key `kind`. There is no `index`, no empty array of selected cards and no remaining-time field. The returned value is a new `{kind: SelectionKind.closed}` object.
docs/sharing/snapshot-selection-notes.md:69:There is no minimum positive move count at this point. A first reveal starts the clock and sets `started`, but a move is counted on the next different eligible reveal. A full snapshot with no matches, `started: true`, zero moves and index `2` revealed is therefore valid. A full snapshot with the same fields and `started: false` is invalid.
docs/sharing/snapshot-selection-notes.md:97:There is no generic recursive object validator here. Each selection branch knows its own key list and semantics. That makes the relationship to `activateCard` direct: closed opens one card; one either matches and closes or becomes a mismatch; mismatch closes after active time. [Turn resolution](../gameplay/turn-resolution.md), [Mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) and [Format versioning](format-versioning-guide.md) provide the adjacent context.
docs/quality/release-checklist.md:73:There is no configured automatic browser retry policy or trace-on-every-failure mechanism in the local wrapper. docs/quality/performance-budget.md:13:There is no numeric first-render, input-latency, frame-rate, bundle-byte or memory budget in the specification or test configuration. docs/decisions/adr-004-no-backend.md:15:Neon Pairs runs its game rules in the browser and needs no application server. There is no account, API key or remote score service. docs/decisions/adr-004-no-backend.md:41:There is no remote recovery promise for an unexported in-memory game. A page reload starts a fresh deal, using a saved supported size when one is available. docs/decisions/adr-050-completion-banner.md:22:`isWon` compares the number of matched positions with the deck length. docs/sound/feedback-without-audio.md:18:`src/game/game.ts` owns selection and matching. `src/game/session/session.ts` derives turn feedback after an accepted activation. `src/game/Game.tsx` brings the board, status and feedback together. docs/sound/feedback-without-audio.md:81:There is no error tone, red failure panel or loss of previously matched cards. The message explains both the outcome and the upcoming closure. The visible faces provide the useful memory information during the interval.
docs/sound/feedback-without-audio.md:113:Both derive their moves and formatted time from the completed game. The board also remains fully matched, and the status stays present. docs/decisions/adr-010-snapshot-json.md:15:Export progress as readable version 1 JSON. The snapshot contains `version`, `boardCode`, `matched`, `selection`, `moves`, `elapsedMs` and `started`. docs/decisions/adr-052-release-tags.md:36:The tag rationale was therefore modest: make history pointable without turning version checking into runtime behavior. docs/decisions/adr-030-move-cap.md:24:At the cap, that same code still creates a mismatch or appends a matched pair. There is no branch that returns early merely because the count cannot increase. docs/decisions/adr-003-single-file.md:27:An offline copy is straightforward to archive and pass between machines. Inline SVG faces need no image directory. The system font needs no font request. There is no runtime account or service configuration to carry alongside the file. These choices reinforce the artifact boundary; see [ADR 004](adr-004-no-backend.md), [ADR 007](adr-007-svg-faces.md) and [ADR 027](adr-027-offline-first.md).
docs/competition/competition-rounds.md:31:This is a useful distinction even in static designs. A review can ask what the round text is describing at the exact moment represented by a screenshot. The labels above identify the event stage, while the remaining competition pages explain the other subjects.
docs/decisions/adr-056-no-feature-flags.md:15:The current game has one supported product behavior for each documented action. It does not choose between old and new turn rules through runtime feature flags. There is no flag client, remote configuration request or player-facing experimental-mode control in the application.
docs/decisions/adr-056-no-feature-flags.md:21:Feature flags are useful when a deployed service needs staged rollout or different cohorts. Neon Pairs is distributed as a complete offline artifact. A person retains the file they have, and the project can build another revision. There is no runtime service coordinating a rollout across players.
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:19:Competition uses a subset of the sizes already supported by the solo game. Quarterfinals are played on 4x4, semifinals on 6x6 and finals on 8x8. There is no new board geometry involved: each is an existing square grid handled by the current deck and board components.
docs/decisions/adr-014-pause-on-hidden.md:46:Synchronization happens before the stored visibility changes. Cleanup removes both future timer work and the listener owned by this effect.
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:33:The examples deliberately separate efficiency from speed. An implementation that adds moves and seconds together, or sorts by time first, would produce a different comparison. There is no weighted combined score in the existing core or in the decision above.
docs/decisions/adr-040-file-size-aim.md:21:React and React DOM are bundled runtime dependencies. Vite and its plugins transform the source during the build. The face renderer describes shapes with a small set of SVG primitives rather than embedding 128 raster images. The system font avoids a downloaded or inlined font asset. There is no audio collection to carry with the file.
docs/decisions/adr-001-react.md:17:React gives those changes a common rendering boundary. The decision was to use React with DOM rendering, rather than to build a bespoke collection of DOM mutation procedures. The current entry, `src/main.tsx`, obtains the root element and renders `Game` inside `StrictMode`. There is no second application root for a score display or reproduction form.
docs/competition/competition-research.md:75:A future research session could explore how different groups feel about spectating, but that is a research question rather than a committed feature. The existing observations support only the narrower conclusion that sharing a device also shares attention in ways that vary with posture, distance and familiarity.
docs/decisions/adr-045-no-i18n-yet.md:16:The current interface is English. The entry document declares `lang="en"`, control and status labels are English, and the specified turn and load messages are English. There is no locale picker, translation catalogue or localization framework in the application.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:29:`boardCode(size, seed)` constructs a string and validates it through `parseBoardCode`, throwing for invalid input. `generateBoard(code)` parses the code, constructs a deck with each face twice and shuffles it. The returned board object and deck array are frozen. There is no participant input in this process.
docs/decisions/adr-026-dark-theme.md:22:The background layers distinguish the page, containers and card states without replacing the face identity system. A hidden card has the same neutral diamond back regardless of its future face. A revealed face has a slightly different surface, while matched cards add the green border and check mark. The palette therefore supports state recognition instead of becoming another matching rule.
docs/decisions/adr-026-dark-theme.md:30:There is no theme picker in the controls and no theme field in `Preferences`. This keeps the saved model focused on the selected board size and best moves. A browser preference for reduced motion is handled separately because it concerns effects rather than selecting a second palette.
docs/decisions/adr-026-dark-theme.md:44:A future appearance discussion would need to consider all those relationships rather than only the page background. For the present code, [Theme tokens](../visuals/theme-tokens.md), [Card artwork](../visuals/card-artwork.md) and [Visuals](../visuals/visuals.md) are the useful references when locating a color and understanding why it belongs to that surface.
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:42:There are no participant names or board codes in that value. A best belongs to a board size across ordinary games, rather than to a particular generated deal. Tournament results live in a separate history key and are not folded into this map.
docs/decisions/adr-044-no-routing.md:35:A query parameter for the initial board could be a separate feature, but it is not implemented in the game. The documented control is the way to load a code in the current game.
docs/decisions/adr-044-no-routing.md:43:This is a scope decision, not a prediction that no future product could benefit from navigation. For the current behavior, routing would supply infrastructure without a corresponding user journey. [ADR 016](adr-016-no-state-library.md), [Reproduction panel](../interface/reproduction-panel.md), [React boundaries](../architecture/react-boundaries.md) and [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md) explain the neighboring structure.
docs/competition/competition-overview.md:27:A shared screen makes the activity visible. People can talk about the artwork, remember a near miss and recognize the effort behind another person's finish. There is no remote opponent waiting behind a network connection, and no account setup between the group and the game. The game already has a compact delivery model: the built game can be opened from one HTML file.
docs/competition/competition-overview.md:51:The core already separates game data from presentation. `src/game/game.ts` contains card transitions and logical elapsed time. `src/game/deck.ts` contains board parsing and deterministic generation. Those files have no participant knowledge. That makes them a useful basis for discussing competition without embedding group administration into card rendering.
docs/decisions/adr-005-vite.md:35:Vite was chosen as a narrow tool rather than as a place to host game logic. Deck generation does not depend on a Vite environment variable. The browser rules can run in Vitest or through Node replay without the development server. A future build-tool change would have to preserve the distribution and command behavior; the current game model is not tied to Vite APIs.
docs/decisions/adr-011-storage-keys.md:48:This is present-day evidence of the original decision’s effect. It is not evidence that every future data family follows the old scheme.
docs/persistence/preferences-store.md:88:`useSavedPreferences` invokes `writePreferences` in a `useEffect` dependent on `[preferences, store]`. Effects run after rendering, including the initial mount. There is no debounce interval, end-of-page listener or pending-save object. The hook has no cleanup because it schedules no continuing background operation.
docs/persistence/preferences-store.md:98:There is no `storage` event listener in this adapter. A tab reads at initialization, keeps its own preference snapshot and writes that aggregate later. Multiple-tab reconciliation is outside the current supported specification. A second tab's newer value is not automatically reflected in the first tab's displayed best.
docs/decisions/adr-046-print-styles.md:48:This is a screen-oriented scroll container. There is no alternate paper layout in this rule set; a print feature would need to define its own intended information and geometry.
docs/decisions/adr-017-colocated-tests.md:41:A central unit-test directory was considered simpler to scan by test type, but it detached examples from the functions under review. The current organization favors the engineer opening one behavior directory to understand both implementation and evidence. It is consistent with the existing architecture and does not imply a new filename convention for future feature modules. [Fixtures guide](../quality/fixtures-guide.md), [Source audit notes](../architecture/source-audit-notes.md) and [ADR 051](adr-051-test-artifacts.md) provide the supporting details.
docs/decisions/adr-021-seeded-decks.md:35:This separation makes investigations repeatable. A tester can specify `np1-4-1`, know the sixteen literal face IDs and perform actions through the real UI. There is no need for a private endpoint exposing the hidden deck. [ADR 009](adr-009-board-codes.md) explains the identifier and [Randomness policy](../architecture/randomness-policy.md) describes the existing boundaries.
docs/persistence/persistence-envelope.md:40:`src/game/competition/storage.ts` reads and writes the tournament-history envelope. `src/game/session/storage.ts` continues to read and write only the preference aggregate. Feeding one representation to the other's reader does not convert it; the two have different jobs and validators.
docs/persistence/persistence-envelope.md:50:There is a useful asymmetry here. Snapshot validation has an exact-key helper available in the shared format module, but the preference reader does not call it. Extra top-level preference properties are ignored if the fields the reader uses are valid. A successful read returns a freshly constructed `Preferences` value containing only `size` and the validated score map. The current preference format accepts extra top-level properties.
docs/persistence/persistence-envelope.md:60:There is no migration chain in the preference store. An unsupported discriminator produces the same fallback as a malformed value. No code attempts to guess an older shape, rename its fields or convert a saved sequence into a best map. Tournament history is a separate collection, not a migration of preferences.
docs/persistence/persistence-envelope.md:68:The tournament envelope serves a similar boundary role for its record collection, but there is no generic persistence framework. The source uses direct imports and a two-method store interface. There is no registry, adapter hierarchy or global storage coordinator.
docs/persistence/persistence-envelope.md:76:Empty data should also be distinguished from unavailable storage. A reader can return an empty state after a denied read, but that return value alone does not prove that the browser is ready to accept a future write. The tournament history API returns an availability flag for its saved-record message; an empty list by itself is not that flag. [Storage failure policy](storage-failure-policy.md) explains both adapters.
docs/decisions/adr-032-best-score-scope.md:22:`Preferences.bestMoves` is a readonly record keyed by canonical side-length strings. `rememberBest` obtains `String(size)`, compares the existing number and returns either the original preferences object or a new map with one changed entry. The equality case is deliberately a no-op rather than a rewrite with identical data.
docs/decisions/adr-032-best-score-scope.md:36:Saved scores are untrusted JSON. The parser accepts only canonical supported size keys and integer counts within the move cap. A stored best also cannot be lower than the board's pair count, because even perfect play needs one move per pair. A 4x4 score below eight is therefore rejected as part of an invalid preference value.
docs/decisions/adr-016-no-state-library.md:43:Format helpers serve both snapshot and replay validation; the board computes face-up positions for rendering. The reason to share is a concrete common meaning, not an expectation that every future feature needs a store. See [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md), [ADR 057](adr-057-small-components.md) and [Game state model](../gameplay/game-state-model.md).
docs/persistence/retention-policy.md:27:The supported set has seven entries. Once read validation has succeeded, the score map can therefore contain at most seven different supported size keys. It can also contain fewer, including none. This bound follows from `GRID_SIZES` and canonical key validation, not from trimming an attempt history. Multiple completed games at the same size compete for the same map entry.
docs/persistence/retention-policy.md:31:The selected size can change while all best entries remain identical. A visit that chooses 16x16 and then reloads may store `size: 16` alongside a score map containing only a 4x4 result. That is a valid aggregate. The remembered preference describes the next board size, while the map describes earlier eligible completions.
docs/persistence/retention-policy.md:37:The preference format contains no creation date, last-played time or expiry value. `readPreferences` does not inspect the current time. It cannot tell whether a valid best was written a minute ago or on a much earlier visit. There is no scheduled cleanup effect, idle purge or age-based deletion in `use-saved-preferences.ts`.
docs/persistence/retention-policy.md:45:The preference writer runs from a React effect whose dependencies are the preferences object and store. This is not a page-exit flush. On initial mounting, the effect writes the current preference state. Later, a new preference object causes another effect run. There is no dependency on active elapsed milliseconds or every move in the game.
docs/persistence/retention-policy.md:51:Tournament retention runs when the final match is completed. The preference effect has no generic event log or timer that scans browser keys, and tournament storage is handled by its feature-specific adapter.
docs/persistence/retention-policy.md:69:The existing preference tests establish aggregate behavior rather than tournament-list retention. `storage.test.ts` checks independent minimums for two sizes and object identity for equal and worse results. The tournament history adapter implements a newest-ten list, but no test evidence is claimed here. Browser journeys check that solo bests survive reloads and game resets.
docs/persistence/storage-failure-policy.md:20:The preference adapter still exposes no blocked-status result: `readPreferences` returns preferences and `writePreferences` returns `void`. The tournament adapter returns history with an `available` flag and a boolean write result. Its warning applies to tournament history; it does not claim that the separate preference write failed.
docs/persistence/storage-failure-policy.md:54:There is no queue, timer-driven retry, backoff or unload handler. Another dependency change can cause another attempt, but the code does not poll for a browser setting to change. A returned `null` store is captured in state for the lifetime of that mounted game; enabling storage later does not replace that state value automatically.
docs/persistence/storage-failure-policy.md:70:The storage adapters call `getItem` and `setItem` only for their own preference or tournament-history key. Neither uses a storage-wide clear call, key enumeration or cleanup routine. Their store interfaces expose only those two methods. The preference storage test explicitly seeds an unrelated key and checks that a preference write leaves its value intact.
docs/persistence/corrupt-data-policy.md:13:Browser storage contains strings outside the type system. A value may have been written by an older build, edited by a person, truncated by a debugging experiment or replaced by another script on the origin. The current preference reader accepts only a usable preference aggregate and otherwise returns its default. It does not try to repair individual score entries.
docs/persistence/corrupt-data-policy.md:109:Stored preference rejection happens during initialization with no draft to correct in the game UI. It returns a playable state quietly. There is no recovery dialog, corrupted-data banner or download of rejected text. Browser access failure also returns defaults, but concerns operation availability rather than text acceptance; see [Storage failure policy](storage-failure-policy.md).
docs/persistence/private-browsing-notes.md:30:There is no server copy, browser-account synchronization or preference export path in the game that restores the earlier aggregate. A board code reproduces a deal, not the private context's remembered settings. A snapshot restores one game position, not the browser's collection of local bests. [Sharing FAQ](../sharing/sharing-faq.md) and [Persistence overview](persistence-overview.md) explain these boundaries.
docs/persistence/private-browsing-notes.md:36:A store can also be obtainable while `getItem` or `setItem` throws. The reader and writer catch those failures independently. There is no need for the game to identify whether the cause is private browsing, a site setting or a browser policy. [Storage failure policy](storage-failure-policy.md) covers the feature presentation and the current adapter's silent behavior.
docs/persistence/storage-testing-guide.md:65:The expected reader result for a rejected aggregate is the whole fallback, including selected size 4 and an empty map. Testing only that one bad entry disappears would miss the actual whole-value behavior. Extra top-level fields are a separate acceptance case because the preference reader currently ignores them.
docs/persistence/storage-testing-guide.md:81:There is no useful assertion that the new board code must differ after every independent page load. Startup creates a fresh deal rather than restoring the old one, but a storage test can establish the intended state through cleared progress and retained preferences without depending on a random coincidence being impossible. New Game's seed handling is a separate behavior.
docs/persistence/persistence-overview.md:24:Here the next page load starts a new 6x6 game. The best displayed while playing that size is 20. Choosing 4x4 exposes the independent best of 9. There is no record for 8x8, so the status displays `none` for that size. The selected size does not have to be the only size represented in the score map.
docs/persistence/storage-quota-notes.md:43:A nominal allowance is not a reservation for Neon Pairs. Browser policy can prevent writes from the beginning. Other values on the same origin can consume capacity. Private browsing can give data a shorter lifetime even if writing works. A small serialized value therefore supports the claim that the application contributes little storage, but does not prove a future write will succeed.
docs/persistence/storage-quota-notes.md:57:There is no test that fills a physical browser storage area to its exact capacity. There is no recorded capacity sweep for Firefox or Safari in the test suite. The README reports Chromium journeys on its named compatibility combination; that is functional evidence for the game, not a general quota benchmark. An engineer should not attach a browser-specific measured threshold to these results.
docs/interface/tables-policy.md:15:The solo UI uses a definition list for one game's statistics. Tournament uses an HTML table for bracket rows, with a caption and scoped column headings. The card board remains a CSS grid of buttons; those different structures serve different data.
docs/interface/tables-policy.md:29:The Best value is one saved move count selected by current size. It does not present a list of people or a comparison across many records. `session.preferences.bestMoves[String(game.size)]` chooses the value before it reaches GameStatus. A single local best is not a table of ordered results.

# Dialog policy

This page records the confirmation policy for leaving unfinished work and its relationship to the game's existing actions.

Tournament uses a native `dialog` when leaving unfinished work or replacing an active event with loaded JSON. The Play controls retain their existing direct behavior: New Game, Restart and reproduction loads do not ask for confirmation.

## The confirmation boundary

A confirmation is useful only when it corresponds to a real decision about abandoning work. Its content and focus need to make the conservative path understandable before the player commits to leaving. Leaving unfinished work asks first in a native dialog element with two buttons, Keep playing and Leave. Keep playing takes focus when it opens, and Escape keeps playing. The decision is about the unfinished work being left; opening a disclosure to inspect a code is not itself that decision.

There is no third action specified by this policy. In particular, the existing snapshot exporter does not turn this confirmation into an automatic save workflow. Export is a separate user action with a text result. A feature that uses the confirmation can draw on that distinction without presenting an unsaved draft as if it had already been preserved.

Tournament owns its dialog state in `Tournament.tsx`; the app still has no router. Changing between Play and Tournament focuses the new screen's h2. [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) covers that main-area replacement.

## What the present controls actually do

`Controls.tsx` renders New Game and Restart as native buttons. Their callbacks in `use-game.ts` reset the clock adapter and commit a replacement game. They do not consult `started`, Moves, Pairs or a dialog result before doing so. The existing game replaces immediately when those buttons are used.

BoardCodeForm validates before replacing. Its `loadBoard` callback returns false for invalid input and true after successful replacement. Snapshot loading decodes the whole draft before replacing as well. These paths protect against invalid external data; they are not implementations of a leave confirmation.

The native `details` panel is also not a modal. It expands in document flow and leaves the rest of the page operable. Calling its summary a dialog trigger would misdescribe both the DOM and its focus behavior. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) documents the actual disclosure.

This distinction matters during incremental work. A new dialog in one feature does not silently change the semantics of every old control. When reading a change, follow the event handler to see whether it reaches a confirmation boundary, a parser, or the replacement directly. Similar visual labels do not establish the same lifecycle.

## Native behavior and application decisions

The policy names a native element because the interface already relies on browser semantics for buttons, forms, selects and details. A dialog has a different interaction boundary from an ordinary panel. Its opening, cancellation and closing need to be considered as a coherent interaction rather than a div painted over the board.

Using the element alone does not decide what leaving means for a game. The application still owns the transition that discards or replaces state. In the current implementation, that transition is represented by controller operations and `replaceGame`. Visual disappearance of an overlay is not evidence that a session was replaced, just as visual appearance is not evidence that play was paused.

The distinction between cancellation and commitment is observable in game state. Continuing leaves the same deal, revealed selection and counters available. A committed departure may dispose of or replace the session, depending on the feature. The current game has no dialog-specific storage write or serialized marker.

Dialog state is local to `Tournament.tsx` and is not part of either game session or exported tournament data. The solo `Session` fields remain `game`, `paused`, `generation`, `feedback`, `loadNotice`, `announcement`, `celebration` and `preferences`. Its `paused` flag still represents unfinished snapshot import.

## Timing questions exposed by an overlay

A mismatch stores its remaining active milliseconds in game selection. The session clock advances it when the page is visible and the imported-pause flag is clear. Merely placing a dialog above the board is not one of those conditions in the current source.

Opening the Tournament confirmation does not pause elapsed time or a pending mismatch: the shared clock continues while the tournament screen remains active and visible. [Clock design](../architecture/clock-design.md) and [Mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) explain the clock model.

Replacement does have a well-defined lifecycle today. `clock.reset()` and the session generation prevent old pending updates from affecting a replacement game. If a leave decision leads to that existing path, stale-timer protection still belongs to the session. The dialog does not need to know the two selected card indices to implement that protection.

The period between opening and making a decision is therefore worth observing in review. It can expose accidental differences between the visual state, current game state and timers. The observation is useful even when the feature's intended behavior is simply to preserve the current clock semantics.

## Focus ownership

Opening the confirmation establishes a temporary interaction context. The policy above states its initial focus and cancellation result. That avoids relying on DOM order alone to make the safe continuation choice the first keyboard target.

After a decision, the durability of the source control matters. Existing action buttons generally remain mounted after a deal replacement, while Resume removes itself. Game handles Resume by moving focus before the button is removed. That is a concrete example of a disappearing source, though it is not a dialog implementation.

A leave feature may keep or remove its trigger as part of its surrounding screen. Its focus return depends on which controls remain mounted. A review can inspect the final active element and its visibility.

The board also remembers focus independently of actual focus. Opening another surface would not, by itself, mean its last card index should become a selected turn. A player returning to the board still needs the distinction between orientation and activation described in [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md).

## Review notes for a proposed implementation

The most useful review evidence separates opening, continuing and leaving. A single screenshot of the open surface cannot establish which element is focused, whether Escape follows the continuation path, or whether the underlying controller already replaced the game before a decision.

A source trace can identify the first state-changing call relative to the decision. A keyboard trace can identify the active element at opening and after cancellation. A populated game, especially one with a pending mismatch, makes unintended early replacement visible. These are ways of observing the stated policy and existing game lifecycle, rather than additional product requirements.

Current browser tests establish focus retention on ordinary buttons, invalid draft preservation, Resume's transfer order and stale-timer protection. They do not establish a dialog journey. Any future report of dialog coverage has to point at the corresponding implementation and evidence, rather than citing those tests because they also involve focus.

The relevant background is [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) for element choice, [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) for page orientation and [New game and restart](../gameplay/new-game-and-restart.md) for the existing replacement boundary. Together they make it possible to review a concrete leave interaction alongside the existing game lifecycle.
