# Source layout

This page is a map of the current Neon Pairs source tree and the responsibilities of its files.

Paths here are relative to the project root. They describe authored source and configured outputs. [Module layout policy](module-layout-policy.md) explains placement decisions; this page is for finding the implementation.

## Entry and project root

`index.html` contains the document metadata, the `root` element and the development module entry `/src/main.tsx`. It declares English, a responsive viewport, the theme color `#090B14` and the title Neon Pairs. The source HTML references a module; the production HTML is assembled by Vite and the single-file plugin.

`src/main.tsx` looks up the root, throws `Missing application root.` if it is absent and renders `<Game />` under React `StrictMode`. There is no second application page or router mounted beside it. The game begins at `src/game/Game.tsx`.

The root also holds `package.json`, `package-lock.json`, four compiler configuration files, three Vite configurations and `vitest.config.ts`. `.prettierrc.json` configures formatting; `.prettierignore` and `.gitignore` identify generated or local work. The README records setup, commands, delivery, replay and the named runtime evidence.

## Game composition

`Game.tsx` calls `useGame`, switches between Play and Tournament, and imports `game.css`. It keeps the solo session mounted while its screen is inactive, pausing its active clock. Tournament screen components and their feature-specific state live under `competition/`.

Its one extra coordination operation is Resume. It asks the board's imperative ref to focus the remembered card, then calls the controller's resume action. That keeps the DOM focus handoff outside the core state. `Board` is keyed by `session.generation`, so a replacement remounts the board's local state.

`game.css` defines root colors and spacing values, system typography, page geometry, global focus styling and the reserved turn-feedback area. The more specific board, control and status rules live beside their components. [CSS organization](css-organization.md) records selectors and cascade relationships.

## Core modules directly under src/game

| File                    | What a reader finds there                                                                                     |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `deck.ts`               | Supported sizes, seed bounds, board-code parser and formatter, seeded shuffle and immutable board description |
| `selection.ts`          | The closed, one-card and mismatch discriminated union                                                         |
| `game.ts`               | `GameState`, caps, creation, victory, face-up positions, activation and logical advancement                   |
| `elapsed-time.ts`       | Display formatting from elapsed milliseconds                                                                  |
| `saved-format.ts`       | Small shared JSON, object, key, integer and byte helpers                                                      |
| `snapshot-selection.ts` | Validation of matched positions and nested selection                                                          |
| `snapshot.ts`           | Snapshot version and bound, serialization and complete-state validation                                       |
| `replay.ts`             | Replay limits, structured problems, ordered actions and final state                                           |

These files use ordinary TypeScript functions and data. The core is not a React context or reducer hook. It can be imported by the session adapter and by the replay CLI without mounting the application.

`generateBoard` returns a frozen description with a frozen deck. `GameState` extends that description. Runtime progress is returned as new objects by transitions; ignored actions can return the existing object. This pattern explains why the board's memoized sets can survive clock-only updates.

## Core test files

`game.test.ts` checks card transitions and logical advancement. `completion.test.ts` finishes every supported size. `move-cap.test.ts` exercises play and records at the maximum move count. `elapsed-time.test.ts` covers the formatter and related elapsed behavior.

`deck.test.ts` checks parsing and generation. `deck-rejection.test.ts` references independently generated vectors for rejection-sampling boundaries. `game.fixture.ts` contains the example code, literal deck, pair positions, initial generator states and shared numerical specification vectors.

`snapshot.test.ts` and `snapshot-selection.test.ts` cover the outer state and nested validation. `replay.test.ts` and `replay-order.test.ts` cover replay acceptance and ordering. These files live near the rules even when a narrow regression deserves a different test filename from the principal module.

## Session directory

`session/session.ts` defines `Session`, the import notices and the pure session operations `initialSession`, `replaceGame`, `tickSession` and `activateSession`. It connects a game transition to feedback, completion state and preferences without itself calling the browser.

`session/use-game.ts` is the React controller. It reads initial preferences, creates the initial fresh board, keeps the latest session ref in step with state, exposes actions and composes the clock and saving hooks. Successful loads replace the game; failed loads publish notices. Exports and activations synchronize the clock first.

`session/browser-clock.ts` defines the 40ms scheduling interval and arithmetic over observed timestamps. `session/use-game-clock.ts` supplies observations, tracks page and screen activity, schedules timeouts and removes pending work on effect cleanup. `session/use-session-clock.ts` adapts the shared hook to solo `Session` updates. `session/browser-clock.test.ts` checks the arithmetic independently.

`session/fresh-board.ts` converts browser entropy into a valid board code, rejecting out-of-range candidates and an optional previous seed. `session/storage.ts` defines the preference key, version, default size, store interface, validators and best-score update. `session/use-saved-preferences.ts` obtains browser storage safely and writes changes in an effect.

`session/session.test.ts` covers state replacement, paused input, generations, repeated feedback events and completion handling. `session/storage.test.ts` uses in-memory and throwing stores to cover persistence decisions. [Session module](session-module.md) follows the exact call paths and state fields.

## Competition directory

`competition/rules.ts` owns tournament phases, match results, winner comparison and advancement. `pairing.ts` creates seeded brackets and stage-sized unique deals. `names.ts` normalizes and validates participant names. The format modules encode and validate tournament JSON, while `storage.ts` retains completed history under its own key. `tournament-session.ts`, `use-tournament.ts` and the Tournament components connect those rules to the shared game and clock.

`Tournament.tsx`, `TournamentSetup.tsx`, `TournamentPlay.tsx`, `Bracket.tsx` and `TournamentHistory.tsx` render the setup, turn flow, bracket and past events. `competition/tournament.css` styles the tournament screen and table.

## Board directory

`board/Board.tsx` maps the immutable deck into cards. It derives a face-up set and a matched set, obtains the focus hook, exposes a remembered-focus method and supplies the `--grid-size` custom property. It keeps the activation callback stable while calling the latest controller action through a ref.

`board/Card.tsx` is memoized. It renders a native button, obtains its class and accessible description from `describeCard`, renders the face only when supplied and adds a matched mark for matched positions. It delegates navigation and focus to callbacks from the board.

`board/Face.tsx` converts a face design into inline SVG primitives. `board/face-design.ts` maps one of 128 face numbers to shape, marker, color, fill style, coordinates and label. `board/card-state.ts` derives a card's closed, revealed or matched description from supplied presentation data.

`board/keyboard.ts` computes arrow-navigation targets with edge stops and modifier handling. `board/use-board-focus.ts` owns the remembered position and DOM focus calls. `board/nearest-scroll.ts` remembers the viewport scroll position so focus can use nearest alignment after Chromium's automatic focus scrolling.

`board/board.css` owns the scrolling board viewport and grid tracks. `board/card.css` owns the button, concealed back, revealed/matched surfaces, corner mark and card transition. The directory's `keyboard.test.ts`, `card-state.test.ts` and `face-design.test.ts` check the numerical and descriptive helpers. Browser tests observe actual focus, artwork and scrolling.

## Controls and status

`controls/Controls.tsx` renders the grid-size select, New Game, Tournament and Restart. It reads the size options from `GRID_SIZES`. `controls/control-labels.ts` owns the exact deal and reproduction control strings consumed by components and tests.

`controls/BoardCodeForm.tsx` renders the board-code field and submit button. Its input is keyed by generation, and successful submission moves focus to the load button because the old input is replaced. An invalid submission leaves the draft available for correction.

`controls/Reproduction.tsx` holds the snapshot textarea draft in local state, renders the details disclosure and export/load buttons, and shows the load notice and conditional Resume button outside the disclosure. It uses the game code and generation passed from the parent rather than reconstructing them.

`controls/control.css` defines the common control surface. `controls/controls.css` lays out deal controls. `controls/reproduction.css` lays out the disclosure, form rows, textarea and notice region.

`status/GameStatus.tsx` renders moves, pair progress, elapsed text, best moves and the completion paragraph. `status/status-labels.ts` owns statistic labels. `status/status.css` styles the statistic layout and completion treatment. The component receives the optional best as `number | undefined` and displays `none` when it is absent.

## Scripts directory

`scripts/replay.ts` is the command entry. It passes command-line arguments to `runReplay` and assigns the returned status to `process.exitCode`. `scripts/replay-cli.ts` handles one input path, caller-directory resolution, file reads, human-readable stderr failures and final snapshot output. `scripts/replay.test.ts` exercises the executable in child processes.

`scripts/source-files.ts` recursively reads ordinary files from a supplied folder and rejects links or special entries. `scripts/source-audit.test.ts` inspects packages, compiler settings, source length, unsafe constructs and selected effect boundaries. `scripts/source-conventions.test.ts` checks recognized exports/imports, yes-or-no naming, test names and environment reads.

These scripts are not imported by the application entry. Some import core functions because they are clients of the same public data behavior. That direction lets command-line replay reuse the rules without putting Node APIs into browser modules.

## Application-level test support

`tests/browser-test.ts` adapts Node tests to Playwright, manages browsers and contexts, records runtime versions, gathers page errors and provides artifact paths. `tests/artifact-server.ts` serves the built HTML over loopback. `tests/game-fixture.ts` contains public-control setup helpers, disk URLs and completion helpers.

`tests/deal-oracle.ts` independently computes a specified deal with BigInt. `tests/focus-bounds.ts`, `tests/readability.ts`, `tests/accessibility-tree.ts` and `tests/ui-snapshot.ts` provide focused measurement or comparison support. They are tools used by journeys, not application modules.

The many `.e2e.test.ts` files are grouped by the observable behavior they examine: controls, input, play, persistence, snapshots, lifecycle, clock edges, layout, motion, artwork, status, accessibility, touch and zoom. [Test policy](test-policy.md) explains the runner and evidence boundaries instead of repeating every assertion here.

## Diagnostic entries and configured outputs

`art/index.html` and `art/face-sheet.tsx` form a separate face-sheet build with `art/face-sheet.css`. It imports the real card and design definitions to render every face at a controlled size. `vite.art.config.ts` writes this entry to `.art`.

`art/session/index.html` and `art/session/session-harness.tsx` form a separate lifecycle harness. It mounts `Game` beside an unmount button. `vite.session.config.ts` writes it to `.session`. The harness exists so the browser suite can measure cleanup rather than infer it from a page navigation.

The production build writes `dist/index.html`. Local dependencies live under `node_modules`; browser downloads, temporary browser files, npm cache and test work have separate ignored directories. `test-results` holds browser runtime and journey artifacts. These directories have operational roles but are not additional application source layers.

There is no generated route tree, backend, API client, asset service or utility framework to discover beyond this map. For command ordering see [Build pipeline](build-pipeline.md); for import and runtime separation see [React boundaries](react-boundaries.md).

# Neon Pairs

Neon Pairs is a browser memory game that asks you to find every pair of matching cards.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Reveal two cards at a time and finish in as few moves as you can. A board code repeats a deal, so you can report a problem with the same starting cards.

## Play

Choose a size, then reveal a card and find its partner. Matches stay face up. A miss closes both cards after 800 active milliseconds. Finding every pair completes the game with your moves and time. New Game gives you another deal. Restart repeats the current deal. Full details are in [Rules](gameplay/rules.md).

## Controls

Use mouse, touch or keyboard for the same card action. Keyboard movement, focus, card names and the screen reader journey are in [Input](interface/input.md). The labels and behavior of game and reproduction actions are in [Controls](interface/controls.md).

## Appearance

The game draws faces on a dark background. Shape, marker and fill distinguish each face without color. Layout, colors, motion, 16x16 behavior and zoom are in [Visuals](visuals/visuals.md). The game stays silent as defined in [Sound](sound/sound.md).

## Repeat a game

A board code describes a deal. A snapshot saves progress. A replay records timed actions. Their algorithms and formats are in [Reproducibility](sharing/reproducibility.md). Tournament JSON has its own `neon-pairs/tournament` format version 1, described with the [tournament requirements](competition/competition-overview.md).

## Tournament

Tournament mode runs a four- or eight-player knockout on one device. Each match gives both players the same deal in sequence, and the bracket records moves, active time and the winner. Finished brackets stay in a local Past tournaments list; Tournament JSON exports or loads setups and progress. The [competition requirements](competition/competition-overview.md) define pairings, rounds, board sizes, ties and score isolation.

## Build

Use React, TypeScript and native DOM controls. Package pins, commands and the offline HTML distribution are in [Technology](architecture/technology.md). Pure game functions, browser effects and behavior placement are in [Architecture](architecture/architecture.md).

Use the journeys in [Acceptance](quality/acceptance.md) to check the finished game. Those examples add no rules beyond the requirement IDs in their defining documents.

## Out of scope

The game doesn't need to support these, so they're never tested:

- Keys and modifier combinations beyond the ones in [Input](interface/input.md#keyboard-movement), which stay with the browser
- Holding a key down
- Several tabs or windows of the game open at once, where each tab may simply overwrite the saved preferences
- How a pointer press behaves when it drifts or is dragged off a card
- Replay or snapshot files with encodings beyond the stated rules, such as a byte-order mark
- Spoken screen-reader output, which stays part of user acceptance as [Input](interface/input.md#screen-reader) describes
- Confirming that a touch long press on a real device opens the context menu without revealing a card, which stays part of user acceptance like spoken output because automated browsers can't produce that gesture

# Neon Pairs

Neon Pairs is a memory game that runs offline from one HTML file and keeps local best moves for each board size.

You can repeat a deal with its board code, save progress as a snapshot or run timed actions through the replay command.

Status: implements product spec version 2.2.

## Install

Use the named test combination, Node 26.12.1, npm 11.20.0 and Playwright 1.64.1 with Chromium 156.0.8078.4. From this folder, install the locked tools:

```powershell
npm ci --cache .npm-cache
```

Chromium 156.0.8078.4 comes with the project's image, so browser tests need no download. Browser tests use fresh contexts. They stop their browser and local HTTP server when they finish.

## Play

Run `npm run build`, then open `dist/index.html` from disk. The game makes no network requests. To keep saved sizes and scores on a stable HTTP origin, run `npm run dev`. Stop it when you finish.

Use Grid size to choose a board. Reveal two cards with a click, tap, Enter or Space. Arrow keys move board focus. Other keys stay with the browser. Tab leaves the board. New Game gives another deal. Restart repeats the current deal.

Open Reproduce a game to load a board code or export progress. Loading an unfinished snapshot pauses it. Resume returns focus to the remembered card and continues the remaining mismatch interval. A completed snapshot loads as completed without Resume. Elapsed time stops at 359999999ms while play continues. The minutes and seconds display reaches 5999:59. Moves stop at 999999. Matching and victory continue at that count. Saved bests use the same move limit.

Select Tournament beside New Game to set up a four- or eight-player knockout on the same device. Players take turns on the same deal within each match; fewer moves wins, with active time and entry seed settling ties. Completed brackets appear in Past tournaments on that browser. Tournament JSON can export or load a setup, active match or finished bracket.

## Replay

Run `npm run --silent replay -- PATH` with a version 1 replay JSON file. Valid input prints only its final version 1 snapshot JSON to stdout and exits 0. Invalid input prints nothing to stdout, writes a message to stderr and exits nonzero. The command's silent flag suppresses its npm banner so stdout stays JSON. Other npm commands keep their errors and warnings. Replay timestamps can reach the safe integer limit. Elapsed time uses the same cap as browser play.

## Check

Run the checks from this folder:

```powershell
npm run typecheck
npm test
$env:NEON_PAIRS_NAMED_COMBINATION = '1'
npm run test:e2e
npm run format:check
```

`npm test` runs the unit and static checks with Vitest 5.0.5. `test:e2e` type checks and builds current source before opening the new HTML. It also builds the face sheet and session harness as separate diagnostic entries. The game distribution contains no diagnostic entry.

The browser command writes the Node, npm, Playwright and Chromium versions it ran on to `test-results/browser-runtime.json`. With `NEON_PAIRS_NAMED_COMBINATION` set to `1`, it also fails unless they match the named combination. Use the flag for named-combination evidence. Other supported runtimes, such as Node 24.19, run without it.

The locked install, type check, Vitest unit tests, build from current source and Chromium journeys have passed on the named combination with the flag set. Other versions have no test record here.

## Accessibility

Keyboard, card names, atomic turn feedback, reduced motion, touch scrolling and the equivalent zoom layout at 640x400 CSS pixels with device scale 2 have browser checks. The diagnostic face sheet draws all 128 faces at 44px.

Playwright checks Chromium's accessibility tree through a complete keyboard journey. It checks controls, card names, states, turn results, the final summary, Tab exit and New Game. The developer provides this tree evidence and the tool record. You confirm spoken output during acceptance with your screen reader.

Tree record: Chromium 156.0.8078.4 and Playwright 1.64.1. Screen reader: not run. Spoken journey: user acceptance.

Delivered projects from document setups keep the product specification in `docs/`.

Follow the requirements in docs/ for this project.

- A02 - Keep the board description and deck immutable. Keep matched positions, current selection, moves, active elapsed milliseconds and whether play started in game state. Derive pair count and victory. Serialize progress using the [reproducibility formats](../sharing/reproducibility.md).

- A03 - Use direct calls and exhaustive branches for the closed, one-card and mismatch states. Keep named states, format versions, timing values and size limits beside the behavior they control.

Proposed game functions:

| Call                               | Result                               |
| ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `createGame(boardCode)`            | Initial state for a valid board code |
| `activateCard(state, index)`       | State after one card activation      |
| `advanceGame(state, milliseconds)` | State after logical time advances    |
| `isWon(state)`                     | Whether every position is matched    |
| `encodeSnapshot(state)`            | Version 1 snapshot JSON              |
| `decodeSnapshot(text)`             | Valid restored state or `null`       |
| `replayGame(text)`                 | Final replay state or `null`         |

## Browser session

- A04 - Keep React state, timer lifecycle and browser visibility handling in `src/game/session`. Use a monotonic browser clock. Clear pending work on unmount and invalidate callbacks when the deal changes. A callback from an earlier deal can't change the current one.

- A05 - Keep preference and best-score reads in the session storage module. Treat saved JSON as unknown input. Validate grid sizes and finite integer scores. Catch read, parse and write failures. Keep unrelated storage keys untouched. A failure leaves the game playable.

- A06 - Keep solo active-game progress in memory until it is exported or imported as a snapshot. Importing a completed snapshot doesn't update best scores or play a celebration. Completing an unfinished imported game records a local best under R10. Tournament history stores completed brackets separately; export/import carries unfinished tournament progress.

## Components

- A07 - `Game.tsx` composes the Play and Tournament screens. Keep board navigation in `src/game/board`, solo controls in `src/game/controls`, tournament behavior in `src/game/competition` and solo session behavior in `src/game/session`. Keep each component's props and styles beside it.

- A08 - A card mounts its face SVG only while revealed or matched. Hidden card identity stays out of DOM attributes, accessible names and diagnostic globals. Tests can know a deck from its documented board code. The app gives them no solver endpoint.

- A09 - Use native browser input and the shared card activation function. Keep focus position in the board component. Focus movement changes presentation, never the deck or move count. [Input](../interface/input.md) defines the keys and focus rules.

## Evidence

- A10 - Keep focused tests beside their behavior. Complete browser journeys live at the application test level. Check generation against independent literal vectors. Check game transitions against stated rules. Test built HTML from disk as well as served storage behavior.

- A11 - Keep development fixtures and diagnostic helpers out of the shipped game. Tests can use the documented board code, snapshot and replay formats. The shipped game exposes only its documented controls.

## Changes

- A12 - Add a new rule at its game behavior, then update its component, tests and specification. Add shared support only when two actual behaviors need the same meaning. Don't add a global store, event bus, router or generic utility folder.

The [game specification](../README.md) defines the behavior this structure implements.

# CSS organization

This page maps the Neon Pairs stylesheets to their components and explains the global cascade, layout formulas and visual-test seams.

Styles sit beside the behavior they present and are imported by components. They remain ordinary global CSS. File adjacency makes ownership discoverable, while selector choice and the cascade determine actual reach. There is no CSS module transformation, CSS-in-JS runtime or component-library theme layer in this source.

## Stylesheet ownership

| Stylesheet                   | Importing component or entry                 | Main responsibility                                                   |
| ---------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `src/game/game.css`          | `Game.tsx`; face-sheet entry also imports it | Root theme, page geometry, typography, focus outline and result space |
| `board/board.css`            | `Board.tsx`                                  | Viewport scrolling and grid dimensions                                |
| `board/card.css`             | `Card.tsx`                                   | Card states, back, face sizing and matched mark                       |
| `controls/control.css`       | Deal and reproduction components             | Shared native-control surface                                         |
| `controls/controls.css`      | `Controls.tsx`                               | Size selector and deal-button arrangement                             |
| `controls/reproduction.css`  | Reproduction components                      | Disclosure, forms, textarea and load notice                           |
| `status/status.css`          | `GameStatus.tsx`                             | Statistics and completion presentation                                |
| `competition/tournament.css` | `Tournament.tsx`                             | Setup fields, tournament actions, bracket table, history and dialog   |
| `art/face-sheet.css`         | Face-sheet entry                             | Diagnostic placement of real cards                                    |

A component import brings its styles into the application graph, and the build embeds the resulting CSS in the finished HTML. The source HTML has no separate stylesheet link to distribute. [Build pipeline](build-pipeline.md) describes that assembly.

## Global foundation

`game.css` sets `system-ui, sans-serif`, a 16px root font size, 24px line height, light text on a dark background and `color-scheme: dark`. It defines the shared variables `--text`, `--secondary`, `--panel`, `--back`, `--face`, `--border` and `--green`.

The current values are `#f4f6ff` for text, `#b8bdd2` for secondary text, `#141827` for panels, `#1b2034` for card backs, `#111625` for face surfaces, `#757c9a` for borders and `#8bea7d` for matched green. The page background is `#090b14`.

The root also defines `--content-max: 1120px` and `--page-padding: 16px`. A global border-box reset applies to every element, body margin is zero and main uses full width up to that maximum with centered margins and page padding. These foundational rules affect diagnostics that deliberately import `game.css` as well as the main game.

Headings, paragraphs and help text have a small set of explicit margins and font sizes. Secondary text is generally 14px. The global `:focus-visible` outline is 3px white with a 2px offset. Because it is global, its interaction with scroll-container padding matters for cards as well as ordinary controls.

## The board owns its geometry

`board.css` defines board-specific custom properties on `.board-viewport`: card minimum 44px, card maximum 88px, gap 6px, padding 6px and border 1px. The viewport uses `overflow: auto`, contained overscroll, a rounded panel and `max-height: min(70dvh, 768px)`.

The viewport has `width: fit-content` and `max-width: 100%`. The inner board is a grid with a number of columns supplied by `--grid-size`, set from the current game size by `Board.tsx`. Track widths range from the card minimum to maximum.

Its width uses a clamp with these conceptual bounds:

```text
minimum = size * card-min + (size - 1) * gap
preferred = 100% of the available content width
maximum = size * card-max + (size - 1) * gap
```

For size 16, the inner minimum is 794px and maximum is 1498px. The viewport's own padding, border and any scrollbar are separate geometry. A narrow screen can therefore scroll the board rather than shrinking every track without limit or making the whole page wider than the viewport.

The width formula uses the scroll area's content box, which already accounts for occupied scrollbar space. `scrollbars.e2e.test.ts` runs with visible scrollbars at several viewport/size combinations to catch a layout that only works when Chromium hides them.

## Card states come from data

`Card.tsx` supplies `card` plus a state class returned by `describeCard`. `.card` is a square grid-placed native button with full available width, zero padding, a 2px border and an 8px radius. It uses the back surface until revealed or matched, when the face surface applies.

Hover changes the border to the text color. The matched selector appears after the hover selector and gives matched cards the green border. This ordering matters when a matched card remains hovered: its matched treatment continues to win. The class is derived from game data, not a CSS pseudo-state pretending to own the match.

The concealed back is a small rotated bordered span. Visible faces are SVG elements sized to the card. The matched check is a separate absolutely positioned SVG in the top-right corner with width and height at 16% of the card. The source comment explains that a mark much wider than roughly 17% would reach the face's top-right marker.

The card has `scroll-margin: 6px`, which works with nearest scrolling and the global focus outline. Its touch-action and user-selection properties support native pointer behavior. These rules are adjacent to the card because the face sheet also renders the same component outside the normal board layout.

## CSS and SVG share one surface value

The face renderer uses a viewBox of 0 0 100 100. Its main geometry takes the design color, with either a solid fill or outline stroke. A marker circle uses the same color, and its surround stroke is `var(--face)`.

That variable ties SVG geometry to the card's face background. Replacing the card surface without considering the marker surround could make the marker appear to have a mismatched halo. This is a direct dependency between the stylesheet and the inline SVG, even though face identity remains a data mapping in `face-design.ts`.

The matched mark is decorative and uses currentColor from CSS. It is separate from the identity marker, so its size and placement are checked for overlap at the smallest rendered card. [Card artwork](../visuals/card-artwork.md) and [Face catalogue](../visuals/face-catalogue.md) cover identity design rather than stylesheet placement.

## Shared controls are deliberately narrow

`control.css` defines `.control`: minimum height 44px, padding 8px 12px, a 1px border, 8px radius, panel background, text color and inherited font. Only button and select controls receive the pointer cursor rule. Inputs and textareas have `min-width: 0` so they can shrink within flex/grid layouts.

This class is applied explicitly to the game's form controls. The card component uses its own class and styling. A broad rule for every button would accidentally affect card rendering and diagnostic comparisons, which is why the current selectors distinguish those surfaces.

`controls.css` uses wrapping flex layout with a 12px gap and 16px bottom margin. The size control aligns label and select with a 12px gap. At widths up to 599px, the size row takes full width with spaced ends, while the direct deal buttons share available space.

These rules handle arrangement without replacing native select and button behavior. The CSS does not define a synthetic menu implementation or a separate touch activation model.

## Reproduction layout

The disclosure panel has 24px top margin, panel background, a 1px border and 12px radius. Its summary has a 44px minimum height and 12px by 16px padding. The open body is a grid with 12px gaps and its own inner padding.

# CSS organization

This page maps the Neon Pairs stylesheets to their components and explains the global cascade, layout formulas and visual-test seams.

Styles sit beside the behavior they present and are imported by components. They remain ordinary global CSS. File adjacency makes ownership discoverable, while selector choice and the cascade determine actual reach. There is no CSS module transformation, CSS-in-JS runtime or component-library theme layer in this source.

## Stylesheet ownership

| Stylesheet                   | Importing component or entry                 | Main responsibility                                                   |
| ---------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `src/game/game.css`          | `Game.tsx`; face-sheet entry also imports it | Root theme, page geometry, typography, focus outline and result space |
| `board/board.css`            | `Board.tsx`                                  | Viewport scrolling and grid dimensions                                |
| `board/card.css`             | `Card.tsx`                                   | Card states, back, face sizing and matched mark                       |
| `controls/control.css`       | Deal and reproduction components             | Shared native-control surface                                         |
| `controls/controls.css`      | `Controls.tsx`                               | Size selector and deal-button arrangement                             |
| `controls/reproduction.css`  | Reproduction components                      | Disclosure, forms, textarea and load notice                           |
| `status/status.css`          | `GameStatus.tsx`                             | Statistics and completion presentation                                |
| `competition/tournament.css` | `Tournament.tsx`                             | Setup fields, tournament actions, bracket table, history and dialog   |
| `art/face-sheet.css`         | Face-sheet entry                             | Diagnostic placement of real cards                                    |

A component import brings its styles into the application graph, and the build embeds the resulting CSS in the finished HTML. The source HTML has no separate stylesheet link to distribute. [Build pipeline](build-pipeline.md) describes that assembly.

## Global foundation

`game.css` sets `system-ui, sans-serif`, a 16px root font size, 24px line height, light text on a dark background and `color-scheme: dark`. It defines the shared variables `--text`, `--secondary`, `--panel`, `--back`, `--face`, `--border` and `--green`.

The current values are `#f4f6ff` for text, `#b8bdd2` for secondary text, `#141827` for panels, `#1b2034` for card backs, `#111625` for face surfaces, `#757c9a` for borders and `#8bea7d` for matched green. The page background is `#090b14`.

The root also defines `--content-max: 1120px` and `--page-padding: 16px`. A global border-box reset applies to every element, body margin is zero and main uses full width up to that maximum with centered margins and page padding. These foundational rules affect diagnostics that deliberately import `game.css` as well as the main game.

Headings, paragraphs and help text have a small set of explicit margins and font sizes. Secondary text is generally 14px. The global `:focus-visible` outline is 3px white with a 2px offset. Because it is global, its interaction with scroll-container padding matters for cards as well as ordinary controls.

## The board owns its geometry

`board.css` defines board-specific custom properties on `.board-viewport`: card minimum 44px, card maximum 88px, gap 6px, padding 6px and border 1px. The viewport uses `overflow: auto`, contained overscroll, a rounded panel and `max-height: min(70dvh, 768px)`.

The viewport has `width: fit-content` and `max-width: 100%`. The inner board is a grid with a number of columns supplied by `--grid-size`, set from the current game size by `Board.tsx`. Track widths range from the card minimum to maximum.

Its width uses a clamp with these conceptual bounds:

```text
minimum = size * card-min + (size - 1) * gap
preferred = 100% of the available content width
maximum = size * card-max + (size - 1) * gap
```

For size 16, the inner minimum is 794px and maximum is 1498px. The viewport's own padding, border and any scrollbar are separate geometry. A narrow screen can therefore scroll the board rather than shrinking every track without limit or making the whole page wider than the viewport.

The width formula uses the scroll area's content box, which already accounts for occupied scrollbar space. `scrollbars.e2e.test.ts` runs with visible scrollbars at several viewport/size combinations to catch a layout that only works when Chromium hides them.

## Card states come from data

`Card.tsx` supplies `card` plus a state class returned by `describeCard`. `.card` is a square grid-placed native button with full available width, zero padding, a 2px border and an 8px radius. It uses the back surface until revealed or matched, when the face surface applies.

Hover changes the border to the text color. The matched selector appears after the hover selector and gives matched cards the green border. This ordering matters when a matched card remains hovered: its matched treatment continues to win. The class is derived from game data, not a CSS pseudo-state pretending to own the match.

The concealed back is a small rotated bordered span. Visible faces are SVG elements sized to the card. The matched check is a separate absolutely positioned SVG in the top-right corner with width and height at 16% of the card. The source comment explains that a mark much wider than roughly 17% would reach the face's top-right marker.

The card has `scroll-margin: 6px`, which works with nearest scrolling and the global focus outline. Its touch-action and user-selection properties support native pointer behavior. These rules are adjacent to the card because the face sheet also renders the same component outside the normal board layout.

## CSS and SVG share one surface value

The face renderer uses a viewBox of 0 0 100 100. Its main geometry takes the design color, with either a solid fill or outline stroke. A marker circle uses the same color, and its surround stroke is `var(--face)`.

That variable ties SVG geometry to the card's face background. Replacing the card surface without considering the marker surround could make the marker appear to have a mismatched halo. This is a direct dependency between the stylesheet and the inline SVG, even though face identity remains a data mapping in `face-design.ts`.

The matched mark is decorative and uses currentColor from CSS. It is separate from the identity marker, so its size and placement are checked for overlap at the smallest rendered card. [Card artwork](../visuals/card-artwork.md) and [Face catalogue](../visuals/face-catalogue.md) cover identity design rather than stylesheet placement.

## Shared controls are deliberately narrow

`control.css` defines `.control`: minimum height 44px, padding 8px 12px, a 1px border, 8px radius, panel background, text color and inherited font. Only button and select controls receive the pointer cursor rule. Inputs and textareas have `min-width: 0` so they can shrink within flex/grid layouts.

This class is applied explicitly to the game's form controls. The card component uses its own class and styling. A broad rule for every button would accidentally affect card rendering and diagnostic comparisons, which is why the current selectors distinguish those surfaces.

`controls.css` uses wrapping flex layout with a 12px gap and 16px bottom margin. The size control aligns label and select with a 12px gap. At widths up to 599px, the size row takes full width with spaced ends, while the direct deal buttons share available space.

These rules handle arrangement without replacing native select and button behavior. The CSS does not define a synthetic menu implementation or a separate touch activation model.

## Reproduction layout

The disclosure panel has 24px top margin, panel background, a 1px border and 12px radius. Its summary has a 44px minimum height and 12px by 16px padding. The open body is a grid with 12px gaps and its own inner padding.

docs/sharing/data-exchange-policy.md:74:All copied or loaded data is untrusted. “Valid snapshot” means that the object satisfies the documented state constraints, not that its claimed result has a verified play history. A hand-edited object can be accepted if its fields remain consistent.
docs/sharing/data-exchange-policy.md:82:For a generation mismatch, begin in `src/game/deck.ts` and compare the literal vector. docs/sharing/format-versioning-guide.md:15:The current product specification is version 2.2. A product release and an exchange format answer different questions: the release says which application behavior was delivered; the format says how an artifact is interpreted. The package's `1.0.0` version is another independent value and does not select a decoder.

A hand-edited object can be accepted if its fields remain consistent.

# Controls

Controls is a specification that defines the game options and reproduction tools in Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.2.

You can start another deal, repeat the current one or load saved progress. Each control keeps the same label, so you can find the same action after a game changes.

## Deal controls

The main controls are:

- C01 - Label the native size select "Grid size". Give it options `4x4`, `6x6`, `8x8`, `10x10`, `12x12`, `14x14` and `16x16`, with numeric side length `N` as each value. After a successful board-code or snapshot load, select the loaded board's size.
- C02 - Label the fresh-deal button "New Game". It creates a fresh seed and keeps the current size.
- C03 - Label the repeat-deal button "Restart". It starts the same board code again.
- C15 - Put a "Tournament" button beside New Game. Open the Tournament screen, where four or eight players can enter a knockout event on the shared device. Each match uses one deal for both turns; the bracket records moves, time and winner. See [Shared-device competition](../competition/competition-overview.md).

Changing size, starting and restarting follow the session rules in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md).

## Reproduction tools

- C04 - Put reproduction controls inside a native `details` element that starts collapsed. Give its summary the exact text "Reproduce a game".

The controls use the board-code and snapshot formats defined in [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md). A board code starts a deal. A snapshot loads progress on a deal.

## Load a board

- C05 - Label the text input "Board code" and limit it to 32 characters. Show the current board code after a new deal, Restart or a successful load. Keep an edited draft when a card action changes the game.

- C06 - Label its button "Load board". Validate the entered code before replacing the current game with that deal's starting state.

For example, loading `np1-4-1` starts its hidden four-column board. Entering that code alone keeps the current game until you select Load board.
---

# Acceptance

Acceptance is a set of journeys that checks whether Neon Pairs meets its product requirements.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Finish a game, then start another one during a mismatch. The first journey checks play and completion. The second checks that an earlier timer can't change a new game.

## Play

Use these journeys with the requirements in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md):

- Finish every supported size with complete pairs.
- Reveal one card twice, then reveal a different card. Check the exact move count.
- Match a pair, then miss a pair. Check the immediate match and the 800ms active mismatch interval.
- Hide the page during a mismatch, then return and finish its remaining interval.
- Start and restart during a mismatch. Check the cleared state and later timer updates.
- Finish games with better, equal and worse move counts. Reload and check the current size's best.

## Controls

Use pointer, touch and keyboard to follow [Input](../interface/input.md) and [Controls](../interface/controls.md). Check control labels, row movement, edge stops, native Tab exit and focus after each action. Check that hidden cards reveal no identity in the DOM.

Follow the keyboard journey in I17 and check its accessibility tree. During user acceptance, confirm spoken results with a screen reader, including consecutive identical results and the final match with its win.

## Appearance

Measure the layout and review all 128 faces against [Visuals](../visuals/visuals.md). Use a 44px grayscale face sheet to distinguish shape, marker and fill. Check 16x16 boards at both stated viewport sizes, full focus outlines and the equivalent zoom layout. Check reduced motion and the static completion banner after its single pulse.

Play through completion and reset while checking [Sound](../sound/sound.md). Every action stays silent.

## Reproduction

Check [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md) with its example deck and replay. Check snapshot round trips and malformed input. Check the exact mismatch timeout before an equal-time replay action.

Load an unfinished snapshot, attempt input while paused, then Resume. Check its remaining active time and focus. Load a completed snapshot and check its static banner and unchanged best score.

## Tournament

Follow [Shared-device competition](../competition/competition-overview.md) with four and eight players. Check the opening pairings, round names and board sizes, then play both turns of a match on its shared deal. Compare moves first, active time second and entry seed for an exact tie. Check the bracket, Next turn, Next match, champion and Back to game flow. Leave an unfinished tournament and keep playing once before confirming Leave.

Export setup and active progress to Tournament JSON. Load valid JSON and reject an unknown field and malformed progress without replacing the current event or its draft. Complete an event, reload on the same origin and check its bracket in Past tournaments. Confirm tournament games do not change solo size or best moves.

## Delivery

Use a locked install, type check, unit tests and a fresh browser build as defined in [Technology](../architecture/technology.md). Open the resulting HTML directly from disk with network access blocked. Use a local HTTP origin for saved preferences.

Review the pure game functions, browser effects, file sizes and behavior placement against [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md).

Back to [Neon Pairs](../README.md).
